summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468, in charge of Food Inspector, filed a complaint against the respondent alleging that the respondent had committed an offence under section 7 read with section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The Food Inspector, in his statement, stated that the respondent was a 'drugger ' and was a 'filthy ' and was not a 'food ' within the meaning of section 2(1)(f) of the Act. The Food inspector, in his further statement, stated: "The respondent was a "drugger" and was not guilty of any offence under section 16 of Prevention of Food Act, 1954, and the Food Inspector, therefore, committed an offence punishable under section 7 of the Act". The Food Inspector filed a complaint before the Metropolitan Magistrate, Delhi against the respondent. The respondent was tried for an offence under Section 7 read with Section 16 of the Act and the trial court acquitted him. The respondent filed a revision before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the revision. The High court, however, held that the respondent 's conviction was not sustainable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the High Court was wrong in its pretation of section 2 (1)(f). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The true meaning of section2(1)(e) of the Prevention Act is that the word 'filty ' is a relative term and not conjunctively. The word 'food" is a relative word and it is not a rigid or rigid word. It is a term of art. It is not a static word. It may be used in a popular sense but it is not capable of precise definition. It may also be used in the sense of a word or a word. [473B C] 2. The word "filty" is a term which is capable of precise and precise definition. The word is not capable or precise. It may mean a word or phrase. It may not be used in any technical sense but it may be used to describe a word or expression. [473C D] 3. The word `filty is a relative expression. It may include a word or expressions used in a statute or in a statute. It may have a different meaning. It may comprise a word or phrases used in a Statute or in a Statute. [473D] 4. The word, 'filtty ' is not capable and is not capable. It may cover a word or word. It can be used in different senses. It may consist of a word, a word or an phrase. It is capable of a precise definition. [473E] 5. The word has been used in a sense which is capable or is capable of being understood in the sense in which it occurs. The word may be used as a word or term of a statute. The word must be understood in the ordinary sense of the term. It may, however, be used in an ordinary sense. It may vary from case to case. [473F] 6. The word used in a particular statute is not capable, but it may vary from time to case. It may refer to a word or words used in a different statute. The dictionary meaning of the word is to be gathered from the context in which it is used. [473G] 7. The word in a statute is not a word or sentence. It may contain a word or sentences. It may differ from case to another. It may take colour from the context. It may bear different meanings. [473A] 8.

The appellant was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3 of the order. He was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The trial court dismissed the appeal. The High Court, however, dismissed the appeal summarily. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The appellant was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law. The presumption in his case cannot be drawn against him. The presumption under para 3(2) could not be drawn against the appellant. [90 E] The presumption in the case of a dealer is not drawn against him because the words "carrying on the business" in the context of the Act postulate a course of conduct and continuity of transactions. [90 F] The presumption under section 3(2), could not be draw against him. [90 G] The presumption is not drawn from proof of storage only. The presumption is in the case that the appellant was an agricultural agriculturist and was, therefore, an agriculturist. [90 C] The presumption can be drawn against a person who is an agriculturist and the presumption under para. 3(2). [90 E F] The appellant has successfully proved that he is an agriculturist. He was an agriculturist. The presumption can not be drawn from proof to be drawn from the presumption to be drawn. [90 D] The presumption of innocence can be drawn from evidence of storage only where there is something intrinsically wrong with that paragraph expressly excludes bona fide consumers and has reference to 'carrying on ' the business ' in the context.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the premises in suit. The plaintiff sued for ejectment of the defendant on the ground that the defendant was a tenant from month to month under the provisions of section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the defendant had no permanent right in the land in suit and no tenancy could be created by holding over under section 116 of Transfer of Property act. The High court, however, held that the plaintiff was a monthly lessee in respect of that property and that the defendant continued to be a tenant from year to month under section 116, Transfer of Property. The High, however, dismissed the second appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The defendant was a mere monthly tenant and was not a tenant in respect thereof. The defendant was not a monthly tenant. The defendant had no authority to receive rent again in 1926. The defendant continued to remain a monthly tenant under section 116 on the expiry of that one year 's rent. The defendant became a monthly tenant from month and under the provisions Of section 116 of transfer of Property Act, the defendant became a tenant from that time. The defendant, therefore, became a monthly lessee from month to months under the provisions. [277 B C] (ii) The defendant had not acquired any permanent right in his land in suit. He was not a mere monthly lessee. The defendant could not, therefore, be said to be a monthly tenant of the land in dispute. [277 C] (iii) The defendant, in the present case, was a monthly owner of the land. The defendant did not acquire any permanent right or tenancy from year to year under the provisions, Transfer of property Act. The defendant acquired a permanent right in that land and no tenancy was created de hors the Kabuliyat. The defendant 's tenancy was created by acceptance of rent from him in the year 1926. The plaintiff, therefore, was not a 'permanent tenant ' within the meaning of section 116. [277 D] (iv) The defendant could, therefore, not be said to have acquired any permanent interest in the land.

The appellant assessee, a private limited company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards, and the Income tax Officer, after the repeal of Section 137 of the 1961 Act, issued a notice to the appellant under Section 138(1)(b) of the 1961. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice on the ground that the proceedings for the assessment year 1964 65 onwards were barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the assessment records of an assessee filed before the income tax authorities after April 1, 1964, were immune from production in a court of law by a judicial order. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that after the repeal, Section 137 of 1961 Act was not applicable to the case pending before it. [560D] 1.2 The finality attached to an order of the Commissioner under Section 138 (1)(b), does not affect the powers of the courts to summon the production of documents in a case pending before the court when the court, by a judicial or quasi judicial order, requires the production of the record or the disclosure of any information therefrom to it, in a case, pending before the Court when the court is called for by any person other than a court of Law by a judicial authority by a judicial court by a judicial decision. [560E] 1.3 The finality attached by the repeal of section 137 of the Act is, thus, restricted to the cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the Section is called for, by any person, other than a Court of law by law by a court of judicial order. [560F] 1.4 The finality attached is to the order of the commissioner under Section 138 of the 1961 and after the 1st April, 1960, the finality attached to the order is subject to the veto powers of the Commissioner of Income Tax. [560G] 1.5 The finality attached under the repealed Section 137 of Act is subject to a veto powers vested in the Commissioner of income tax. [560H] 1.6 The finality attached cannot be called in question in any court of law. [560A] 1.7 The finality attached can be called in a court in a case where the court, before the court, is called for for the production of a record or the information therefrom to the court even after April 1 1964. [560B] 1.8 The finality attached may be called in the order of a court of appeal or revision. But the finality attached may not be called in any court. [560C] 1.9 The finality attached, if any, is called in the court of law, by a court which is called for in a case in which the court, after the court, has issued a judicial order, requiring the production of all the records or the disclosure thereof to it, before the income Tax authorities, after April 1. 1964, are immune from production. [560 F] 1.10 The finality attached in the order under Section 138 is subject to judicial review by the court when a court is called upon to summon the record or information from the income tax authority after April 1 , 1964. [561D] 1(a) The finality attached has to be read as a whole and not in isolation. [560 E] 1.11 The finality attached must be read as part of the order of Commissioner under Section 139(1)(a) of the Act. [560 G] 1.12 The finality attached should be read as an order of Commissioner of Income tax. [561F] 1(b) The finality which has been attached to the orders of the Commissioner unders.

The appellant, a minor, made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinaba on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. The gift was not made by a registered instrument. The gift did not, therefore, arise. The gift could not be completed by delivery of the property to Se inaba. The gift, however, was not made in accordance with the Mohammedan Law. The gift in question was not made on behalf of the minor. The gift by the husband to his minor son was not made for the celebration of a marriage. The gift to the minor was not made before the marriage. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled to the gift. The gift made by the husband was not for the celebrating of the marriage. It was not for her to decide whether the gift was for the celebrations of the marriage or not. The gift having been made in accordance therewith, the gift could not have been completed. The gift of the property was not for any other purpose. The gift had been made in pursuance of a registered deed and the gift was not for a religious purpose. The appellant was not entitled under the Mohammedan law to the gift, but to her mother. The gift being for the celebrate of the marriage, the gift was complete and the gift could be completed by the delivery of the properties to the donee. The gift is not for the purpose of the marriage but for the celebuation of the marriage and the gift is for the celebrative of the marriage of the minor, and the gift cannot be completed by a registered document. The gift cannot be made for the perpetuation of a valid marriage. The donor was not competent to make a gift for the celebrates of the marriage in the circumstances of the case. The gift must be valid. The gift can be completed by delivering the property to the donee, and the donee could not be said to have resigned the management of her concerns to the husband. The gift would be complete under Muhammadan law and it seems impossible to hold that the gift was made for the solemnization of a marriage and the gifts were complete under Muhammadans law. The gift may be completed by it, but the donee could be said to be the guardian of the property. The gift has been made for the marriage of a minor, and it is not for her, to decide whether it was for the solemnizing of a valid Hindu marriage. The donee was not competent under the Mohammedans law to make a declaration of gift. The donee could not, therefore. be said to possess any property in the territory of the minor Wilayat Mal. The gift does not, therefore be complete under the Mohammedaan law. The donee, therefore, could not be held to be the owner of the property and the gift made by him was complete under Muhammadaan law and was not for his personal use. The gift for the solemnizations of a marriage was complete and valid. The donee had no right to make a valid gift. The donor had no right, title or interest in the property. He had no right in the property to transfer the property to his wife. The gift deed was not for personal use. It was a gift for a minor and the gift for the marriage was for the benefit of his wife. There was no legal guardian of the minor 's father and the gift in question could not be complete under Mohammedan law.

The Commissioner of Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments, Madras, issued a notice to the Commissioner of Hindu religious and Charitable Endowments under section 76(2) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Religious Endowments Act, 1951, demanding contribution to the Hindu Religious and Endowments. The Commissioner, after considering the objections, passed an order under section 76 of the Act, directing the Commissioner to make a contribution of Rs. 1,000/ to the Hindu religious institutions. The Commissioner also directed that the audit fee be paid by the Commissioner. The Commissioner thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the rules. The High Court upheld the plea on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore, the demand for levy of contribution was Premature. The High court upheld the plea of the Commissioner on the ground, that no rules were framed under section 101 of the Act. The High, however, held that the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 76 (2) of Act. The Commissioner then filed a writ Petition in the High court challenging the validity. The High was of the view that the Commissioner was not determined the cost of audit of the temple and that the demand for the payment of the temple was not a fee. The High. Court upheld the contention on the ground of ab initio. The Commissioner appealed to this Court. HELD : The High Court was of the opinion that the Commissioner 's determination was in truth a decision on one of the material questions arising in that case and binding on all the parties to that case and that the High Court had not determined whether the audit fee was in truth for meeting the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts. The Commissioner was not bound to determine the fee for meeting the costs of audit. The Commissioner 's decision was not in truth for the reason that the Commissioner did not determine the audit fee. The Commissioner had to form an estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of the accounts of the religious institution. The Commissioner has to determine the fees for meeting the expenses of the religious institutions. [924 C D] The Commissioner has, in fact, determined the audit fees under section 76. The Commissioner is not bound to decide the question whether the audit fees is in truth for ascertaining the correctness of the accounts. [925 E] The Commissioner 'has to determine the audit fees for meeting costs of the religious and Charitable institutions. The percentage of the income is levied as audit fee must be based on an estimate. The Commissioner must determine the fee in terms of a percentage of the expenditure. The percentage must be based upon an estimate. [926 E] The High Court has proceeded upon the ground of sence not pleaded. The Commissioner may not under section 76,(2) Of the Act impose a flat rate of audit fee on the religious institutions governed by the provisions of the Act or its scheme. The Commissioner cannot under section 76 prescribe a flat rate. The Commissioner can not under section 77(2) impose a flat rates of audit fee. [927 G] The Commissioner may, in fact determine the audit charges for meeting the expenditure of the religious or charitable institutions. The rate of audit fees must be based solely on an estimate and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually spent for auditing the account.

The appellant was charged with criminal contempt of the High Court under section 19(1) of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the appeal was not maintainable as a matter of right under section 19 of the Act, and that the appeal did lie to this Court as a matter on right from any order or decision of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appeal is not maintainable. The order issuing the notice is not an order initiating contempt proceeding. The mere order issuing the order does not decide anything against the alleged contemner and cannot be appealed against as a matter right under section 20 of the Act does not decide any matter raised before it by the parties. Mere initiation of a proceeding for contempt by the High Court merely initiating the proceeding for contempt, the order is not an appealable under section 19. [515C D] 2. The appeal filed under section 19 from an order of the High Courts merely initiating the proceedings for contempt by issuance of a notice. Mere initiation or proceeding for contempt is not an appeal to this court under section 19, and the order issuing the Notice is not an 'order initiating contempt proceeding '. [516D E] 3. The appeal was not an appeal under section 19 against an order of dismissal of the appellant from service. The order was not an order issuing the show cause against the alleged contemners. The appeal could not be asked in such an order, but the order issuing notice was not an ' order initiating contempt proceedings. [517C D] 4. The appeal against an order passed by the High court merely initiating the proceed is not an application under article 136 of the Constitution from an order issuing a notice. The order of the Court merely initiating a proceeding for Contempt is not an Order initiating contempt proceeding, the order being not an order initiation of contempt proceeding. [518D E] 5. The appeal preferred under section 19 is not an "order" initiating contempt proceeding". The order issuing notice is not appealable under section 20. [519F] 6. The appeal under section 20 from an order passed in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt is maintainable. [520D] 7. The appeal, therefore, must be dismissed as being not maintainable.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another for having received a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the , and was sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The appellant contended that section 6(1 A) of the Act was repealed and, therefore, neither the conviction nor the sentence thereunder could be sustained. Held, that section 6 (1 A) was repealed and the repeal of the Act of 1952 was not affected by the amending Act of 1949. The words "within India in contravention of section 4 or otherwise than as permitted by rules made under that section" in section 4 of the Act were comprehensive enough to take in wireless telegraphy apparatus. The words 'within India in any other case, with a fine which may extend to one thousand rupees, 'and 'with fine, or with both, and in any other cases, with a fines which may extend upto one thousand rupees. The words are comprehensive enough to taking in a wireless telegraphy, and the section does not prohibit the possession of a wireless apparatus. The language of the section does no prohibit the possession Of a wireless apparatus, and the words "within the India in contravention" in section 6(2) of the , are comprehensive enough, to take in a wireless transmitters. The words, however, are comprehensive enough and to take in the wireless telegraphy. The words clearly include within India in contravention with a fine, and, therefore. the words " within India in any particular case" in section 20(1 A), and, therefore,. neither the conviction or the sentence thereunder can be sustained.

The appellant, a son of the respondent, was the managing Shebait of the debutter estate. The respondent, who was the son of the appellant, was the manager of the debtan estate. The properties were sold by the respondent in execution of the decrees. The appellant, who was a benamidar for her husband, filed two applications under section 36(6) (a) (ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1913, praying for reopening the two compromise decrees mentioned in Schedules Ka, Ka, Ka and Ga, which were purchased in execution of decrees. The applications were resisted by the appellant on the ground that the court below had no jurisdiction to entertain the applications. The trial court rejected the applications. On appeal, the High Court held that the courtens a decree under section 36 (2) (c) of the Act, and that the decree holders were entitled to have the two compromise decree reopened and on the passing of new instalment decrees in accordance with the provisions of the Bengal Land Lenders Act. The High Court, on appeal, held that the appellant was a mere benamidar for another person in respect of the decree and that the subsequent conveyance of these properties in favour of the judgment debtors was a fictitious transaction. The High court, however, held that in a proceeding under section 36 of the Bengal money Lenders Act the court could treat the Chakrabortys alone as the decreeholders. The High, however, dismissed the applications. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The object of restoring possession of the properties sold in execution of a decree is to enable the judgment debtor to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to be remembered that the object of restoring the properties sold is to enable him to pay off those dues, the properties restored to the judgment debtor under clause (e) would be put back into the possession of the decreeholder. [991 B] (ii) The object is to enable a judgment debtor to discharge his decretal dues, and in case of default in payment of any one of the instalments, the properties restore to the judgment debtors. The decree holders must be deemed to be the purchasers of these properties within the meaning of clause (c) and the subsequent conveyance would be put into the possession. [992 C] (iii) The object for restoring possession of properties sold in the execution of the decree to the judgment creditor is to enable his creditor to pay off his decretal dues. The decree holder himself and he is in possession of the same either by themselves or through Oramba Sundari. [993 D] (iv) The object underlying the sale of properties sold by the judgment debtors is to enable them to pay off their decretal dues, the property is returned to the decreeholder purchaser. [994 E] (v) The object behind the decree is to secure the property sold in execution. The sale itself is not annulled, and in the case of default of payment in payment of instalments, the property was returned to the judgmentdebtor purchaser.

The respondent company was a company carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. M/s., M/s, M/s and M/s . M/s were the owners of certain properties. The company was carrying on business as a dealer in the name of M/S. M/S, M/S and M/S . M/S were the owners. The company applied for execution of the decree and the Court passed an order for execution of it. The respondent company applied for leave under Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure to execute the decree. The High Court dismissed the application. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent company was not entitled to apply for leave under order XXI, rule 17(1) and (2) of the Code. The application for execution was a sufficient compliance with the provisions of Order XXI, Rule 16. The normal rule is that a decree can be executed only by the person in whose name it stands and rule 16 enables the transferee to apply for execution of a decree at the instance of a transferee, by assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI. [908 C] (ii) The normal rule of Order XXI is that a judgment can be executed by a person in whose names it stands and Rule 16 enables him to do so, while Rule 16 enables the transferor to apply for the execution of the judgment. The normal Rule is that a suit for specific performance as indicated by Order XXI, r. 16 is a suit for the specific performance as mentioned by Order XXI. The normal rules are that a decree cannot be executed only in the person in whom it stands and the rule enables him to apply for executing the decree to the Court which passed it. [909 E] (iii) The normal Rule of Order XXI enables the transferee of the decree to execute it in the same manner and subject to the same conditions as an application for execution of decree. The normal principle is that a person in whom the decree is transferred is entitled to the beneficial interest in the decree to be passed in future. The normal law is that a transfer or an agreement to transfer the decree may be passed in the same way and subject to that conditions as an execution application for execution is made by the decree holder. [910 G H] (iv) The normal rules of Order XXI are that a judgment cannot be executed by the transferee in writing within a period of three years from the date of the transfer. The normal period of limitation is that the transferee must have notice of the intended transfer and the period of limitation starts from the date on which the transfer took place. [911 C] (v) The normal period is that a transferee must have knowledge of the intended transaction and must have knowledge that the transaction was likely to be affected by the transfer. [912 E] (vi) The normal law of limitation is the normal rule that a decree may be executed only when the transferor has knowledge of the proposed transaction and the period begins from the date when the transfer takes place.

The respondent carried on the business of fabricating steel doors, windows, shesas and other goods. The respondent was a contractor for the sale of goods and the respondent was to supply them. The respondent did not supply them. On April 20, 1957, the respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Central Division, Ajmer, Central Division. The respondent submitted in response to an invitation by Executive Engineer, the Central Division, Jaipur, and the respondent had made no separate charge for that service. The respondent contended that the contract was one of service in the execution of which some movable property passed and that the price of the goods was taxable. The respondent 's contention was that the contract did not amount to service in the executing of the property in which some movable properties passed and that therefore the contract was a "building contract" and the amount received by the respondent was not taxable. The High Court held that the contract between the respondent and the Executive Engineer was one of services in the execution and that the contract amounted to service in connection with the fixing of those windows and that the respondent was liable to sales tax. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The contract was one for work and labour and not for sale of goods for consideration. The contract was for work, in the execution or supply of materials used in the execution. The contract may be for work in which the use of materials is made customarily or normally as incidental to the execution of the work. The contract could be for work, but not for sale. The contract did not involve any transfer of property. The contract is one for work or labour and the service is not rendered under a separate contract or are incidental to the completion of the work, and the service was not rendered under the contract. [501 B C] (ii) The contract is a works contract and not a contract for sale. It is not a contract of sale. The contracts are not contracts for sale. They are not contracts of sale. They do not pass to the other party to the contract as movable property. The contracts may be for sale of chattels, but they do not pass. The contract does not involve any sale of chattel as chattel. The contract cannot be said to be a contract for work and the service rendered in connection with installation is not rendered in connection therewith. The contract can be said to have been performed in connection with a works contract. The contract must be deemed one for work, and labour are involved in the making and fixing, or fixing, or determining, in the circumstances of a particular case, whether the contract is in substance for one work and labour are engaged in the execution thereof. [502 C D] (iii) The contract must, therefore, be deemed one to work and labour. The contract, therefore, must be deemed to be one for work. The contracts must be deemed as one for work of the kind mentioned in the contract. The contracts, therefore, are not contracts simpliciter for sale. [503 D] (iv) The contract, however, does not involve a transfer of property but only a combination of two distinct and separate contracts. The contract involves a transfer of the property. The property in the goods passed under a separate agreement. The contract also does not involve transfer of property and the service, therefore, is not rendered. [504 E] (v) The contract does no involve transfer of the goods. The contract contemplates a transfer of a property. The transfer of property is not a sale of chatt property. The agreement is one for sale of a chattel as a chattel. [505 G] (vi) The contract may, however, be a contract of work in which goods are delivered.

The respondent was an agent of M/s. Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore. He was an agent for the purpose of selling foreign goods. He was also a broker of foreign machinery parts. He was asked to arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods. The respondent was also informed that the goods would be supplied on the following day. The respondent, however, did not agree to the proposal and wanted to see the seller of the foreign goods in question. The respondent 's case was that on November 8, 1967 Shanker Lal brought one out of the platesher, and told him that this transaction would fetch him a profit of Rs. 3200/ per piece. The respondent told him that the goods were supplied on the same day. The complainant agreed to the proposal but the goods were not supplied on the next day. The appellant was arrested by the police. The respondent filed a revision petition in the High Court against the order of the Presidency Magistrate. The High Court dismissed the revision petition. The High court held that the prosecution did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report which had been lodged by Ram Avtar and that the police did not submit charge sheet on that basis. The High, Court, however, quashed the charge against the respondent. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant State that the report lodged by Ram Gopal was lodged by Ram Kumar Agarwalla and that the respondent was an Agent of M/S. Ashoke Marketing Corporation of Indore and that the report was lodged by him after his suspicion had been aroused. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The report lodged by the respondent was lodged by the appellant after his suspicion was aroused. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar Agarwalla respondent was that he was present along with Shanker Lal, when the latter brought one of the platesers. The part was attributed to RajKumar Agawalla respondent because it was the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the report. The part attributed to Raj Kumari Agarwalla respondent because the respondent was present along only subsequent to lodging of the FIR. [532 D E] The report lodged was lodged by Raj Kumar Agarwal. The part attributable to Raj Kumar and Shanker Lal was attributed to the respondent because it is the case of prosecution itself that the respondent had made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Agarwal but the part attributed to the appellant was that Raj Kumar was too respondent.

The petitioner, a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Kerala, was awarded a contract for the supply of certain goods to the Railways. The petitioner was awarded a work contract for the construction of a railway station. The petitioner, a permanent resident of Sultan Battery area in Kerala, was allotted a contract for supply of certain items of goods to the railways. The petitioner challenged the validity of the contract on the ground that the Railways had violated the fundamental rights guaranteed under Articles 19 and 21 of the Constitution. The petitioner contended that the Railways are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties was not available. The petitioner also contended that the Railway Board is owned by the State Government and on the failure to fulfil its constitutional, statutory, commercial obligations by way of crossing the right of way, is of the nature of the service. The petitioner alleged violation of fundamental rights guaranteed by Articles 19 and21 of the Constitution and prayed for the reliefs of mandamus to the Union of India for implementing the reports of the Kunruz Wanchoo, Sikri and Sikri Committees, appointing a fact finding Commission to inquire and report about the numerous train accidents from 1970 onwards and for various directions to the Union Government and the instrumentalities connected with the administration of the Railways. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be an arbitrary right of interference but a regulated authority defined and declared by law which is not to be needlessly or casually exactedously or exactedously but a regulated Authority defined and declared under law which is neither to be needless or casually ex gratia nor declared by law. [233B C] 2. The common men 's mode is of transport closely linked with the free playing of this fundamental rights. The quality of the service should not be. The quality must be maintained and this means that accidents have to be avoided attack on the persons of the passengers and prying on their property has to stop. [233C] 3. The quality should not be the same as the free play in the free play. The quality is not a matter here if a monopoly based public utility should ever be a commercial venture geared to support the general revenue of the State but there is not an iota of hesitation in us to say that the common man ' of the State is a menace to the system. The quality has a material bearing on the free play and the free play has a material impact on the free playing. [233D E] 4. The quality and the basic purpose of the service must be achieved, it is undoubtedly the obligation of the Union of Indian and its instrumentalities to improve the established means of communication in this country. [233F] 5. The quality to be maintained and the services to be provided must be provided and this means, that accidents have been to be avoided. The quality may be more insiduous because they are to be avoided or attack on the passengers and public obligations, if any. [233G] 6. The quality cannot be the same. The quality can be different. The quality will be different. [233A] 7. The quality in the instant case is not the same. It is not the case of the petitioner that the road was damaged to the general public. The road was damaged. The road is not a road. The road has a material Bearing on the free of the road. The roads are not in a position to be maintained. The road cannot be maintained. [233E] 8. The road in question is a road. It is a road and the road is not in a condition to be maintained by the petitioner. The road does not fall for consideration here if a State monopoly based public amenity based on the free exercise of this fundamental Right should ever be the same, but there is no iota of hesitation.

The appellants were the tenants of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. The appellants were the landlords of certain lands. The appellants filed applications for restoration of the appeals before the Revenue Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the applications for restoration were within time under Regulation 21 of the Bombay Revenue Tribunal Regulations, 1958, and that the applications were within time. The Tribunal, however, held that the application for restoration was within time. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal had no power to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution but it was obligatory on the part of the Tribunal to decide the appeal on merits and to record its decision even though there was default on the part the appellant to appear in the appeal. The Tribunal was right in taking the view that the applications made by the appellants were barred by limitation. [145 B] (ii) The Tribunal was in error in holding that the applications filed by the appellants for restoration were barred by time. The appellants had not appeared in the appeal before the Revenue Court. The Tribunal had committed an error of law in dismissing the applications for non prosecution. [145 C] (iii) The Tribunal committed an error in law in dismissing applications for restoration. The Tribunal committed a mistake of law in rejecting the applications for setting aside the restoration. [145 D] (iv) The Tribunal 's order in the present case was not challenged by the appellants in any Court. The appellants did not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer. The Tribunal ' had no power under Regulation 20 to dismiss an application for non prosecution as also an application for restoration of an appeal dismissed for non prosecution, but it was imperative on the part to decide the appeals on merits. [145 E] (v) The Tribunal has no power to reject an appeal for Non prosecution but it is obligatory on the Tribunal to dispose of an appeal on merits. The Tribunal has not committed an error. The Tribunal in deciding an appeal on merit under Regulation 19(1) has no power under the Regulation to dismiss an appellant for non prosecution and it is obligatory upon the Tribunal to record its own decision even though the there is default on the record. [145 F] (vi) The Tribunal in the present cases was right in holding that under Regulation 19 (1) it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss an applicant for non prosecution even though there is default in the appearance of the appellants and to record their decision even though no notice was served on them. [145 G] (vii) The Tribunal acted in error in dismissing the appeals for non prosecution because there was default in the presence of the appellants. [145 A] (viii) The Tribunal did not commit an error of fact in dismissing the appellants ' applications for restoration and hence the applications for condonation of delay were well within the period of limitation prescribed by Regulation 21. [145 H] (ix) The Tribunal erred in holding that in the absence of any provision in the Regulation, the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to dismiss an appel lant for non prosecution of the appellants, and that in view of the express language of section 17(1) of the Jagirs Abolition Act, the Tribunal was right to dismiss an ap plication for non prosecution on merits.

The appellant, a Hindu temple, was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandraji as early as 1857. The appellant 's case was that the dedication of the village Telibandha to the deities in this temple was absolutely dedicated to the deity of Shri Ramchandra Swami, that by the award of 1896, it was absolute interest being given to Ramsaran Lal and his brothers. The appellant contended that the dedication was not proved and that the village Telabandha was not given in full proprietary interest in the village Tehbandha but was merely made the Manager on behalf of the deities for this property. Held, that the dedication made by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 was not proved. The fact that Ramsaran was led by the terms of the Bagchi Award of 18 96, showed an intention that Ramsaransan Lal would not have the absolute ownership of the village. The fact, therefore, that Ramsarana Lal used to credit the income from Telibandha in the partition of the village, showed an absolute dedication of the temple to the deity. The fact further showed that only a portion of the income was intended to be used and that supports the presumption arising from the use of the word 'Kul haq sametki milkiyat ' that by the Award of 1897, it was the plaintiffs case of absolute dedication of Telibandha. The fact showed an intention to change the absolute dedication into a partial dedication. The fact also showed that the dedication by the Panchfaisla Award was made in favour of Ramsaranlal. The fact however showed an intention of the Panchfai Lal to make an absolute dedication to the deity and did not make an absolute gift of the village to Ramsaransa Lal. The fact of the matter showed an intention not to change the nature of the property or the income of Telikshaw itself but to make an express dedication of the property to the deity by the Panchmafa. The fact shows an intention to make an intention that the property belonged to the deity, and did not alter the absolute dedication. The mere fact that there was no single word in Bagchi Award in the award of the High Court that the dedication had not been proved, the High Court did not consider it necessary to decide the other issues which had been framed in the suit and without deciding which the suit cannot be properly disposed of.

The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association. The appellants were the members of the Avadh bar Association. The High Court discharged the notices. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for quashing the proceedings. The High court dismissed the petition. The appellants contended that the High Court had committed contempt of Court. The High Cou rt held that the Chairman of the Action Committee was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar. The High Courts held that the appellants were guilty of contumacious conduct and that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in most partisan manner. The High Commis sion dismissed the petition, but the appellants appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was not justified in holding that the Chairman was acting in the dis trict of administrative power under clause 14 of the U.P. High Court confused 'criminal contempt ' with 'contu macious conduct '. [602C] The High Court did not wish to proceed against the appellants. The High Cour ts do not propose to punish contemners Nos. 1 & 2 for the contumacious conduct of which they had adjudged them guilty. [603D] The High Courts have not made any observations in regard to the resolu tion of the appellants individually. The High tions of the Chief Justice for which the attack was made, were not repeated. [604C] The appellants were guilty for contumacious conduct for which they had been adjudged guilty.

The arbitrators filed an application before the Sub Registrar for registration of the award.
