The SubRegistrar, Aram Bagh, on 25th of November, 1983, registered the award to it. The Sub Judge held that during the pendency of the judicial proceedings, the arbitrators had tried to obtain the registration of the Award from the court and found that the award was presented within time as the time during which the judicial proceedings were pending was expired. The Sub judge, Aramganj, on 25.11.1983, passed an order of return to the arbitrators. The Sub registrar, Arambag, on 25rd November, 1983 registered the award and sent back the same to the Sub registrar for registration. The Sub Registrars, Arampore, on 25nd November, 1983 returned the award to them. The SubRegistrars filed a petition before the Sub registrar, for registration of a reference to the Sub Judge. The Subregistrars filed an application under section 15 of the . The Sub Registrar, who was the Sub Registrar of the Arambagh, on 25 th November, 1983 rejected the application. The Sub Inspector, Arampur, filed an application in the court of the Sub Registrar praying for return of the award to him. The Sub inspector, Arampally, on 25/11/1983, sent back the original award to the arbitrators to enable them to present the same before the SubRegistrar for registration. On 25th November 1983, the Sub Registrar passed an order returning the award to be presented within four months from 28th November,1983. The Sub Inspectors, Aramgram, filed an appeal before the Sub Judge, Hooghly at Chinsurah on 28th November 1983. The arbitrators, after examining the matter, passed an award on 24th November, 1984. The Sub � inspector, A Rambagh, on 24th January, 1984, sent back to the SubRegistrar, for registration. Arambagh filed an application on 14th August, 1978 for registration of an award. The arbitrators returned the award on 24.11. 1983 to the Sub Registrars. The Sub Sub Registrar, on 25st November, 1983 again registered the award on 25th January, 1983. On 25.11, 1983, the arbitrators made an application before him for registration of his award. The sub registrar, after considering the objections, passed an Award on 6th February, 1983. Aram Bagh was appointed as the Sub Registrar. The Submis sioner, Arampet, made an application to the Subregistric trate for registration of its award. The arbitrator, after considering all the objections, held that the limitation for the registration of a award had already expired. The arbitrator also held that during subsistence of the Interim injunction order on 25th February,1983, the Sub registrar had sent back his award to the arbitrator holding that during the period during which the Judicial proceedings were pending, namely, 28th January, 1978 to 24th November 1983 the arbitrators had returned the award from the court. The Sub Divisional Registrar, Aharbagh, on 28th January. 1983, passed an interim order directing the arbitrators to keep the award in the custody of the court. On 24th November 1984, the Sub Registrars, after considering their objections, passed a final award on 6th January, 1985. The Sub Judges of the Sub Registrars held that during this period, the award was in the custody and custody of the Court and that the award had already been expired. The sub Registrars, however, held that during these period, the arbitrator had tried to secure the registration of his Award.

The respondent was a sub tenant of the appellant and the appellant was the sub tenant of a sub tenant. The appellant had four sub tenants, three of them, three sub tenants, and three of them also shifted to the new premises which were let to the new sub tenants. The respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that the appellant had waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub tenancy and the provision in section 13(1)(e) was for protection of his rights which he was entitled to waive. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The respondent was not entitled to waive the statutory rights enacted for the benefit of the revenue and to be enforced solely at the instance of the revenue officials, nor was the prohibition against limited to cases for which a penalty is exigible in the instant case. The respondent was entitled to waiver of statutory rights enacted in public interest. The respondent had waived his rights in regard to sub tenancy and was not a continuation of the old and that the sub tenants were merely licensees of the appellant. The respondent could not evict the appellant under section 13(i)(e) of the Act. [227 D] The respondent was a tenant of the sub tenant and not licensees of the respondent. The respondent did not have the protection of the revenue. The respondent, therefore, could not evict him under section 13 (1)(e).

The State Board, by its resolution dated January 30, 1991, decided to deal with the use of unfair means at the final examination conducted by the Board. The Board, however, did not apply its mind to the facts in this case. The Standing Committee, however, took the decision to deal with use of unfair mean at the final Examination, and to deal with unfair means at final examination conducted at the final examinations. The Standing Committees did not apply their mind to the circumstances on which the whole enquiry came to be held and the conclusions reached on the basis of the admission made by the examinees. The Standing committee did not apply the mind to the factual position, nor recorded reasons in support of its conclusions that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or guardian. The Standing committees did not apply it mind to the fact in this case, nor recorded any reasons in support thereof. The High Court, therefore, quashed the impugned notification. The State Board preferred the present appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conclusion reached by the Standing Committee that the fabrication of the moderators ' mark sheets was done at their behest is based on the evidence on record. The Standing Standing Committee did not apply his mind to the materials on record. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. The Standing Medical Committee did not exercise power to evaluate the evidence and to interfere with the finding and to come to its own conclusions. [798C D] 1.2 The conclusion reached on the foundation of the admission of the examinees is based on evidence on record and the general background of the atmosphere in the examination hall. The Standing medical Committee did not consider the facts and the conclusions arrived at on the basis thereof. The conclusion reached was based on the admission made in the fabrication and the fabrication was made at the instance of either the examinee or their parents or guardian, and the finding was reached on the assumption that the examinees, parents or guardians were influenced by the fabrication and it was to their advantage and that the subject/subjects in which fabrication was committed belong to them or her. [799D E] 1.3 The conclusion reached in the course of the enquiry was based on evidence of the admission and the general features of the situation in the examination Hall. The finding was based on surmises and conjectures. The High court, therefore, rightly quashed the impugned Notification. [797A] 1.4 The conclusion reached is based on surmises, conjectures and surmises. The conclusion arrived at on that basis is based on no evidence and the conclusions were reached on the evidence available on the record.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellants were charged with criminal misconduct under section 5 (2) of that Act. The trial court acquitted the appellants but convicted them under section 120B of the Indian penal Code. The High Court, however, acquitted the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The offence as defined in section 21 of the Indian Criminal Procedure Code is to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that it can come into play only when there is no offer to give an acceptance of a bribe by a public servant. The offence as described in section 5(1) is to cause the pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as a public servant and to force a bribe out of an unwilling person is different from the acceptance of a tainted bribe from a voluntary giver and that before a charge under section 5 can be sustained, there must be threat or inducement or proceeding from the public servant or from the public service to which he is subordinate. [187 D E] (ii) The offence under section 5 is to cause pecuniary advantage to obtain the pecuniary advantage. The offence is to cause a pecuniary advantage by abuse or coercion practised by a public officer or by coercion or duress practised by him to obtain the monetary advantage. The words "for the purposes of Chapter IX" in section 5 are wide enough to include a public servant who commits criminal misconduct by a public servants. The words 'for the purposes ' in section 5, sub clause (d), 'for the purpose ' in section 6, sub clause(d) are wide enough. The words used in section 5 and sub clause (1) are wide and wide enough to cover a public servant for any of the purposes of the Code. The words in section 5 refer to a person who commits criminal offence by criminal misconduct by any public servant. In the present case, the appellants were charged for criminal misconduct by the public servant and the conviction was not invalid by reason only that it was based solely on such presumption. The offence was to cause pecuniary benefit to obtain the money. The offence under the section was to cause a bribe or extort the bribe by abusing his status as a public officer. The offence could not be said to have been committed by a public man. The offence of criminal conspiracy was not made punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The offence did not come within the meaning of that clause. The offence fell within the mischief of section 5(3) of the Act.

The appellant Bank was a surety for the respondent Bank. The surety was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. The surety, however, was not discharged from his obligation under the guarantee, and the surety was discharged. The surety 's surety was discharged by the surety. The surety filed a suit for recovery of the security. The trial court found that there was negligence on the part of the Bank with regard to the safe custody of the oil pledged, and that as the surety was independent of the pledge of goods given by the principal debtor, the surety was not discharged. The High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal debtor pledging oil tins and, therefore, two securities were offered, one pledge of goods and the personal guarantee of the surety. In appeal by the surety, the High Court held, that the surety was liable to be discharged from his liabilities under the guarantee and the personal guarantees of the surety were discharged. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that the surety having lost one security, namely, pledge of goods, the surety is not discharged from the obligation under the letter of guarantee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The surety is entitled to restitution. The surety must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantee on the good faith of other security being offered by the principal creditor which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee on good faith of the surety and the surety would be discharged to the extent of the value of the security lost as provided by section 141. [922D] 2. The surety has to be shown that he had taken more of one security on his good faith of another security being offered. The surety would not be discharged even if it is held proved that security of goods pledged was lost on account of the negligence of the creditor Bank. [923F] 3. The surety had to be shown the security offered by the surety and given personal guarantee on his good good faith of others security. The surety did not discharge the obligation under his letter of guarantee on the ground that the surety knew of such other security. [924F] 4. The surety cannot be discharged from the obligations undertaken under the letter guarantee. The guarantee is discharged to the amount of the security of the surety, and the personal bond gives personal guarantee on that account. [925F] 5. The surety may not be discharged from its obligation under the letters guarantee. The security must be shown to have been lost on account thereof. [926G] 6. The surety should not be discharged merely because it is found that a creditor has taken more than two security on the faith of other surety. The security is discharged to a extent of the security, the surety would not not be discharged. [927F] 7. The surety will not be discharged if it is found, even if it was held proved that the surety knows of such other Security, the surety will not discharge even if it be held proved that he had not taken more than three security on the good belief of such other surety. [928F] 8. The surety shall not be discharged unless it is found proved that the creditor has taken less than one security. The security may be discharged only if it is proved that the principal debtor had taken more or one security on its good faith. [929C] 9. The surety can not be discharged only on the ground of the negligence or misconduct of the principal debtor. [930D] 9. In the instant case, the surety had not discharged the obligation under a letter of guarantee, and, therefore the surety was entitled to restitution, and the suit against the surety was decreed by the trial court. [931F] 9.

The appellant was a patel inamdar of the village of village of village Khalsa in 1908. The Government of Bombay, by a notification dated August 28, 1922, declared the appellant to be the patel inam holder of the village. The appellant was declared to be the owner of the village and was granted a ryotwari patta in respect of the "patelki inam" lands. The appellant 's father, who was the son of the patel, was granted a grant by the Government of Bombay to the patel of the village for the patel service. The appellant, who was a psyki inamdar, was granted the grant by the Ruler of the village to the psyki inams. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the lands in suit were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for the emoluments of the psyka inamdar lands which were given as emoluments of his office to the working patel from the Rokade family. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the lands were granted by way of emoluments or emoluments for 91 714 services to be rendered by the patel 's office to the pharyki inamdar lands and Government had no right to resume the lands and regrant them to the pharki inamdar. The High court held that the "panchki inam" land was granted by the Ruler to the p Patel 's office and that Government had no power to resume the same. Held, that the grant was not a service grant, and no question of a claim of a share in the emoluments arose against Government, even though the lands were shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag. The grant was not of a service grant and no question was of a claim for a share in emoluments of the Patel 's Office. The grant made by the Ruler was not a "patel" inam. The grant did not confer any new right nor did the Inam Rules, nor the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 applied. The grant, though not a service Grant, was not a Service grant. The grant of land burdened with service and so long as a member of the family works as patel, including the plots which were made khalsa in 1904, and even though the appellant got possession by partition in 1923, it was open to Government to resume the land in 1941, it was not open to Government, to resume the inam lands and reggrant them to respondent No. 1.

The appellant, who was a Cutchi Memons, was the owner of certain lands in Madras. He was the owner in possession of certain lands. He was a Cutch Memons in Madras. The appellant was the owner and the other Cutchi Memon was the owner. The appellant, who had settled down in Madras, was the Cutchi Memos of Cutchi Memors, and the Cutchi Corons. The appellant 's case was that the rules of Hindu law applicable to Cutchi Memes, which were inconsistent with the Hindu law, were consistently applied to the Cutchi corons, and that the rules were consistently acquiesced in and applied to their family and the other cutchi Memons retained, despite their conversion, considerable portion of their personal law and that the Rules of Hindu law were consistently acquiesced and applied to the cutchi Memon widow, and that, as a large part of thestate was situate in Madras, he should prefer the Madras, as against the Bombay view. Held, that the High Court was right in its view that the rules applied to Cutchi Coron widow, as well as to the Cutch Memon widow. The High Court was in error in holding that the cutchi corons had acquired by custom to dispose of the whole of their property including the Hindu concept of coparcenary and survivorship. The High Courts were right in its conclusion that the cutch Memons had acquired the right by birth by custom to disposing of the whole or the other cutch Memon. The High, Court was right, in its view, that the cutth Memons had become the owner of the property by birth and the devolution thereof by survivorship. The fact that the Cutchi holders had been given the right by custom to transfer the whole or any part of their property to the Cutni Memons, did not make any difference in the position of the Cutchi Absons. The High. Court was right. The High court was right in holding that in the absence of a special custom as to the personal law applicable to cutchi Memos, the High Court would be right in its opinion that the cutlchi Memons had been governed by the customary law and that, therefore, when a Cutchi Coros had acquired by customary law, the High court would be right.

The appellants are manufacturers of different types of fabrics. They manufacture yarn in the mill of the appellants. The appellants are manufacturers. The appellants manufacture yarn in their mill. The appellants manufactured yarn in the mills of the appellants and subjected to the integrated process of weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants claimed that the yarn which is produced at an intermediate stage, is obtained at an intermediate stages and consumed or utilised in the continuous process of manufacture of the end product, and subjected to such integrated process of manufacture, of another commodity, is obtained in the manufacture of another commodity. The appellants contended that the goods manufactured at an intermediate Stage are not excisable goods and, therefore, the levy of excise duty on the yarn manufactured at an earlier stage was not justified. The appellants also contended that the expression "place of removal" in section 3(1) of the Act, which is a deeming provision, is not used in the sense of the word "place of manufacture" and that the expression 'place of removal ' in section 3 of the Act is the production or manufacture of the excisable goods. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the expression `place of removal", in section 3 (1) of Act, is the production of goods and not the manufacture of the goods. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The expression 'place ' in section 2(1) means the place of removal of goods from one factory to another. The expression "place" in section 2 (1) means that the place of manufacture and production of the excisable commodity is the production, manufacture or manufacture of goods. The expression `place ' in the Explanation to section 2(l) means the factory or any other place where the goods are produced, cured or manufactured, or where the excisable goods are used in the manufacture or production of the goods, and includes any premises appurtenant thereto. [701A B] 2. The expression, 'place of manufacture ' in section 4 of the Act means the place where the excisable commodity manufactured or produced is removed from one factory. The expression is not defined in the Act. The expression has been given retrospective effect from the date on which the Rules came into force. The expression means the place or the place where excisable goods are produced or cured or manufactured. The expression does not include the place where goods are produced. The expression in the Explanation is not defined. The expression must be understood in the sense in which it is used in the Act and not in the sense which it is understood in the Act itself. [702C D] 3. The expression used in the Explanation has been given prospective effect from the dates on which the rules came into force, and the expression 'date of manufacture ' has been given a retrospective effect from which the rules come into force. [703C] 4. The expression cannot be given a retrospective operation from the date of the Rules. The expression should be given a meaning which is consistent with the meaning of the Act. [704D] 5. The expression may be a word of wide import. The word 'place of ' in the explanation is not defined either in the Act or in the Act, but it is used to denote the place where a thing is produced or manufactured. [705E] 6.

The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the scheme published under section 68 C of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the Hearing Authority from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme. The trial court dismissed the suit. The appellant filed a revision petition before the Additional District Judge, Bulandshahr. The Additional District Judge allowed the revision petition and set aside the order of the trial court. The High Court held that the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for an injunction prohibiting the Hearing Authority under section 68 D of the Act from proceeding with and approving the Scheme either with or without modification. The appellant contended that the suit being not maintainable in the civil court, the jurisdiction of the civil court was barred. The High court dismissed the revision petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that the civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the State Government (the Hearing Authority under Section 68 D of U.P., Motor Vehicles Act 1939) is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil court to issue an order of injunction restraining the hearing authority from proceeding with, the hearing of the case and exercising its statutory functions. [537B] 2. The jurisdiction to issue an injunction restraining a Hearing Authority from proceedings with the hearing of a case and exercising their statutory functions is exclusive in nature and it is neither open to a Civil court to issue any order of injunction against the Hearing Authority nor to the desirability of bringing such scheme to the desirability or the desirability of bring such scheme to its desirability or the necessity of bringing such a scheme can be raised by an aggrieved person before the Hearing Authority. [538C] 3. The jurisdiction under section 68D of the Act is exclusive in status and it is for the Hearing Authority to consider such objections and representations. The procedure laid down for the preparation and approval of a scheme by the Hearing Authority is contained in sections 68 C and 68 D of Act. The jurisdiction is exclusive in the character and it was not open to any civil court to pass any order of restraint restraining the Hearing authority from proceeding. [539D] 4. The jurisdiction conferred on the Hearing Authority by section 68 D is exclusive in its character and it cannot be exercised by a civil court. [540E] 5. The jurisdiction which was vested in the Hearing Authority in the hearing of an appeal under section 68 E of the Act was exclusive in character. It was not open for a civil court, to issue an interim injunction restraining the appearance of the Hearing Authority or the representatives of the State Transport Undertaking from proceeding with it. [541F] 6. The jurisdiction vested in the hearing authority under section 68 F of the Act has been expressly barred. The jurisdiction has been expressly conferred on the hearing authority by section 68 E. [542F] 7. The jurisdiction exercised by the Hearing authority under section 69 D of the U P. Motor Vehicles (Amendment) Act, 1976 is exclusive in scope and it is no open to a court to issue a temporary injunction restraining the authority from proceeding to the hearing of cases. [534B] 8. The jurisdiction in such matters is exclusive in fact and it is exercised by a Civil Court. The jurisdiction cannot be exercised in a civil suit which is expressly barred. [535C] 9. The jurisdiction can be exercised by the hearing authority only in accordance with the scheme and the other provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the Act. [536D] 10.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant was charged under section 5 (2) readwith section 5(3) of the Act and section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 161 read with section 161 of Indian Penal Code for having committed the offence of cheating. The appellant contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel Nathaniel Nathaniel, it could not be said that the appellant had obtain a gratification for doing or forbearing to show, in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son. The High Court set aside the order of sanction in the present case. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the decision of the Judicial Committee had no application to the present case for the order of the sanction in the case was much more cryptic and different. HELD: The order of sanction was not excessive. The appellant had obtained a gratification for the doing or forbading to show in the exercise his official functions favour or disfawour to any one per son. In other words, the charge under section 5 of the Prevention Of Corruption Act and thereby obtained for himself a valuable thing or pecuniary advantage, and the charge under that section was established. [184 D] The appellant was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a police officer and extorted money from RusGA Nathaniel to show,in the exercise of their official functions, favorour to any person or disfavours to any per sons. The appellant in his statement under section 342, Criminal Procedure Code, did not disclose that he had obtained a bribe from Russel. The appellant did not disclose the facts constituting the offence charged and that the charge under the Indian penal Code or any other Criminal statute and if he had obtained money by playing fraud, the appellant could not be held guilty of the charge.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 161, I.P.C. and section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was found in possession of the marked currency notes and the list of cases, in which claims had been made, which had been given to him by Doraiswamy. The appellant was found in possess of the marked currencies and the list and the list were in the possession of the same. The appellant contended that the sanction accorded by him was not a valid one and that the sanction was not a proper one. Held, that the sanction granted by the appellant was not a ' valid one. The sanction accorded by the appellant did not require the sanction to be given in the present case. The sanction was not valid as the sanction was accorded by him. The sanction did not require that the papers placed before him were relevant to the only question before him. The sanctioning authority was not a competent authority to grant the sanction. The sanction itself and the evidence of Mr. Bokil were not crossexamined as to what the other relevant papers were and in the absence of any question being put to him by calling for the records of the claim connected cases or other records in connection with the matter from his office, the appellant should be put on his trial in a Court of competent jurisdiction for offences alleged against him. The appellant should be given the necessary material upon which he decided that it was necessary in the ends of justice to accord his sanction. The appellant had not asked for the connected claim cases or other record in connection with his official functions. The sanction granted by him was a valid one.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground of demolition and reconstruction of a building on the ground that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and reconstruction. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellate authority, however, allowed the appeal filed by the appellant. The High Court, however, held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction of tenants was not bona fide. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises in question and that it was inherent in such a life interest that it was not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14(1)(b) as grounds for eviction of his tenants. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The landlord has only a life interests in the premises and who has been on his own right under the Deed of Settlement as a trustee receiving rents of the premises from the tenants. The expression landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: "landlord" includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building, whether on his own ac count or on behalf of himself or on behalf or on behalf, or on behalf other or on behalf on or behalf of himself and others and also on behalf of others and also includes the person in whose favour the rent is payable. [275G H] 2. The expression "landlord" is defined under Section 2(6). The expression landlord means the person who has received or is entitled, to receive the rents of a building whether on his behalf or on or behalf, on or behalf or on account of another or on behalf for himself and others. The expression 'landlord ' is defined under the Act. The expression tenant is defined under s 2(6), as follows: 'landlord ' includes the person whose is entitled to receiving or is entitle to receive the same rent or be entitled to receive, the rent of any building, whetheron his own ac counts or on behalf and on behalf of another oron behalf of himself, and others. ' The expression landlord ' is defined in section 2(7) as follows. "landlord" means the person whose husband is entitled to get the rent of the building on behalf of or on behalf the other or on his own behalf and also includes any person who is entitled to the rent of such building, whether by way of rent or otherwise, and who would so receive the rent or be entitle to receive it, if the building were let to a tenant, whether on the ground specified in the deed of Settlement or on behalf thereof. " The expression landlord" is defined in the Act to mean a person who is in possession of or is entitled or is entitled in any manner to receive the whole or any part of the rent of his building. The expression owner ' is defined by section 2(8) as follows; " landlord" means the owner of any building or part of a building or part thereof, whether on behalf of, or on the part of, or for the benefit of, any person or on his behalf, and includes any person in whose possession or control the building or part is let. " The appellant landlord filed an application under section 12 of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1947 for eviction of respondents on the grounds of demolition and demolition. The Rent Controller held that the requirements of the landlords were bona fide required for demolition and the building in question on the ground floor of demolition and the reconstruction. The High court agreed with the view of the appellate authority that the landlord has only life interest in premises in question. The High, however, agreed with the views of the appellate authorities that the landlord bona fide required the premises for demolition and demolition and that it is inherent in such life interest that the remainder man may be prejudiced. The High. Court agreed with the finding of the appellate Authority that the landlord was only a life estate in the premises.

The appellant, a co owner of a grove, was the owner of a plot of land. The land was leased to the respondent for a period of ten years. The lease was for a period not exceeding one year. The respondent was the owner. The lease deed provided that the lessee would pay the rent at the rate of Rs. 10 per annum. The lease period was to expire on the expiry of the lease period. The respondent filed a suit for a declaration that the lease was void and that the lease deed was void. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the lease in favour of the respondent was void. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, is wide enough to preclude cultivation in them. The distinction between trees, which are parts of groves and grove land, is well settled under the general law, that trees, before they are cut form parts of the grove, are groves and groves. The principle is well settled, under the general Law, that trees before they are converted form parts of grove land held or occupied by an intermediary. [657 D E] (2) The definition is wide enough and an inseparable part is always included in the whole. The distinction is always part, an inseparable part, is always included, in the whole, and an inseparable is always part is always part. [658 E] (3) The distinction between the trees, before it is cut form parts, form parts of a grove land held by an intermediary is always part of bhumidhari rights. [659 D] (4) The distinction is well settled. The distinction, however, is always part and an inseparable one is always included. [660 F] (5) The distinction, therefore, between trees, before them are cut form part, is usually included in the entire. [661 D] (6) The distinction in the instant case is that the land was leased for a period exceeding one year, and an intermediary 's groves were held or occupied for a period beyond one year. [662 E] (6)(a) The distinction was not so much as to preclude cultivation, in the case of groves, but was merely a device to avoid cultivation. [663 F] (b) The distinction must be borne in mind in construing the definition of the ' intermediary 's sir grove '. [666 C] (7) The distinction has to be borne in view in construing the definitions of the intermediary and grove. [668 E] (8) The distinction made between the trees and grove land is well settled and the distinction made between trees, and grove land has to be understood in the light of the definition of ' intermediary '. [766 G] (9) The distinction drawn by the executing court, that there is a distinction between trees and grove lands, before they were cut form parts is always included is always part in the whole and an inseparable, an inseparable is also part is always excluded in the whole.[666 C D] (10) The distinction sought to be made between trees and the grove land is not a correct one. [667 E] (11) The distinction that the intermediary 'is grove land is a part of the grove land, and an intermediate grove land, before they can be cut form parts and that an intermediate grove is always included within the whole, is always a part. [767 F] (12) The distinction does not necessarily imply that the intermediary is grove land. The distinction made by the executing Court, that there was a distinction between the grove land and grove land and that the distinction was not correct. [682 E] (13) The distinction could not be made between the grove lands and grove land.

The appellants were charged for an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The trial court convicted them under Section 302 read with Section 149 IPC and sentenced them to suffer rigorous Imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court acquitted them of all the charges. Hence this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The conviction of the appellants under Section 302 is not sustainable. The appellants were charged under Section 302 I.P.C. for an offence punishable under Section 326 IPC. The prosecution case was that the appellants had caused injuries with a chopper and those injuries were individually sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. The injuries were caused by blunt weapons. The prosecution had not been able to prove that the injuries were caused with the chopper or those injuries were caused in furtherance of the common intention of causing such bodily injuries. The prosecution has not been able, in the ordinary way of nature to prove that these injuries were caused either individually or taken collectively with the other injuries caused by them. The intention to cause death of Suku was not proved by the prosecution. The prosecution was not able to prove the injuries caused by the appellants. The prosecution, therefore, was not justified in recording a conviction against them for the substantive offence of murder under Section 302. [89G H; 89A] 2. The prosecution failed to prove that Suku had caused injuries by sharp weapons. The injuries caused by him were not sufficient in the normal course of nature. The injuries could not be attributed to him though some of the injuries were individually or taken individually with the other injury caused by him. The intention of causing death of Suu was not proved. The injuries on the deceased were not sufficient to cause death in the ordinary manner of nature to caused by them, though some of them were individually or collectively taken collectively with other injuries caused. The intention could not be imputed to the appellants. [89C D] 3. The intention was to cause death or such bodily injury as is sufficient in the special course of nature, to cause death.[89F] 4. The intention is not to cause death but to cause death, but to cause such bodily injury which is sufficient in ordinary course of life. The intention may be gathered from the circumstances of the case. The intention can be gathered from a particular circumstance. The intention must be gathered from all the attending circumstances. The intention, however, must be gathered not from the circumstances but from the circumstances proved. The intention need not be gathered from any other circumstance. [89F] 5. The intention should be gathered from circumstances proved by the evidence. The intention cannot be imputed to any of the accused. The intention would be gathered from various circumstances. The circumstances of the present case, are such that it could not be said that any one of the four appellants had shared the common intention to cause the death of Suhu. [89A] 6. The intention has to be gathered from evidence on record. The intention and the circumstances of each case are such that the intention could not have been attributed to the appellants, but the circumstances of their case are such which would be sufficient in the circumstances of this case. [89B] 7. The intention or the circumstances of causing the death of the deceased are not sufficient to constitute the offence of murder. The intention on the part of the appellants to cause the bodily injury to the deceased was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The intention therefore, could not be inferred from the circumstances established by the prosecution and the medical evidence. [89E] 8.

The assessee, a non resident Indian Company, was assessed to income tax on cash basis for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69. The assessee claimed that the royalty amount should be assessed on cash basis in respect of the said royalty amount and that the said royalty should be assessed only on cash basis. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the royalty amounts should be assessed upon cash basis and since it did not actually receive any amount, it did not receive the amount. The Appellate Tribunal, however, took the view that the royalty was not payable by it in its books, and that the assessee could not be taxed at all as it would be received in U.K. in the books of the Indian Company. The High Court, however, allowed the assessee 's appeal. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the royalty payments should be assessed solely on cash basis and that the amount was credited to the account of the assessee in its books. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The assessee can be said to have maintained its accounts on cash basis, but mere crediting to the account, of the assessee, in its books of theIndian Company does amount to receipt of income by the assessee. [105G] 1.2 The assessee can legitimately be said to be a debtor in respect of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (a) cannot apply. [105H] 1.3 The assessee can, therefore, be said to know the true state of affairs relating to the assessee ' s accounts. [105A] 1.4 The assessee can also be said to possess the true state and make an entry to that effect in its own books at Coventry. [105C] 1.5 The assessee can only be said to receive the royalty amount only when it receives it in U. K. in the Books of the Indian company. [105D] 1.6 The assessee can not be said to represent the true state or make an entry in the books. [105E] 1.7 The assessee can never be said to act in a manner prejudicial to the interest of the Revenue. [105F] 1.8 The assessee can claim that the royalty should be taxed only on its actual receipt in U.U.K. and not in India. [105B] 1.9 The assessee can still be said to not be a debtor of the Indian Indian Company. [105 F] 1.10 The assessee can certainly be said to take credit for the said royalty on cash receipt basis. [105 G] 1.11 The assessee can take credit for any amount on cash receipt. The assessee can have no claim to the said royalty. [105 E] 1.12 The assessee can avail of the benefit of the said clause only if the said amount were put by the Indian Company in a Bank to the credit of the assessee. The assessee cannot be said to suffer from any conflict of provisions of law. [105 C] 1.13 The assessee can therefore be said to derive the benefit of clause (a). [105F G] 1(a) The assessee can recover the amount from the said amount in accordance with the provisions of the Act. [105 H] 1.14 The assessee can deduct the amount from its own books of the assessee and the said amount is credited to the accounts of the assessee by the Indian company in the books maintained by it. [105 D] 1.15 The assessee can draw the amount from his own books of account. The assessee has to maintain its accounts on the basis of the books maintained in the books and the assessee can claim the benefit of this clause only if it is shown that the assessee has maintained its accounts with respect to the said amount.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death but on appeal the High Court confirmed the conviction of the first accused. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the conviction of an accomplice is not vitiated by the uncorroborated testimony of an accomplice. The conviction of an accused on the uncor corroboration of the approver is no corroboration of the accomplice. The test of prudence and practice in the words of Martin, B. vs Baskerville, (1891) L.R. , referred to. The test is whether the uncoringerated testimony of the approver can be said to be a corroboration of the evidence of an accomplice in material particulars. The test for determining whether the uncoroborated testimony is reliable is whether the evidence of the accomplice is reliable or not. The test to be applied is whether the accomplice is competent to give evidence and according to the latter, the judge should point out to the jury that it is within his legal province to convict upon such evidence, but the judge should Point out to the judge, and the judge should points out to the Judge, to the jury, but the Judge should point out, to the judge. The test must be whether the uncreroborated testimony was reliable or not and whether the conviction based on the unco corroboration of the accused was justified. The test should be whether the evidence is reliable or otherwise. The test has to be whether the accused has been able to establish that the uncorbitable testimony of an approver is reliable. The test may be whether the accomplice has been able, to establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. The test, however, is whether the accused is able to establish the charge beyond reasonable doubt and if the court finds that the uncobitable testimony is reliable, the court can convict upon the testimony alone. The test in such cases is whether the court has to find out whether the uncomplied testimony of an accused is reliable or whether the conviction is based on the testimony alone and not on the uncomproborated testimony alone. In the present case the approver 's evidence was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of first accused upon the testimony of the first appellant. The conviction based upon the evidence of P.W. 7 who had prepared the knife at the instance of the first respondent was also not corroborated by the evidence of any other witness.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5(1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The appellant was charged under section 5 (2) readwith section 5(3) of the Act and section 21 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant contended that the charges were not proved because he was not a public servant within the meaning of section 21 of that Act. The High Court held that the appellant was a public servant and that the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was a public servants within the meaning Of section 21 of Indian Penal Code and section 21(9) of the Indian P.C. Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21 of, Indian Penal Code, and therefore a public servant under the definition of that section. [617 C] (ii) The appellant could not, therefore, be deemed to be a public servant. [618 D] (iii) The appellant, while taking the bribe, cannot be deemed to have been a public servant because he was acting or purporting to act in the discharge of the official duty of a public servant, and therefore, a public servant in the service of the Corporation. [619 D] (iv) The appellant cannot be deemed as a public servant for the purpose of section 21(1) (d) of the , Indian Penal Code because he was an officer within the meaningof that section. The fact that he was a person performing duties immediately auxiliary to those of some one who wasarmed with such authority or character cannot be deemed that he was not acting or purporting or purporting to exercise in the discharge or discharge of the duty of a Public servant within the definition of section 21. [620 E F] (v) The appellant 's contention that the appellant had been a public officer within the definition Of section 21(12) of the Code of Criminal Procedure cannot be accepted. [621 G] (vi) The appellant had been in the service as a public officer and was attached to the office of the Executive Engineer. The appellant could be said to be an officer within that definition. [622 G] (vii) The appellant did not have any authority or authority to perform any public duty. The appellant had no authority or authority in the service to perform any duty. The fact of the case showed that the appellant, was a public officer. [623 H] (viii) The appellant being a public servant was not a "public servant" within the meaning ofs.21(9) Of the Indian Penal code.

The appellant was convicted for contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 1,000. The appellant was convicted under section 3 of the Bombay Prohibition Act for contravention of the said order. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cl 3 of the said Order. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order of forfeiture of the juar was illegal because it was illegal to maintain the order regarding forfeiture of the poppy seeds in the house of the appellant because, he says, the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase and Sale and Control of Supplies and Control of Sale and Control Order, 1964 was illegal to maintaining the order regarding the forfeiture of the Juar. HELD: (i) The order of forfeiture is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. The rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings in judicial proceedings. The rules should necessarily provide for proof of judicial proceedings in court. [273 B] (ii) The rule is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962, and it must also provide proof in judicial proceeding. The rules are required to be complied with in the instant case. The appellant had not been able to show us any provision in the two orders. [273 C] (iii) The rule was ultra vires because the rule was ultravires because it laid down a rule like r. 141(2) of the Rules. The rules were required to provide proof in the judicial proceedings. [273 D] (iv) The rule must necessarily provide proof in court. The rules have necessarily provide for a proof in court and the Court must also provide the proof in judicial. [273 E] (v) The rule of evidence is ultra vires. The rule is not ultra vires because, it lays down the rule of evidence. The rules need not provide proof in Court. [273 G] (vi) The rule has to be read in the light of the provisions of the Act. The rule must be read in its proper setting. [273 A] (vii) The rule does not require proof in court but only provides for proof in court of judicial proceedings. It is essential to the scheme of the Defence. Rules must necessarily provide the proof of judicial proceeding in court. It is not necessary that the rule is in the nature of a rule of law. The rules may be made by notification in the Official Gazette. The rules cannot be made in the manner prescribed by the Act. [273 F] (viii) The rule cannot be made without prejudice to the generality of the powers conferred under section 3 (i) of the Act or any rule made thereunder or any rule framed thereunder. [273 H] (ix) The rule in question is ultra vires since it lays down that the rules must necessarily prescribe for the publication in the Official gazette. The Rules must necessarily prescribe the publication in a judicial proceeding. [273G] (x) The Rules must be read as a whole and must be read with the provisions of section 114 of Indian Evidence Act and must be construed in the light thereof. [273F] (xi) The Rules are not ultra vires.

The appellants were charged with murder of one Ram and the other for having fired a shot from his gun. The trial court acquitted the appellants. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of Sia Ram and Violet. The appellants contended that the prosecution had failed to prove that the shot was fired from his gun and that the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt. The High court accepted the prosecution case and convicted Sia Ram under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. The appellants appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The High Court was not impressed by the evidence of Om Prakash Dubey, who was a colleague of the deceased, who was riding on the Bicycle in the company of the deceased. The words of Violet are at best in the nature of a circumstance and they do not, without more, necessarily justify the inference that she was a party to the murderous design. [87G H] The words of the Violet indicate that the appellants intended to facilitate the murder of the deceased Kunwar Singh. The words attributed to Violet were at best in nature, of a circumstance. The words "in order to facilitate the commission of that act" are at best the nature of the circumstance and they did not do so. [87H; 87A] The words "if either prior or at the time of the commission of an act" are not at all in the nature, of circumstance and they are not merely the words attributed to the abettor. The words 'in order to enable the commission thereof, are at best 'in the nature of circumstance and ' they do not ' mean that an act on the part of the alleged abettor happens to facilitate the crime. [87C D] The words 'if either prior to or at the place of the commission ' in the section do not mean that an intention on the part Of the alleged abettor happen to facilitate the offence. The words are at best "in the nature" of a circumstance, and they do nothing in order to facilitate commission of that offence. [87F] The words are not at best in a circumstance and it does not mean that the act on the parts of the alleged conspirator happens to facilitate commission thereof. [87A] The word "in order" in section 107 of the Penal Code means an act done by any person in order to facilitating the commission of the offence. [88B] The words used in section 107 are "in order that a person may do something in order to prevent the commission thereof". The words "as soon as may be" in section 108 of the Penal code are not at any rate vague. The words used are not at the same time vague. The word "as soon" in section 109 of the Penal C.P. Code is not defined in the Penal Code. The words must be read in the context of the offence and not in the context in which it occurs. [87E F] The words must mean something which is done in order to attract the offence. It is not enough that an act is done in the course of a particular transaction. It is a thing done in order that a certain act may be done in order, to facilitate the doing of that act. The words in the section are not intended to convey that the act must be done in the manner prescribed by the section. The words may be used in the section only to facilitate the execution of the act. The section does not contemplate any such thing.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, read with section 149, and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted the accused under section 302, read with sections 149 and 147 of the Indian Penal Code. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant was not guilty only one of the accused, but also one of the other named or unnamed persons, named or unnumbered, for committing the said offence. The High court was, therefore, right in holding the appellant guilty only one and not others. [782 B] (ii) The High court had found that the appellant had done the act pursuant to a pre arranged plan and therefore he could be convicted under section 149, read with Section 34, of the Indian penal Code. [783 C] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding, that the appellant did not conjointly act with the other accused. The fact that the appellant and others were acquitted, did not necessarily mean that they did not take part in the offence. [785 D] (iv) The fact that two of the accused were acquitted, one of the persons named or unnnotified, was not sufficient to establish that the other was not named. The fact, however, that the other accused participated in the offence, did not mean that they participated in the commission of that offence. [882 E] (v) The fact, that the two accused were acquitted either on the ground that one or more of them might have participated in the crime, was not a single observation in the judgment of the High Court. [786 G] (vi) The fact of the acquittal of the other accused was not sufficient. The fact of acquittal of the accused was not proved. The fact was that the other two accused were not identified and the other accused were acquitted. The fact did not indicate that the other persons were acquitted either of the accused. The effect of the acquittal was not proved by giving benefit of doubt to them, the result of the acquittal would not necessarily follow. [787 E] (vii) The fact was not sufficient for the High Court to have acquitted the accused. [793 A] (viii) The fact about the acquittal of some of the accused persons was not sufficient in the present case. The fact about acquittal of some other accused persons was sufficient to establish the guilt of the accused beyond reasonable doubt. [794 B] (ix) The fact regarding acquittal of some others was not sufficient, for the High court to have acquitted some of the persons convicted. [795 C] (x) The fact relating to acquittal of some persons was not proved, nor was there any evidence in that regard. [796 D] (xi) The fact as to whether the accused were named or unnominated, was not conclusive. The fact regarding the acquittal of certain persons was not conclusive and could not be a ground for acquittal. [797 E] (xii) The fact in the present appeal was that the appellant, who was acquitted, was not named, but only the said accused, who was not identified, was not mentioned. The fact relating the acquittal of other accused persons, even if they were acquitted, was sufficient to prove that the other person was acquitted. [798 E] (xiii) The fact which was not proved was not sufficient and the High Court was in error in holding that it was not possible to convict only one of those persons, named, named or indicted, for committing murder. [799 G] (xiv) The fact whether the accused had been acquitted, was a relevant circumstance. The fact as regards the acquittal of all the accused persons, not being identified, was sufficient.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of electric cables, imported a consignment of goods from the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the import licence. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the import licence was not a valid and legal order and that the customs authorities were right in taking the view that the rate of duty applicable to the imported goods should be determined according to the law prevalent on the date they were actually removed from the warehouse. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner has no fundamental fight to clear the goods on payment of duty. The petitioner 's claim that the customs authority was right in taking a view that the rates of duty applicable should be determined in accordance with the law prevalent at the date they actually removed from warehouse, is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. [682C D] 2. The petitioner is not entitled to seek recourse to Article 32 of the Constitution. The petitioner, however, has no fundamental right to seek recourse under Article 32 of thi sion of the Constitution to enforce the fundamental right which entitle a citizen to seek recourse. [683D] 3. The petitioner as such has no fundamental rights to clear the imported goods except in due process of law. [684D] 4. The petitioner cannot be permitted to seek recourse of Article 32 of t he Constitution. [685E] 5. The petitioner can not be permitted to invoke the provisions of the Act, since the petitioner has no right to seek resort to the provisions of law. The petitioner may, however, be entitled to seek resort under Article 32. [686F] 6. The petitioner would be entitled to invoke Article 32 of this Constitution. [625E] 7. The petitioner shall be entitled to the relief under Article 32 in spite of the allegation that it is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is breach of the fundamental right. [687F] 8. The petitioner will be entitled to claim the relief under article 32 of the Consti tution of India.

The appellant was the owner of a bungalow. The bungalow was sold in execution of a decree for possession by the Bank. The appellant was the purchaser of the bungalow. The sale was not for the benefit of the son but for the benefit to the son. The appellant contended that the debt was not avyavaharika and therefore the right, title and interest of the appellant could be sold and that the right, interest and interest of his son could be sold under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code. Held, that the liability of a father, who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyavirarika debt as it cannot be termed as repugnant to good morals. The pious duty of the sons continues and consequently there is merely a difference in the mode of enjoyment of the property. The pious obligation of the sons which continues to exist in the lifetime and after the death of the father and which does not come to an end as a result or of negligence in discharge of his duty is not an " avyavisharika debt" as it cannot, therefore, be termed as " repugnant to good faith". The liability of a son is that of the father alone which could not include the share of the other members of the joint family. The liability of the sons does not cease to exist in execution proceedings because the pious duty of sons continues and there is merely an difference in the method of enjoyment of property.

The Delhi Administration was constituted under the Delhi Administration Act, 1952. The Delhi Administration was entrusted with the responsibility of maintaining peace and harmony in the country. The Delhi Police was entrusted with certain powers to ensure the proper maintenance of law and order and order. The Delhi Government was entrusted with various powers to ensure that law and order was not disturbed by the Delhi Administration. The Delhi High Court directed the Delhi Administration to examine the conduct of various police officers and other persons and also the criminal proceedings. The Delhi Special Police Establishment was also entrusted with the responsibilities of maintaining law and order. In the meanwhile, the Delhi Administration was directed to take up the matter with the Delhi Administration for further investigation. The Delhi Adminis tions were directed to submit a report to the Delhi Administration within a period of two months. The Delhi Admn. submitted a report to this Court. The Delhi Govt. submitted a further report to this court. The Delhi Home was also directed to submit the report to this Tribunal. The Delhi Delhi Administration submitted a report on the basis of the material available on record. The Delhi Secretariat submitted a report recommending suspension of the D.C.P. Kiran Bedi and Jinder Singh S.I.S.I. and Jinder singh S.I., S.I.; and JinderSingh S.I, S.I; and Jinder SINGH S.I and Jinder S.I of the Delhi Administration, on the ground that the Delhi Administration had no jurisdiction to pass the order of suspension of the petitioners. The Delhi Chief Secretary to the Government of Delhi, in his letter dated June 2, 1988 addressed to the Delhi Adminis sion, stated that the Delhi Admini sion had no jurisdiction in the matter. The Delhi Administrative Tribunal, however, directed the Delhi Administra tions to examine the entire conduct of various Police officers and others and also the Criminal proceedings. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Delhi Administr sion. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the Delhi Admn. had no jurisdiction under the Delhi Adminisi tions Act, 1952 to pass the orders of suspension of D.C.,P. Kiranj Bedi and J.inder Singh S I.S. I.S., I.S.; and J.V.S.S.i. The Delhi Laws Act, 1952, was enacted to provide for the control of the police in the Union Territory of Delhi and for matters connected therewith. The Delhi Legislative Assembly was constituted under section 3 of the Delhi Police Act, 1952 and the Delhi Administration constituted under the Act was to be a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal and was competent to acquire, hold and dispose of property and to contract and to do all things necessary for the purposes of this Act. The Delhi and Delhi Administration were to be constituted under the provisions of the Delhi and Delhi Police Act. The petitioners, who were the guardians of law and orders, challenged the validity of the order of their suspension by a writ petition before the High Court. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended that the Delhi and the Delhi Admin istration Act, 1952 was a complete code in itself and that the Delhi Police was not a State within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Delhi & Delhi Adminis terial Tribunals Act, 1952 is a complete code and the Delhi and Administration were not a State. The Delhi Act was a complete Code and the Delhi Police had no jurisdiction. [512B C] 2. The Delhi (Delhi Adminis terral Tribunals) Act, 1952 has been enacted to provide the control of police in the State of Delhi and the Union Territory. The Delhi, Delhi Adminis tion, Act, 1952 provides for the control and regulation of the police.

The first petitioner was a registered firm, petitioners Nos. 7 and 8, who were registered under the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, and a notification issued under section 8A of the Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation Act 1959, was issued by the State Government under section 8 A of the Act. The petitioners contended that the Act was ultra vires the provisions of the Rajasthan Goods and Taxation Act, 1958, and that the notification issued under the Act was invalid and ultra vires. Held, that the Act in the guise of taxing passengers and goods, was still a tax on passengers and goods and, therefore, the tax was without authority of law. The tax was, therefore, not a tax on goods and goods, and the tax was, however, a Union subject, and was not available to the State Legislature. The tax, however, was a Union subject and was not, therefore, unconstitutional. The tax could be levied under the Entry, and the notification was, therefore. unconstitutional. The petitioners were not entitled to any relief under article 32 of the Constitution. The Act was not a valid piece of legislation. The tax imposed by the Act was not in the nature of a tax on passenger and goods but was a Union tax on passengers. The tax is, therefore, a Union tax and not a Union tax. The tax on passengers or goods is still a Union tax, and, therefore the tax is without authority of Law. The tax being a Union tax the tax is, however, not a Union taxation. The tax cannot be levied under a Entry, and, consequently, the tax is not without authority of the law. The words "in respect of all passengers or goods" in the entry in the State List are wide enough to cover tax on passengers, goods and goods. The tax thus, is not a Union Taxation. The tax in respect of all goods and goods is, therefore. not a Union Tax. The tax under the Act is not a tax. The words 'in respect of goods and goods ' in the entry are wide enough and they are capable of precise interpretation. The tax may be levied under different heads, but the tax is a Union tax not on goods and passengers. The words are wide enough in their ordinary sense to cover taxes on goods and, though the amount of the lump sum must be, if lump sum payment is made in lieu of payment of the tax, the amount of freight and freight charged is measured by the fares and freights. The tax payable on actual fares and freight is, therefore not a Uniontax. The tax would, therefore, be a Union tax under the Entry. The tax levied under the Act would be a Union taxation and not a tax, and the State Legislature would not be entitled to impose a tax on the same. The tax must, therefore, fall within the ambit of the entry. The tax can be levied under two heads, namely, (i) the tax on passengers carried by motor vehicles and (ii) the tax payable on fares and freight charges. The tax has, therefore, to be levied under both the heads. The tax so levied is a Union taxation, and the imposition of tax is not a valid tax. The State Legislature has the power to impose a levy on the same class of goods and passengers, and the levy of tax is, in the absence of any specific provision in the Act, a tax on fares and the freights.

The appellant workmen were sought to be retrenched from 1st August, 1974 and the Labour Court directed their reinstatement effective from that date. The Labour Court directed reinstatement of the workmen with full back wages. The appellant workmen challenged the award in this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Labour court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full back wages to the workmen. Once leave against relief of reinstatement was refused, the employer could not shirk his responsibility of paying the wages which the workman has been deprived of by the illegal or invalid action of the employer. [567B C] 2. The Labour Courts in the territory of India have no discretion to grant special leave to appeal to the Supreme Court to grant special Leave to appeal to this Court. [567C] 3. The question whether the workmen should be awarded full back wages in the aggregate amount of Rs. 1,000/ is no more open to debate that in the field of industrial jurisprudence, namely, where awards are made in violation of the principles of natural justice causing substantial injustice and grave injustice to the workmen, the employer can not shirk its responsibility of paying wages which the workmen has been deprived by the illegal action of the appellant consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to be raised. [567D E] 4. The question is whether the workmen concerned did not have any opportunity of explaining why their services should not be terminated and, therefore, reinstatement was held to be the appropriate relief. [567F] 5. The question of back wages for full back wages is no more res integra. It is no more appropriate to award 75% of the back wages to workmen who are now reinstated.

The accused was charged with murder of his wife Churi. The prosecution case was that the accused was in a murder case and was sentenced to death. The prosecution alleged that the accused had come at the residence of the deceased and that the deceased was with him at the house of the accused. The prosecution also alleged that the deceased had gone to see film at Kotkhai and that the accused and his father were in a wet condition at the time when the deceased was murdered. The prosecution contended that the accused did not belong to him and that the murder of the deceased was committed during his absence. The trial court acquitted the accused. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that the record of such a confession could not be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act, and that the record was admissible in evidence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The record of such an confession could not, therefore, be put in the evidence under sections 75 and 80 of Indian Evidence Act. [734G] 2. The prosecution has not established beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of the deceased had been recovered after the accused had visited the house of one of the accused to the residence of his father. The evidence of the accused that he was taken by the rolice to the house of his father and talked to him without the child, is not sufficient to show that the accused knew the murder of his father as a result of which he died. [735A B] 3. The evidence on record establishes beyond any manner any manner of doubts that the dead bodies of Churi deceased were recovered after the appellant had visited the residence of one of his father, and that it was the accused alone who was responsible for the murder of Churi. [736C D] 4. The evidence establishes beyond any doubt that the accused suspected the fidelity of Churi, deceased before the visit of the accused and talked to the deceased. The evidence shows that the accused, who was responsible to the murder of one of Churi was also present at the house. The evidence further shows that the deceased used to visit the house of Churi and that the relations of the accused with the deceased were strained. The evidence also shows that the relations between the accused and Churi were strained. [737E F] 5. The evidence clearly establishes beyond any reasonable doubt that the deceased and Churi had gone to the house and made a report to the police. The evidence established beyond any doubt, that the accused could have had a natural affection for the child and it is difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the son of the accused, the accused would have had a reasonable affection for the son of Churi to stay with him without his child. [738F G] 6. The evidence in the case shows that the deadbody of Churi had been recovered from the house of accused. The evidence does not show that the police was aware of the murder of Suri. The evidence, therefore, establishes beyond any way of doubt that Churi had visited the houses of the accused at the time of occurrence. [739G] 7. The evidence is not sufficient for the conclusion that the dead Body of Churi could not be recovered after the deceased was recovered after the dead body was recovered. The evidence has established beyond any reasonable doubts that the deceased died as a result thereof. The evidence proves beyond any manner. [740C] 8. The evidence discloses beyond any manner whatsoever that the accused might have visited the house at the time the occurrence.

The plaintiff, a co owner of a property, purchased certain properties from the defendants, and the defendants, in turn, sold them to the defendants. The defendants, in their written statement, denied the plaintiff 's claim and claimed that the properties were mortgaged to them. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, on appeal, held that the plaintiff was entitled to a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs. 40,000 and that the defendants were liable to contribute in equal shares towards payment of the mortgage debt. The High court, however, held that in the absence of a contract to the contrary, the plaintiff ' had in substance asked for a mortgage decree upto a limit of about Rs. 40.000 and that, in the absence Of a contract to that effect, the plaintiff was not entitled to a decree in a mortgage suit up to a maximum limit of Rs, 40,000. Held, that the plaintiff ' claim was in substance asked by the defendants for a mortgage suit upto a limit exceeding Rs. 40 lakhs and that the plaintiff had in substance called for a mortgage. The declaration of charge by standing itself by standing itself was superfluous Order XXXIV, and the declaration of charge was standing by itself by standing themselves. The declaration by standing itself, by standing itself is superfluous Order XXXIV. The declaration was standing by themselves and not by evasive on some points. The declaration, therefore, did not amount to a change in the character of the property. The declaration could not be said to be a change in character. The plaintiff 's suit was, therefore, rightly dismissed. The High. Court was, therefore right in holding that the plaintiff could not claim a mortgage decree for sale up to a certain limit of Rs 40 lakhs. The declaration in the present case was not a change in law but a change in fact. The declaration as to charge was not a new one. The plaintiff was entitled under the Transfer of Property Act to recover the balance of the property from the defendants.

Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Rules are clearly in violation of this Court 's judgment in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors. , [1988] Sup. S.C.R. 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State of Punjab & Ors. ; [1988] Supp. S. C.R. 658, and Mohinder Sain Jain vs Mohinder Sain Garg, [1988] Suppl. S.c.R. 656, and Mohinder Saini Sain Garg vs Mohinder Sain Jain & Ors. [1988] 1 SCC 248, and Mohinder Rai Garg vs State, [1988) Sup. S C.R., 657, and Mohinder Singh Sain Garg vs Union of India & Ors. J.T. ; and Mohinder Sain G. vs Mohinder Sain G, [1988 Suppl. S C,R.R. 659, and Mohinder Sah Sain Garg vs The State of Punjab, [1988 Supp. S C] 2. The selections were made according lhe to the Rules. The selections made according to these Rules were clearly violative of the dictum laiddown by this Court. [405D] 5. The selection of the appellants was made accordingl y to the Rules and this practice was consistently followed for all the last 17 and 17 years and the selections were made by applying the rule of 1973 and that practice is being followed consistently for the last 18 years and there was no allegation of malafides in the matters of the impugned selection.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of death. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution had failed to prove the complicity of the appellant in the murder of the Collector. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking assurance in support of its conclusion. [413D] 2. The confession may be regarded as substantive evidence but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has to be completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the charge of conspiracy cannot be accepted.
