[413E] 3. The confession is not substantive evidence and cannot be treated to be substantive evidence. It is a fact that a set of witnesses who according to the prosecution, were present when Yadav was taken into custody, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that they were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. [413F] 4. The High court has rightly held that the prosecution has established by circumstantial evidence that the chain has been established and the link has to been established and, after it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evidence, it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after it has formation its opinion with regards to the quality, effect of the alleged evidence, then it is permissible for turn to the confessional in order to accept the conclusion of the guilt which the Judicial mind is about reach on the said other evidence. [413G H] 5. The High Courts have not been able to agree with the High Court that the prosecution was able to establish by circumstantial evidence, that the chain had been established and that the chain was complete one and the chain had to be completed otherwise it would be hazardous to accepted a part of that link as a full and on the foundation of such incomplete prosecution evidence, the allegation of conspiracy cannot, therefore, be accepted. The High. Court has rightly held in the present case that the prosecution failed to prove that the chain of circumstantial evidence was complete one. [413A B] 6. The High, Court has rightly pointed out that the prosecution evidence has established by direct evidence in every case but if the evidence relied upon by the prosecution is found to be exculpatory in nature and, therefore, would not be admissible against the co accused.

The appellants, who were working as clerical and subordinate staff in the four companies, were working as such in the four concerns. The Tribunal found that the total wage packet of the concerns was Rs. 1,000 and Rs. 1.000 respectively. The Tribunal also found that the appellants were working as the clerical and subordinate employees and that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wages and dearness allowance. The Tribunal, however, ignored the total wage packets including basic wages and dearness allowances prevalent in comparable concerns. The appellants contended that the Tribunal was wrong in applying a region cum region formula for fixing the same scales of dearness allowance and dearness allowance together as it should have done, for the purpose of finding out whether the total wage package of concerns could bear comparison with the total wage unit including basic wages, dearness allowance and that the tribunal had gone wrong on the basis of the comparable concerns. Held, that the Tribunal has gone wrong in looking at the industry cum industry formula and the Tribunal has not considered what the total wage price packet including basic wages plus dearness allowance and has made the total wage difference including basic wages. The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the daily wage packet including basic wage and dearness allowance are less than the highest in the comparable concerns and thus arrive at a just figure for basic wage. The Tribunal had not considered what wages for these categories of factories and workmen were comparable. The Tribunal was in error in applying the region cum region method which was the foundation for fixing the wage and dearness allowances. The Tribunal ignored the total wages packet including basic pay packet including basic salary and dearness allowance and made the total wages for clerical and subordinate Staff. The Tribunal did not consider the total wage out of which the Tribunal had dealt with the matter and had made the total number of wage packet including dearness allowance prevalent in comparable concern which it took into account. The Tribunal therefore was in error.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa, filed a suit against the respondents for the redemption of certain mortgaged property and for placing the mortgaged property in their name. The trial Court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the Rajinama had not the effect of transferring the interest of Annappa to the mortgagees and hence the appellants were entitled to redeem the mortgage in the suit land. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Rajinama was a complete relinquishment of his interest, but as regards Annappa, the Rajinamama was a full relinquishment of his rights of both the brothers Shiddappa and Annappa. The Rajinamma was the registered occupant. The Raj inama was a part of the estate of Annaappa. The Rajiama was a registered occupant. He was the registered owner of the suit land and the mortgagee was the registered occupants. The Rajnama was a joint family property. The Rajmama was the registered tenant. The Rajmaama was the owner of the land. The Rajiniama was the tenant of the land and the mortgagees were the legal heirs of the mortgagees. The Rajniama was the recorded occupant. The appellants, therefore, could not claim redemption of the mortgage in their favour. [648 C D] (ii) The Rajinima was a complete relinquished of his interest. The Rajaniama was a separate property. The appellants were not the legal representatives. The Rajesama was a consolidated property. The Raja was the registered occupancy tenant. The appellants had no right to alienate the property. The respondent, therefore, was not entitled to redeem his mortgage. [649 D] (iii) The Rajnmaama was a clear relinquishment of his right of both the sons. The Rajnaama was a partition of the property. It was not a transfer of title from the mortgagors to the mortgagees. [650 E] (iv) The Rajnimaama was not a full relinquishment. The Rajanaama was a transfer of the interest of the mortgagees and the mortgagees. It was a transfer from the mortgagors. The Rajmiama was a document of title. The Rajainama was a deed of title. It was executed by the Rajinmaama in favour of the mortgagees, and the mortgagees had redeemed themselves. The Rajnatama was a mortgage deed of title and the mortgagees became the owners of the property and the mortgagees continued to be the owners of that property. The Ramanaama was not the registered occupant of the suit property. The suit was therefore not barred by limitation.

The respondent, a dealer, was assessed to sales tax at the rate of 2 per cent. The Sales Tax Officer, Kanpur, did not accede to the conten tions of the respondent and holding that carbon paper was a part of the typewriter, its turnover could not be subjected to sales tax. The Sales tax Officer, Kanpur did not accede, to the contens tions of respondent and holding, that carbon paper does not lose its character as paper even after being subjected to chemical processes and that ribbon was a part thereof. The Salestax Officer, Kanpur also did not accede. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10%. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the levy. The High Court, however, held that carbon paper did not lose its nature as paper even though paper even after going through certain chemical processes and had become a part of typewriter. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'paper ' has not been defined in the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1947 and that sale of stencil paper is not an essen tial part of a typewriter so as to attract tax as per entry 18 of the Second Schedule to the Act. [838F] 2. The word paper ' has not necessarily been defined in Entry 42 in the First Schedule to the Sales Tax Act. The word "paper" has not been used in the sense in which it has been understood in common parlance. The wordpaper ' has been defined in popular parlance, the word 'paper" has been used for bearing, writing, or printing or for drawing on, or for drawing or for drawing, on or for drawing. or for drawing a, on or from, or for getting, on or over, or for receiving, on or after the typewriter. [839C D] 3. The word `paper ' has also not been defined either in the U P. Sales Tax Rules, 1948 or in the Act or the Rules. The word,paper ' has neither been defined in any of the U. P. Sales tax Rules, 1948. [840F] 4. The word newspaper ' has not even been defined in entry 42 in the Schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax Act 1957. [841F] 5. The word printing ' has not defined in the Act nor in the Act. The words 'popular sense ' in popular parlance are not decisive of the question whether carbon paper is not paper as envisaged by entry 2 of the aforesaid Notification. [842F] 6. The word Paper ' has not yet been defined in a popular sense, meaning in popular parlance. The words "popular" in popular parlance means paper which is used for printing, writing or printing. [843G] 7. The word printed is used for bearing or printing or writing for drawing on or for or drawing on, for or on, or from, any of the typewriters. The word used in the entry is not decisive of whether the question whether the article is paper generally understood as a sub stance which is used in the common parlance or in the common sense, meaning thereby, the word paper ' in the sense which people conversant with the sub ject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [844C D] 8. The word in popular parlance is a sub stance used for printing or writing. The word is used in popular parlance and in the common man sense, meaning which people conversant in the sub jection matter with which it is dealing. The word has not been specifically defined in the Sales Tax Rules. The words used in popular sense are not decisive.

The appellant, a company, was carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar at Amroha. The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the owners of the appellant Mills at Amroha. On February 2, 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents 1 to4 from service on the ground that they had disobeyed the order of the management. The appellant filed an appeal to the Labour Appellate Tribunal of India. The Tribunal held that the management had no right to transfer the respondents 1, to the new factory and that the appellant had disobeyed his order of transfer and thus he was guilty of misconduct under Standing Order No. 3. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant was within its rights and that the order of dismissal was illegal. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court. Held, that the appeal must be dismissed. The question whether the appellant had the right to transfer his employees from one concern to another was a substantial question of law within the meaning of section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. The question was whether the appellant was entitled to transfer the respondent from one concern. The question of law involved in the present case was one of law, namely, whether the appellant has the right to transferred the respondents 1 and 4 to the new concern. The appellant was not a condition of service of the respondents either express or implied that the employer had the inherent right to transfer their employees to another place where the business of the employer in the same line was situated. The question as to whether the appellant could be transferred to another concern was one of fact. The appellant had no such right. The question arose in the case and the question was whether in the circumstances of the case the liability to be transferred must be deemed to be an implied condition of service. Held, further, that the appellant in the present ease had no such rights. The question raised was one of Law, namely, that the employer in a business subsequent to the date of the employment, was not a 'workman ' within the meaning Of section 2(s) of the Act. The question, therefore, was one of the fact. The question which arose in the present appeal was one of general law relating to the right of an employer to transfer his employee if he had the right of transfer to another concern. The essential distinction between that case and the present one was that the employer has the inherent right of transfer his employee to transfer his employer to another place, where the business is situated, unless there was an express condition to the contrary in the contract of employment. The essential difference between that case is that the employer must be the owner of the business of that concern and the employer in that case must be the employer. The essential ingredient of the relationship of master and servant is that the employee must be a person employed by the employer in connection with the business of his employer. The test is whether the employer has a right to transfer an employee if he has the right of appointment to another place. The essential element of the relationship is that the master and servant must be a servant of the employer. If the employer has no such right, the employer has to establish that the employee has been employed in a particular trade or business.

The appellant company was incorporated in 1948 under the . The appellant company was a company incorporated under the . In the year 1948, the appellant company was paying special contribution to the Employees ' State Insurance Corporation. The appellant company made a contribution of Rs. 1,000 to the Employees State Insurance Corporation, which was to be paid by the appellant company. The appellant 's contribution was to be made by the employer under Chapter V A of the . The employees ' State Insurance Act, 1948 was enacted in 1948. The appellant Company was a company registered under the . It was, however, not a company. The employees 'State Insurance Corporation were not in force. The appellant, however, made contribution of Rs, 1,000. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act. The High Court held that the contribution payable under Chapter VA was a fee and its levy was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. The High court held that the contributions payable under Chapter IV A were not fees and its levy is illegal as the appellant company itself was not a tax. The appellant appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contribution under Chapter V of the Act is a fee and not a fee inorder to attain legitimacy. The Act does not contemplate the making of any service, or the conferment or the conferment thereof of any benefit or the conferment. The Act is only a fee and does not contemplate rendering of any services or the conferment, of any benefit thereto to the appellant Company or its employees. The scheme is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they be, in the case of employers who straightaway receive the benefits of the insurance scheme, their rate of contribution is lower. [1088G H] 2. The appellant is a company incorporated in 1948. It is pursuant to the power entrusted in respect of entries 23 and 24 of List III of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, the Parliament has enacted the . The expression 'appropriate contribution ' in the Act is used in the sense of a fee. The expression 'fee ' in the context of entry 23 and 24 is used in Entry 24 of List II. The expression "appropriate contribution" in Entry 24 is used to mean the amount of the contribution payable by an employer under Chapter IV. The expression is used in a sense of a tax. [1089F G] 3. The expression, 'appropriate contribution" is used in entry 23 and 25 of List III. The expression has been used in Entry 23 and 25 in the sense in which it is used in connection with the levy of taxes. The expression means the amount of contribution payable by the employer. The expression does not mean the amount payable by the employee to the employer. It is not a tax, fee or fee in order that the employee may be liable to pay the same. The expression in Entry 24 has been used to mean a tax. It is a tax. There is no distinction between a tax and a fee. [1090F G] 4. The expression used in Entry 25 is used in relation to taxes. The word 'appropriate ' is used in different senses. The expression takes in the sense that the amount of tax is to be determined by the authority competent to impose the tax. The expression may be used in different contexts. The expression must be understood in the sense as understood in the Act. [1091F G] 5. The expression `appropriate contribution ' is used to denote the amount of contributions payable by the employers. The expression cannot be used in a narrow sense. The expression should be understood in its ordinary sense. The word "appropriate" in the context in which it occurs in the Act has been used.

The petitioners are not regular employees, they do not have any specific job to do, they do no work for a long time. The petitioners are not regularly employed on the rolls and paid their daily wages. The management has denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that the petitioners are discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The petitioners have been continuing on rolls and paid the same duties. The management, therefore, denied the petition ers claim and alleged to be daily rated workmen for a long period. The petitioners contended that the petitioners were not regular employees and that their claim was denied throughout the petition ices and that the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds. The High Court rejected the petitioners ' claim and held that the petitioners ' case was not covered by the principle of regularisation of a daily rated workmen. Allowing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation is not arise. The principle is that the daily rated workmen are doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not paid the equal pay for the period during which the same work is taken from him. [655D] 2. The principle does not arise when the daily rated workman is doing the same job as the regular workmen. The principle has been consistently followed by this Court in several decisions. [656F] 3. The principle that regularisation of a Daily rated workman and payment of equal pay for a period during which he is doing the work as regular workman and also there being a post available for him is not absorbed in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners and that for some time they have been continued in spite of there being no work for them. [657F] 4. The principle applies to all daily rated workmen and the principle of regularization of a daily wage workman and payment for the period after which the same works is taken from them. [625B] 5. The principle regarding regularisation of a casual worker is not applicable when the daily wage workman is doing a work as the permanent workman and there is a vacancy available in the establishment. The principle cannot be applied to all daily wage workmen. [625C] 6. The principle in regularisation of a regular workman and payment to him 'to him 's equal pay for equal work is not applicable in the instant case.

The appellants, who were the co sharers of the Azamabad Tea Estate, purchased the entire land in question from the respondent, who was the sole proprietor of the land in question. The appellants claimed title to the property and the recovery of possession of the property. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, on appeal, held that the appellants were precluded by 0. r. 1 of the Bengal Revenue Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, from questioning the validity of the mortgage and the sale of the property in execution of the decree obtained by the respondent. The appellants contended that the sale in execution of a mortgage decree obtained by them was not the full owner of the property and that the mortgage decree obtained in pursuance thereof and of the court sale in execution thereof was not the real owner of the entire interest effected by him under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that the co heirs were estopped from questioning the legality of the mortgage of the entire property and that in conse quence the sale passed the entire property. The High court rejected the contention of the appellants that the sale was not the sole proprietor or owner of the whole interest effected by the respondent under section 41. The High, Court, on a reference, held that when the sale in the execution of the mortgage decree was made by the National Agency Co. Ismail was not the owner of the land and that the sale did not amount to a mortgage, the sale was illegal and void. The High. Court, however, held that though Ismail was the full owner, was an ostensible owner of the properties and that the transaction by which the mortgage decree had been obtained by Ismail was not a full owner of that property and that as the mortgage decree did not amount only to the extent of 2 1/2 as share belonging to Ismail, the mortgage decree passed by the National agency Co. Ismail could not be upheld as frivolous. The High 'Court, however, rejected the contention that the sale by the sale in favour of the 1st defendant was not the exclusive owner of the suit property and that it was only the interest of Ismail who was not the ostensible owner of that land and that therefore the mortgage decree could not be sustained. The HighCourt, however held that the sale made by the 1st respondent in execution of that decree was not a valid sale and that the appellants could not be allowed to raise any further plea touching their right to the share in the property. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the sale under exhibit 12(i) was not a genuine sale and that it could not be said that the sale had been made in pursuance of the decree in execution of which the mortgage was executed. [212 A B] (ii) The High court was right in not holding that the transaction was a sham one and that the appellant had no right to the property. [212 C] (iii) The High.Court was right in rejecting the contention that if the sale was a real one, the plaintiffs would be entitled to a decree for a declaration that the entire interest of the property conveyed under exhibit 12 (i) was a real and intended to pass title to Pir Baksh and in the event of the sale not being held to be real, it would stand on the same footing as the 8 pies share granted to them by the High Court to a further transaction to which it was real.

The appellant was charged with offences under sections 302 and 201 of the Indian Penal Code, and was convicted by the Sessions Judge. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him under section 302 and 201, and sentenced him to imprisonment for life. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the provisions of sections 173(4) and 207A(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, were not complied with, and the trial were vitiated by the omission of the police officer in charge of the investigation. The High court was, therefore, justified in holding that the provisions Of section 207A were mandatory and that the failure of justice had caused a complete failure of justice. The High Courts were, therefore, right in holding that they had not complied with the provisions of section 207A(4) of the Criminal Procedure Code. The High, Court, while dealing with the ground of appeal, had observed that the mandatory provisions of sections 207A and other sections of the Code had not been complied with, but had caused a full failure of justice, and that the irregularity was curable by reference to section 537 of the Code. Held, further, that the High Court was right in holding, that the mandatory sections of the Criminal procedure Code had not not been complied. The High. Court was, therefore. right in holding the appellant guilty of the offences under sections 207A, 207A and 207A of the Code, and that, as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial have not been vitiated by the admitted non compliance with the provisions Of the Code. The irregularity is curable by referring to section 537 Of the Code, as no case of prejudice has been made out.

The respondent Municipality was constituted under the , for the purpose of carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling of oil and oil. The respondent Municipality issued a notice to the appellant under section 153A of the Act to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in the manner specified in the notice. The appellant filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of mandamus directing the Municipality to take action against the appellant for the breach of the provisions of the Act. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The scheme of section 153A was to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality. Once the notice has issued, the person to whom the notice has been issued does not deny the existence of the nuisance in question and is prepared to comply with the direction to arrange the discharge of effluent in the specified manner. The scheme under section 153 A is to leave it for the subjective satisfaction to the Municipality. The scheme is to leave the subjective satisfaction before a notice is issued to the person on whom the notice is issued. Once the authority has issued the notice, it would not require a judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge to enquire into the dispute and make its report only as to the manner in which the effluent should be discharged. [437 C D] The scheme under the section is to leave a discretion to the subjective subjective satisfaction of a Municipality. Once a notice has been given to the Municipality, the Municipality is bound to enquire into and report only as regards the manner in Which the effluent should, be discharged. The scheme does not deny that the nuisance in the terms of sub section (1) exists or not. Once the Notice has issued, it would be open to the person to accept the assertion of the Municipality that the nuisance was one which ought to be set aside.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the prosecution was not called upon to prove that the articles were not railway stores within the meaning of section 2 of the Act. HELD: The prosecution was not calling upon to prove the articles belonging to a particular railway administration but only those which were used or intended to be used in the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The prosecution was therefore not called upon. to prove that articles were not meant or intended to have been used in the execution, operation or maintaining of a railway, and that the goods were in a serviceable condition. [191 D] The prosecution was, therefore, not called upon, to prove that they belonged to any particular railway administration. [191 E] The prosecution could not successfully establish that the articles belonged to any railway administration. The prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that the articles in question were not only the property belonging to a railway administration but they were used or meant to be used for the construction, operations or maintenance of railway. The evidence that they were intended to be use in the construction or operation of a railway is not an offence. [191 F] The prosecution is not called upon tO account of the stores being stolen or unlawfully obtained. The prosecution is, therefore, entitled to prove that these articles were not Railway stores within the definition of railway stores.

The appellants, who were the tenants of the demised premises, filed a suit for ejectment of the respondents from the demised premises on the ground that on the death of the tenant, the appellants had no right to continue in occupation of the demised property. The suit was decreed by the trial court and the decree was confirmed by the first appellate court. The appellants filed second appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the appellants were entitled to remain in possession of the demised shop in question till the appellants were duly evicted in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The appellants have filed this appeal by special leave against the High Court 's judgment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the demised premises governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Act and also subject to the right in favour of the respond ent created under section 13(1)(a) to (k) and other provi sions of the Act subject only to the rights in favour of a person who had been in possession even after the determination of his tenancy, as has been done in the case of heirs of the tenant without any hiatus and restriction on the heritable interest of the tenant. [10C D] 1.2 The appellants succeeded in September 1966 to the estate of the tenant by virtue of intestate succession under the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. The appellants succeeded on the heritable estate of the tenants without any hikiatus and restrictions on the heritable rights in the demised property governed by the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent) Act, 1950. [10D E] 1.3 The appellants succeeded only to the heritable estate or interest in the tenanted premises governed by section 13(i)(a) of the Act and subject to the provi sion of the Act, an irrepara mischief which the Legislature would never have intended is likely to be caused. [10E F] 1.4 The appellants succeeded not to the heritable right in the demised shop but to the heirs of the tenants. The appellants were duly evict ed in accordance with law. [10F] 1.5 The appellants succeeded the heritable interest which they continued to remain in the possession of the premises. [10H] 1.6 The appellants succeeded by virtue of succession under the law of the land and they succeeded in September, 1966 to the appellants and succeeded in September 1967 to the estate. [10G] 1.7 The appellants succeeded before the High court on the ground of limitation. The appellants failed to establish that the tenancy was not heritable on the death or the heirs of their tenants. [10A] 1.8 The appellants succeeded. The appellants are entitled to enjoy the protection of the Act as amended from time to time. [10B] 1.9 The appellants succeeded and succeeded in October, 1966 to their estate. The appellants lost their right to the heritable and heritable interest in their tenancy. [10 F] 1(a) The appellants succeeded, to the heritable rights of the tenancy held by the tenant. The appellants became entitled to enjoy protection under the Act subject, to the rights of the heirs of such tenants.

The appellant Board was a public sector undertaking. The appellant Board was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who were on deputation and those to whom the Provident Fund Act applies. The appellant company was willing to pay the provident fund scheme to all its employees except the Government employees who were on the deputation and those who contributed to the Provident Fund scheme. The appellant, however, claimed that the services of the workmen of the Board should have been transferred from one establishment to another and that there should be no distinction between the Board 's Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The appellant contended that the services should be transferred from one employer to another and the employees contributing equally. The Tribunal held that the employees of the Board were liable to be transferred from the one establishment to other both which may not be covered by the same scheme under the Act and therefore the appellant was entitled to the benefits of the Provident Fund Scheme. The Tribunal also held that the services were liable to been transferred from the other establishment to the other establishment both of which may not he covered by the Act. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant Board was entitled to a higher rate of interest than what it was earlier and that the Board should extend the benefits of Provident Fund to all the employees of its Board. The appellant 's appeal to the Industrial Tribunal was dismissed. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the employees in question were not liable to be shifted from one establishment and that the employees were not entitled to the benefit of the Provident Funds Act. HELD: (1) The employees of the appellant Board were not entitled under the Provident Fund Schemes and the scheme framed under the Employees ' Provident Fund Act, 1952. The employees of a public sector Undertaking are not entitled to any higher rate of bonus than what they are entitled to. [47C] (2) The employees in question are not entitled under any scheme under the Provident Funds Scheme. The employees in the instant case are not entitled for the benefit of Provident Fund Scheme as they are not governed by the Provident Fund Rules. The employees are not entitled in the matter of bonus. The employees who are covered by the Provident Funds Schemes are not entitled. [47D] (3) The employees are entitled to the same benefits as are given to the employees of a private sector undertaking. [47E] (4) The employees who were governed by the Act are not entitled, under the Provident fund Scheme to any additional amount to the depreciation reserve. The contribution to the Provident fund scheme is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion. It will certainly result in some reduction in profits. The contribution is a statutory liability and is a positive proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the provident fund and gratuity is a definite percentage. [47F G] (5) The financial capacity to implement the Provident Fund schemes as well as the scheme under section 67 of the Act is to be taken into account in calculating the profits. The financial capacity of the employer is to be considered in calculating the profit. The contribution in the instant cases is not borne out by the provisions of the Act. [47G] (6) The financial position shows a very large amount in the shape of interest payable to the Government. The financial position of the employer shows a very small amount in the form of interest payable. The contribution has to be taken in working out the profits. [47H] (7) The financial capability of the employer to implement the provident fund schemes as well the scheme under sections 67 and 68 of the Act are to be taken care of in calculating the financial capacity of an employer. [47A] (8) The financial status of the employer cannot be ignored in working out its profits. The employees contribute to the Provident Funds scheme.

The respondent wife filed a petition for maintenance under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Magistrate, Ahmedabad, allowed the application filed by the respondent for maintenance and set aside the order of the Metropolitan Magistrate, Ahmedabad. The High Court, however, held that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for refusing to live with the husband merely because her husband was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligations. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts erred in ignoring the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125 of Cr. P.C. and setting aside the order. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that the wife was impotence which had been held by a number of authorities under the Civil law to be a just reason for refusing to maintain the wife. [701C] 1.2 The High Court erred in ignoring that the ground of impotence was no good ground or reason for the wife to refuse to live with her husband. [702D] 1.3 The High Court has overlooked the legal effect and object of the second Proviso for the wife 's refusal to live with him. The High Courts have overlooked the legal effects and object of both the provisos for the wife. The High court erred in ignoring this legal effect of second proviso for the wife, because, if this could be a ground for divorce or for an action for restitution of conjugal rights, it could be said with any show of neglect or refusal to maintain the husband. [802D] 2.1 The second proviso to section 125 of Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, which was also a proviso to sub s.(3) of s. 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973, was also a substantive ground for refusing the wife ' to live with his husband. [777E] 2.2 The second proviso was introduced with the clear object of arming the wife with a cause of action for refusing to keep with her husband, as the one which she was seeking to live with a wife, as the other which she was not entitled to maintenance from her husband. The second proviso, therefore, was not good law and were hereby overruled. [777G H] 2.3 The second proviso in sub section (1) of section125 of the Code, 1973 was also a procedural provision which was introduced with clear object of the arming the husband with a cause for refusing to reside with her husband and the wife would be entitled to maintenance. [777H] 2.4 The second proviso is a substantive provision which is introduced with the object of armting the wife with the husband. The proviso is a procedural provision and the conduct of the husband from which the Court may draw the inference of neglect or refuse to maintain the spouse. [777A] 2.5 The second proviso does not apply to cases under the Hindu Law or other laws. The second Proviso to sub section(3) of Section 125 of the Cr. Pc. is a substantive one and is not a bar to the application of the second sub section. [777B] 2.6 The second proviso has no application to cases under Hindu Law or any other laws. [777C] 2.7 The second proviso cannot be said to be a substantive provision. The second sub section (2) of section 127 of the Code is a substantive law and is not applicable to cases under other laws. It is a very different thing from holding that no evidence of cruelty can be admitted in a proceeding under the section. [703D] 2(a) The second proviso which is a substantive part of the section is a substantive substantive provision and is not an exception to the general rule of construction of statutes.

The plaintiff, a Municipal Corporation, was granted a lease of the suit property for a period of 99 years. The plaintiff was in possession of the suit land. The plaintiff filed a suit for possession based on title to the suit property. The plaintiff claimed that the suit property was leased to the plaintiff for a period from 1st January, 1964 till possession of the property was delivered to him. The plaintiff also claimed that the defendant was in possession thereof till the date of his possession. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The first defendant Union of India filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the vesting of the land in the Municipality was not a vesting of the title itself in the State to dispose of the land. The High court also held that the plaintiff had not shown possession of the land as claimed by the Municipality. The High, however, held that the suit was also liable to be dismissed as barred by limitation. The plaintiff appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have erred in holding that the vesting was of the title to the land as representing the Government but not a vesting as agent of the State to the Municipality. [222B] 2. The High was right in holding that vesting was of title in the Municipality. It was not necessary for the Court to give a finding on title to a suit property. [222C] 3. The plaintiff had not pleaded adverse possession. The plaintiff has also admitted that the structures in Rasala Lines were not shown to be that of the Municipality. In fact, the plaintiff had also admitted that they were vested in the Municipality and remained in possession of Government of India. The plaintiff, therefore, had denied title of the suit building. [222D] 4. The plaintiff having admitted that the structure in Rasala Line was not shown to have been vested in the municipality, there was nothing on record to show that the Municipality was formally handed over the land in question. The plaintiff could not, therefore, be said to have been in possession of any Government. [222E] 5. The plaintiff 's claim that the structures were not shown as belonging to the Municipality was erroneous and that the land was vested in the State. The plaintiff did not claim that the structure was not vested in it. The plaintiff therefore, had not pleaded any adverse possession. [222F] 6. The plaintiff is not entitled to any relief. The plaintiff cannot, therefore, claim any relief.

The appellant was a lessee of a railway Carriage Workshop at Ajmer. He was charged with offences under section 5(1)(d) of the Indian Penal Code and was convicted under section 5 (1)(d), Indian Penal Code. The appellant was convicted under sections 5(1) (d) and 5(1), Indian Penal code and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant 's appeal to the Judicial Commissioner was dismissed. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The Judicial Commissioner held that the appellant was not an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) of the Act and was not an "officer" within the meaning Of that term as used in section 21(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The appellant contended that the appellant had not been an officer within that term as defined in section 21 (9) of Act II of 1947 and could not be convicted of the offence under section 5 of the Act. Held, that the appellant 's contention that the Quarter Master 's clerk was not an 'officer ' within the meaningof section 21(8) of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of1947 was not correct. The appellant had been rightly convicted under section 6(1) read with section 5(2) of the Bombay Prevention of Corruption act, 1947. The appellant, therefore, was an officer within section 21(2) (d), Indian Railway Establishment Code, and was, therefore, a public servant within the meaning ofs. 21(9). The appellant was, therefore. an officer within s. 21(1)(c) of the General Clauses Act, 1897. The appellant could not be a public servant for the purposes of the Act 11 of 1947 and was, consequently, a public officer within the definition of section 21 (8) of Act 11 of 1948.

The Respondent was granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69 under the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887. The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala C, Patiala, for recovery of the said share of the Respondent in the said property. The Respondent 's suit was decreed by the Sub Judge, Patiala, on the ground that the property attached and notified for sale was not exempt from attachment and sale under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Respondent then filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,00,000/ from the Respondent. The Respondent contended that the property was not exempt under clause (c) of sub section (l) of section 61 of the Code. The Trial Court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the property in question was exempt from attachment. The Respondent appealed to the District Judge, Patiala. The District Judge, however, allowed the appeal holding that the property belonged to the Respondent and that the Respondent was not exempt. The Respondent preferred an appeal to the District judge, Patiala, which was allowed by the High Court. The Respondent thereafter filed a second appeal before the High Court in second appeal being Regular Second Appeal No. 2944 of 1980. The High Court allowed the second appeal holding that section 60 of Code of Civil procedure, 1908 applies only to execution of a decree of a civil court. The High court also held that the Respondent 's half share was exempt from the attachment and sale. The Respondent thereupon filed a second second appeal before this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were wrong in both the criticism of the subordinate courts and in allowing the Respondent 'S half share of the respondent in the said properties were not exempt from the attached and sale under cl. (ccc), of the proviso. [848D] 2. The opening words of sub section(1) of Section 60 set out the properties which are liable to attachment and sale in execution of a money decree. The opening word of sub section is "such attachment or sale" in the said proviso refers to the attachment and sell mentioned in sub section (I) of section60 set out the property which are liable for attachment and sale mentioned in sub s.(1) of that section. The opening portion in which the liquor shop was situated. is also under the provisions of the said Act and the sale which was notified for sale is also under sub section (c) thereof. [849E F] 3. The opening sentence of sub section.(1) is "such sale or sale" and the said proviso is "such property as are so exempted by the said Act would be only such properties as are so exempt by the said act". The opening words in sub section(l) of Section 61 set out the assets which are liable "to attachment and sale" in sub section.(l) of that Section. The opening part of sub section refers to the sale and the sale mentioned in the proviso to subsection (1) thereof. The opening terms of sub section are "such attachment and sale". The opening sentence in sub section is the "such attachment of sale or sale". The proviso to sub s.(l) is "the attachment of sale and the said sale mentioned in subsection (1). "such attachment, sale or sale mentioned in clause (cc c) of the said proviso. "such attachment is "such "such property" as are so exemption from attachment and sell in revenue recovery proceedings under the said Act.

The respondent, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 and 1964 66. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice issued under s.61 of the Act on the ground that the respondent had not issued it on the basis that such right to compensation had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and that the enhanced compensation had been wrongly valued as at the date of the death of the deceased. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not entitled to receive the compensation as on the date of death of the original assessment under s.73 A of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the respondent did not estimate the market value of the lands on the date when the original assessment was made. The respondent had merely accepted the value of the acquired lands as determined by the Special Deputy Collector. The respondent was therefore, not entitled to any compensation as on that date. [331C D] 2. The High Courts have attempted to distinguish the above decision by stating that in the instant case the respon dent had merely accepted that the acquired lands still formed part of the estate of the deceased properly under s.36 of the Act and when he accepted the compensation fixed by the Special Assistant Collector, he must resort to provisions of section 59 and proceed to make reassessment but such reassessment has to be done within the period of three years from the date of original assessment under section 73 A of the. [332D E] 3. The High ' Court was right in taking the view that the respondent himself did not estimate its value of the land on the date the original assessment had been undervalued. [333G] 4. The High. Court was right, in holding that such valuation was obviously wrong in view of the enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court. [334B] 5. The High, Court was right.

The appellant, a Cooperative Society, was elected as a Director of the Bank on 8.1.1987. The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected as the Director on 8.2.1987. On 8.1,1987, the Deputy Registrar issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of the Bank. The appellant challenged the said notice before the Divisional Joint Registrar, who dismissed the appellant 's revision petition. The appellant 's Revision Petition under section 154 of the Act was dismissed by the Divisional JointRegistrar on 30.8.1989. The appellant preferred a revision petition before the Divisional Deputy Registrar which was dismissed on 30.9.1989. In the revision petition under section 154, the appellant contended that section 73FF of the Act had no application to the case of the appellant and that the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. The appellant contended that the disqualification on account of his having repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section 78 (1) of Act was invalid and hence the appellant was disqualified under section 73FF(1) and that the Assistant Registrar could not have acted under section 78 of the Act. The Divisional Joint Registrar dismissed the revision petition. In the Revision Petition under Section 154, the petitioner contended that section 74FF of the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act was without jurisdiction inasmuch as the Act prescribes a separate procedure for calling in question the appellant ' s election as a Director and that the procedure having not been followed the Assistant Registrar was not a defaulter in presenti on the date of the notice and the provisions of section 78(I) of the Act were not attracted. The appellant also contended that the Assistant Regisrar, Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors of Chandrapur District Central Cooperative Bank, Chandrapur by holding that the appellant had repaid the entire loans before the impugned order. The appellant, therefore, contended that section 78FF of the said Act was not applicable to the case. The appellant further contended that section 76FF of the Bombay Cooperative Societies Act had no applicability to the case and that the disqualification of the appellant was extinguished and hence the Assistant Registrar should not have acted in the absence of the Assistant Registrar. The respondent, on the other hand, contended that the appellant having repaid the loan before the said notice was issued would not be material for the purpose of taking action under section 78. The appellant was not a defaulters in presenti, on the date when he was declared elected as Director. The appellant having repaid before the impugned show cause notice under section 79(1) was issued, he was clearly not a defaulter. The appellant had not repaid the entire amount before the impugned notices under section 78 were issued. The appellant did not dispute the fact that he repaid the entire of loan before the notice was issued. The Assistant Registrar, Cooperative Societies rejected the appellant ' revision petition under Section 154 of the said act on the ground that the appellant ' having repaid the whole loan before the aforesaid impugned notice under Section 78(1), the disqualification continued from 18.8.1986 to 21.10.1986 and the appellant having been a defaulter under the provisions of Section 73FF of that Act, the disqualification continued for both common for election and for continuation as a Director. The Assistant Regisar Cooperative Societies, Nagpur, by its order dated 7th December, 1987 removed the appellant ' from the Committee. The appellant then filed a revision petition under the said act before the Divisional Assistant Registrar, who allowed the revision petition and set aside the order of removal. The appellant thereafter filed a revision before the Divisional Commissioner, who dismissed it. The appellant thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. The appellant came to this Court by special leave.

The respondent was in the service of the State Government. He retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. The State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent. The State of Maharashtra issued orders on November 4, 1982 enhancing the amount of pension payable to respondent by 50%. The State Govt. issued orders on January 13, 1987 reducing the amount of Pension payable to the Respondent by 50 percent. The State government issued orders on February 13, 1987 enhancing the pension payable by 50 per centum. The State was aggrieved by the reduction of the pension by 50 per percent. The State filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court quashed the State Government 's order reducing the respondent 's pension by 50 percent. The High court held that the initiation of disciplinary proceedings and the order of punishment was unauthorised and illegal. The State, however, reduced the pension by the 50 per cent to the extent of Re. 1 per month. The State appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The State has power to reduce the pension payable in case of a Government servant who has been found guilty of grave misconduct while he was in service or after the completion of his service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a Government servant depends upon the good conduct of the Government servant. The State is entitled to withhold or withdraw any part of the pension payable. [34D] 2. The State 's power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. The State cannot impose any punishment. [35E] 3. The State may withhold or withdraw a pension or any part of it if the pensioner is found guilty of serious crime or is found to have been guilty of grave crime or of any financial irregularities which he may has committed during the period of his service or after completion of his services. Grant of pensions and its continuance should be taken into consideration. [35F] 4. The State should have taken into consideration the fact that the respondent had retired from service and the reduction of pension by 50% would seriously affect his living. [35G] 5. The State had power to reduce, or withhold pension. The State did not impose any punishment; instead the proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. The High Courts in the instant case were not justified in holding that the State Government had no authority to initiate any proceedings against the respondent. [35H] 6. The State by its order reducing the pension by 100 per cent to 50 per cent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the respondent and the Government was entitled to withhold pension by the taking into consideration the facts and circumstances of the case. [35D] 7. The State in its order reducing pension by 50 percentage to 50 percent was too harsh. The State could not have imposed any punishment. The State can impose any punishment without taking into consideration all the facts and circumstance of the case and without giving any opportunity to the respondent to show cause against the proposed reduction. [35B] 8. The State as well as the State Government should have taken the into consideration the circumstance of the respondent 'S case. The State while reducing the pension, by 50 per majority, would seriously affect the living. [36C] 9. The State must have taken into account the fact that respondent had retired on attaining the superannuation of superannuation. The State does not have power to reduce pension payable to a Government employee. [35C] 10. The State having regard to the facts and situation of the case, the reduction of 50 per cent is too harsh and arbitrary. [35A] 11. The State and the State Government are entitled to withhold the pension granted to a Government Servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that the tenant was in arrears of rent for more than six months. The trial court decreed the suit but the District Magistrate granted permission to the landlord to sue the tenant for eviction. The High Court held that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) of the Act was invalid in law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was in error in coming to the conclu sion that the plea against the validity of the order passed by the District Magistrate was not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the revisionalvisional power conferred on the Commissioner by section 3(4) of the U.P. Act III of 1947. [7 F] The High Court had not committed any error in coming out of the conclusion that the permission was invalid in fact. [7 G] The High court was not justified by introducing a limitation relating to questions of law in determining the nature of the revisional provision. [7 C] The High Courts were not justified in introduce a limitation pertaining only to questions of fact and law in determining whether the order passed in violation of the principles of natural justice was a nullity. [7 E] The High, Court was not justified to introduce a limitation relating only to questions which could be raised before a civil court in relation to orders passed under the relevant provisions of the Act. [7 D] The High. Court was not right in introducing a limit relating to questions which were not raised before the civil court.

The appellant, a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission, was appointed as a member of a Public Service Commission. He was appointed as the Chairman of the Punjab Service Commission. The appellant was appointed as Chairman of the Commission. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of the Chairman of a Commission. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant filed a writ appeal in this Court. The High court dismissed the writ appeal. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the case of his client was that he was guilty of misconduct and that the punishment of removal was disproportionate to the charges levelled against him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The appellant has been rightly convicted by the High Court. The fact that the evidence of any particular witness is recorded by the learned Judge will not conclude the issue as regards the admissibility or relevance of that evidence. [603G] 2. The fact of the matter is that the evidence has been examined and found upon by some other body or authority. The fact, that the evidence is recorded by a court of first instance, will not conclude that the person concerned is guilty of misconduct. [604B] 3. The fact whether the person concerned was guilty of misbehaviour and ought to be removed from his office on the ground of misbehaviour and that its function is limited to determining whether the person is guilty of misbehaviour is of such a nature as to warrant the removal of the person from his office. [605C] 4. The fact as to whether the person against whom the charge of misbehaviour is made out and whether the misbehaviour is of a nature as lo warrant the removal is in direct opposition to the plain words of article 317(1) of the Constitution, is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other authority or authority. That Article 317(1), which provides that subject to the provisions of clause (3), the Chairman or any other member of a public service Commission can only be removed from office on the grounds of misbehaviour and the Chairman or other member, as the case may be, ought to be remove from his office only by the order of the President on the ground that the misbehaviour is such a nature that to warrant the dismissal of the person concerned. [606E F] 5. The fact the evidence to be recorded by the President, the charge of misconduct is made out, and whether the misbehavior is of such nature as to justify his removal is in order opposition to the clear words of article 316(1) and that its functions is limited to deciding whether the person Concerned is guilty of the charge of assault and he will have to suffer a decree for damages in a civil court. [607F G] 6. The fact in a reference under article 317(l) is not subject matter of the inquiry which this Court is required to hold is not over that by the Supreme Court and not by a court. [707F] 7. The fact is that the appellant was not guilty of misconduct, and that the charge of misbehavior was made out and that it would be impossible for him to prove his case unless he is allowed to cross examine witnesses on those aspects of the matter. [608C] 8. The fact remains that the appellant has been acquitted of the charge. The fact which the appellant has stated in his affidavit that he was not guilty is not a ground to hold that the charge was proved. The fact however remains that the evidence to the limited question is not over by that date, the learned Judge may write to the Registrar (Judicial) of this Court immediately after the entire evidence is recorded.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. VIII of 1939) for the recovery of a sum of Rs. 1,00,000/ from the defendant. The plaintiffs alleged that the endowment was a private endowment and the deity installed in the temple was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the endowment in question was a private one and the deity was a private temple and the deity had nothing to do therewith. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the approach made by the High Court was wholly incorrect and it had misconstrued the evidence and documents produced in the case to show that the endowment had been a private one. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The mere fact that members of the public had a right to worship in the temple by itself would not determine the nature of the endowment. [830E] 2. The mere circumstance that members of a public were allowed to worship at the shrine of the deity can only be the members of the family, and that is an ascertained group of individuals. The mere factum of worship would not determine, the nature and character of the endowment and the recitals of the document show that the founder of the endowment did not make any stipulation for offerings or contributions to be made by members of the community or their descendants. Other factors that may be considered would be the nature of right and not as a matter of concession. [831F] 3. The mere existence of the endowment in the temple is merely to instal a family deity in the temple. The mere possibility of the founder being a public temple is merely a possibility of the temple being used for the benefit of the members of a family or their descendants, the endowment would be an important intrinsic circumstance to indicate the private nature of the endowments. [832G] 4. The mere possession of the endowment does not determine the character of the temple. [833A] 5. The mere absence of any averment in the deed to show that there was any stipulation for taking offerings from the members of public to the temple, this would be an intrinsic circumstance to show that it was of a private nature. [834B] 6. The mere presence of the founder of a public temple in the temple cannot be proved that the founder was merely to instal the family deity in a temple. [820C] 7. The mere mere fact that the founder did not make a stipulation for offerings from the public to the deity, and there is nothing to show that any contribution was called for from members of the Hindu or his descendants, the temple was merely toERSUS a family deity. [835D] 8. The mere receipt of the founder from the public or his descendants does not establish that the founder had any obligation to perform all the work on the members of his public.

The appellant Bank was a contractor to finance contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against bills for supplies under the contracts. The appellant Bank was to finance contracts with the Government in its various departments and had entered into certain contracts and will in future enter into certain contracts. The respondent Bank was to pay the bills for payments to be received by it under the contracts directly in their own name or in the payment of such bills or other amounts and to receive the amount due in connection with the contracts directly. The appellant bank was to pay to the respondent Bank the amounts due under the bills for payment to the respondent. The respondent bank was to make payment to the appellant Bank out of the monies receivable under the bills. The appellant was also authorised to sue for recovery of the monies due in connection therewith under the contracts and to pay the same to the respondent bank. The appellant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhatmal for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhatmal had no right to attach it. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the power of attorney was expressed to be irrevocable and that the document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. The High court held that the appellant bank was the assignee of the BiLl and Takhathal had no right, to attach it, and that the power was irrevocable. The High. Court, however, held that the powers of attorney were irrevocable and that there was no equitable assignment of the debt due under the bill. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The power of attorney in favour of the appellant bank is an equitable assignment of a specific fund in favour of a borrower or which might be passed in his favour in his favour and in the payment to Bharat Bank Ltd., the power of Attorney is expressed to be unconditional. The power of Attorney coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 created an equitable assignment. The power coupled with the endorsements on the bill on the bill was expressed to have been irrevocable. [782 B C] (ii) The power conferred on the attorney coupled with the endorsed on the bill is expressed to have the same effect as the power of the attorney. The power conferred upon the attorney is expressed to operate as an equitable assignment and is irrevocable. The power to attorney is expressed in the following terms: "The power of attorney is expressed as an equitable assign of the debts or fund coming to the debtor, or an order given by a debtor to his creditor upon a person owing money or holding funds belonging to the giver of the order, directing such person to pay such funds to the creditor will create a valid equitable charge upon such fund in other words, wll operate as an equity assignment of the debts and fund. The power is expressed to run as an equitable assigning of the debts, in other words the equity assignment of a particular fund in favour or fund coming into the debtor, will create a equitable assignment of all the debts or funds belonging to him in the hands of the Government authorities. [785 D E] (iii) The power to sell or sell or sell any property belonging to the Government authorities is expressed to vest in the Government authorities and the Government is entitled to sell or dispose of the property belonging to them. The power under the power of sale or purchase of property is expressed to include the power of alienation or sale of the property. The power can be exercised only in accordance with the terms of the contract. The power cannot be exercised in a manner which is not inconsistent with the terms and conditions of the contract or in the absence of any express provision in the contract. [786 E F] (iv) The power is not absolute and is subject to the conditions of the agreement. The power may be exercised in accordance with law.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gilland Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The said Co. had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. The said Provident Fund was not a recognised one. The assessee retired during the previous year relevant to assessment year 1963 64. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the receipt in question was not a legal. The Tribunal, however, took the view that the receipt was not profits in lieu of salary. The Tribunal also held that the receipts in question were not taxable as salary. The High Court answered the question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The receipt in question cannot be considered as salary. It is undoubtedly that though undoubtedly that is an income, it is undoubtedly that is undoubtedly that being an income. The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ representing the interest on such contributions. The receipt is undoubtedly an income. [441 D] The receipt of a Rs. 27948 is undoubtedly an Income. The receipt in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered to be either interest on the securities income or on the income from other source. [441 E] The receipt in respect of the interest on the investments is dealt with by section 16. The receipt was not income. The interest on the investment was defined in section 17 as including any payment. The income from other heads specified in section 1.4 was brought to tax under section 56. [441 F] The receipt was income from other income. The income was not income from other items. The receipt could not be considered as income in the relevant account year.

The Bihar Act, 1950, was passed by the Bihar Legislature in the year 1951, which was replaced by the Bihar Act of 1951. The Bihar Act was passed by a majority of the States in the year 1954. The Bihar Legislature enacted the Bihar Act, 1951, which came into force on April 1, 1951, and the Bihar Act was replaced by Act of 1951, which provided that the slaughter of cows and calves of cows and cows of calves of buffaloes and calves shall be deemed to be a slaughter of cows, male and female, and the slaughter of buffaloes and buffalo shall be deemed always to be a breeding of cows and buffaloes, and the provisions of the Bihar Act shall apply to the slaughter of bulls and buffaloes, bulls and working bullocks, and buffalo, and the provision of the Bihar Acts shall apply to such slaughter. The Bihar Acts were passed by the State Legislature in the years 1951, 1951, 1951 and 1951, and were passed by a unanimous majority of the State Legislatures. The Bihar and Orissa Acts were passed in the year 1952, and the Act was passed in the years 1952, and 1953, and the validity of the Act was challenged on the ground that the Act was invalid, because it was not passed in the manner prescribed by the Act, and that the Act violated article 19 (1) (g) and was therefore void. Held, that the Bihar Act in so far as it prohibits the slaughter of cow and calves, male and male, was valid in so far it prohibits the Slaughter of cows and buffalo, without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness, and the restriction on the slaughter of the cows and calve of cows, female and calves for cattle, and buffalo was not valid. The Bihar Agricultural Produce Markets Act, 1950 was passed by Parliament in the year 1953, and was passed by an unanimous majority of two Judges of the High Court. The Bihar legislature had no power to enact the Bihar Act with respect to the slaughter or buffalo of all ages and calves and the provisions Of the Bihar Act were not valid.

The respondent company, a public limited company, was incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, with its registered office at Nagpur. The Company was incorporated under section 3 of the Indian Companies (Acquisition and Development) Act, 1956, with its objects and purposes, for the purpose of carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling of electrical energy. The Company, a public company, was formed under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1956. The Company had its registered office in Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh, its Manager and Assistant Manager. The Company 's name and ticket number were not mentioned in the departmental muster. The respondent company, however, filed a suit against the Company for wrongful dismissal and damages for wrongful dismissal. The Company resisted the suit on the ground that the Standing Orders did not apply to the respondent and the remedy of the respondent was to sue the Company in damages for wrongful termination. The trial court held that the respondent was a 'employee ' within the meaning of the Standing Orders and was not entitled to sue the company in damages for the wrongful dismissal. On appeal the High Court held that the Standing Order did not apply and the respondent was not a 'employee as defined for the Standing Orders. The High Court held in favour of the respondent. On appeal by special leave, Held, that the Standing orders applied to the respondent, and his service had been terminated in accordance with Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Order No, Standing Order No., Standing Order No.; Standing Order No; Standing Order No: Standing Order No.(e) of standing Order No. Standing Order No.' Standing Order No '. Standing Order ' No. (f) of Standing Orders No. (g) of Standing order No. (h) of Standing No. (i) of Standing Standing Order No,. (g) was not applicable to the respondent. The respondent was not an 'employee ' as defined for Standing Orders No, Standing Orders No., Standing Orders No.; Standing Orders No; Standing Orders No.(h) of standing Orders No. 1, Standing Order (g) did not apply. The respondent, therefore, was not a "employee" within the meaning Of the Standing Orders No,. 1, Standing Orders. No. (j) of Standing orders No. (k) of Standing Rules No. (l) of Standing Regulations No. (m) of Standing Rule No. (n) of Standing. Standing Orders No . The respondent was a "employee " within the meaningof the Central Act and an "employee" as defined in the Standing Orders, and the mere fact of employment in the office, Mains Department, Stores, Power House or Receiving Station of the Company was not enough to make a person so employed an 'employee within the meaning thereof. The respondent had no ticket in the departmental work. The respondent did not fulfil the necessary condition of having his name and ticket numbers included in the departmental ' muster. The High court, therefore, erred in holding that the inclusion of the name and ticket No. in the departmental " muster was an essential characteristic of an employee. The respondent 's case was that the respondent had committed a breach of the statutory provisions in section 30 of the local Act in the sense that no Standing Orders had been made in respect of the respondent and his service has been terminated in contravention of Standing Order. The respondent could not, therefore, be said to have committed a breach in terms of Standing Order Nos.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. It was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling steel products. The Company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956. The Company had its own establishment in the year 1961 and it went into production in the year 1964. The Company claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965. The workmen claimed bonus at a minimum rate prescribed by the Payment of bonus Act, 1965, and claimed bonus at that minimum rate. The workmen contended that the Company was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until this Project itself earned profits, so that exemption could not be granted to this company in respect of payment of bonus under section 16 of the Act. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project was a separate Establishment in respect of whom separate balance sheets were maintained, and that the point raised had to be decided on the basis of consolidated profits of all the units. The Tribunal, however, held that alloys Project was a distinct establishment in respect whereof separate balance sheets, profit and loss account and profit statements were maintained, that no bonus could be granted to the Company in respect of payments of bonus under the Payment Of Bonus Act, 1966. The Tribunal also held that all theoy Steel Project could not be treated as a separate establishment for purposes of section 16 of Act, and that, therefore, the claim of the workmen was resisted by the Company on the ground that the Company had not been treated as a new establishment for purposes Of section 16 of . The Tribunal held, that alloy steel Project was a part of the Hindustan Steel Ltd. and could not be regarded as a separate Establishment for purposes of Section 16 of the . The Tribunal, therefore, held that the Company itself was an establishment which had been in existence for a long period and had been in operation for a long time and had been functioning for all the units on the basis thereof, and consequently, the point raised by the workmen was disallowed. The Tribunal further held that all theseoy Steel Project would be treated as part of the same establishment for purposes for purposes of computation of bonus under Section 16 of Act. The Company appealed to this Court. HELD : The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that merely because alloy Steel Projects was owned, controlled and managed by Hindustan Steel Ltd., it had to be treated as parts of one single establishment for purposes, of computation of the bonus under the Act. [682 C] The Tribunal went wholly wrong in holding, that merely because Alloy Steel Project is owned, controlled or managed by Hindustan steel Ltd., it has to be treated a separate establishment, or is to be treated separately for the purpose of computation of Bonus under the Act, but the proviso to sub section (2) of section 16 does not stand in the way of this claim, because, alloy Steel project is owned, managed and controlled by one single Company and managed by one single company and managed by another single Company and, therefore, no bonus was paid in any year to the employees of all the Units on the basis Of consolidated profits of each unit.
