[683 D E] The proviso to sub s. (2) does not stand the way of the claim, because there is no evidence at all that in any year, after alloy Steel projects were set up bonus was paid to the employees. The proviso to subsection (2) is not applicable in view of the provision contained in section 1, sub section (1) of section 6 of the Act, and the proviso to that sub section does not stand on the way of that claim.

The appellant, a sugar manufacturing company, was manufacturing sugar from sugarcane juice. The appellant, a company, was carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar from the sugarcane juice and was manufacturing sugar in the same area. The appellant was manufacturing sugar at the factory premises of the respondent company. The respondent company was manufacturing sugar on the basis of water consumed by it. The appellant company was manufacturing sugarcane juice from sugarcane juices. The respondent Company was manufacturing sugar for the purpose of manufacturing sugar. The appellant 's factory was closed by the respondent company on the ground that the sugar manufacturing industry would come within Entry 15 of Schedule I to the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The High court held that the sugar industry would come under Entry 15 of the Schedule I to The Cess Act, 1976 and that the sugar manufactured by the respondent Company was not an industry within the meaning of Entry 15 of List I of Schedule I. The High Cou rt held that the appellant was not an 'industry ' within the meaning Of Entry 15 of list I to the Cess Act, and that the appellant 's sugar manufacturing industry did not come within Entry 45 of Schedule I of the Cess Act. The High Courts dismissed the writ peti tion. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sugar produced by the respondent was not an "industry" within the meaning and Entry 15 of Sch. I to the cess Act. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'vegetable ' in Entry 15 of schedule I to the Tax Act is used in the sense in which the word 'veliable ' is used in Entry 15. The word vegetable in Entry 15 is used in contradistinction to vegetable. The word "vegetable" in Entry 15 has to be understood in common parlance and it must be given its popular sense that sense which people conversant with the subject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [517C D] 2. The word `vegetable product ' means of or made or of product out of vegetable. The term vegetable in Entry15 is used in connection with the sense in Which the word 'ves it. The word is used in relation to vegetable products. The word, vegetable in Entry 16 is used in contrast to vegetable products and vegetable products. In the context in which the term 'vegetables ' is used, it has to be construed as understood in common sense and it must mean that vegetable products are not understood in common terminology. [518D E] 3. The word edible in Entry 15 in Schedule I is used in different senses and it has a wider amplitude. The word Vegetable in Entry 15, therefore, comes within Entry 15. [519F] 4. The word oil is used in entry 15 in contradistinction to oil. The word crude oil is used for the purpose and purpose of the statute in which it is occurring and to the fitness of the thing to the matter to the statute. In the instant case, the word vegetable in entry 15 is used for purposes and vegetables. The word taste is used in respect of vegetable products. It is used in a sense to mean that vegetable product means of or is made or of the product out of the vegetable product. The word refined is used in common parlance. The word botanic meaning is used in its ordinary sense in which people conversantwith the subject matter of the statute are dealing with. The word in vegetable product means a product of or made out of vegetable product. [520G H] 5. The word fruit product means a commodity of or made of or made from vegetable product. It is a commodity of food. It is not a commodity of vegetable product but a commodity of fruit. It is an article of food.

The respondent landlord filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant on the ground that he required the premises for the purpose of carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller rejected the application. The High Court, in revision, held that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the practice was not business in the sense of a profession of an advocate and that the tenancy was not such as could be split up. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression business occurring in Section 10(1)(a)(iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice of a profession. The word 'business ' in the context of the statute in which it occurs in other statutes or in a manner alien to the context of other statutes or the in a manner applicable to the context. [14D E] 2. The word "business" in the context in which it occur in the statute in question is used in the wider sense so as not to include any profession. [14E] 3. The word business occurring in the Andhra Pradesh Act broadly classified buildings into residential and non residential buildings, the landlord bona fide proposes to commence. The word used in the Andhra Act is used in wide sense so that as to include any professional. The word in the context is used in different statutes or in different contexts to include any professions. [14F] 4. The word `business ' in Section 10 (3) (b) (iii), is used in an wide sense so to include the practices of a profession and it plainly includes the practice of profession of an Advocates. [14G] 5. The word, business ' in the definition of the word 'business" in Section 10 of the Andhra Act includes the practice or profession of an advocates. [14H] 6. The word is used in Section 10. The word must be interpreted in the context and the statute in a wide and liberal sense so as t he word may have been used in a wider sense so that the word may have reference to the provisions of the Constitution or other statutes where the expression is used cannot be of any assistance in determining its meaning in Section 10.(3)(a)(iv) only.

The respondent was a debtor to the respondent for the approximate sum of Rs. 4,00,000. The respondent deposited a sum of Rs, 4,00000 in the deposit account of the appellant with the appellant. The respondent filed the suit on 16 May, 1953 against the appellant for the recovery of Rs.4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The respondent contended that the appellant was not liable to pay the amount of Rs. 3,00,500 as a banker and that the suit was barred by time. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appellant had not proved that the amount was deposited under an agreement and that it was not a case of deposit of the sum of Rs 4,00.000 and that the respondent was not liable for the deposit. The High court, however, held that the suit had been barred by time and that the appellant could not be allowed to withdraw the deposit on demand. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant 's case was covered by the award. The High Courts were right in holding, that the appellant did not prove that the amount deposited under an arbitration agreement was not covered by the arbitration agreement. [575 C] (ii) The High Courts had erred in holding that there was a demand for a part of the amount in the year 1943 for a part. The fact that the appellant paid the amount of the respondent with the traders was not sufficient to make the payment of the dues of the respondent. [575 D] (iii) The fact that in the year 1942 the respondent was paying the amount of money to the traders was immaterial. The fact of the transaction between the appellant and the respondent was that the appellant gave the use of the sum. The fact, however, that the respondent had to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills was immaterial. [575 E] (iv) The fact of payment of Rs. 2,00, 000 to the appellant by the respondent to the appellant was immaterial. It was not a question of the deposit of the amount of a banker and the appellant was liable to pay it. [575 G] (v) The fact, that the transaction was between the appellant, the respondent and Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mill, that the payment of Rs 4.00,000 was debited to India Supplies on the one hand and the appellant had to pay it to the traders, was immaterial. There was no question of the appellant giving the loan to the respondent. The fact was that the respondent paid the amount to the traders and the appellant did pay it to them. [575 A] (vi) The fact was not a ground for the appellant giving loan to the traders. The fact did not show that the appellant made payment of the amount to them. The fact showed that the appellant deposited the amount with the traders. [575 B] (vii) The fact showed the appellant not to pay the amounts of the respondent to them. It was a case of an ordinary loan of Rs. 5,00,00. The respondent was not bound to pay the money to the appellant. [575 F] (viii) The fact did show that the respondent made payment of Rs 2,00.00, 000. The fact however showed that the respondent did not pay the amount to him. The fact also showed that the payment was made to the traders in the year 1944.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, Department of Finance, Ministry of Revenue, Ministry of Home, Department of Personnel, Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Personnel, Government of India. The petitioner made an application to this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution for his release on the ground that the period of parole from May 15, 1986 to February 28, 1987 could not be added to the maximum period of imprison ment of the detenu Shital Kumar for one year as specified in the order of Detention. The petitioner contended that the period from May 15 1986 to February 27, 1987 could be added to his maximum period of incarcera tion of the detenu, Shital Kumar, and that the order of detention was illegal and invalid. The respondents contended that the petitioner had a strong prima facie case on merits and that the detention order was liable to be quashed. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of detention is liable to be set aside. The detaining authority was aware of the fact that the petitioner was already in custody and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his detention was necessary for preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The detaining author ity had a strong case on merits but he was very keen to have the question of exclusion of the parole period decided since it arose squarely in this case. [845G H] 2. The detaining authorities were aware of the facts that the petitioner is already in custody, the order of his detention became necessary. The detaining autho cient material to show that the detaining authority was conscious of the fact, that the petitioner, was aware of it, yet he was Sub jectivelyatisfied that his detention is imminent and the order of re spect of which he may be granted bail may not in all circumstances entitle an authority to direct preventive detention. [846A B] 3. The detaining Authority was aware of that the petitioner 's detention was imminent and the detention order of detention became necessary for putting him back in jail. The detaining Authorities were aware of this fact that the detenu was already in detention and yet he had been remanded to the judicial custody on the 27th of February, 1986. [847C D] 4. The detaining Authori ty was aware of this position and did not dispute the fact that he was already in jail for a period of one year as provided in the order. The fact that the detaining authori ty was unaware of the fact when the order was made, yet he had a strong reason to have the issue of exclusion of parole period decided. [848E F] 5. The detaining aut hority was aware of its fact that the detenue was already in judicial custody and yet the order of release was necessary for putting the detenu back in jail, and that he was not aware of the proceedings in the Court and did not contest the fact that his detention became imperative. [849G H] 6.

The petitioners were working as casual labourers in the Telecom Department of the Union of India. They were engaged in digging, carrying and other similar types of work. The petitioners were engaged in excavation, carrying and allied loads and other similar type of work. They were employed as casual labourers, helpers, peons etc. and were mostly engaged in digging and carrying other similar types. The petitioners, who were working for the last ten years as casual labourers were given the benefits of increments, pension, leave, gratuity etc. which were enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. The petitioners filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the said orders. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labour and are not being regularly employed, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. Dismissing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioners belong to category of casual labourers and are not regularly employed, They are not being employed, they cannot be denied the same privileges as the regular employees of the Telecom Department. [602B] 2. The petitioners are not being directly employed, they were not being regularly recruited. They are not entitled for the same privileges, which the regular workmen are enjoying. [603C] 3. The petitioners belonged to the category in which they have been working for more than six months. They are being paid wages to the regular employees in accordance with the job content of corresponding regular posts in scales of Rs.210 and Rs.260. The petitioners have been working continuously for more than 6 months. The petitioners do not fall within the category of Casual Labour and are not be regularly employed, but are being regularly employed. The petitioners cannot be denied their same privileges which they are enjoying. The petitioners also do not fall under the category of temporary employees. [604D E] 4. The petitioners in the writ petitions are not being paid wages and other benefits as are being paid to the regular workers of the Telecom department. The petitioners belongs to the category referred to above in the Postal and Telegraphs Department at the rates equivalent to the minimum pay in the pay scales of semi skilled/skilled labour. The petitioners belonging to the various categories of employees referred to above are not entitled the same privileges. [605E F] 5. The petitioners ' claim that they belong to the categories of casual labourers who have been continuously working for more a period of 5 years in the Posts and Telegraphs department at the rates equal to 1/30th of the minimum of the pay scale of semi skilled (Rs.260 350) as the case may be and that there should not be any variation in the respective job con tent. 12. The petitioners claim that since the Petitioners belong to the class of casual labourers, they are being regularly appointed, they are entitled to the similar privileges which the petitioners are enjoying. They are also entitled to the privileges which the permanent employees are enjoying, and they are being paid the same privileges and which the regular workers are enjoying.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1950 52 and 1952 53. The Income tax Officer, however, issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Act on January 5, 1950, to the assessee, stating that the assessment was completed before March 31, 1950, and that the notice was not issued within the time fixed by the notice. The assessee filed a return on January 5. 1950, and the Income tax Officer issued a notice on January 5 1950, under section 22 (3) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, to the effect that the assessee had submitted a return under section 22, and that he was entitled to make a " voluntary return " on the date he did, and that, in any event, the assessment was not barred by limitation. The assessee contended that the notice under section 34(3) was not available in this case, and that since the return was filed within the time prescribed by the notice, the Department should have proceeded under section 23(4) to a "best judgment assessment" and that the Department should not have issued a notice unders. 22(2), and that the department should have proceeded to issue a notice under s. 22(3) within the assessment year and if no return was made within the time specified by the notice the Department should had proceeded under section 22. Held, that the notice issued under section 22 was not available to the assessee and the assessee was not entitled to make the " voluntary return" under section 24(3) of that Act. The notice could be issued only after a return was filed under section 22 and not after a return had been filed. The notice under section 24 was not available when the return was made. The notice was not a return of income. The notice issued under s.22(3) could not be treated as a return under s.24(3) and consequently the return in answer to a notice under that section could not be regarded as a return of taxable income.

The respondent State of Maharashtra issued a notification dated 23.8.1983 inviting applications for appointment of members of the Board of Directors of the Reserve Bank of India. The respondent State of Bombay issued a notification on 23.8,1983 inviting applications from the eligible candidates for appointment to the Board of directors of the Reserve bank of India. In the notification, the respondent State of Gujarat made a proposal to the Central Government for the constitution of the Board. The Central Government, after consultation with the Reserve Bank, made the Scheme. The respondent, a company, was appointed by the Central Government from amongst the employees of the nationalised bank, who were workmen, to be appointed by the Board of the Directors of the respondent State. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the ReserveBank that the Act and the Scheme were ultra vires the Act and that the Scheme was ultra vires the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The scheme was ultra vires and void. The scheme was not ultra vires the provisions of the Act and was, therefore, void. [857F] 1.2 The scheme was framed by the Central Govern ment in consultation with the State Bank of India and the Scheme was not ultravi sive. The scheme, therefore, was ultra vires. [858F] 1.(a) The scheme was in effect a nomination of the employees of nationalised bank, which was in effect an independent agency of the Reserve. The scheme could not be said to be ultra vires. The scheme did not contain any provision for the nomination of the members of the board of directors. The scheme had been framed by the Reserve Bank in consultation with Reserve Bank of lndia. The scheme contained a provision for the constitution and the nomination of members of Board of Directors. The scheme provided for the constitution, nomination and nomination of members. The scheme contemplated the nomination of persons from amongst the members of Board. The scheme also provided for nomination of members by nomination of the Board and the nomination was to be made by the Central Govt. from amongst the names of three employees furnished by the representative Union of workmen or Association of workmen. The scheme further provided that the nomination of a person from amongst the representatives of the employees furnished by one of the employees, shall be made by nomination of one person out of the panel furnished by the representatives of employees. The scheme provides for nomination of persons, who are not workmen, to the Board. [859G H] 1.(b) The scheme, however, does not contain any provisions for nomination of the representatives of non workmen, as the case may be, and the scheme does not contain provisions for nomination. The scheme is not intended to be exhaustive of all employees. The Scheme is not intended for the purpose of giving the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. The scheme does not contemplate nomination of the non workmen, and the Scheme does not contemplate any nomination of the nominees of the employees. [860H; 861A] 2.(c) The scheme is in the nature of a scheme for the constitution or nomination of members, and it is not intended merely to give the maximum scope of the scheme. The scheme may be framed by the Board in consultation with it. The scheme must be read in the light of the scheme and the scheme. [861D] 3.(d) The scheme must, therefore, be read in its entirety and the scheme must be construed in its entirety. [862E] 4.(e) The scheme should be read in a manner which would be consistent with the scheme.

The respondent was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 1,000/ on the appellant. The respondent challenged the imposition of the penalties before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the imposition of penalties and directed the recovery of the penalty. The respondent appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the Tribunal had the power to stay the recovery proceedings as also the collection of the penalties. The Tribunal also held that the Appellate Tribunal had the jurisdiction to stay the proceedings as also to the collection of penalties. The High Court held that the tribunal had the power under the relevant provisions of the Income tax Act, 1961 to stay the collection of penalty. The High court held that the order of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal was not a stay. The High, Court, however, held that the appellate Tribunal had the powers to stay the Recovery proceedings and on what conditions and conditions the stay should be made, quashed the recovery proceedings and directed the Recovery Officer to stay the execution proceedings. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Appellate Tribunal must be held to have the power to grant stay as incidental or ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner or the Appellate Tribunal is given the power to suspend the recovery proceedings or penalties payable by or imposed on the assessees as a matter of practice prevailing in the department. [69E F] (2) The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner is not given the power of stay by the Tribunal. The Appellate Tribu nal is not given to the Appellate Assistant Commissi sioner. The Appellate Authority is given the powers to pass interim orders as incidental or incidental to its appellate jurisdic tion. [69F] (3) The Appellate Tribun nal is entitled to stay the operation of the recovery proceedings pending before the Appellate Tribunal under section 220(6) of the Act. [69G] (4) The Appellate Authority must be held not to have the powers of granting stay as incidental ancillary or ancillary to the appellate jurisdiction.

The respondent was charged under section 7 of the Police Act with remissness in the discharge of his duty and unfitness for the same. The trial was conducted by the Superintendent of Police and the respondent was placed under suspension and on August 18, 1953, he was placed under the suspension and on September 12, 1953, the District Magistrate sent an endorsement to the Superintendent of police to the effect that the respondent had also received such complaints and that his general reputation for integrity was not good, but that his general integrity was not satisfactory. The respondent was charged with the offence of dishonesty, corruption and misbehaviour in that he had received such complaints. The respondent challenged the order of dismissal on the ground that the District Magistrate had found substantial complaints against the integrity of the respondent and that his integrity was not bad, but that the Superintendent of the Police had no power to dismiss him, since an order in such circumstances could only be made by a police officer in senior rank to a Superintendent; and that the District Superintendent had no power under the statutory power to dismiss the respondent. Held, that the order of the District Magistrate was not in any way affected by the order of his dismissal. The order of dismissal was not in the nature of administrative directions but was merely directory in nature and inasmuch as no prejudice was caused to the respondent, the order of discharge was invalid. The District Magistrate was the only step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent in regard whereto the magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage. The District Superintendent of Police was the only authority competent to dismiss the Respondent. The District Collector was the only competent authority to dismiss the appellant. The District Inspector of Police was not competent to dismiss him. The District Deputy Superintendent of Police had no jurisdiction to proceed with a departmental trial without complying with the provisions of subparagraph (1) of para 486 of the Police Regulations. The District Officer was not competent under the statutory powers conferred upon the Superintendent ofPolice to make an enquiry into the conduct of the respondent. The District Government had no power in the matter to dismiss the respondents. The District officer was not competent in the matter of the departmental trial. The District Judge was not competent, under the statutory authority to dismiss a respondent. The order was not in accordance with the provisions Of para 486 of Police Regulations.

The appellant was appointed as a Specialists Grade II in the Central Government Health Service on February 8, 1971. He was promoted to supertime grade II on February 8. 1971. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the promotion of the appellant to supertime Grade II on February 9, 1971. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the promotion of one post from unspecified specialists Grade ' posts in supertime grade I was converted into a specified post by conversion of one post amongst specialists grade ' posts in the supertime grade ' grade II and that the post could only be filled in, in accordance with the relevant rule; (ii) the promotion was not a promotion from which promotion was to be given; (iii) the promotion to supertime scale II was not a selection post; (iv) the promotion could only be made by promotion from amongst those belonging to Specialists ' grade ' grade ' and the post could be filled in only by promotion from those belonging to specialists ' grade and (v) the promotion did not amount to a promotion from the date on which the appellant was promoted to the supertime scale. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The appellant was fully qualified for promotion to super time grade II because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists ' Grade ' posts. He was not qualified for promotion from the post of Director of Health Services, Manipur, but the post was not unqualified for the post of the Director of Health Service, Manipur. [53G H] 1.2. The appellant had not put him in 8 years ' service in the post vacated by him which was deemed to have fallen vacant in September 1971 from which date he claims as being eligible for promotion to Supertime Grade II. [53H] 1.3. The appellant is fully qualified for the post which was deemed vacant in September, 1971 from which he claims as having been eligible for promotion from that date. [53A] 1.4. The appellant has been fully qualified for being promoted to super time scale II. He was, therefore, not entitled to be considered for the post in which he claims. [53C] 1.5. The appellant, therefore, was fully qualified to be promoted to super Time grade II because his refusal to accept promotion at Simla appellant was never superseded by any one junior to him in his speciality. [53D] 1.6. The appellant cannot be said to have been fully qualified to the post which he claims to super time Scale II because he was not qualified to be appointed to supertime grades II because he has not put in a specified post to which one who is on top of the general seniority list in Specialists ' Grade. [53F] 1.7. The appellant could not be said to be fully qualified for super time scale I because he was fully qualified and, therefore, he must be considered eligible for promotion. [53E] 1.8. The appellant did not have put in 8 year ' service in that grade. He was fully qualified in the post which is deemed to have been filled in by him. He was also not offered to be considered in the speciality in which the post was created. [53B] 1.9. The appellant would be the Head of the Department and would continue to be in supertime scale I. [53 F] 1.10. The appellant should be considered for promotion from super time scale III to supertime Scale II. [54G] 1.11.

The appellants were tenants of certain lands in the State of Punjab. The appellants were tenants in the said lands. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the provisions of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 1953) and the High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants contended that the land inherited by them and later transferred to their sons and wife were not hit by section 10A and section 19B of the Act. The High Court dismissed their writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the land owned by the appellants was not hit by the ceiling set up by section 10 A of the Act and that the appellants were not hit on section 10A. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the surplus pool will be adversely affected if gifts and other transfers which will skim off were to be affected if gifts or other transfers which would skim off are to be affected by the interdict of section 10 A. [616C D] The object of the Act is to provide for the acquisition of land by the State Government for utilization under section 10A of the Act, and the object of the legislation is to provide a machinery for the acquisition and disposal of surplus area. [617D] The object is to provide machinery for the disposal of surplus areas. The object is not to provide for any surplus area. The language of the section is plain and unambiguous. The language is plain and clear. The language used in the section is clear and unambiguous. [618E F] The object sought to be achieved is to provide an machinery for the transfer of surplus area to the son or the son or daughter of the tenant so settled. The language in the section does not indicate that the surplus area is to be transferred to the son of the tenant. The language does not indicate any intention to transfer the surplus area to his son or daughter. The language indicates that the surplus land is to be retained. The language clearly indicates that the transfer of the surplus area will not be affected by any interdict of section. [619F G] The language of section 19B is plain and simple. The language requires that the surplus surplus pool will not be transferred to any son or daughter or the son of a tenant. The words "any person" in section 19B are clear and unambiguous and are intended to give some time to the heir, to ascertain the assets he has inherited, make the choice of his 'reserved area which he likes to keep and make the necessary declaration. The language has to be read in the context of the scheme of the Act which is consistent with the scheme of section 19 B. [620D E] The object in the section was to provide for a machinery for disposal of surplus land acquired by the State. The language was clear and unambiguous that the surplus was to be distributed among the heirs of the tenants. The language did not indicate that any one held in excess of the permissible area and since by the gift to the son, the son or son of a person was situated in more than one patwar circle, he had only lands within permissible limits. The language could only be that though in the hands of the propositus, it was surplus land, if among the heirs it was surplus, it was not, then their transfers will not be effected by the interdict.

The plaintiffs claimed the other estate of Amarshah in devisees under the will of Amarshha. The defendants contended that the geneal table set up by the plaintiffs represented the true relationship between the descendants of Gangashah and that the geninal table set up was incorrect, that by the order of the Governor of Madhya Pradesh dated November 9, 1951, the Zamindari was conferred upon the plaintiffs, that the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act, 1 of 1951, had become binding and conclusive against the plaintiffs because no suit was filed by the plaintiffs against the defendants. The High Court held that the plaintiffs were entitled to receive compensation in respect of the Malguzars lands and that the decision was binding upon the plaintiffs. The High court held that the decision in Malguzart lands was not binding on the plaintiffs because the decision of Governor in 1950 declaring Dayaram to be the successor on the death of Amarshashah was not binding and that the plaintiffs had no right or title upon the Zamindari. The High, Court, however, held that the suit was not barred by the decision of this Court in Malguza Land and that the suit had become binding on the defendants. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The decision of the Governor in 1950 declared Dayaram to be a successor on the demise of Amarshih was not a binding decision of the Government. The decision of this court in Malguja Land was not binding upon the defendants because the decision in the Malguza land was not binding. [319 B] (ii) The decision in Mal Guzart lands did not affect the rights of the plaintiffs on the death or of Amarshanh. The decision in theMalguzart land was not conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date. [320 C] (iii) The decision was binding on the plaintiff and the plaintiffs. [321 D] (iv) The decision did not affect rights of the defendants on the death, or of Amarha. The plaintiffs were entitled under the will set up by them to the estate devised in their favour by Amarsha. The decision was not binding as the plaintiffs had not filed any suit against the defendants because no suit had been filed against them. [322 E] (v) The decision could not be reviewed in a suit instituted more than six months after that date and if no suit was instituted, the order became final and conclusive. [323 E] (vi) The decision to set up by Amarshh was not conclusive. [322 G] (vii) The decision on the question of the right to the estate created by the operation of section 3 was not binding because the decision was not final and conclusive and could be reopened in the suit filed more over six years after the date. [322 C] (viii) The decision must be made conclusive and can be reopened in proceedings instituted more than 6 years after that day.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession of the premises on the ground that the respondent was not entitled to raise a dispute as to standard rent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the provisions contained in section 12(3)(a) of the Act do not apply to the suit, but that the suit was governed by the provisions contained therein. The High court took the view that the provisions of section 12(2) (a) of Act do not come into operation to the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the provisions in section 12 (3)(a), (b) and (c) of the Bombay High Court Act do not cover the suit. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was in error in holding that the dispute in section 12 was a dispute within the meaning of section 12 (1) (a). [682 B] (2) The High court was in error. The view taken by the Bombay High court in Ambalal 's case was that the dispute was governed by section 12(1)(a) and (b) of the said Act and would take the suit out of the provisions of that sub section. [682 C] (3) The latest point of time when according to Ambalal was the date of service of notice under section 12(4) (a), the operation of section 12 of the Act was the expiry of one month from the date of the service of the notice. [683 D] (4) The latest points of time when the notice was served under section 12 (2) (b) would be excluded. [684 E] (5) The latest position of time when under section 12 of Act the tenant can claim protection from the operation of Section 12(3) (a); and (6) The latest date of service under section 12 is the expiry of the one month from date of service. [685 E] (6) In the instant case, the notice was issued under section 12 and the respondent was entitled to raise the dispute. [686 E] (7) The High Courts in Amballa 's case (supra) held that the dispute as to the standard rent must be raised within one month of the notice of the service. The view of the Bombay and Gujarat High Court in Amballi 's case is not correct. [687 E] (8) The Bombay High Court in the decision Ambalal vs Chimanlal Nagindas, [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869, held that the view taken by Bombay High Court was correct.

The respondent company was a director of the respondent company. The respondent company was incorporated in the year 1939. The respondent was a director in the respondent company and was appointed as a director of a company. The company was a private limited company. The appellant was a director. The respondent, who was the managing director of the company, was appointed a director of its company. The Income tax Officer held that the directors of the respondent Company had a controlling interest in the respondent 's shares and had no beneficial interest in the shares held by it in the respondent. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the respondent company had a controlling interests in the respondent and, therefore, the directors of it were not liable to be taxed under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act. The Appellate Tribunal, however, answered the question in the affirmative. The High Court answered the question against the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The directors of the company in fact held the majority of the shares as trustees and, as such, had no beneficial interests in the shares. The controlling interest remained vested in the Aluminium Ltd. and was at no time vested in the respondent Company. The controlling interests remained vested in them, though as between them and their beneficiaries, the shareholders and the right to vote were vested in them. [191 D] (ii) The directors, who hold the majority of shares as trustees, are the directors of a company and are the registered in the name of the Aluminium Ltd., and are the shareholders, and as such, have "a controlling interest" in the respondent, and as between them, they cannot be said to have "a Controlling interest" in them as long as their authority is not revoked, as long as his authority is not revocation, as long his authority is neither revoked nor is he bound to cast the votes according to the directions of his principals. [191 E] (iii) The directors are not liable to pay the costs of the appellant in this Court and is at no time vest in the Aluminium Limited.

The respondent was appointed as an Assistant Director of the Electricity Board on 30th December, 1966. He was promoted to the post of Assistant Director on 30th January, 1970. He was denied promotion on the ground that he had not passed the examination. The Board by its resolution dated 19th May, 1969 decided to promote him to the post with effect from that date. The respondent challenged the said resolution before the High Court. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition and quashed the resolution. The Board filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. The Board appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The resolution of the Board dated 19th April, 1969 was not relaxed by amending the Regulations. The passing of the S.A.S. Examination was not insisted upon. The Resolution did not have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed by the Board under section 79(c) of the Act. The passing o f the resolution by the Board was not relaxed. The passing or passing of the resolution by a subsequent Resolution was not insisted on. [509G H] The Resolution did indicate that the allottees were not required to pass the Departmental Exami nation and the Kannada language test. The Resolution required the passing of the Departmental Exam cation test as a consequence of the judgment of the High Court cannot be upheld as the binding nature of the Regulations passed by the board under section 79 (c) has not been insisted upon.

The petitioner 's son Suman Behera was taken from his home in police custody at about 8 a.m. on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, a Sub Inspector of Police. He was taken from the home in police remand custody at about 9.00 a.m., on 1.11.1987 by the respondent No. 6, SaratChandra Barik. The petitioner 's mother, the mother of Suman Behera, was taken from her home in police detention at about 8.00 a., on 1 12.12.87 by respondent No 6, Sarats Chandra Barik. She was taken from home in police force at about 8 p.m. and was taken to a hospital at about 8 P.m. The petitioner, who was a Sub Inspector, was taken to the hospital at about 9 p.m., and was taken from there. The petitioner was taken to hospital at about 10 p.m, and was taken in police custody. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court, which was dismissed. The petitioner appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner ' son Suman Beher, aged about 22 years, in police custody, at about 8p.m. was taken to police custody at around 8 p.M. on 1 12th December, 1987 by respondent No6, Sarats Chand Barik, and his sustaining the injuries in a train accident was not acceptable. The relief of monetary compensation as exemplary damages, in proceedings under Article 32 or 226 of the Constitution, is a remedy available in public law based on strict liability for contravention of fundamental rights to which the principle of sovereign immunity does not apply, even though it may be available as a defence in public law. [606B C] 1.2 The payment of compensation in this proceeding for violation of fundamental rights, in the larger sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends ' under the public law for damages under the public duty to protect the fundamental rights of the citizen, notwithstanding the right of the citizen to the remedy by way of a civil suit or criminal proceedings. of course, relief in exercise of its jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 of the constitution seeking enforcement or protection of fundamental rights is claimed by resort to the remedy in public law under the Constitution. [607C D] 1.3 The payment of the compensation in this proceedings is in the nature of superannpellary damages awarded against the wrong doer for the breach of its public duty to safeguard the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The compensation is in the character of superannpendary damages awarded for breach of public duty, not protecting the fundamental rights. [608D] 1.4 The compensation in this case is in the manner of compensating the wrongdoer and fixing the liability for the public wrong on the State which has failed in its public duty, to protect the rights of the citizens, notwithstanding the rights available under the public Law. [609E] 1.5 The compensation in the instant case is in nature of superannupellary damage awarded against the wrongful doer for breach of its statutory duty to protect fundamental rights of citizens. [610F] 1.6 The compensation in these proceedings is in nature, of superannu pellary damages. The compensation in such cases is not to be understood, as it is generally understood in a civil action based on tort. [611D] 1(a) The compensation in a proceeding under Article 32 of the Constitution is a remedy provided in public law, based on strict responsibility for contravention of the fundamental rights to the citizen, irrespective of the right available to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under the public act.

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The petitioner filed a petition under article 32 of the Constitution in the High Court of Delhi for commutation of his sentence. The High Court rejected the petitions filed by the petitioner and the petitions filed in this Court were rejected by the President of India. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner was not entitled to interview the prisoners for commutation of their sentence to imprisonment for life. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right, nor does it confer any right on the Press, to have an unrestricted access to means of information. [1186F] 2. The right to means of any information through the medium of an interview of the two prisoners who are sentenced to death is not an exclusive right nor does it conferred any right on a Press unless in the first instance, the person sought to be interviewed, the interviews can be permitted only subject to the rules and regulations governing the interviews. [1187G] 3. The right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right to means any particular view, or opinion but is the right to mean any particular view. [1189G] 4. The right of an interview under clause (4) of rule 549(4) of the Manual for the Superintendence and administration of Jails, which is applicable to Delhi, provides that every prisoner under a sentence of death shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends, legal advisers and approved religious ministers. [1190G] 5. The petitioner has been asking permission to interview the prisoner. The petitioner should be allowed to interview the Prisoners as we are disposed to give to the petitioner in the main writ petition.

The appellant was the Receiver of the tea garden. The Receiver took possession of the estate on 22nd January, 1950. The Receiver filed a suit against the Receiver for recovery of the amount due under the mortgage. The Receiver contended that the Receiver was not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956. The Subordinate judge decreed the suit but the Subordinate Judge decreed it on May 31. 1956. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court which was dismissed on December 18, 1959. The appellant 's appeal to the Supreme Court was dismissed on January 20, 1960. The Subordinate Judges of the High Court transferred the suit to the court of the Subordinate Judge. The Subordinate Court transferred the mortgage suit to the Court of the Subordinate judge. The Subordinate court transferred the suit on January 20. The SubordinateJudge transferred the suit. The Subordinate judges of the High court transferred the mortgage to the court. The Subordinate District Judge transferred the suit for recovery of damages. The Subordinate Subordinate Judge decreed a suit on May 30, 1956. On appeal the Subordinate Judge held that the bond could be enforced only by or at the instance of the District Judge because "successor in office" would mean successor of the District judge because "sucessor in office would mean successor in office of the District Court because "suecessor in office", would mean successor. The Subordinate Courts decreed the suit. On appeal by special leave, the High Court held that the Subordinate Judge was entitled to exercise the same powers in the matter of enforcement of the bond as the District Judge himself. The Subordinate High Court held in favour of the Receiver. The Subordinate Division Bench of the High ' Court held that in the absence of the Receiver, the Receiver was entitled to the protection of the bond. The Subordinate. Judge held that in view of the provisions of section 150 of the Civil Procedure Code, the appellant was not answerable to the loss caused by the Receiver 's negligence in the performance of his duties. The Subordinate 'Court held that the appellant was liable to make good the loss caused. The Subordinate .Court further held that the Receiver ' was not answerable in respect of the loss caused and the Receiver ' liability was limited to the stock in trade, machinery and movables in the tea garden and to the factory premises and since the Receiver 'is not answerable for loss caused to him by the fire, the appellant would not be liable for the loss occasioned to the tea Garden by fire. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The Subordinate Judge was not entitled to exercise any of the powers in the matters of enforcement of a bond as the district judge himself. The surety bond was executed in and for the purposes of the particular proceedings which were pending before the District Judge. The surety bonds were executed in and For the purposes of that proceedings, a successor of the district judge. The surety Bond was executed in favour of "successors in office" and "succession in office" was a part of the proceedings pending before the district judge because " successor inoffice" would mean the successor of the State Judge. [360 E] The surety bond is executed in and on behalf of "succcessor in Office" and "Successor in offices" would mean successors in office of "suecession in office". [360 G] The surety Bond is executed in favour and for the purpose of the particular proceeding which were pending in the District Judge, but the Receiver owes no obligation in relation to the tea plantation. The surety is executed in the name of "suicessor in office". The surety bond has undoubtedly, to be construed strictly but it is impossible to accept the contention that the Receiver owed no duty or obligation in respect of tea garden.

The appellant, a dealer in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller, was assessed to sales tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat purchased by him during the period of the Order. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the Act on the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat to the Regional Controller. The appellant challenged the validity of the assessment on the ground that the sales made to the Regional Manager were not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the U. P. Sales Tax (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales tax Officer held that the turnover resulting therefrom sales to the Regional Director were not taxable because there was no sale within the meaning Of the U.p. Sales Tax. The appellant contended that the sales were not taxable as there was no 'sale ' within the meaningof the U. Pradesh Sales Tax Act. The Salestax Officer held that there was no taxable event of sale and that the turnover resulted from supplies of rice to the Regional Directorate. The appellant 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was dismissed. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that there was a contract between the appellant and the State pursuant to which the goods were sold within the meaning. of the U P. Sales tax Act. The State Government was of the opinion that it was necessary and expedient so to do for maintaining supplies of wheat and for securing equitable distribution and availability at fair prices Now, THEREFORE, in exercise of the powers conferred by clauses (e) and (f) of sub section (2) of section 3 of the UP. Sales tax (Levy) Act, 1959, the State Government was pleased to make the following order: "The State Government is of the opinion, that it is necessary and expedient to do for securing the supplies of wheat. The State Govt. may, by notification, declare that the turnover of wheat purchased or purchased by the dealer during the period the Order shall be deemed to be the sales turnover of the dealer. The State Governments may, by like notification, declare the turnover of the dealers to be the sale turnover of the goods. The State Gov ernment may, by a like notification, direct that the turnover shall be deemed not to be the turnover of a dealer. The notification is accordingly issued. The State of U.P., is directed to issue a notification to the effect that the turnover in question shall be deemed as taxable turnover. The State may also direct that the dealer shall pay the turnover tax on the turnover of sales effected during the period. The State shall also direct that in the event of failure to pay the tax the dealer shall be liable to pay the sales tax on the sales effected during that period. The dealer shall be entitled to take delivery of the wheat held in stock by him at the commencement of the Order until such time as the State Government otherwise directs. " The State Government, therefore, issued a notification to that effect. The appellant, a manufacturer of wheat, was directed to sell the wheat to the State Government. The State did not pay the tax. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of that notification. The High Court held that the sales effected to the Regional Sales Controller were not taxable. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court rightly held that the transactions of supply did not result in sales. The State was not entitled to take the delivery of the goods pursuant to the directions issued under cl. 5 of the Order and not pursuant to the direction issued under cl 5 of the order. [582 C] The State Government had no volition in the matter. The State had no volition to the matter. [583 D] The State of Uttar Pradesh, is directed to carry out the directions of the Controller and it had no volition.

The petitioner was convicted by the trial court for offences under sections 302, 201 and 201 IPC and sentenced to death. He was also convicted for offences under section 201 IPC and was sentenced to imprisonment for life. The petitioner challenged the order of his detention before the High Court which dismissed his petition. The petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution in this Court. The petitioner contended that the detention order was illegal as it was within three months of the date of detention and that the Advisory Board had no power to make the detention of the petitioner beyond three months. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of detention was illegal as the Advisory Board was not made within three months from the date of the second order of detention. The order was passed on August 7, 1986. The report of the Advisory Board is to be obtained within three months. The order is not a sufficient answer to say that the report of the advisory Board was not in existence to which a reference could be made under the Act and whose report could be obtained within 3 months. [10E F] 2. The report was not made by the Advisory Board within three months, but it was received within three months after the date of its report. The report could be produced within three months and it was not answer to say whether the report was obtained within three weeks. If the report was not obtained within three month, it is not answer to saying that the reference was made within three weeks, it is no answer to say, though not made within 3 months, it is a sufficient answer. [10F G] 3. The report is to be received within three weeks from the date on which its report is to he obtained. If the Advisory Board has reported within the period of three months, it was not answered to say that it is necessary to continue the detention of a person for a longer period than three months after its date on which it was made. [10H; 10A] 4. The report must be obtained within a period of three weeks after the date on whi ch the order of detention is made. If the representation made by the detenu is required to be disposed of within a stipulated period, it is to be made within three days. If the order of the advisory board is not made within the period specified, it is the duty of the detaining authority to consider the representation made and to pass a fresh order. If the opinion of the advisory committee is not received within three month it is not a proper answer to say the least that the procedural requirements of the Constitution and the statute have been complied with before the date of hearing and therefore, the detention becomes illegal notwithstanding that it is within three months before the date onwhich its report or beyond the period of 3 months after the detention becomes invalid. [10C D] 5. The report should be obtained within two months of the detention. If the reports of the advisory Committee are not received within the period stipulated, it is for the detaining authority, to consider whether the detention of such person is necessary to be continued. If the advisory board has reported within three months it is not answered to the say that the representation, though not filed within three months was disposed of before the hearing of the case. If the Report of the advisory body is to be taken within three months the detention becomes unlawful notwithstanding that it was within 3 months of the subsequent order of detention, the detention would be invalid notwithstanding that it has been within three months without the Advisory Board having reported within the time specified.

The respondent was the father of the petitioner. He was the father and the petitioner was the father. He was appointed as an arbitrator to resolve the disputes between the parties. The respondent filed an application under section 17 of the for setting aside the award.
