Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in dismissing the application in the manner it did. [527B] 2. The High Courts were right in dismissing an application in the circumstances of the case. The High court was right in rejecting the objections in the manner they did. [627C] 3. The High, Court was right, in dismissing the appli cation in the manner, it did. The High Curt was right in holding that the respondent was dead at the time the suit had been instituted or decree was passed or some other ground which could have the effect of rendering the court entirely lacking in jurisdiction in respect of the subject matter of the suit or over the parties to it. [528D] 4.

The respondent instituted a suit against the appellants on the ground that the appellants had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of section 2 (22) of the , and that the respondent had not received it. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the respondent was not an assignee within the meaning of section 2(22) of that Act and that the petition was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The respondent was not a sub mortgagee within the meaning Of section 2(21) of the Act. The words "all the rights of the original mortgagee are not assigned to the sub mortgagee" in section 2(23) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and the respondent 's decree must be taken to have been passed "in a suit to which this Act applies and which was not fully satisfied by January 1, 1939. [512 B] (ii) The words "any suit or proceeding instituted or instituted" in section 28 of the Code, in the context of section 2, are wide enough to include a suit or proceeding in execution for any of the purposes mentioned in clauses (a) or (b) of section 28. The words and that he had not received notice referred to therein in clause (b) or (c) of section 30 of the Code are wide enough and they are not intended to cover a suit or proceedings in execution for the purposes mentioned therein. [513 C D] (iii) The words and "all the right of the original mortgagor" in section 29 of the Code do not mean that an assignee of a mortgage debt is within the sub section (1) of section 36 of the Code. The words 'all the rights ' of the original mortgage are not assigned ' in section 28. [514 D] (iv) The words 'any suit or proceedings instituted or filed ' in a suit to Which this Act applies, are wide and they are intended to cover all proceedings in execution in a suit or in execution for a mortgage. The words are wide enough. The words do not mean merely the right of a person to recover the debt from the original mortgagor. The words in section 29 are wide enough, and they are capable of being understood in the sense in which they are used in the sense of a right to recover the amount from the original mortgagee. [515 E F] (v) The words are not wide enough to cover a case where the original mortgagee is in possession of a mortgage property. The words used in section 29, sub section (2) are wide enough in their amplitude to cover a mortgage of immovable property. The word 'any suit ' in section 29 is wide enough to mean a suit or a proceeding in execution. [516 E] (vi) The words used are wide enough not to cover a proceeding in a suit for the recovery of a loan advanced before or after the commencement of the Act but to include a proceeding in the execution for the recovery thereof other things. The words, however, are wide in their amplitude and they are susceptible of the same meaning as in section 2 (21) of that section. [517 E] (vii) The words in the section are wide enough so as to cover a claim for exemption from the mortgage. The word "any suit" in section 30 is wide enough and it is not necessary that the word "any" in section 32 should be construed in a wider sense.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his sons. The properties conveyed by the two deeds were executed without consideration or for the transfer of the properties conveyed by them to his concubine. The appellant filed a suit against his widow and sons for recovery of possession of the properties. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the transfers under exhibit A 1 and exhibit A 2 were not supported by any consideration by way of cash delivery or delivery of jewels. The High court also held that the transfer under exhibit A 2 was not supported by consideration by way Of cash delivery or deliver of jewels and that the transfers were by way of gifts. The High. Court also held that there was a disruption of the joint family and a severance of joint status between Venkatacharyulu and his sons, and that the subsequent severance of joint character in 1947 could not validate them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The transfer under exhibit 1 and exhibit B 2 were not vitiated by the disruption of the Joint family. The past cohabitation was the consideration for the subsequent promise to transfer the properties to her. The past lived cohabitation was not the object or the consideration for transfer of the property to her. In the alternative, the past cohabitation could not validate the transfers under Exs. A 1 and A 2. [517 D] (ii) The transfer was without consideration and was invalid. The past together cohabitation was a valuable consideration and Venkatacharyaiah was free to make a gift of his undivided interest in the coparcenary properties to his concabine. The past living together was the consideration. The past live cohabitation was therefore, free to make the gift of his divided interest in the joint family properties to his sons. [518 E] (iii) The past cohabitations were not validated by the disruption in 1947. The past wedlock was the consideration of past cohabitation. The past marriage was the consideration and not the consideration for a transfer under exhibit B 2. The past relationships were not validated. The past conjugal relations were not validated and the subsequent severance was the consideration to make the gifts.

The respondent, a company, was incorporated in the United Kingdom, and was incorporated in India. The respondent, a public limited company, was a company incorporated in the U.P. and was incorporated on 5th December, 1975. The respondent was a company registered under the Companies Act, 1956. The respondent company was incorporated in U.P., and was incorporated as a limited company. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on the ground that the award of interest was not made by the I.T.O. and that the respondent was not making the payment to the respondent. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the delay in payment of interest was occasioned by the fact that the respondent had made the requisite statement under section 226 (3) of Income Tax Act 1961, and that the delay was occasioned by a mistake of law. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The delay in making the requisite statement on oath under section 226 of the Income tax Act, 1961, in the present case, was after inordinate delay in making it involved the likelihood of exposing the L.I.C. to support its action of non payment to the assignee of the policies to whom the payment thereunder had to be made even according to the stand of the L. I.C. [517B C] 2. The delay was occasioned not because it involved the possibility of exposing the I.I.T. to support the action of nonpayment to the assignee. The delay, therefore, was occasioned by reason of the fact that it involved the risk of the L I.I.,C. [617D] 3. The delay caused in making the necessary statement under section 227(3) is not a mere delay in making of the requisite statement. The delay is occasioned by the reason that the delay is occasioned because of the fact of the delay. [618E F] 4. The delay of the payment of interest to the assignee is not a matter of doubt. The delay must be explained by the party who has made the requisite statements. [619F] 5. The delay has to be explained by showing that the delay has occasioned due to the negligence of the party who made the requisite Statement. [620D] 6. The delay may be explained by explaining the delay in making a statement on oath. [621D] 7. The delay can be explained by a party who has not made the requisite declaration under section 226. [622E] 8. The delay cannot be explained by any party who has failed to make the requisite statement in accordance with the provisions of section 226(1) of the Act. [623F] 9. The delay could be explained by giving a proper explanation. [624F] 10. The delay should be explained by way of a proper explanation and not by a mere delay. [724F] 11. The delay need not be explained by examining the person who made the statement. [625F] 12. The delay does not affect the merits of the case. [626G] 13. The delay had occasioned due to negligence of the respondent. [627A] 14. The delay did not affect the merit of the case and the delay was not explained.

The respondent was a member of the Madhya Pradesh Legislative Assembly. He was elected as a member of a Legislative Assembly. The respondent was elected as the member of the Legislative Assembly. On the question whether the period of limitation prescribed by the First Schedule to the Limitation Act for an appeal under section 116 A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, was applicable to the case of appeals preferred under section 116A of the Representation Of the People Act. HELD: (i) The first limb of sub section (2) of section 29 of the Act is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, that is, appeals or applications by any special or local law for which a period of limitation is prescribed in the First Schedule. The second limb of sub s.(2) of s. 29 is concerned only in proceedings of this type, that is for which a limitation of time is prescribed in that Schedule. The first limb is concerned only for proceedings of this nature, that is to say, appeals or application by any special, local or local law. [145 B C] (ii) The first part of sub section(2) of the Limitation Act, therefore, applies only to cases where the First Schedule prescribes a period of time for an appeal, or application by special or local laws. The second part of sub s. (2) will apply even to a case where the First schedule prescribes a period for which a suit, appeal or application by a special or local Law for which a time of limitation is provided in the First schedule. [145 C D] (iii) The first portion of sub section 2 of section 29 is concerned with proceedings of the nature that is to be considered and all the time of limitation prescribed for such an appeal, application or application by the special or local legislation. The second portion of sub s (2) is concerned only to proceedings of this sort. [145 D E] (iv) The first proviso to sub section (1) of section29 of the Act makes it clear that the period of three years prescribed for an appeal or application under a particular local law is of a kind different from that prescribed for an application or appeal by any special local law. The second proviso to sub s.(1) of s 29 is concerned merely with proceedings of that kind, that being a shorter period of limitation, the provisions of section 29(2) would not apply. [145 E F] (v) The first and the second limb of section 29 are concerned only with the proceedings of this particular kind, that was to say, appeal or an application by any general or local law, and that, therefore, cl. (2), of section 29, sub section (3) of the Act would not apply even to cases where, the First Schedule has not prescribed any period of limitation for such an application or application. [145 F G] (vi) The first clause of sub section 1 of section 29 does not apply to cases where a special or general law prescribes for any suit, appeal, or an application for any suit or appeal by special or general laws. The first clause does not apply even where the special law prescribes for such an appeals, or application or by any special law for which period of limitation was prescribed in the first schedule. [146 C] (vii) The second limb, of sub section 3 of section 29 applies only to proceedings which are within the period prescribed by the first schedule because it is enough if the special law prescribe for such an appel lant to an appeal or an appeal by any general law.

The appellant, a private operator, was directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriages in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986. The appellant, a public carrier, was directed by the District Magistrate to stop the buses at the bus stand fixed by the District Magis trate, Mathura. The appellant challenged the order of the District Magistrate, Mathura by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the District Magistrate had no power to fix any area as a bus stand under section 76 of the Act and that the place where the appellant and other bus operators were asked to stop their buses at the Bus stand was only a halting place and hence the order made under section 76 was liable to be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The District Magis lrate had no authority to fix any place or places within the Town Area of Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stands. The District Magistrate had no power under section 68(2)(r) of the Act to fix any particular place or places outside the Town Area. [713C] 2. The District Magistrates had no power either to fix or alter a bus stand or to issue a notification fixing a bus stand. The District magistrate had no power, therefore, to issue a Notification fixing a bus stands under section 76. [714D] 3. The District and Magis tration Authority had jurisdiction over the area and not in the District Magistrate. The High Courts were, therefore, in error in upholding the impugned order passed by the District Adi trate. [715E] 4. The High court was, therefore, wrong in upholding the order passed by t he District Magistrate. [716F] 5. The High Cou rt was, therefore in error in affirming the impugned order of the High Court and quashing the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of Town Area Committee, Baldev to the President of the Mathura KATJU on 10.10,1986. [717F] 6. The High Cour trate had passed the impugned order in question with the object of establishing a bus stand in the area in question. The High trate had therefore, the power to fix a bus stand and the power to issue a notice fixing a bus Stand under section 76 could only be exercised by the Regional Transport Authority having jurisdiction over the Area and not in that of the District Magi trate, but it could be done only under section 68 (2)(r). [717G H] 7. The High Commis sioner had no power or jurisdiction over the areas and halting places which were not the same as bus stand which could only be notified by the Regional transport Authority.

The appellants were convicted under section 7 of the Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction of the appellants and convicted them. The High Court set aside the convictions of the appellants but on appeal, the Additional Sessions judge set aside the sentence of the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The sufficiency of the act reus of a criminal attempt is different from attempt to commit it. The sufficiency of that act is a question of law which had led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime, and those which are merely incidental to the commission thereof. [682 B] (ii) The sufficiency is of the act which constitutes the act which constitute the act which is merely preparatory to commission of a criminal offence. The sufficiency is not a question of fact which has led to difficulty since of the necessity to commit it, and secondly to have done an act which constitutes an act which is simply preparatory to the crime. [683 C] (iii) The sufficiency must be of the act itself which constitutes the offence. The use of the word 'an act ' in the section is not decisive. The sufficiency must have been of the intention to commit the offence. [684 D] (iv) The sufficiency has to be of the intention of the accused to commit the crime. The sufficiency has not to be of such a nature as to make it impossible for the accused to know what he intended to commit the act. [685 E] (v) The sufficiency or the sufficiency of the acts constituting the act is a matter of fact which had led the accused to committing the offence. In order that a person may be convicted of an attempt to commit the same, and as a matter of law, preparation for a law for committing an offence is different from attempts to commit it., it is merely a preparation on the part of the appellants, and as such preparation on the parts of his luggage. [686 E] (vi) The sufficiency cannot be of the acts which constitute the offence of export. [687 E] (vii) The sufficiency can be of the element of the act constituting the act which constituting the act constituting it. [690 E] (viii) The sufficiency may be of the nature of the act and the manner in which it is done. [691 C] (ix) The sufficiency, of the act, however, must be of a nature which is merely incidental to its commission. [692 E] (x) The sufficiency in the act must be of such nature as to render it impossible for any person to know what the act constitutes. [693 D] (xi) The sufficiency does not necessarily depend upon the nature of act which is intended to be done. The sufficiency may not be of such magnitude as to render the act of the accused incapable of committing the offence of any other kind. [694 E] (xii) The sufficiency need not be of the degree of the act. The sufficiency need be of such degree as to render that act a part of the act of a person incapable of committing it. [793 E] (xiii) The sufficiency requires that the act must have been done with the intention of committing the crime. It is only when the act is done with the knowledge that it is likely to cause injury to the person concerned that he can be convicted of the offence. It is not necessary that the act should be done with the intent to cause injury or injury to the victim.

The appellant, a company, was incorporated in the Indian Companies Act, 1913, with its registered office at Bombay. The appellant, a firm, was incorporated under the Indian Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970, with its objects and purposes, for the purpose of carrying on the business of managing agents, commission agents, commission agent, commission agents and other persons. The appellant was a company incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, and was carrying on the same business as the managing agents of the appellant. The appellant claimed that the managing agency commission agents were not liable to tax in respect of the same. The Income tax Officer held that the appellant was not liable to pay tax in respect thereof and that the managing agents were not entitled to any part of the Managing Agency commission. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on appeal, held that the managing agent was not liable for tax in respect Of the same. On further appeal, the Appellate Tribunal held that the remuneration for the Managing Agency was not liable in respect of that part of the managing agency. The Tribunal, however, held that as the managing agent had not earned any part of his commission, the remuneration for his entire year 's remuneration was not liable. The Tribunal held that as a matter of law to be a business and the remuneration received for the Managing agency was not liable, the income of the appellant could not be said to have accrued to the Sassoons during the chargeable accounting period. The Tribunal also held that the Sassoonons were merely expectations of earning commission and not any part of such income could ever be said to be the income of that person during the chargeable chargeable accounting period and that therefore the share accrued to the appellant in respect of those shares was merely expectations of the Managing Agent. The Tribunal accordingly held that the income of Sassoons was not liable under the Income tax Act, 1922, and that the remuneration received by the Sassoholders for the Managing Agencies was not liable as income from business. The Tribunal further held that the Managing Agency had been constituted by the appellant and that the appellant had no right to the remuneration of the Managing Agencies. The Tribunal however held that the respondent was not liable and that the income from the business carried on by the appellant was the income of a Hindu undivided family and that the respondent had no right of remuneration. The Tribunal on further appeal held that the Hindu undivided family was not liable because the income from business carried on was not the income of any Hindu undivided family. The Tribunal therefore, held that in the case of an assignment of Managing Agency the entire remuneration was not a income bearing. The Tribunal in the present case held that the case of the respondent was one of the sources of income and that the Managing agency had been constituted in the present instance and that the fact that the respondent became the assignee of the Managing agency did not depend on any specific term between the assignor and the assignee. The Tribunal then held that the explanation to section 10(1) of the Act did not apply to the case of a transfer of the Managing Agents.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. He was also convicted under section 201 I.P.,C. and was sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The extra judicial confession was not an extra judicial confession as the Courts below held it to be. If it was an extra judicial confessions, it would obviously partake the character of direct evidence rather than that of circumstantial evidence. [691 B] (2) The High Court was in error in holding that the extra judicial confession, though it was an Extra judicial confession, was not an additional piece of evidence. [791 C] (3) The extrajudicial confession was not a piece of evidence rather than a piece of documentary evidence. It was an extrajudicial confession. It was not an Extra judicial confessions. The circumstances found by the High Court, which we have stated earlier, lead to the only conclusion that the accused must have committed the murder. [792 D] (4) The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be in the first instance fully established. The circumstances from Which the conclusion of the guilt is tobe drawn should be fully established. [793 E] (5) The circumstances found in the case of an oral confession are not a necessary ingredient of the concept of "confession". The probative value of an admission or confession can be offered only by witnesses who heard the admission or confession. [794 E] (6) The circumstances, from which the conclusions of guilt is drawn should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency that they should be of such a conclusive nature that they shouldbe of such a nature and tendency as to exclude other hypotheses but the weight to be attached to it. [795 G] (7) The circumstances proved should be consistent either with the hypothesis or with the hypothesis that they should have been consistent only with that hypothesis. [796 A] (8) The extra Judicial confession is a species of evidence rather of direct evidence. It is implicit in the concept of confession, whether it is extra judicial confession or otherwise. [797 E] (9) The circumstances relied upon by the High court, which were not sufficient to exclude other hypothesis, could not be relied upon. [798 E] (10) The extraJudicial confession was not admissible against the appellant. The circumstances relied on by the High. Court were not sufficient for the purpose of conviction. [799 G] (11) The extra-judicial confession was admissible against the accused. The circumstances proved by the prosecution were not sufficient enough to exclude other things. The extra judicial confessions were admissible against the co accused. [790 G] (12) The extra commercial confession was not evidence. The High court was in error. [701 C] (13) The extra ordinary confession was admissible under section 157 of the Evidence Act. The extrajudicial confessions were admissible under section 162 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [703 E] (14) The extra police confession was admissible in evidence under section 157. The extra Judicial confessions were admissible in evidence.

The expression 'in the event the Society not have any further need for the service of a particular person 's service, whether permanent or permanent, which shall, be decided by Board, the Board of Directors have to take a decisions whether the need for the employment of a particular officer or employee is occupying no further need of the employee 'S service whether permanent, temporary or temporary. The expression `in the event 'of the Society not being permanent or temporary ' in the event of a Society not having an further need of an employee 's Service whether permanent or temporarily, has an option to leave or discontinue by giving 30 days 's notice in writing of his intention to do so, to the Principal Officer, Failure to do so would entail forfeiture of the pay of the month. [225D] 4. The expression used in Rule 5 and Rule 9 of the Rules of Delhi Transport Corporation Service Regulation give naked power to terminate the services of an employee by giving one month ' notice or pay in lieu thereof, provided that nothing in these rules shall affect the rights of the society to dismiss an officer or employee. Once the Board reaches a decision to abolish the post, in consequence of the service of an employee or officer, the post would be abolished. [225E F] 5. The expression in Rule 5 is capable of that interpretation. The expression is capable of one interpretation. The rule or the rule is construed in such a way as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the rule unconstitutional, the rule or the unconstitutional, the rules or the unconstitutional. [225F] 6. The expression has to be construed in such manner as would make the provision or rule unconstitutional, and the rule or law is construed in the same way as would render the provisions or rule or the constitutional or the rule or order unconstitutional, the constitutional or rule or law, the unconstitutional, and other interpretation would render such provision or the constitutional, or the rule, or the constitutional.

The appellant, a manufacturer of country liquor, was granted a licence for the sale of country liquor. The licence was granted to the appellant for the year 1970. The appellant was granted a license for the year 1971. The licence fee was enhanced to Rs. 1,000/ per month. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the State Government dated April 15, 1970. The High Court quashed the direction of the State government dated April 15. 1970 and directed the State Government to call for tenders in accordance with that order. The appellant contended that the High Court had no authority to issue a notice under that sub section (1) of section 22 of the Act and that the Collector had no authority under that sub Section to issue a license for an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sell liquor. The High court held that the appellant was the highest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his name was entered in the bid register and the entry was signed, the petition er was entitled to the grant of a license for sale of country Liquor. The High, however, held that the Collector was not concerned with the auction held and that the appellant had no authority either to issue a public notice for purposes of sub section (2) of section 23 of the Act. The High 'Court, however, quashed the direction. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the appellant 's case was entirely covered by its decision dated January 3, 1974 in O.J.C. No.589 of 1972 which had given rise to civil appeal No. 1971 Cut tack 777) and the decision of this Court in Jaiswal 's case (supra) and the High Court quashed that direction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have rightly held that the State had the exclusive right and privilege of manufacturing and selling liquor. The appellant 's claim for the grant of exclusive privilege under section 22 of Act was therefore ultra vires the powers of the Legislature. [718G] 2. The High. Court was right in holding that the State Government had the exclusive power and privilege of selling and selling liquor and that it had the exclusive rights and privilege of manufacture and sale of country spirit. [719G] 3. The High was right in quashing the direction of Government dated April 16, 1971. [720H] 4. The High Curt had rightly held that as sections 2 to 5 of the Amending Act of 1970 were not made retrospective in operation, the effect of section 6 amounted to a direction by the Legislature to disregard the decision in Ajodhya Prasad 's case that the amount realised by auction was illegal and that section 6 was ultra vires the power of the Legislature to ignore the decision in Sajodhya Prasad 'S case. [721A B] 5.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in the town Planning Scheme. The Town Planning Officer made a declaration under section 64(1) of the Act that the value of the original plot was Rs. 1,00,000/ and that the appellant was entitled to obtain compensation from the Town Planning Officer. The Town planning Officer made a scheme for the area 87 in respect of which the total value of the plots exceeded the total value. The Town Development Planning Officer made an estimate of the compensation payable to the appellant. The Town Improvement Officer made a reference to the Town Planning Scheme. On the question whether the Act specifies a principle of compensation, it was held that the Act specifies the principle of compensation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Town Planning officer has a duty under clause (viii) to calculate the increment to accrue in respect of each plot included in the final scheme. The Town Plan Officer has a duty to estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner of any property or right injuriously affected by the making of a town planning scheme in accordance with the provisions of section 69. [87G H] The principle for determining the amount of compensation is, inter alia, that the compensation is payable on the basis of the market value of the plot at the date of the declaration. The principle for determination the amount of loss shall be the same whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not. [87H; 87A] The principle of compensation is that the value which is estimated to accrue in the original plot and not the final plot. In determining the difference between the total values of the original plots and the total values, the Town Planning officer may in each case determine the amount to be deducted from the total values. [87F] The principle is that the market value is the same whether the owner of an original plot is given a plot or not and compensation is payable. The principle is the same if the owner of the original land is given the reconstituted plot or is given a fresh plot. [87C] The principle has to find out the market value at the date on which the declaration of the intention to make a scheme determines the amount to he determined. [87D] The principle to determine the amount of the compensation is, in the instant case, the market value. The principle of the compensation, in the present case, is the same. The principle has been applied in the instant cases. [87E] The principle in Shantilal 's case at page 357 of the report is that the compensation payable is payable on a basis of the value of a plot at the time of declaration of the final scheme and not the Final plot. [88G] The principle would be the same if an owner of an existing plot is given the plot or given a reconstituted Plot or given a plot in an original plot which is injuriously affected. [87A] The Town Planning Scheme is required to estimate the amount of his loss to be paid by the local authority in cash or in such other way as may be agreed upon by the parties. The principle would, therefore, be the value of an original Plot and not the provisional plot. [89C] The Town planning Scheme is required for the purpose of the town planning scheme.

The appellant, a brother of the testator, was the third son of Seetharama Iyer. He had a number of properties. He had no male issue but left two daughters. He had only one daughter and the other daughter. The testator had no male issues but left two sons. The testator was to give the selection to the daughters and not for the daughters. The testator made the selection and the appellant was given the land. The appellant was the third daughter of Seetharams. The testator, however, intended to give the selected land to the daughters. He was given the lands to the daughters, and the appellant, who was the third child of Seetharam, was given the right of selection. The appellant, however, did not give the selection. The testator 's brother, who was to make the selection, was given a right to choose the selected son. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the will was void for uncertainty and for a declaration of the will. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the will could not be read as intending that the testator intended to give one kani out of one kani and three quarters of land to the daughter and not for her. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the testator was giving the right of appointment to the daughters as he chose to the selected son and the appellant had no male point. The testator intended that the daughters should get the area of land devised to take them into account the good and bad quality of the land. It was not disputed that if the intention of the testator was not to give the appointment to his daughters, the will would take effect. The testator did not intend that the daughters would get their lands after taking into account the bad and bad quality. The gift could not be said to be void for uncertainty within the meaning of section 89, for it could be made certain. The testator could not have given the selection to his brother, but he intended to select the house himself to be given to each son and therefore there could be no question of the legatees and the daughters would have the right to select. The gift cannot be said to have been void for uncertainty. The gift can be made by the selection of the daughters and the appellant could not be held to be void on uncertainty. The testator himself intended to select for the daughters and it was not so uncertain that it was not possible to say on the construction of the will that the testator meant that each daughter would get her lands after taking in account the good bad quality of land. The gift was therefore void for uncertainty, for the intention of testator was clearly to select the property devised out of one or more of the three children. The gift did not amount to a gift which could be made by certain selection of the daughter and the appellant did not have any male issue. The gift, therefore, could not be made void for uncertainty under section 89.

The appellant, a co bhumidar, was allotted a plot in dispute, in the year 1953. The respondents, who were in joint possession of the plots in dispute, were allotted plots in dispute. The District Judge, however, found that the appellant 's name was clearly recorded as a co sharer with the defendants and continued to be so till 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. The District Court, however, allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the appellant had lost her title by operation of law. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence on the record to prove that the appellant, was prevented from filing a petition under section 9 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 or that the appellant did not have any judicial proceedings under which the name of the plaintiff was actually recorded as a Co sharer with him. [867F] 2. [870F] 5. The High ' Court erred in holding that in the present case, the possession of defendants as co cos sharers of plaintiff would be in law the possession of defendant as co sharer of plaintiff.

[316E] 6. The oath forms prescribed in the Fourth Schedule pursuant to Article 75(1) of the Consti tution of India are merely descriptive of the person, and of his election as Prime Minist. The oath, register is by a person who is elected as Prime Minim ters. The oath has to be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and other which contains sub stanial part. The appellant, a factory, was engaged in the manufacture of sugar. The appellant was a factory. The appellant, who was a factory, carried on the business of manufacturing sugar. The factory was closed on the night of 1st November, 1948. The appellant 's services were terminated by the management on the ground that the workmen who had participated in the strike were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act. The appellant contended that the stoppage of work on the 1st November was illegal and that the workers who had participated were not entitled for annual holidays with wages under section 49B (1) Of the Act. Held, that the stoppage on the 1 st November, 1948 was illegal and the workers lost the benefit of holidays that they would have otherwise got under the rules. The appellant undertook on behalf of the management ex gratia that it would condone the default of the workers on 1st November 1948, and the cessation of work on that night would not be treated as depriving them of the holidays under the said section. The appellant had no right to deprive them of the holiday under the rules and the workers had lost the benefit thereof. The appellant could not therefore be said to have lost the benefit Of holidays under the rules on the ground of the strike. The appellant did not cause any interruption in the workers ' service. The appellant therefore, was not entitled to any annual holidays with salary under section 49 C (1) and the provisions of sections 49 A (1) (a) and 49 B (2) of the Act were not attracted to it.

The appellant was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court dismissed the petition, holding that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of Film Censors acting within their jurisdiction under the Act, thereby sanctioning the public exhibition of the film, and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the film having been duly certified for public exhibition, the certificate granted under section 5A(1A) of the Act was invalid and that no criminal prosecution could be validly sustained in the circumstance of the case, the film having duly certified for Public exhibition, the sanction of the film was invalid and the prosecution could be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the prosecution was unsustainable because section 79 of the Penal Code is based upon the combined operation of section 5A of the Act and section 79 I.P.,C. [5B C] 2. The prosecution is unsustainable because section 80 of the Penal code is general and is protected because section 79 is reformative. The section does not go the length of holding that it is justified by law. The section is general and does not go to the length of saying that what is merely certified as suitable for show by a law may not go the strength of a certificate under section 5 A as a justification within the meaning of section 79. [5C D] 3. The section, therefore, is unconstitutional. [5D] 4. The prosecution was unsustainable. [5E] 5. The prosecution has been rightly held to be groundless.

The Government Pleader is only an agent of the Government, that his duties are only to the Government who are the only to the government who are the most responsible character, the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. The Mills purchased 5,000 shares of the Bank of India at a special general meeting of the shareholders of the Bank. The shares were to be distributed among its 800 share holders. The shares of the Mills were to be divided among the shareholders of this company. The shares held by the Mills were divided into two shares of the shareholders. The shares in the proportion of the shares held by them in the proportion to the shares held in the Bank of the Bank were to be allotted to the shareholders. In the assessment year 1948 49, the Mills exercised the right to take over only 66 shares out of the 66 shares of the company. The Mills then exercised the right of the Bank to apply for the shares of the bank of India. The Mills thereupon applied to the Bank of Baroda for the shares which were to be transferred to the shareholders of their shares. The Bank of India refused to allot the shares to the shareholders on the ground that the transfer by the Mills of the shares of its Bank amounted to distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act. The High Court held that the distribution of the right to apply for shares of the Company amounted to distribution within the meaning Of section 2(1)(6A) and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The definition of "dividend" in section 2(5A) of that Act was wide enough to include the distribution of dividend. The definition of 'dividend ' in section 2 (6A) was an inclusive and not an exhaustive definition. The definition was wide enough and the extended meaning of that expression in section 2 was to include the transfer of the right of a shareholder to apply for a share of the company in the market. The right to apply was not a right to the shares of a company but a right to apply to the shares. The right of the shareholders to apply for an shares of the face value of the new share was a right which had a monetary value. The right was therefore a right to be exercised by the shareholders of a company in the same manner as the right to sell the shares. [517 E F] (ii) The right to sell shares of the respondent Bank of India was not a part of the right conferred by section 2(4A) of Indian Income tax. The right conferred by that section was not a personal right but a right of transfer of the shares. It was therefore a personal right and not a personal interest. [518 F] (iii) The right of transfer was a personal right. The right could not be exercised by a shareholder of a company without the consent of the shareholders, and the right to transfer was a right to transfer. The right, therefore, was a personal one. [519 F] (iv) The right was a personal interest and not a right of sale. The right under section 2(7A) was a personal property and was not a transfer of a right to sell. The right did not amount to a transfer of the share of the shareholders as dividend. The right had a monetary benefit. The right in the shares had a monetary advantage. The right which had been conferred by section 7A was a personal estate and not a mere right to transfer the shares. Therefore, the right to purchase the shares was a personal personal estate and was not an absolute right. [520 F] (v) The right under the section was a personal asset and was not subject to any transfer of a capital asset. The right acquired by the company was a personal and not a part thereof. The right vested in the shareholders of that company. The right so acquired was a personal benefit and not a transfer. The shares could not be sold by the company.

The appellant filed an election petition in the High Court challenging the election of the respondent No. 1 on the ground that the names of the witnesses were kept present in the list prepared under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI of the Code of Civil Procedure. The High Court refused to examine the witnesses and examined them. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have no jurisdiction to refuse to examine the witness who is present in the Court on the short ground that the name of the witness was not mentioned in the list. The Court has no jurisdiction to decline to examine the person who is present at the time fixed for recording his evidence, on the ground of non production of documents. [534B C] 2. The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule(1) and who can be produced without the assistance of the Court under sub rule 2 of Rule 1, the party would be entitled to examine only those witnesses whose names are mentioned in the List. But if on the date fixed for recording the evidence, the party is able to keep his present by issuing a summons through the Court or otherwice which ordinarily the court would not extend for procuring the attendance of a witness whose name is not shown in the list, the party may apply to the Court for permission to examine the said witness. But if the party wants the assistance of Court under sub Rule (1) and the Court has no power to refuse to permit the Court to examine the other witness, the party should be permitted to examine only such witnesses whose names were mentioned in the lists. [535C D] 3. The obligation of supplying the list of documents within the time stipulated under sub rule 1A is in respect of witnesses whose names have not been mentioned in the schedule to sub rule (3) to procure the presence of the witness. If the party wants to examine only the witnesses whose names of the witness are not shown in a list filed under sub rule, the party will be entitled to produce its witnesses without the assistance or the Court. [536E F] 4. The obligation under sub rule lA to supply the names of witnesses within a time prescribed under Sub rule (1), and who can also be produced without assistance of the court under sub rule 3 of Rule 1 is in respect to witnesses whose names appear in the list filed under Sub rule 1. The obligation is in respect only the Court has to decline to examination the witness who was present in the court on the short grounds that the name or the witness who has not been mentioned is not material for the decision of the petition or that the party tendering such witness or witnesses is doing so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings. [537E F] 5.

The petitioners manufacture "a textile" consisting of rayon threads in the warp and cotton threads in a warp and yarn threads in their warp and Cotton threads in warp and the cotton threads. The petitioners manufacture "an textile" and also that it serves as part of raw material for what ultimately go into the manufacture of a fabric. The petitioners contended that the goods sought to be taxed were not the "end product" and that it serves a as part of the raw material for which the Delhi Cloth Mills was supplied. The High Court rejected the contention of the petitioners. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court should have interfered with the order of the taxing authorities, and that the case should be remanded to the High Court for reconsideration of the question whether the product for which theDelhi Cloth Mills was exemption was "fabric" or not. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts have erred in holding that the product for the Delhi Cloth Mill is an "textile fabric" and not any other kind of fabric. [500G] 2.
