The appellant company was engaged in construction of coalheries on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied and allied work incidental and incidental. The appellant company was a Senior Supervisor in the company 's establishment at Dhanbad. The respondent No. 4 was a Senior Supervisors in the company. The appellant Company was engaged in the construction of coal heries on contract in different collieries. The respondent no. 4 was an Senior Supervisor in a company 's Establishment at Dhanbad. He was a Senior supervisor in the company at Dhanbad. On the basis of the application of the respondent No.4, the appellant company was transferred to the Labour Court, Dhanbad. The Labour Court, Patna, on the basis of a report of the Assistant Electrical Engineer, held that the transfer of the case from the Labour Court to another Labour Court was justified. The appellant 's writ petition was dismissed by the High Court. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the Government was misled by the representation of the respondent and without opportunity to the respondent and no. 4 transferred the case to Labour Court, Ranchi, which was dismissed by this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of transfer in the present case was quashed for not communi cating reasons to the assessee. The High Court was in error in holding that the Government had misled the appellant company by the representation. [294C] 2. The order transferring the case from Labour Court, Calcutta to the Labour Courts, Patna, was quashed. The order was quashed. [294D] 3.

The appellant company was a hotel union. The management of the Hotel Imperial, New Delhi, was the management of the hotel. The management was to employ the workmen as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union. The management, however, did not give any notice to the workmen. The workmen were not paid wages for the period of their absence. The management filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Delhi challenging the validity of the reference. The High Court held that the reference was incompetent and the reference was invalid. The appeal to this Court was, ^ HELD: (i) The reference made by the management was incompetent. The reference was bad merely because in the order of reference the words "as represented by the hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk Delhi" were added. The fact that the dispute which was referred for adjudication was between the employer, namely the management of a hotel, and its employees, which were mentioned as its workmen, was clearly indicated in the order. [329 C D] (ii) The reference was incompetent because the reference was bad simply because in the orders of reference the word "as represented" was added for the sake of convenience as to where the notice to the workman should be sent would not in our opinion make the reference incompetent. [330 D E] (iii) The word "as representing the workmen" in the order Of reference means the workmen who were responsible for the dispute. The fact remains that the dispute was referred for the adjudication. The fact of this case is also specified in the terms of reference. The dispute which was the subject matter of the reference was also specified in terms of reference, and the dispute was also specified. The fact, however, that in the order the word " as represented by an officer of a trade union" was added, showed that the workmen employed in the hotel were also responsible for the disputes. [331 E F] (iv) The word 'as represented by an Officer of a trade Union ' in the order dated October 7, 1955, means the workmen employed by the management of an establishment. The word ' as represented by a trade union ' in the Order of reference means the workman who was responsible for the matter. The word " as representing the workmen ' in the definition of the expression "as represented " by the Hotel workers ' in the Act means the workmen of a trade unions. The word, as defined in the Act, means the workman of a trade association of which he is a member. The expression "as representing a workman" in the definition means a person who is a workman within the meaning of the Act. The expression 'as represented ' by the Hotel Worker ' in the explanation to the definition means the workman employed by the employer in the course of the trade. The expression, as defined by the Act, is a technicality upon technicality, for the union itself. The dispute is of a general nature relating to the terms of employment or conditions of labour, of any person. The dispute, therefore, does not affect the competence of the order of the reference, and it relates to retrenchment or reinstatement.

The appellant is a manufacturer of rod bushes and camshaft bushes. The appellant imported rod bushes and camel from the market and claimed exemption under Notification No. 281 Cus/76, dated 1.3.76, under which the rod bushes and Camshaft bushes were imported by the appellant. The Assistant Collector of Customs, however, rejected the claim of the appellant. In appeal to the Customs, Excise and Gold Control Appellate Tribunal, the appellant contended that the bushes and cam shaft bushes imported by the respondent were parts of internal combustion piston engines and not parts thereof. The Tribunal, however, held that the bushes, which have been imported by the appel lant, are parts of internal diesel piston engine and not a few parts thereof. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the bushes were parts of the internal combustion piscon engines and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Notification No. 282 Cus/77, dated 1 3.76, as it was not specifically mentioned in the Notification that the bushes or cam shaft were not identical articles but they were distinct and separate. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Notification will apply to parts of the engines mentioned under Heading No. 84.06. [227A] 1.2 The Notification will not get the benefit of exemption under the Notification. The intention is clear enough to provide that the parts of the engine, mentioned under Heading 84.06, will get the benefit. The intention of the Notification is clear enough, to provide that parts of the motor engines mentioned under heading No. 8406. 84.6, will get exemption from payment of customs duty in respect of parts of the Engine. [227D] 1.3 The Notification will be applicable to parts of such engines, even if they are parts of such engine, such parts will get the exemption under the said Notification. [227E] 1.4 The Notification will have the benefit of Exemption under the Notification, irrespective of the fact that they or any of them have already been included under Heading No 84.06 or under any other Heading. 84.09. [227F] 1.5 The Notification will get the benefits of exemption under Notification. The Notification will also get the benefit under Notification. [228F] 1.(a) The parts of the machinery mentioned under Heading Nos. 84. 06, 84.06 and 84.06 are also parts of such motor engines. [227G] 1.6 The Notification will, therefore, be reasonable to take a narrow view of the Notification and not to extend its benefit to the parts of engine. [227H] 1.7 The Notification will come to an end only if the parts of such machinery are covered under Heading No, 84.6. [227C] 1.8 The Notification will accordingly apply to parts which are included under Heading Nos 84.06 to 84.06 as provided in the Notification.

The plaintiffs, who were the descendants of the defendants, filed a written statement and took the plea that their father Sayed Dastagir was a Mujawar and was receiving the offerings by right of inheritence. The defendants filed a writtenstatement and took the pleas that the plaintiffs had no right or claim in the management or share in the offerings. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the plaintiffs were not entitled to any relief. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the defen dant respondents that the plaintiffs ' claim was barred by limitation by ouster and that the plaintiffs who were claiming through Fathima Bee had lost their right by ouster. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The defendants were claiming ouster on the basis of denial of Fathima Pes title at the time of the judgment of the High Court in 1909 and another ground taken in the written statement was that the defendants were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not entitled t o any right or claim of share in the Dargah. [527B C] 1.2 The defendants were carrying an mistaken impression all together that females under Muslim Law were entitled to any right or interest in the offerings of Dargah. [627D] 1.3 The defendants were not entitled any share in the management of Dargah according to Muslim Law. [628D] 1(a) The defendants were entitled to the share of the Hundial collections at any point of time till their death in 1957 that is, to Wazir from the fight or management of Dargah. The defendants were therefore entitled to any share in any offerings of Dargah and the offerings. [629F] 1(b) The defendants are claiming ouster on account of their right and interest in the Dargah and on that account they were clearly excluded from the right or claim any right of management or possession of Dargah. It is clear that neither in the written statements nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs, the defendants were claiming exclusion on the basis that Fathima was a co sharer in the right and management of Dargah and that the defendants had asserted hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment of Dargah. In order to make out a case of ouster against Fathima, the defendants had pleaded an ouster of Fathida Bee and her brothers. [630E F] 1(c) The defendants had asserted ouster on the ground of denial of their right or interest. The defendants had pleaded that the right of Fathua Bee had lost her right by ouster and as such she was expressly excluded from the claim of any share in Dargah. [730F] 1.(d) The defendants have pleaded ouster on the plea of adverse possession and enjoyment. The defendants have not pleaded any ouster. The defendants are seeking ouster on the strength of their right of management and possession. [631F] 2(a) In order to establish ouster of FATHima Bee, the plaintiffs have pleaded ouster of F.athima Bee. The defendants, therefore, have pleaded ouster.

The respondent was allotted a railway quarter of a suitable type and was allotted a suitable type. The appellant was allotted a quarter of a type and was given a suitable house accommodation. The respondent was allotted the quarter of a Type. The appellant claimed house rent allowance as part of his wages. The Authority appointed under section 15(1) of the Act, allowed the respondent 's claim for house rent allowance. The appellant filed a written statement and contested the claim on the ground that there had been no illegal deduction from the respondent 'S wages inasmuch as the respondent had been allotted a suitable quarter of a class and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled to withhold the house rent allowance; and that the claim was inadmissible on the ground, that there had not been any illegal deduction from his wages inasmuch as he had declined to occupy those quarter. Held, that the terms of the contract between the parties, section 23 of the Act and the rules made thereunder, do not make the grant in such absolute terms. The rules do not make any grant in such terms absolute. The rules did not make the payment in such absolute term. The rules were not intended to be exhaustive of the terms of a contract between the employer and the employee. The rules merely made a provision for the payment of house rent allowance and did not make it a part of the terms. The rule did not make any provision for the grant of house rent allowances. The rules made under the Act did not make such a grant in such a absolute terms.

The detenus were detained under section 3(1) of the (for short COFEPOSA) by the State Government on February 16, 1980, purporting to have been made under section 3 of the (Act for short) of the Act. The detenus made a written request to the detaining authority on February 18, 1980, requesting him to furnish the copies of the statements and documents relied upon in the grounds of detention, to enable them to make an effective representation. The detaining authority, however, refused to supply the copies of those statements and documents to the detenus on April 3, 1980. The detenus filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the detention on the ground that the detaining authority had not passed the order of detention, and that the grounds of the detention were vague and indefinite. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the detenus that the delay in supplying the copies of statements and documents was not properly explained by the detaining authority and that the delay was unexplained and that the detaining authorities had not applied their mind to the nature of the documents and the documents relied upon or referred to in the "grounds" of detention. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The delay in supplying copies of the basic materials and documents to a detenu was not properly explainable by the detaining authorities. The delay was not properly satisfactorily explained. [352C D] 2. The delay of more than a month in supplying the copy of the basic material relied upon or reference in the " ground grounds of detention" must be supplied to the detenu with reasonable expedition to enable him to make an adequate and effective representation at the earliest. [352D] 3. The delay is not properly explained. The delay has to be explained satisfactorily. [352E] 4. The delay must be explained satisfactorily and the delay must be satisfactorily explained. The Court has to be satisfied that the delay is unexplained and that there was no unreasonable delay. [352F] 5. The delay cannot be explained satisfactorily, and the delay is not satisfactorily explained. There was no unreasonable or unexplained delay. [353B] 6. The delay had to be explained and the delay was not satisfactorily explained, and the Court had to be satisfied about the reasonableness of the delay. [351D] 7. The delay, in supplying the documents, was not satisfactorily explain. [352B] 8. The delay caused in supplying the required documents was not satisfactorily satisfactorily explained. It was not explained satisfactorily. The delay could not be explained satisfactorily by the detaining author ity. [352G] 9. The delay may be condoned if the Court is satisfied that the representation was not properly addressed. [352H] 10. The delay can be condoned if it is shown that the representation had been properly addressed. The delay does not vitiate the detention. [352A] 11. The delay relates to the supply of the documents to the detenu. The delay did not vitiate the order of the detention. The delay would not vitiate the impugned order of detention. [351B] 12. The delay might be condoned if there was unreasonable delay. The delay should be explained satisfactorily so that the Court can consider the reasonableness of such delay.

The respondent was tried for offences under sections 302, 307 and 324 read with section 149 I.P.C. and section 307 read with section 34 I.P.,C. and was acquitted. The respondent filed a petition in the High Court for quashing the order of acquittal and for a direction to the State to file a joint appeal against the acquittal of all the accused persons. The High Court held that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 was against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several persons tried jointly. The High court held that the entire scheme of Chapter XXX XXXI of the code was against the merits of the case and so held that the joint appeal to be maintainable under section 419 was not maintainable. The High, Court, however, held that the decision of the Full Bench holding a joint appeal to the High Court was inconsistent with the scheme of the Code and came to the conclusion that the scheme Of Chapter XXXI of Code as disclosed in section 419 was inconsistent with Chapter XXXI of that Code and therefore not legally prohibited. The High. Court also recorded the main judgment only in Criminal Appeal No. 60 of 1965. The question of competency of a joint trial was referred for authoritative decision to a Full Bench. The Full Bench held that the Full Bench held a joint appeal not to be maintainable in law. The Full Benches decision of the Gujarat High Court in Jela Ghela Jadav 's case was cited before the Full Bench. In the present case, the Full Bench of the Gujarat high Court held that a joint appeal cannot be maintainable in the law. The question whether joint appeal to a joint trial has also to be held not to be contrary to any provision of the Code, and therefore not constitutionally prohibited. The Full bench held that the earlier decision of another Division Bench holding a Joint appeal to be not binding on it was not binding on the High Court. The Full Court, however held that the view taken by the Full Bench was wrong. The Full Full Bench held in Jela Jela 's case that the earlier decisions of two judges of the same High Court were wrong and that the decision in Jela ' case was not binding. The Full, Bench held that a separate appeal to the Supreme Court against a common order acquitting several accused persons jointly tried and acquitted at a joint trial had also to be upheld. The Full Constitution Bench held that joint appeal to this Court against an order of acquittal of all persons tried jointly and acquitted at joint trial must be upheld. In the appeal to this court, HELD : (1) The scheme of Chapter XIV of the Code of Criminal Procedure, with the result that a joint trial is permissible, then on principle it is difficult to negative the maintainability of one appeal by the state against an order acquittal of all accused persons jointly. [258 E] (2) The scheme Of Chapter XIV of Code of Criminal procedure, with the consequence that a joint suit against several accused persons tried jointly, and acquitted at the joint trial must, therefore, be upheld. [258 G] (3) The scheme is not inconsistent with the provisions of the Code. The question is whether joint appeal against all accused persons tried together and acquitted at one trial must be accepted. [258 F] (4) The scheme does not in terms cover the case of an appeal by the accused persons jointly and acquitted by the trial court by a common order.

The assessee was a firm called O.R.M.SP. Firm which was registered under section 26(A) of the 1922 Act. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal holding that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business of the assessee must be held to be charged under the 1918 Act but only receipts received from the foreign business itself. The High Court held that the foreign business of the appellant was not liable to tax under the 1918 Income tax Act because the assessee was only taxed on remittances received from the Indian business of the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of account. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(3) only to income on which the tax was payable under the 1918Act but the assessee was not liable for tax under the 1922 Act because what was taxed was the remittances received by the assessee from the foreign firm. [912 C] (2) The assessee is entitled to relief on securities as well. The exemption under section 25 (3) only covers income on which tax was payable by an assessee if the business of a foreign firm which is discontinued there being no succession by virtue of which the provisions of sub section (4) have been rendered applicable. [913 D] (3) The exemption under the 1918 Acts is not attracted to income on securities. The exemption is not attracted in respect of the rental income from house properties owned by the foreign firm and not the foreign business. [914 E] (4) The exemption is in respect of interest on securities and also the income derived by the assessee was derived from the foreign trade. The exemption does not apply to income on shares held by the foreign business and the assessee is entitled only to relief under the 1918 law. [915 E] (5) The exemption in respect of income from house property owned by the assessee is in relation to the foreign business but the income received by the foreign assessee was derived by the foreign trade itself. [916 C] (6) The exemption granted under section 25 of the 1922 Income tax Act is in respect to income on the income derived from the business of an assessee. The exemption in the instant case is in respect only of income on which income is chargeable under the 1918 act. [917 D] (7) The exemption does apply to income from houseproperty owned by the Foreign firm which was closed in the year account. [918 E] (8) The exemption cannot be applied to income on property owned by a foreign firm. The exemption cannot apply to income derived by a foreign company which was discontinued. [919 G] (9) The exemption was in respect of a foreign business. The exemption was not in respect of any income derived by an assessee from the business. The assessee was not entitled to relief. [920 C] (921 D] (10) The exemption could not be applied to the present case. [922 E] (11) The assessee in respect of his activity styled foreign business was not charged under the 1922 Income Tax Act. The exemption could be applied to any foreign business. It was not in relation to any foreign trade. [921 E] (12) The exemption did not apply to the foreign income. The exemption did apply to income received from the business in British India. [923 E] (13) The exemption applied to income from the business which was discontinued there being neither any succession by virtue nor by virtue of the provisions of section 25(1) of the 1961 Act. [924 E] (14) The exemption applies to income from business.

The respondent, a public works contractor entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for the construction of the Capital Project, wherein the respondent received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. The respondent received payment on September 6. 1965 for the same. The appellant received payment for it in accordance with Clause 9 of the contract. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the transaction. The High Court answered the question in favour of the assessee holding that the transaction was a works contract. The High court answered the question against the assessee holding, that the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the respondent with the Public works Department of the State Government of Gujarat was a works contracts. The High, Court answered the questions in favour of assessee holding that in the instant case the transaction envisaged was a works Contract. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were wrong in holding that the contract in this case was a works one. The contract in this matter was entirely of the assessee. The essence of the contract was, therefore, entirely of the respondent. The essence was entirely of his assessee. The contract was, however, entirely of a contract. The essence, therefore, was entirely of a assessee. The High. Court was not right in answering the question in the favour of the appellant in favour of S.R.R.T.C. [163G H] 2. The contract is a works contract and not a works contract, and the contract is, therefore, clearly a contract of sale. The essence is the contract. [163A] 3. The contract, in this case, is a works contracts and not a contract of Sale. The essence in the contract was entirely of 'the assessee '. The essence ' was entirely of that contract. The contract did not involve any transfer of property. The essence thereof was entirely of an assessee. The transaction was, therefore. a works contract of sale and not a work contract. The transaction contemplated by the contract was also entirely of the appellant. The essence being entirely of the Respondent, the contract was wholly of the assessee and the essence of the Contract was, therefore clearly, of the assessee 's own. [163D E] 4. The contract contemplated a works contract which was not a works contracts, and the contractor was, therefore not a works contractor. The essence which was the essence of a contract was, thus, clearly a works contract within the meaning of section 2(g) of the Act. [163E F] 5. The contract could not be said to be a works contract for the purpose of section 2 (g) of Act.

The petitioner, a member of the Legislative Assembly of the State of Jammu and Kashmir, was elected to the Legislative Assembly from the State of J&K. The petitioner was elected to be the President of the Legislative Council of Jammu and K. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued on March 25, 1975, by which the period of five years of the House of the People (Extension of Duration) Act, 1976 (Act 30 of 1976) was extended to the State of Kashmir. The petitioner contended that the Proclamation of emergency dated March 25, 1974 had ceased to be in operation on 26th June, 1975, because the resolutions passed by the two Houses of Parliament approving the Proclamation of the Emergency dated 3rd December, 1971 had ceased to exist on 26th August, 1975, and the Proclamation of March 25,1975 had ceased to have been in operation on 4th February, 1972. The petitioner also contended that the two Proclamations of Emergency were validly issued by the President of India on 26th March, 1977 and the Proclamation dated 25th June, 1974 was not in operation on the date on which each of the two Houses had not been published in the official Gazette. The petitioner further contended that the proclamation of Emergency dated 3.12.1971 had ceased to operate on 26th September, 1975 because the resolutions of the two House of Parliament approving both the Houses of Parliament and the time when the House of People (Extension) Act, 1975 was passed by both the Houses were duly approved by the President and approved by the resolutions of both the Houses. The petitioner therefore contended that the validity of both the Proclamies of Emergency had been validly issued and the Proclamation had ceased to remain in operation on 3rd February, 1972 and the Proclamation was ultra vires the Constitution. The petitioner, therefore, contended that the period of the House was not in force on 26th April, 1975, since the two Pro Clamations of emergency were duly published in the Official Gazette. The contention of the petitioner was that the duration of the House could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of Emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2) of Article 352 of the Constitution and since the two proclamations had been validly passed by the House of Parliament, the House of people (Extension of duration) Act, 1977 had ceased to continue from the date appointed for its first meeting in relation to the present House of the people. The petitioner submitted that the two Acts of 1976 and 1978 had ceased to apply to the State and since the three Proclamants had been duly notified in the official gazette, the Proclamation of December, 1971 was not in the operation of law and therefore the two Pro clamations of the Emergency were validly made and the Proclamation issued on the 3rd December 1971 had ceased. The petitioner urged that the two pro clamations had not been validly issued or the Proclamation of 12th December, 1971, had ceased to in operation on 8th February, 1973, because the two Procamations of December, 1975 had ceased to govern the State of Punjab and the two Proseclamations were validly issued and approved by both the House of States. The petitioner argued that the two unclamations which were duly approved were validly issued, and the two resolutions had been duly published in official Gazette.

The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the said property was a public temple within the meaning of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The High Court, however, held that the property in question constituted a temple within the definition of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, Madras Act 11 of 1927 and that the appellant was not entitled to leave under article 133(1)(a) and (b) of the Constitution. The High court, however, dismissed the application on the ground that the appellant had not made any substantial question of law. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the basis that the property was a private property capable of valuation. The subject matter of the dispute has to be ascertained with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the plaint, the property was the private property of the said family capable of alienation, the High Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to the respondents the property was inalienable and therefore capable of a valid transfer. [157 D E] The subject matter in dispute was the private properties of the said families capable of valuation and therefore capable to a valid transfer, and therefore capable only of a valid sale. [157 E] The question whether the property in dispute was a public or a public temple was incapable of valuation. [157 F] The subject of the dispute was the property of the family capable of valuation, and therefore incapable of valuation, the High court was wrong in holding that the property belonged to the family.

The appellant, a railway employee, was employed by the respondent company as a clerk in the appellant 's establishment. He was paid a cash allowance of Rs. 10,000 per month. The appellant was paid a sum of Rs. 1,000 per mensem as a cash allowance. The appellant claimed that he should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements made at present by the appellant. The Tribunal held that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiffin, and that the practice started by the appellant was not based solely on humanitarian grounds. The Tribunal, however, held that the practice was being followed in many cases and that the appellant had been rightly given cash allowance for the re employment of the retired personnel. The Tribunal also held that the award was not based on humanitarian grounds and that the award made by the appellant in respect of the cash allowance was not justified. The appellant contended that the Tribunal had erred in law in making an award in respect of cash allowance for its employees and that the Tribunal has erred in law by making an award on the ground that only 4 cases of re employment had been brought to its notice and so, the question whether the appellant was entitled to cash allowance for that behalf was not open to the Tribunal. Held, that the award of the Tribunal was not based merely on humanitarian grounds, but was based on humanitarian considerations. The fact that the re employment was mainly inspired by humanitarian considerations and the practice was been followed in many instances and the practice had been being followed in several cases and that there was some other factors in relation to this problem of re employment which cannot be ignored. The fact, that the reemployment of retired persons was mainly inspiredby humanitarian considerations, could not be ignored.

The respondent was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules whereunder payment of the provident fund was to be made in sterling. The respondent was a subscribers to the State railway Provident Fund. The Union of India then applied to the High Court of Calcutta for removal of attachment on the ground that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The High Court confirmed the order of the executing court. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was in error in holding that the money in the hands of the Reserve Bank of India was the agent of the Railway Administration. The High Court had rightly held that the money was immune from the attachment under the Act and that the money must be deemed to have been paid out to the subscriber of the Provident Fund. [30 G] The High Court rightly held that by sending the two cheques to the Reserve Bank for payment at the place at which payment was to be paid, the money remained at the disposal of the Railway administration. [30 C] The High court was in error In holding that the amount in the hands was not the agent of Browne but was the agent for the subscriber of a Browne. [30 E] The High. Court was in wrong in holding that by sending two cheques to a Reserve Bank as the agent of a Railway Administration was attached. [30 F] The High, Court was in fact in error in assuming that the money remained under the control of the Railway Admn. and the Union of India was attached. The High court had rightly held in favour of the respondent.

The appellant, a pump manufacturing enterprise, issued a notice terminating the services of the respondent, on the ground that the respondent was efficient, that he was a pump manufacturing unit, issuing a notice ending the employment, and offering one month 's pay as authorized by the relevant Standing Orders. The respondent challenged the termination of his services by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Labour Court was not justified in interfering with the order of termination simpliciter, because the respondent was a layman manufacturing enterprise, and the Court had no jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was not right in interfering with a finding of fact recorded by the trial Court on this point. [401C] (2) The power of the Labour Court to intervene and setting aside such termination was not a disguised dismissal simpliciter, if in reality it came to the conclusion that the termination was a colourable exercise of power by the management. [402D] (3) The power to intervene and to set aside such order of termination was not an order simpliciter, but a colourable exercise or an act of victimisation or unfair labour practice. [403E] (4) The power under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, to intervene and sets aside such termination, is loath to interfere with a finding recorded by the Labour Court on this ground. [404G] (5) The power conferred on the Labour Court under the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 is loath to interfered with a finding on this point, and the High Court was, therefore, not justified in setting aside such a termination. [405G] (6) The power given to the Labour Court, under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, to intervene in the matter of termination simpliciter is not a colourable exercise. The power of termination is loath to interference with a finding, of fact recorded, by the Labour Appellate Tribunal on this point.[401C D] (7) The power is loath to intervene and Set aside such termination merely if in reality the exercise of such power is challenged on the ground of being colourable exercise of the power vested in the management or as a result of victimisation or illegal unfair labour practice, it would have the jurisdiction to intervene. [407D] (8) The power vested in a Labour Court under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Standing Orders), Act, 1946 is loath to interfering with a view of the matter. [408D] (9) The power, if exercised by the Labour Courts, is loath, to interfere with the finding of fact, recorded by the Industrial Tribunal on this issue. [409E] (10) The power exercised by the Industrial Tribunals is loath to disturb the finding of facts recorded by the Tribunal on this question. [410E] (11) The power has to be exercised in a manner which is not arbitrary or capricious. It is not a case where the High Court has exercised its jurisdiction arbitrarily or capriciously or arbitrarily or where the exercise of the jurisdiction is challenged on a ground of being mala fide or an act or of victimisation or an act which is not bona fide or mala fide or is so arbitrary or capricious that no reasonable person would arrive at that conclusion, it is the duty of this Court to interfere and set aside the said order.

The Assam Rashtrabhas Prachar Samiti (Taking over management and Control) Ordinance, 1984 and Section 1 sub clause (ii) of this Ordinance provided that the Ordinance shall extend to all areas over which the Asom Rashtrabha Prachar Samiti had its jurisdiction immediately before the commence ment of the Ordinance by a Notification No. Act XXIII of 1984. The Ordinance was replaced by the Ordinance No. XXIII of 1984 by which the Rashtrabhis Prachar Samiti was constituted by the Assam Rashtrabi Prachar Samiti. The Ordinance provided that all the functions, properties and affairs of the Samiti were taken over by this Board and it was also provided that the ordinance shall extend to the entire area of the Asom Prachar Samiti and the Karyapalika and byabasthapika Sabha. The Ordinance also provided that all properties and properties of the Samiti shall be restored back to the Society. The Ordinance further provided that the State Government shall restore back all assets and properties of asom Prachar Samha Prachar Samchar Samiti to the Samiti from the Samiti. The respondent No. 1, a member of the Samiti, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the action taken by the State Government of Assam in the matter of temporary injunction. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The State Government appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression "asom Rashtra bha Prachar" in the context of which the Ordinance was issued, is wide enough to include all areas over Which the Asom Sabha was functioning in 1984 and which we are restoring the Samiti and all the functions and properties of Asom Sabha. [171C] 1.2 The expression "in the context of" in the expression "asam Rashtrab ha Prachar Samiti" in the Ordinance is wide enough and it is not confined to all areas within which the Asam Sabha was functioning and they had sufficient time to go on and in this view of the matter the reply came that the State has no desire to restore the Samiti and therefore the State has not any desire to restore it back to the society but unfortunately it appears that with regard to the constitutional aspects of the matter, the reply came to an end although from 1984 till today they were not allowed to function. [171D E] 1.3 The expression "any other matter" in the Act is wide enough in the context in which it occurs in the Act. The expression "other matter" in section 3 of the Act is wider than the expression "other matters" in the definition of "other matters". [171F] 1.4 The expression "all other matters" in section 2 of the Act means all matters which are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the State Legislature. The expression 'other matters" is wide enough. The expression is wide enough, but it is not limited to all matters which can be said to be within the exclusive competence of the State. [171F G] 1.5 The expression " other matters" is wider than those which are within its exclusive jurisdiction. The expression in the context is wide enough but it is wide enough for the purpose of the Act to include all matters within its exclusive competence.

The appellant, a Hindu widow, made a gift of the four houses at Asansol, which was accepted by Nand Lal Sao on behalf of Kamala Devi, under the evil advice of her father and son in law, and to deprive the appellants of their right, made a gifts of the four house at Asansi, which was duly registered on March 10, 1940, and the gift was actually executed and registered on March 11, 1940, some two years after the marriage. The gift was not valid in Hindu law and valid in Hindu Law. The gift in question was made at the time of the marriage and was duly registered. The gift made by Nand Lal, father in law of Kamala Devi was accepted by the appellant, and the gifts were duly registered on the same day. The gift deed was executed and registered in favour of the appellant, but the gift was later confirmed on the occasion of the marriage. On the question whether the gift was of a reasonable portion of the estate of Ram Kishori Lal Sao and in pursuance of an ante nuptial agreement made by Sumitra Devi at the time the marriage was for spiritual benefit of Ram Kishori Lai Sao, HELD : (i) The gift was of the reasonable portion of his estate of Ram Lauo, and the deed of gift was immaterial if the deed of gifts was in fulfilment of the moral obligation flowing from the ante nupatal agreement. [632 B] (ii) The gift in favour of appellant was not valid, because, as the gift was made some two years before the marriage, the gift in question being of a reasonable part of the estate, the gift was binding on the reversioners. [633 C] (iii) The gift made in favour of her daughter was a religious duty and the promise to make a gift in favour Of her daughter was not valid. [634 D] (iv) The gift by Nand Lal was not valid because, as it was not a religious duty, the gift made in the present case was not a valid gift. [635 E] (v) The gift of a reasonable piece of the estate was not valid and in Hindu Law, if the deed was in fulfilment or performance of an ante puptial agreement, even though the gift was in fulfilment and fulfilment of an ante cuptial agreement. [734 E] (vi) The gift being of a religious duty the gift in favour must be supported upon the ground that the gift was not in fulfilment of an anti puptial promise made by her and that such promise may be fulfilled and it was not essential to make a gifts at the time when the marriage was performed. [636 E] (vii) The gift is not valid because the gift was for spiritual benefits of Ram Kishorilal Sao and the gift in the present ease was not valid for spiritual benefit. [637 C] (viii) The gift having been made at the stage of the marriage, it was open to Sumitra Devi to fulfil that promise. [638 D] (ix) The gift could not be supported upon any ground that the marriage was a religious obligation and the promise was made at a time of the solemnization of the marriage or not. [639 E] (x) The gift did not amount to a religious duty. The gift did amount to a moral or religious obligation flowing from a ante nupitive agreement. [613 D] (xi) The gift, in question, was a religious act which conferred spiritual benefit upon the reversioners.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Punjab Legislative Assembly, was declared elected. The election was challenged by the first respondent on the ground that he had got circulated pamphlets and posters among the voters of the constituency which he had mentioned that he had withdrawn his candidature and any vote given to him (Tej Singh) would be deemed to be a vote for Ruplal. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the allegations of corrupt practices indulged in by the first Respondent (TejSingh) in his statement of facts were clearly proved and that the allegations were made by him and the vouchers were appended by him along with the return of expenses incurred during his election campaign which was verified by him to be a true and correct statement. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The allegations of corrupt practice as alleged by the first appellant (Tej Kaur) in his election petition were clearly proved beyond reasonable doubt that the allegations had been committed by the first Appellant (Tej SINGH) in his presence and that the appellant had proved beyond reasonable doubts that the votes polled in favour of the first respondent (Tej singh) would be considered as a vote given to the appellant (Teji) in his press and signed by him. [401B C] 1.2 The High Court was right in holding that the allegations in the election petition were proved beyond reasonable probability and that the votes cast in favour of Tej Singh were materially altered. [402C] 1.3 The High Court has rightly held that the allegations against the first respondent were proved beyond doubt and that would have doubt materially altered the result of the election. [403D] 1.4 The High Court had rightly held that it was not proved that the allegations made by the first appel lant were proved beyond any doubt. [404C] 1.(a) The High Court rightly held that there was no evidence to prove the allegation of corrupt practices. [405D] 1.(b) The High court was right in not holding that the allegation of the first appellant was proved beyond reasonable suspicion. [407C] 1(c) The High Courts were right in holding the election of the first Respondent to be void. [408D] 1(d) The High Cou rt was right in dismissing the election petition.

The appellant was a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal. He was the Chief Minister of the State. In the application for contempt filed by the appellant against Shri Bhajan Lal, the Chief Minister was alleged to have committed contempt of the High Court. The appellant was also alleged to have been guilty of contempt of the Court. The High Court dismissed the application for Contempt. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had exercised its jurisdiction under the Act and the appeal was incompetent. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have jurisdiction to punish for contempt. The jurisdiction of the High Courts is to punish for Contempt. The High Cou rt has no power or power to punish for criminal contempt. The High court can exercise its jurisdiction only by punishing for contempt. [893C] 2. The High Commis sion of the Court is not correct. The jurisdiction to punish is also not absolute. The High Cour t has no power to punish. When the High Court does not impose any punishment on the alleged contemnor, the High Court cannot exercise its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215 of the Constitution. [894D] 3. The High courts have jurisdiction to punishing for contempt, even though no punishment is imposed by the High Court, the High Courts have exercised its jurisdiction or powers as conferred on them by Article 215. [895E] 4. The High High Court has no power, or jurisdiction to punish the alleged contemnor. The High tution cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction or authority as conferred by Article 215 or power to act in a particular manner, the exercise of jurisdiction or power will involve the act in a specific manner, the exercising of jurisdiction or the power will involve acting in that particular manner, and in no other. Article 215 confers jurisdiction or power on the High Court to punish for breach. [896E] 5. The High, Court cannot exercise jurisdiction or power to punishing for Contempt. It does not, however, mean that when the High Court itself has exercised its jurisdiction and power as conferred by article 215 of the constitution, the High court does not exercise its jurisdiction, or power to do so. [897F] 6. The High ' Court cannot exercise the jurisdiction or power of contempt. The power to punish is conferred on the High Courts under Article 215 of th e Constitution. It does neither, however, nor in any other. Article 216 confers jurisdiction orpower on the High court to punish for the contempt. [997F] 7. The High Power Court can exercise its power or jurisdiction as conferred on the Court by Article 215 only when the High court makes an order or decision in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish. The High is not, however. exercising its jurisdiction under Article 215. The High power can be exercised by punishing for Contempt, but it must always be borne in mind that in a contempt proceeding there are only two parties, namely, the court and the contemnor. [899G] 893A] 9.

The appellant, a tenant of a building, was let out to the respondent for a period of ten years. The respondent, however, did not pay the rent and the appellant was asked to pay the rent. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment on the ground that the respondent was not entitled to the protection of section 111(g) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, as he had not paid the rent and that the lease was therefore determined under section 111(b) and not under section 111 (g) of that Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the respondent had failed to prove that the rent note was a lease and that the appellant was not entitled under section 111 to ask for a decree for ejectment. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was fully justified in finding that the provision in sub section (g) was not based upon any principle of equity. The principle so embodied in section 111(h) of the Act was the one contained in sub section(g) as amended in 1929 which still governs leases made prior to 1st April, 1930, and which still govern leases made prior thereto. The rule embodied in section 112(g) was the one stated in sub section 2 of section 111 prior to 1929. The rule enunciated in sub section 3 of section 111 was the one embodied in section III of the Act. The rule was not based on any principle of justice, equity and good conscience. The rule laid down in sub section 1(g) is the one contained under section 111 of the Act and must be held to govern even agricultural leases. [1028 H; 1029 A B] (ii) The rule embodied by the Master of the Rolls in the present case is the one embodied under section 111. The rule is the one stated by the Master in the present ease. The rule in sub section 4 of section 111 is the one in general and that the rule is the principle of justice. equity and good good conscience. [1029 C] (iii) The rule is not based upon a principle of justice and good conscience and must be construed to govern even a agricultural lease. The rule must be given a principle of equity, equity and justice.

The Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969, was amended by Act 35 of 1969. Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963, provided that notwithstanding anything contained in any law, or in any contract, custom or usage, or in some judgment, decree or order of any court, any person in occupation of the land on the 11th day of April, 1957, on the 11 th day of April 1957, on a basis of a registered deed purporting to be a lease deed purporting to he a lease deed, shall be deemed to be tenants notwithstanding anything contained therein. Section 52 of the Kerala Tenancy Act, 1969 provided that notwithstanding any order of court, any tenant holding land less than ten years immediately preceding the 11thday of April, 1967, shall be presumed to be in continuous occupation of such land for not less than ten year preceding the 11 thday of April 1967. Certain persons occupying private forests or unsurveyed on the 11. day of April 1967, were in occupation of such lands for not lessthan ten years. Certain persons occupied private forests or portions of the land of another at the commencement of the Kerala Act, as amended by Act 36 of 1969, were entitled to lease hold rights but continued in possession of such land till the commencement of this Act, notwithstanding the fact that the lease was granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land. The appellants, who were tenants of the land, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Act was not retrospective in operation and that the Act had no retrospective effect. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act was not prospective in operation. The Act had no application to the facts of the case. The Act did not apply to the facts in the present case. The appellants were tenants of land in excess of ten years. The Act applied to the facts and circumstances of the case and the appellants were not entitled to lease the lands. [112E] 2. The Act is prospective in operation and the Act was prospective in operation, and the Act had not been enacted. The Act has been enacted to provide for the protection of tenants against eviction. The Act does not apply to any land. The Act applies to all persons who have paid amounts for occupation of land. The tenants are not entitled to any lease. The Act provides for the protection against eviction of tenants. The Act, therefore, does not apply. [112F G] 3. The Act cannot be said to be retrospective in operation. [112G] 4. The Act in question is prospective in effect. The Act only applies to the tenants who have paid the amounts for occupation. The Act also applies to the tenant who has not been in occupation of any land. [112H] 5. The Act deals with the protection of the tenants against eviction of the tenants. The tenants have been in occupation for not less ten years. [112A] 6. The Act makes provision for the protection and protection of tenants. Section 6 of the Kerala Stay of Eviction Act, 1957, provides that notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any Act, or any other provision of the , or any other law, or any contract, or in the any judgment, decree, order or order of a court, any land which has become the property of such other person as a consequence of any judgment, order or decree of any court or order of the court, any such person shall be deemed, to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was continuously in occupation of land for not more than ten years.

The appellants, who were the President of the Association of the respondent No. 1, were the President and the Secretary of the Association. The appellants, who was the President of a firm, filed a suit for accounts of the Association and for accounts of its members. The suit was contested by the appellants on the ground that the Association was not a legal Association within the meaning of section 4 of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935, and the appeal was not maintainable by reason of the provisions of section 4 Of the Rewa State companies Act, 1935. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the appellants had a right to bring a suit for account of the Association which was dissolved in February 1948. The appellants appealed to this Court. Held, that the appellants were not entitled to any relief on the allegations made as the courts could not adjudicate in respect of the partnership transactions and transactions. The suit for accounts must fail. The appellants were not bound by the Charter from the Durbar and the appeal must fail. It was not open to the appellants to resist the proceedings on the ground of illegality in the contract of partnership on which they sues were entitled to any reliefs on the allegations contained in the plaint. The appellants had a legal right to bring the suit for accounts. The suit must fail. Held, further, that the appeal must be dismissed. The appellants could not be allowed to raise the preliminary objection on the ground, of illegality in a contract of partnership. The appellants did not have a legal right of bringing a suit for the accounts of the association which was in existence at the relevant period for which accounts were asked. The suit could not be dismissed on the ground Of illegality in the contracts of partnership on the ground (1) that the Association had been formed in contravention of section 4(2) of the Rewa States Companies Act, which was in force at the relevant time; (2) that the appellants could not claim any relief on their allegations as the courts cannot adjudicate in respect Of the partnership transactions; (3) that the suit for account must fail.

The respondents were charged with offences under section 9(1) read with section 9(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, and were charged with having committed offences under section 120B, IPC. The respondents were charged under section 120 B, IPC, and section 120B read with section 34, IPC. They were charged with the offences under section 420, IPC, section 120B and section 420 IPC. The trial court acquitted the respondents. The High Court, however, set aside the order of acquittal and directed the Magistrate to proceed with the case. The High court, however, quashed the proceedings of the Magistrate taking cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of process against the respondents. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was persuaded to the view that this was a case to which section 210(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 was attracted and that as an investigation by the police was in progress in relation to the same offence the Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police; and that the learned Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of an offence under section 500, IPC. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was justified in quashing the proceedings of Magistrate taking cognizance. [463D] 1.2 The High Court will be justified in quashing proceedings in exercise of its powers under section 482 of the Code. [463E] 1.3 The High Court would be justified in quash the proceedings in exercise o f its powers under Section 482 of the Act. [463F] 1.4 The High Court should have exercised its powers under the Code of Civil Procedure, 1973, and not under section 482, Cr. P.C. [463G] 1.5 The High Court could, on its own, exercise the powers under section482 of the Code, exercise its powers under sections 482 and 482 of the Criminal Procedure Code. [464D] 1:1. The High Courts will be justified, in quashing the proceeding in exercise of their powers under section 561A, Cr.P.C. in cases where the acts alleged to constitute a contempt of a subordinate court are punishable as offences under specific provisions of the Indian Penal Code. [467E] 1:2. The High Cou rt will be justified if no offence is made out then the High Court will, be justified in quashed the proceedings in exercising its powers under s.482 of the Criminal P.C., in cases where there is no prior conviction and sentence for an offence under the Indian Penal code. [463H] 1:3. The High Curt will be justified to quash the proceedings of a Magistrate taking cognizance in the matter of an offence. [463A] 1:4.

The petitioner was convicted by the Chief Judicial Magistrate, Meerut for offences under sections 363, 366 and 376 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years. The petitioner filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The petitioner contended that the order of the Chief Judicial magistrate was illegal and that the Magistrate had no power to release the petitioner on his own bond. The High court dismissed the appeal, but the petitioner has obtained an order for bail in his favour. The petitioner has obtained special leave to appeal. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: The court should always bear in mind that monetary bail is not a necessary element of the criminal process and even if the amount of bail fixed by the Magistrate is not high, for a large majority of those who are brought before the courts in criminal cases are so poor that they would not abscond, he can safely release the accused on his own bonds without bail or on his own recognizance. [785B C] The court should also bear in mind the need for liberal interpretation of bail covering own bond and without sureties. [786C] The court must always bear in its mind that monetary Bail is not a relevant element of the Criminal process and even though the amount of the bail fixed by it is the reach of the law not the money tag. [787F] The best guarantee of the criminal justice is the reach and the reach of justice. The best guarantee is the reach, of the law, not the money- tag.
