In the assessment year 1951 52, the assessee claimed exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in the undertaking 'Eldee '. The Income tax Officer, Special Circle, Amritsar, and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the business of the two businesses 'Castle ' and 'Castles ' was a branch of the assessee and that the constitution of both the businesses 'CTHle ' and the ownership of the two undertakings being the same, the assessee was not entitled to include the amount of Rs. 3,21,460 in the computation of capital employed in 'Elder '. The Appellate Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to 'Castl ' and directed in elusion of the said amount to 'CTHl '. The High Court, on a reference, held that in the assessment for the year 1951 52 the income from 'Casts ' had not been computed and included in the assessment of the assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court had the power merely to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of the order of the Tribunal. The High court had the power to call upon the Tribunal to state a case and refer to it, if it, satisfied that the case in its view had been one of fact as it was based on some evidence to support the finding of the Tribunal on a question of law. [440 F] (ii) The High court has the power merelyto advise the Tribunal upon questions of law which arose out of the orders of the Tribunal, and also if the Tribunal has misdirected itself in law in arriving at its finding. The High, Court has the power to ask the Tribunal to. state the case if in its view a question of fact arises out of the decision of the Tribunal is based upon some evidence ignoring other essential matters. [441 C] (iii) The High Courts have the power merely because on a review of the evidence the Court might have arrived at a different conclusion. The High Courts, in the present case, have the power to advise the tribunal on questions of fact. [442 D] (iv) The High,Court has the power only to advise the tribunals on questions of facts, if there is some evidence to justify the finding of fact, if there are some evidence to supported the finding of Tribunal on a point of law. The High ' Court has the jurisdiction merely to advise it on questions of Law arising out of its order. [445 E] (v) The High 'Court has the jurisdiction to call upon it to state a particular case and refer it to the case. The High. Court has the powers merely to advise. The High , Court has the discretion merely to advise, but not to refer to a case. [446 F] (vi) The High.Court has the powers to advise the Tribunals on questions of laws arising out of an order of the tribunal.

The respondent was a party in the writ petition filed by the appellant. The Minister concerned was also directed to file his personal affidavit. The Minister was also directed that the Minister concerned might give a personal hearing to the parties and thereafter pass the necessary order in the matter. The Minister, however, did not file his personal affidavits. The Minister filed an affidavit in regard to the allegations made in the writ peti tion. The Minister made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 confirming the earlier seniority list. The Minister heard the parties and made a speaking Order on February 18. 1975 confirming the later seniority list. On February 18,1975 the Minister passed the order in the writ Petition. The Minister also directed that he should file his personal Affidavit. The Minister thereafter heard the parties. The Minister passed the necessary order on February 19, 1975 confirming that the Minister was a necessary party. The Minister then heard the parties, and made a reasoned order on February 20, 1975 confirming his earlier seniority list, and directed that the Secretary should file his affidavit in regard thereto. The Minister accordingly heard the parties on February 18 1975 and passed the necessary orders in the matter, and thereafter passed the necessary consequential order in the case. The Minister thereupon heard the parties in the matter and passed a speaking order. The Minister in charge of Irrigation Department was also directed by the High Court to file his affidavit. The respondent filed an affidavit on February 18 1974 confirming the earlier order of February 18, 1974 fixing the seniority of the engineers. The Minister did not file any affidavit in regard tain to the allegations in the writ application. The Minister who heard the parties submitted his personal affidavit on February 19 1975. The Minister recorded his personal affidavit and the Minister was also asked to file his own affidavit. The High Court, however, in its order dated February 18, 1976, observed that the Minister should file his own personal affidavit in regard lo the allegations made against the Minister concerned and as such the High Court was in error in directing that the Minister be impleaded as a party. The High court also directed that in the event the Minister concerned should file his sworn affidavit, the Minister concerned may give a personal hear ing to the parties. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Minister who was impleaded as a respondent in the writ proceedings was directed to file an affidavit in respect of the allegations made by the Minister concerned. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The direction for the impleading of the Minister as a party was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations in his petition. The Minister should file an affidavit. The Secretary concerned should file the affidavit in regard thereof. [97B] 2. The Minister must file his personal counter affidavit in regard whereto the Minister concerned was directed to place the allegations made. The Minister may file his personalaffidavit in regard to allegations made in his petition and thus to afford an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. [97C] 3.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of arrears of rent on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent from the respondent under section 259 of the Act on the ground of arrears of rents. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that arrears of rent due under a lease cannot be recovered under section 259. The High court held that arrears due under a contract of lease cannot be recoverable under section 259 and dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the rent in this case was not claimed by the Board under the Act or the Rules. [259 B] The words "rent on land and buildings" in section 259 of Act cannot be used to mean rent payable by the lessee. The words "amount due" in section 260 of the Act are wide enough to cover rent payable by a lessee. The word "amount due", in section 259, means the amount due as rent from the lessee. [259 C] The words 'amount due" are wide enough in the sense of rent. The word 'amount due ' in section 260, in the context of rent of land and buildings, means the rent payable by him in respect of such property, as it does not refer to rent. The words 'rent on land or buildings ' in section 259 must be construed in their widest sense. [259 D] The words used in section 259 are wide enough and they are not intended to cover rent of land or buildings. The word rent ' in section 258, in the sense in which it is used, is wide enough to include rent payable by lessee. The expression 'amount due in section 260 is wide enough in its amplitude to include rent of land, buildings or buildings. [259 E] The word 'compensation ' in section 261 is wide enough and it is not confined to rent of land. The word compensation ' in section 262 is wide enough. The word amount due in section 259 is wide enough, to include rent. The expression "amount due in the section" in section 261, in the wider sense, includes rent payable by lessor. The word money is wide enough not to include rent but it is wide enough for the purpose of the Act to include rent in the section. [259 G H] The word "compensation" in section 258 is wide enough so as to include rent which is payable by the lessor. The words in section 259 refer to rent of lands and buildings. The words are wide enough. [259 A] The word compensation is wide enough than the rent payable in section 260. The word is wide enough but it is not limited to rent. [259 F] The word rent is wide enough as to include the rent payable. The word in section 259 refers to rent of buildings or buildings and not to rent. In the present case, the rent in the case of rent of buildings and buildings was not claimed or recoverable under any express provision of the Act.

The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman in the respondent company. He was appointed as an Section Salesman for the districts of Bikaner, Ganganagar, Merta and Barmer. He was also appointed as a section salesman for the district of Bikaner, Merta, Merta. He was later appointed as a s Salesman for various districts. He was paid a sum equivalent to three years salary at the rate he was drawing when the appellant 's services were controlled by the head office of the company. The appellant was appointed on 12th July, 1973 as a section Salesman for certain number of local salesmen. He was given a commission of Rs. 2,000/ per month. The appellant 's service was controlled by the Head office of the Company. He was not paid any remuneration for the services of the Company and was not paid his remuneration. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the termination of his services. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Labour Court had given findings in favour of the appel lant on the question whether the termination of the services of his appellant by the respondent company was legal and justified and if not to what relief he was entitled to. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Labour Court has given findings in the favour of the appellant without any remedy at this stage. The finding of the Tribu nal on the nature of the work is a finding on a question of fact and it is also borne out by the document produced before the Labour Court. [474B C] 2. The Labour court has given findings on the question of fact. The finding on a fact is a finding of fact and the question whether it is a workman has to be decided by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the area of his operation. [474C] 3. The finding recorded by the Tribu lal on the question that the appellant was employed to do canvassing and promoting the sale of the product of the company in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company. None of the salesmen were employed to sell the product of a company in any specific area or collecting sale proceeds and deposit the same with it. The supervising work of the other local salesmen was part of his work considered by the Tribunal.

The Company was a Government lessee under section 181 of the M.P. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 (Act No. 66 of 1950) for the purpose of carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling sugar. The Company was a private limited company. The Company had been carrying on the said business. The Company, therefore, was not a Government lessee within the meaning of section 181 of M.P Land Revenue and Revenue Act, Sampattee. The Company filed a suit for eviction of the Company from the land in dispute on the ground that the Company had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue and Land Revenue Act, 1954. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the Company was not a 'Government lessee ' within the meaning Of section 181 of Madhya Pradesh Land revenue and Tenancy Act. The High court, however, dismissed the suit. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Company that the Company did not enjoy the status of Gairusi tenant and did not enjoy it as a 'pakka ' tenant. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the Company, was not an occupancy tenant under section 185 of the Code. [178G] 2. The High, however, was wrong in having recourse to the proceeding prescribed under section 182 of the Code and that the Company could not be evicted by the summary proceeding provided for under that section. [178H] 3. The High. Court was, therefore, in error in holding that in terms of sub section 2(i) of section 181, the Company was a 'phakka ' tenant '. [178A] 4. The High ' Court was, in error, completely unjustified and opposed to law.

The Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1965, was passed by the State Legislature in exercise of the power conferred by Part III of the Constitution. By section 1(3) of the Act, the State Government of the United State was formed. The Act was amended by Act 13 of 1965. By section 47 of the Act the State Government was empowered to make rules for the purpose of carrying out the provisions of the Act. The Act provided for the acquisition of certain land in an estate under the personal cultivation of a person who was in possession of the land. The Act came into force on July 1, 1949. The Act, however, provided for the payment of compensation to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the market value of the land but at fifteen times the fair and equitable rent was in consistent with article 3 1 A of the Constitution and the Act. By section 45 of the Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time direct. The Act also provided for the compulsory acquisition of land which may be laid only if the law providing for the acquisition by the State of any estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any portion of such land as is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force. The Act made a declaration that the land in question was liable to be acquired for the public purpose and that the notification was issued in exercise of that power. The appellants contended that the notification issued in exercise Of the power under section 1(1) of the Travancore Act 14 of 1124 (M.E.) was invalid and invalid as it was inconsistent with article 31(2) of the Constitution, and that the notifications were invalid. The High Court held that the notification did not contravene article 31(1) and that the appellants were entitled to compensation under the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The notification issued in the exercise of the powers under section 1 (3) of Act 14 of 1965 was not law in force. [924 C] (2) The notification was not a law in force when the United State came into force. The notification issued under section 1 of the Act was not a valid law in force, but was repealed by Act 15 of 1965. The notification was issued under section I(3) on the date appointed by the State Government by notification. The notification did not violate article 31(3) and was therefore invalid. [925 D] (3) The notification dated July 1, 1959 was not a notification under section 1. The notification dated August 1, 1959, was not a declaration under section 1 Of the Act. [926 E] (4) The notification did come into force on August 1, 1960, and the notification was therefore invalid on the ground that it was inconsistent. [927 C] (5) The notification under section I of the Act did not contravene the provisions of article 31(4) of the constitution. [928 D] (6) The notification could not be questioned because section 1(4) was in operation on July 1. 1949. [929 E] (7) The notification in question was not a statute in force when it was passed.

The widow of her husband, who was a widow of her deceased husband, was in possession of certain properties. The widow, after the death of her husband and after the death, became the absolute owner of the properties. The property was sold by the widow of her father to the widow, and the widow was given a limited interest in the property. The widow was in possession and enjoyment of the properties and she was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Hindu law. The widow filed a suit for a declaration that the reversion of her husband to her husband 's estate was in violation of the Hindu Law and for a declaration to that effect. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, on appeal, held that the widow was in the position of a Hindu widow and that on a surrender by her of her husband ' estate, the reversionary right of the reversions could not be defeated by a surrender made by the widow. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The widow was not an alienation and as the reversioner did not derive her title from her, there was no principle of law under which the acts of the widow could bind her self effacement by the widow could not be surrendered to the reversioner. [355 E] (ii) The reversionary right to recover possession of the property during the entire period of the widow 's natural life is not an alienation but an alienation which she has made herself. The reversionary rights of the widow were not extinguished by a surrender on the part of the widow. [355 G] (iii) The reversion of the widow to her husband was not an absolute act on the part, of the widow, but was an act of self effatification by the widow, which no doubt was not an alienations. [355 A] (iv) The reversion was not an act of an alienation and the reversioner did no longer acquire title by adverse possession against her. The reversion of her widow to her estate was not an incident of a voluntary act on the whole of the widow and she was not under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate. [355 B] (v) The reversion is not an incident or an act of fraud or collusion that might arise, be in a position to recover possession from the widow ' of her husband or her estate at all and, therefore, could not be surrender to the reversioner merely because the widow was not in the position to recover the possession of the properties during the entire term of her widow. [356 E] (vi) The reversion to the widow 'of her husband ' s estate at all was not an ex parte act on the ground of fraud or connivance that might arise. [355 D] (vii) The reversion must take place subject to such prior interest. The reversion is a voluntary act of self repre sentation which she has rendered.

The appellant, a Director of the respondent Company, was appointed as a Receiver in respect of the Cotton Mills. He made a further order under section 149 of the Land Revenue Act read with section 5 of the U.P. Government Electrical Undertakings (Dues Recovery) Act, 1958 appointing a Receiver in the respect of the cotton Mills. The appellant, a director of the respondent company, was appointed a Receiver in terms of the order of the High Court. The Receiver filed a suit for a declaration that the order of attachment was illegal and void. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The High Court, however, held that the order was an order in the nature of a charging order and that the suit was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the order passed by the Collector being an order in nature of a charge, the Receiver had obtained an equitable right in the shares in question and there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the Cotton Mills Company had lost its right to the shares pledged in its favour. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The charge order under the English Law is not the same as an attachment of property or appointment of a Receiver under the Land Revenue Code. The charge is not the one which is attached by the Collector, that a charge is the same as a attachment of property and appointment of a receiver under the Land revenue Act. [877 D] 2. The charge under the English law is not the former but the latter. The charge in the present case is the same. The charge was not the same. [878 D] 3. The charge against the appellant was that the appellant had lost its rights to the shares in the Polytex Company held by the Cotton Mills, the Cotton Mill, and the manner in which those voting rights were to be exercised was to be determined by the Board of Directors. The appellant had lost his right to the share pledged in its name. [879 E] 4. The High court was right in holding that the attachment of the shares in Polytex Company was not the property of the Cotton Mill. [880 F] 5. The High. Court was right in not holding that the order under the Indian Law was an order of attachment of property. [882 F] 6. The High, Court was right. [886 A] 7. The High Courts were right in holding, that the attachment was not the proper or equitable right of the Cotton Company to vote at the meetings of the company or to issue a notice under section 169 of the Act. [820 G] 8. The High 'Court was right in taking the view that the attachment had lost its legal right to the equity in question and the High Court was right, in holding that it had no bearing on the case before it.

The petitioners filed a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat, Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala, District Sangrur in the State of Punjab (hereinafter referred to as 'the Panchayat ') had no sort of right in the suit land and that the suit land had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat. The trial court dismissed the suit. The petitioners filed a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed. Hence this petition by special leave. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the suit was not maintainable before the civil court. [836C] 2. The plaintiffs who claimed to be the owners along with some other of the suit lands had not claimed a declaration that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat deh. They had also questioned the correctness of the entries in the revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the suit land. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by drawing their Plaint cleverly claim that the land belonged to it. [837F] 3. The plaintiffs had no right or title in it. They had no right to claim any right or interest in it. The plaintiffs have no right or interest. They had not claimed that the suit property belonged to it or that it did not belong to the Gram Panchayat. The plaintiffs could not by drawing their own plaint cleverally by drawing their written statement inter alia pleaded that the land was shamlat deh and that the plaintiffs had no sort or right in it. [820H] 4. The plaintiffs were not entitled to the relief claimed by them. The plaintiffs did not claim any right, title or interest in the suit property. They had merely claimed a declaration in their favour that the land had been validly vested in the Panchayat. They had expressly claimed that the land which had been vested in the Gram Panchayat had expressly claimed the suit land as shamlat. They had, however, questioned the correctness and the correctness of entries in the Revenue records which showed the that the Panchayat had expressly asserted that the land belongs to it. The High court held in the circumstances of that case that the suit had been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat. [838F] 5. The plaintiffs are not entitled to any relief. The plaintiffs can by drawing their suit cleverly seek a declaration that their land was shamot deh. They have, however, challenged the correctness of entry in the revenue record which showed that it belonged to the Panchayat and had expressly claimed a declaration. [839G] 6. The plaintiffs, therefore, cannot by drawing the plaint cleverfully claim that the suit is not shamlat deh conferred jurisdiction on the civil court when by virtue of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 (Punjab Act No. 10 of 1961) the jurisdiction of civil courts to try such suits had been taken away.

The respondent Board issued a notice to the appellant Board under Section 49(1) of the Andhra Pradesh Electricity Supply Undertakings (Acquisition) Act, 1976 to show cause why the Board should not pay interest on the security deposit. The appellant Board filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The High court held that the Board was not entitled to levy interest on the amount of security deposit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Board that the Board had no authority to levy interest. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumer in trust with the Board to secure the payment of consumption charges. The liability to pay interest to the consumer in respect of the consumption security deposit has a direct bearing on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. [278C] 1.2 The levy of interest on the amounts due to the Board is not arbitrary or unreasonable. The levy of the interest is not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. [278D] 1.3 The levy of a penalty is not arbitrary. The levy is not arbitrary but is based on a commercial transaction. The levy has a direct impact on the operation of the Board. The levy does not contemplate appropriation. It stands to reason that if there is a revision in the rate of tariff there must be an upward revision in the consumption security deposits since it has direct bearing to the level of supply in the context of wide scale theft of energy, tempering with the meters and such other methods adopted by the consumers. The levy cannot be struck down as arbitrary on the basis of a commercial transaction governing a bank deposit. [278E F] 1.4 The levy of penalty is not unreasonable. It is not unreasonable as to shock or shock the conscience. The levy, therefore, is not arbitrary and unreasonable. [278F] 1.5 The levy of additional security deposit is not arbitrary, but is based upon a commercial transaction governed by a commercial transaction which operates harshly on a small section of the public. [278G] 1.6 The levy of an additional security deposit with interest at the rate of 3 per cent was made in January 1987. The demand for payment of interest was made in February 1987. The revision in the form of an additional Security deposit with interest was made on June 30, 1987. The rate of interest was fixed at the rate applicable to the consumer. The rate was fixed at 3 per cent. The revision was made in the form as a result of the revision in the price of electricity. The rate for the consumption of electricity was fixed at Rs.

The petitioners are members of the Telecommunication Research Centre under the Telecommunication Department of the Government of India. They are working as Assistants in the Telecommunication Organisation. The petitioners are members in the Telecommunications Research Centre under Recruitment Rules, 1962. The petitioners belong to the Indian Telecommunications Service Group A and Group B Field Officers who are working in the Tele Communication Research Centre under recruitment Rules, 1962 and are working in Telecommunications. The petitioners have raised two grounds, namely, the denial of Special Pay to the direct recruits and the transfer of Group B Field officers recruited through the Union Public Service Commission after a rigorous competition examination followed by an interview followed by an written examination followed by interview followed by interview, and the petitioners belong to this category. The petitioners also raised two grounds namely, (i) the denial of special pay to the direct recruit and the transfer from the Indian Telecommunication Research Center to the Telecommuni cation Centre is not grant ing them the same special pay which is granted to the trans ferred officers who are direct recruits working in the Telecom Research Centre; and (ii) the transfer of the Group B Field Officer recruited through the union Public Service Commission without the Special Pay is sought to be justified by the Government in the Counter affidavit filed by the Government. The petitioners contended that the denial of the Special Pay to direct recruits was mala fide and was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. The petitioners further contended that the discrimination between direct recruits and direct recruits was sought to be justify by the Government and that the denial was mala fide. The petitioners submitted that the denial to the Special Pay was mala fide, and was violative o f Article 14 of Consti tution. The petitioners raised two grounds: (i) The denial of Special pay to the promotees was mala fide; and (2) the denial was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India. The petitioners ' contention was that the denial is mala fide. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The denial of special Pay to the promotees is mala fide and is violative of Article 16 of the Consti tive. The denial is mala fides. The denial was mala fides. [1010C] 2. The denial to the special pay is mala fide, mala fide and has been made mala fide. [1011D] 3. The denial in the counter affidavit filed by respondent No. 1 is mala fide; the denial is not mala fide. It is not the case of the Government that the petitioners are not competent and are not able to discharge their duties. All the direct recruits to the same pay are entitled to the Special pay. [1012E] 4. The denial by the Government of the Special pay to direct recruits working throughout the Telecommunication Centre is mala fide because the transfer of officers from the Indian Telecom Service to the Telecommunication Institute is not in their general line. The denial has been mala fide. There is no justification to deny the Special Pay. [1013G H] 5. The denial on the ground of mala fide is not mala fides. It is a matter of record that the petitioners were not able to perform their duties. The denial does not amount to mala fide. They are not entitled to any Special Pay but the transferred officers have to perform in the Tele communication Research Centre which are not in their General line. [1014H; 1015A] 6. The denial cannot be said to be mala fide. A person who is not a direct recruit cannot claim the same pay at the same rates at which it is paid to the direct ent recruits. [1015B] 7.

The appellant was employed as a driver in the respondent company. He was dismissed from service on the ground that he had failed to comply with the provisions of section 42(4) of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act, 1946. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending inter alia that the third respondent had failed to observe the provisions of the Act in that he did not make an application under section 42(1) of the Act for relief under section 8(1) D. The Labour Court held that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42(2) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour Court for relief under Section 8(1). The appellant preferred a writ petition to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the third Respondent had failed to follow the provisions of Section 42(4), including the proviso to sub section (4) of section 42, and that the third and the third respondents had failed to do so in that they did not make any application under section 43(4) including the Proviso before the Labour Court. HELD: (i) The scheme of the Act is that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side side by all this step by all this steps. The scheme of section 7(1) is that disputes which should be settled in respect of matters covered by section 42(I) should be settled by a direct reference to the Labour court. [707 D] (ii) The scheme is that disputes must be settled as expeditiously as possible and exclusively through conciliation and settlement agreement. The scheme is a part of the scheme of the Industrial Disputes Act. The scheme has been arrived at in respect of disputes falling under clause (a) of sub section (1) of section 78. The scheme does not stand on the same footing as that of a settlement under section 7(2). [707 G] (iii) The scheme has to be worked out in accordance with the provisions contained in the Act. The Scheme of the Act has to be implemented in the light of the provisions contained therein. [708 A] (iv) The scheme must be worked out by a competent authority. The scheme must first be made by the employer intending to effect any change in respect of any order passed by the employer under standing orders applicable under the Act. [709 C] (v) The scheme should be worked out on an application made by any of the parties to the dispute. The scheme should first be made in the prescribed form and from time to time. [710 D] (vi) The scheme shall be worked out and the application to the labour court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute and no agreement had been arrived at. [711 E] (vii) The scheme was not in accordance with law. The scheme was arrived at in accordance with section 7(4) and the award of the Labour Court was set aside.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were occupying the property under a registered lease for a period of 20 years which expired on 31.7.1971. The appellants ' application under section 12 of the Act was allowed and an appeal therefrom filed by the respondents was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner. The appellants filed a revision petition before the High Court which was dismissed by a Single Judge. The appellants then moved the Patna High Court in its revisional jurisdiction under section 12. The appellants contended that the application under section 13 of the Act before the Munsif was not maintainable before the Civil Court and the High Court was in error in holding otherwise. The appellants also contended that the respondents were occupying the premises under a registered Lease for a period 20 years which expires on 31.07.1971 and that the appellants would have to make another application under section 11 of the Act for evicting the respondents if they did not vacate within the time allowed by the court. The Single Judge dismissed the revision petition. The appellants preferred a Letters Patent Appeal before the Division Bench which allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Single Judge. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The proceedings have to be treated as a suit and the judgment of a learned Munsif as a decree therein. The question does not affect the substantive right of the parties as the judgment of an appellate court in favour of the appellants. The question is whether the petition which was filed by the appellants as an application under section12 of the Act is not maintainable in the facts and circumstances of the case. The question whether the petition was filed by a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term tenancy, and it is for him to choose which course to follow. The question, whether the petition filed by the appellant as an application for eviction under section 12 is wholly inapplicable in the facts of the case, as the respondents, did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent 's election of the Secretary of the Society, alleging that the respondent 'as the Secretary of a Society was elected as the Secretary of that Society. The trial court decreed the suit and the appellant 's appeal was dismissed by the High Court. The appellant 's revision application to the High Court was also dismissed by the District Judge. The High Court, however, held that the appellant ' s application filed under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. The appellant Society challenged the order before the High Court by a petition under section 15 of the Code. The High court, however, dismissed the revision application holding that the appellant had no locus standi to withdraw the suit. The appellant filed a petition under Section 15 of the Civil Procedure Code for restoration of the suit. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the application under section 15 was not maintainable, and the High Court had rightly held that the only remedy of the appellant was to file a fresh suit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The application under section 14 of the Code is not maintainable. It is a well settled principle of law that the inherent power of the court under section 15 is not to be exercised in a routine manner. It is not necessary that the court should be satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree on a fraudulent repre sentation to it that the party had actually consented to it. [237A B] 1.2 The High Court was wrong in dismissing the appellant ' application as not maintainable. [237B] 1.3 The High Court had committed serious errors in deciding the question as to who was the duly elected Secretary of the appellant Society and had, therefore, full authority to withdraw the case of the appellant at all and the impugned order was passed as a result of the court being misled. [237C] 1.4 The High Court has rightly held that in the exercise of inherent power under section 15, the trial court has no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting withdrawal of the suit under its inherent power, if it is ultimately satisfied that the compromise petition filed in the case was true that Hari Narain Swami was not the Secretary of appellant Society and was, therefore, not authorised to withdraw the same. [237D] 1.5 The High Court rightly held that only remedy of a party is to institute a suit. The High Courts were, therefore, wrong in dismissing a appellant 's application as not competent to withdraw the appeal. [237F] 1.6 The High Court in the exercise Of inherent power under Section 15 1 of Civil Procedure Code, a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it. The High Cou rt was wrong in holding that the application of the appellant under Section 15 was not competent to file a suit. [237G] 1.7 The High Court erred in holding that in the exercising inherent power under its inherent powers under section 15 I of the Code, the trial Court had no jurisdiction to cancel the order permitting withdrawal. [237H; 237A] 1.8 The High Court committed serious errors of law in deciding the matter in favour of the respondent ' s case.

The appellant was a company carrying on business in the name and style of "The Indian Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, and was a company incorporated in the Indian Burma (Fmergency Provisions), Act, 1940. The appellant was a firm carrying on business as a dealer in the name of "The Burma (Eachmergency Provisions Act, 1940". The appellant was the managing agent of the Burma (Echmergency Provisions). The appellant was appointed as the managing agent and was appointed as managing agent of Burma (Ethmergency Provisions and Burma (Embmergency Provisions ) Act, 1940 by the Government of India. The appellant, who was the managing agents of the Burma, was appointed as an managing agent of a company. The appellant filed a complaint against the company and the company and its managing agent for the alleged contravention of the provisions of the Act. The company contended that the Ordinance was not a law within the meaning of article 12 of the Constitution and that the Ordinance had been promulgated in exercise of the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of Indian India and Burma (Fixation of Emergency) Order, 1946, in spite of the words "for the space of not more than six months from its promulgation " in spite of this words "for not more than 6 months from its enactment " in spite Of the words " for the space of less than six months" in section 72 of that Act, the Ordinance had ceased to be in operation after April 1, 1946, and that the Act was not a valid law within the scope of article 12. Held, that the Ordinance having continued in operation even after the declaration of the emergency having come to an end, the Ordinance in question was not limited to the space of more than six month from its promulgation but was perpetual in its duration with the result that it continued in operation only after April 1. 1946, and not after April 1 , 1946, and the Ordinance having ceased to be effective after April 1., 1946, the said notes continued to be ineffective as legal tender in India, though the position in Jammu and Kashmir in regard to the same could not be affected by reason of the words 'for not more more than sixmonths from its promulgation '. The Ordinance having continued to be in force even after the declarations of the emergency had come to an "continuance" of the Ordinance in respect of the same could no longer be affected by the words "For the space of the not more than four months from its commencement" in section 3 of that Act. The Ordinance had continued in operation in spite of its words restored to its original position after April 1 1946, and it was perpetual in Its duration with the consequence that it continued to be operative in operation even before April 1, 1947, and that it continued till it was repealed.

The appellant was a dealer in a cinema theatre. He was suspended on 30th September, 1953, by the Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., Lucknow, on the ground that he had entered into partnership with others, under the name of Gautam Cycle Mart, Meerut, in 1939, in contravention of the Government Servants ' Conduct Rules. The appellant was placed under suspension on 30th November, 1953, on the basis of a preliminary enquiry conducted into some of the matters mentioned in the charges. The appellant challenged the order of suspension on the ground, inter alia, that the order passed by the Commissioner was void and inoperative. The High Court dismissed the application for revocation of special leave. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the questions raised by the appellant depended on findings of fact and that the appellant had been exonerated of the charges involving corruption and violation of service rules. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to meet a new case or not was essentially a question of fact. The question whether a departmental proceeding was null and void depends on findings of facts. The question of fact is essentially a question which could be raised on behalf of a person who had been convicted of a criminal charge involving corruption in the discharge of his duties that he was given the lesser punishment of demotion and neither dismissed nor removed from service. [583H; 584A B] (2) The question of prejudice to a departmental proceeding is a question of law. The question is essentially a mixed question of fact and it is not necessary for the High Court to decide whether the departmental proceedings were null and void. [583B C] (3) The question is one of fact. It is only when an opportunity is denied to the appellant that it can be said that the departmental proceedings are null and void and the result of the trial is that it goes to the root of the jurisdiction and the conduct of the trial. [583F] (4) The question as to whether the departmental proceeding was void or not depends on findings on facts. The test is whether the departmental enquiry was null and the result thereof was materially affected. [583G] (5) The question that arose for consideration was whether the departmental action was null and invalid. The question was whether the appellant had made a reasonable opportunity of being heard and to be heard. The question as regards the validity of the departmental proceedings was not raised before the High Court. [583C] (6) The question was not raised in the first regular enquiry in the course of which charges were actually framed as a result of any previous enquiry. The question that fell for consideration was not whether the departmental inquiry was null and/or void. The question which arose for consideration in the second regular enquiry was whether the disciplinary proceedings were null. The question, therefore, was whether the enquiry was vitiated by the failure of the officers to report that earlier charges had been framed. [583D E] (7) The question, whether the appellant could have been permitted to meet a case in the course at which the departmental proceedings had been initiated, was one of fact and the High Court was right in holding that the departmental enquiry had been held as a result thereof. [583E] (8) The question which fell for consideration in this case was whether the Departmental proceedings were null or void. The appellant had been acquitted of the charges of corruption involving corruption in his discharge of his duty that he was giving the lesser punishment. The question for consideration was, whether the departmental authorities were justified in holding that there was no violation of the mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi 521 Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. He was terminated by letter dated 12th October, 1974 with effect from 19th October,1974 with effect from 1st October, 1974. He challenged the termination of his service by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court held that the termination of service of the appellant was not automatically effective by a certain date as set out in the order of appointment it would nonetheless be a retrenchment within the meaning of section 2(oo) and in the absence of strict compliance with the requirements of section 25F, termination was held to be invalid. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the termination was not automatically valid by a certain day as set out therein and that the termination could not be said to be a retrenchment under section 2(o) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The termination of service is not a retrenchment within section 2(O) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The termination is not a termination simpliciter but a discharge of a temporary employee, and the declaration follows that the workman concerned continues to be in service with all consequential benefits. [529B] 2. The termination was not a retrenchment under the Act. The termination must be held to be valid only by a certain event or an accident or an accident. The termination does not involve any termination of service. The termination in the instant case was not a termination simplicitor but a discharge simpliciter. The termination did not involve any retrenchment. The termination, therefore, was not a dismissal simpliciter. [530C D] 3. The termination by itself was not a discharge simpliciter but a termination simpliciter. The appellant was not a workman within the meaning section 2(u) of the and the termination of the service of the respondent was ab initio void. [531D] 4. The termination having been made without any notice or opportunity to the respondent, the termination of services of the appellant could not be held to have been invalid. [532D] 5. The termination being illegal, the appellant was entitled to reinstatement with all consequential benefit. [533E] 6. The termination order of the appellant is void and inoperative. The declaration follows that he continues to be a workman in service with no other benefits.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953, and was confirmed on March 17, 1955. He was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the Settlement Officer 's report with which the finding was based, the appellant was not liable to be dismissed or removed from service. The appellant applied to the High Court for a writ under article 226 of the Constitution quashing the order of dismissal from service and the High Court held that the order of termination was in contravention of article 311(2) of the Constitution as no reasonable opportunity to show cause against the order of removal was given to him. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court. Held, that the order passed by the Settlement Officer was in contravention to article 311(1) of the constitution and the appellant was entitled to the protection of article 311 (2) of Constitution. The order of termination of service was passed without affording him an opportunity to make his defence and it was not a punishment. The order was not a penalty. The appellant was not entitled to the benefit of article 311 of the Constitution. The appellant had no right to hold the post he was occupying and by the impugned order the termination of his employment was not a dismissal. The appellant, therefore, was not liable for any evil consequences of his appointment. The order passed by him was not a termination simpliciter. The appellant could not be said to have been a probationer. The order did not amount to a penalty. It was not a case of misconduct. The order could not be regarded as one by way of punishment. The appellant did not have the opportunity to make a representation against the order. The order had been passed without affording the appellant an opportunity of making his representation. The order must be held to be one by way Of punishment. The termination of service of the appellant was by way of penalty, because it put a stigma on his competence and thus affects his future career of the public servant by the order terminating his employment. The order terminating his service was passed by the appellant without giving him an opportunity of being heard. The order made by the Settlement officer was not a valid order. The appellant 's case was not covered by article 311(3) of theConstitution. The order, therefore, could not be sustained.

The appellant, a Public Service Commission, was appointed by the State Government to the posts of Professors in the colleges. The appellant was appointed by a Committee consisting of three members, one of whom was the Chairman of the Commission and the other one of whom, was the Chairman. The appellant, who was the Chairman, was appointed the Chairman of a Committee. The Committee was to consist of two members, one from the Chairman and the other from the Chairman. In the year 1969, the State Government issued a notification under section 133 of the Constitution of Jammu and Kashmir, which provided that the Public Service Commission shall be consulted on the suitability of the candidates for promotion to the posts. The appellant challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that the Commission was consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making appointments to civil services and posts and in making promotions to the posts and in effecting promotions to the civil services and post and in making appointments, promotions to the post of Professors were not made by the Commission. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Public Services Commission was consulted only in regard to principles to be adopted in making appointments and transfers and that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court erred in holding that the Commission had not consulted either in regard to any principles to be taken in making appointments or transfers. The Commission was consulted on the eligibility of the candidates to the posts, and that the Selection Committee 's report was formally submitted to the Commission under the Chairman 's note dated June 2, 1969, and the Commission was therefore consulted on the fitness of the candidates. [875F G] (2) The Commission was not consulted either on the suitability or suitability of the selected candidates for promotion as Professors and the second requirement of clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 133 was also complied with.

The petitioner was a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly. He was elected as a member of a Legislative Assembly. The petitioner was elected as the member of the Legislative Assembly. On the question whether the petitioner was entitled to the privileges of a House of Commons, the Court ^ HELD: (i) The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the provisions of the Constitution. The privilege conferred upon the Legislature of the State is subject only to the provisions in the Constitution. [603 B] (ii) The privilege of preventing the publication of its proceedings without the authority of the House to be expunged is not preserved despite the provisions of article 194(3) of the Constitution, and, as in this case, the petitioner is not alleged to have done so, the Legislature has no power to take any action in respect of the said publication. [604 C] (iii) The privilege to prevent the publication of the proceedings directed by the Speaker to be expunged cannot be said to have been conferred on the legislature of a State. [605 D] (iv) The Legislature has the privilege of preventing publication of its Proceedings without the authority or the House has never formally rescinded the orders from which time to time it has made with regard to the publication of that part of the proceedings ordered by the Speaker. [606 E] (v) The privilege under article 194(1) is preserved despite the provision of article 194 (3) of that article. [607 D] (vi) The privilege is preserved despite article 194(2) of the constitution. [608 E] (vii) The privilege granted to the Legislature of India under article 194 (1) is protected despite the provisions Of article 194(4) of the . [608 D] (viii) The privilege given to the Legislature under article 194 is preserved despite Article 194(3). [608 F] (ix) The privilege which the Legislature has under article 194 has the power to prevent the publications of its proceedings, or at any rate of the expunged portions of it, the Legislature of any State in India has also a similar privilege or power to prevent publication of its proceeding without the authority thereof. [609 E] (x) The privilege in article 194(5) is preserved notwithstanding the provisions of Article 194(1).

The Government of Orissa took over the management of the College on and from March 9, 1971, and a formal agreement was executed between the managing committee of the College and the Governor of the State. The Government of Orissa, after taking over the management, took over the College on March 9,1971, and appointed a formal agreement. The Government, however, prescribed the qualifica tions for appointment as Readers in the private colleges in the town of Behrampur, Ganjam District, Orissa. The Government prescribed the qualifi cial qualifications for appointment as Reader in the private college. The Government also prescribed the quali cial qualification for appointment as Professor in the private College. The Government issued a formal agreement on July 30, 1970, and a regular agreement was executed on July 30. 1970, and the formal agreement was signed between the managing Committee of the College, and the Governor. The Government then issued a formal order on July 30 1970, appointing the respondents as Readers in different faculties in the private Colleges in the town. The respondents challenged the validity of the said order by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the respondents were not entitled to be appointed as Readers in a private college. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court erred in directing the Government to take into account the experience as a Reader in the college and that the High court erred in directing that the Government should take into account, as experience, the service of the respondents while they were in the private institution, first time presented before this Court, the teaching experience of the Readers in the college on the date of taking over.
