The High Courts erred in directing appointment of the respondents as Reader in private colleges in spite of the fact that they were drawing a salary of less than Rs.600/ on the date when taking over were in receipt of pay of Rs.600. [776F] 3. The High Cou rt erred in directing to take into consider the experience as the Reader in a college. [778F] 4.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) A of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Act, 1939. The State Transport Authority, the Regional Transport Authority, Allahabad, rejected the applications of the appellants on the ground that the route in question was an inter regional route and therefore an application for temporary permits was not made by the Corporation. The State Government, however, rejected the appellants ' applications. The appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the State Transport Authority and the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the route was an inter Regional route and therefore the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Courts fell into an error by interpreting section 68 F (1 A) C. The State transport Authority, the State Transport Tribunal and the State Appellate Tribunal fell into an erroneous error by interpreting Section 68 F(2) C.P.C. and that the High Court fell into an wrong error by interpreting the section 68 F. The State of U.P., the Regional Transport Authorities and the State Transport Authorities have power under sub section (1 C) to grant temporary permits to any one else. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State, Transport Authority, and the Regional Transport Officer, are entitled to grant temporary permit. The State Road Transport Authority, in exercise of power conferred by section 68 F, can grant temporary permits only to persons who are willing to obtain temporary permits. The State or the Regional Transport authority, as the case may be, in exercise Of power conferred by sub section (l C) to order temporary permits, once the Corporation made an application for the temporary permits, the State or the Transport Authority as the case might be, will have to examine the application for temporary permit and if such application is made by the corporation and section 68 F is squarely attracted. [985 D F] 2. The State ' Transport Authority, while considering the applications of other appellants for the remaining 4 vacancies and grant four permits according to law, has to consider the applications of each of the appellants for the balance remaining permits. The appellants have to apply for temporary permits only after the Corporation made its application for the remaining remaining permits. [986 D] 3. The State has power under sub s. (1 C ) to grant temporary temporary permits not for the full strength but something short it there was no power left in 985 the State Transport authority to grant temporary or permanent permits. The Corporation was not entitled to grant any temporary permits. [ 986 D] 4. The State Govt. has power under section 68F(1 C) of the U P. Motor Vehicles Rules, 1939 to grant temporary stage permits. The Regional Transport Authority or the Regional transport Authority as the situation may be, can grant only temporary permits for the full number of vehicles operating on the route for which the scheme is published. The State as the case maybe will have to consider the application for the balance of the permits. But if the Corporation is willing to operate on the route, then the State Transport Undertaking will have to grant temporary and permanent permits. But, if the Corporation applied for all the permits, the Corporation would be entitled to all the temporary permits and the Corporation will have to apply only for the remaining permits. But the Corporation will not be entitled to any temporary permits because in respect of the remaining strength there would be no application by the Corporation and section 68F (1 A ) to the exclusion of any other applicant. [987 E F] 5. The State is not entitled to any permanent permit. The Corporation is not entitled under section 68G(1 A) to the exclusion.

The appellant, a son of the respondent, was the son of the appellant. He died in the year 1947. The respondent 's father, who was the son, died in the years 1947. The appellant 's father died in the meantime. The respondent, who was a son of his maternal grandfather, filed a suit for a declaration that the property inherited by him from his maternal grandfather was ancestral property and that the appellant was entitled to recover possession of the same from the respondent. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the property in suit could be held to be ancestral property between the appellant and respondent 10. The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court. The question for determination was whether the property in the suit could be said to be ancestral properties between the appellant, and respondent 10, and so it allowed the appeal preferred by respondents 1 to 9 and dismissed the appellant 's suit. Held, that the decision of the Full Bench in Narotam Chand 's case (2) was wholly unsustainable as a decision on the question of law was not binding on the High Court. The decision of the High Court was wholly unsustainable. The decision in Narotham Chand 's Case (2) did not rest upon any evidence relating to custom. The decision was not based on any evidence relating thereto. The decision on the doctrine of stare decisis was not binding. The decision did not rest on any evidence regarding custom. The law on the question was not binding as the decision of this Court in Narotappa vs Musammat Thakri (I.L.R. , followed.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum, for offences under section 449 and section 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The appellants were tried for offences under sections 449 and 302 read with section 149 of the Indian penal Code and for two years under section 449 of the Indian Evidence Act. The appellants contended that the charge under section 449 was not sustainable in law. The High Court rejected the contention and convicted the appellants under section 449. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The charge under section 307 read and section 34 of Indian Penal Code is not sustainable in the law. The fact that the offence was committed by a number of persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed the entire criminal act. The position is that each individual act of a person in furtherance of his common intention of All, the legal consequences that are mentioned in the section and so, where the act is done by a number or persons jointly, it can have no application. But once it is decided that the act is so done by a person in pursuance of the common intent of all, it can no have application. [982 B C] (ii) The position is in no way when different persons are acting jointly in furtherance of common intention of each, the legal principle that each person must be held to be jointly in furtherance and in furtherance of their common intention of both. The position in law is that each one person shall be holding to have committed an offence punishable with imprisonment for life or to suc h punishment as is hereinbefore mentioned. [983 C D] (iii) The position in the present case is that when it is found that the four appellants attacked Haji Ebrar Ali with the dagger on the neck as if the act had been actually committed or not, the house trespass was committed. The position was in no way different when Matiullah was not acting alone but several others were acting jointly in pursuance of their common intent of both. So, he became punishable under section 307 of the Indian P.C. for injuring Ebrar.

The appellant, a Sarswat Brahmin, resident of Pathankot, filed a suit for a declaration of his title as collaterals within four degrees of Gurdial, and for a declaration that the properties in suit were not ancestral, and the respondent was not a collateral of the father who was the last male holder excluded the daughter from succession to the selfacquired property of her father. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, on appeal, held that the appellant was not a " collaterals" within the fourth degree and that the respondent was entitled to succeed to the self acquired property of her grandfather. The High court, however, held that there was no custom in the Gurdaspur district to exclude the collaterals from succession to their self acquired property. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the appellant had failed to discharge the onus that was thrown on her as a result of the production by the appellant of the Riwaj i am. of 1913 and which had been discredited in judicial proceedings and had been discounted in judicial proceedings. [153 C D] (ii) The appellant 's right to succeed to her father 's ancestral property was varied by a special local custom excluding the daughter which is binding on the parties. The appellant ' claim to have discharged this initial presumption of the general custom in favour of the daughter who is the res pondent. [153 D] (iii) The appellant had failed in proving the custom in favour or otherwise. The High, Court was right, in holding that there was a custom in the Pathankot district of Gurdaspur which was compiled by the appellant. [153 E] (iv) The appellant was not entitled to succeed in preference to collaterals even though they were within the fourth degrees. [153 F] (v) The appellant has failed to discharge this initial presumption. [153 G] (vi) The appellant, a sarswat Brahmins of Gurdaspur district prepared by Mr. Kennaway in 1913 and (2) by producing the Riwi am of 1913 and the same Riwaji am of the same Rivaji am, was not a reliable and trustworthy document. [153 A] (vii) The appellant could not succeed in preference only to collaterals. [153 B] (viii) The appellant cannot, therefore, succeed. [153 H] (ix) The appellant is not entitled to the declaration of his right to succeed in the suit. [153A] (x) The appellant must succeed. [155 B] (xi) The appellant can not, therefore, be allowed to succeed. [156 D] (xii) The appellant should succeed. [154 D] (xiii) The appellant would not, therefore be entitled to succeed. The appeal must accordingly be allowed.

The respondent was a Managing Agent of certain companies registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent was a managing agent of certain companies. The respondent, who was acting as Managing Agent of the companies, was acting as managing agents of several companies registered under section 5 of the Indian Companies Acts. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant and the Managing Agent of some of the companies for a declaration that the instrument was chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect of each of those capacities. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the instrument in question was a power of attorney and that the instrument could not be split up into separate instruments and that the respondent was not entitled to exercise all the powers in relation thereto. The High Court held in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The instrument in question did not comprise a single power of attorney liable for a single duty under article 48(d) (1) of the Schedule. The instrument in the present case did not comprise one matter but consisted one matter and that matter was the execution of a general power of attorney. The instrument was not one of the modes of exercising all the powers of attorney. It was within the very nature of the general power of Attorney executed by the respondent. [855 C D] (ii) The instrument was a single power and not a distinct matter. The instrument could not therefore be split up in separate instruments and could be split up only into separate instruments. [856 D] (iii) The instrument could be split into separate instruments only and not separate instruments. The instrument must be construed as distinct matters but that is the execution of general power of agent. The instrument cannot be split up as separate instruments. It is within the very essence of the general powers of attorney that all acts which the donor is capable of performing whether in his individual capacity or in his representative capacity as trustee, whatever be the capacity or capacities which he enjoys and cannot be splitup into separate instruments, and thus requiring the operation of section 5 would apply even when the instrument consists of several capacities. [857 E] (iv) The instrument must, therefore, be construed as separate matters but that does not mean that he is not entitled to exercising all these powers in relation to a distinct matter, and thus requires to be dealt with so as to attract the operation of the section. [858 C] (v) The instrument is a single power. It is a part of the general function of the attorney to act for him in all the capacities which he enjoyed and cannot be mixed up into separate instrument. The instrument is capable of forming one distinct matter and thus requiring to be dealt therewith. [859 D] (vi) The instrument cannot, therefore, split up into two separate instruments. A general power of GPA is not necessarily a part of a general function of a attorney. The fact that the instrument is executed by one person, if he fills a particular capacities, is not sufficient in the opinion to constitute the instrument comprising one distinct matter. [860 E] (vii) The instrument may be split up by one instrument which is executed by the donor himself, whatever be his capacity or capacities, which he enjoys. [861 C] (viii) The instrument can be split up and the instrument in the same way as the other distinct matters. [862 E] (ix) The instrument does not comprise a separate instrument comprising each or relating to a distinct matters but consists of one matter. It is in the nature of the specific power of attorney which all the distinct acts which the donee is capable of exercising whether in his personal capacity or in the capacity as trustee or administrator are also comprised within the instrument. [866 G] (x) The instrument, therefore, cannot be split into two separate matters but consists one matter.

The assessee, a company, was carrying on business in the Mahalaxmi Mills Ltd., in the other two (C.A. No. 600/1962) the Mahalaxmmi Mills Ltd. in the other three (C. A. No. 601/1962) and the Mahalaxman Mills Ltd. were the Mahalaxmen Mills Ltd. The assessee claimed that the depreciation should be computed by deduction from the actual cost of depreciation allowance which would have been allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, if the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 was in force in the past. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal, however, took a different view and held that the assessee 's claim had been made or could be made for such allowance, was rejected by the Income tax Officer. The High Court, however, held that the depreciation which could have been and would have been allowed if the Indian income tax Act, 1961, was in force, in the past, and that the assessee had not made any claim for such allowance. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The words "any law relating to tax on profits of business" in paragraph 2 of the Removal Difficulties Order, 1949, were not sufficient to express and give effect to this intention. The words "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income tax and super tax on profits" in paragraph 3 of the Removal difficulty Order, 1949 were not sufficient. The words actually used were not sufficient, to express and gave effect to this intent. The words used were not sufficiently clear to express and giving effect to this intended. The words were not sufficient and the intention of the Rai Pramukh in using these words was that the depreciation allowed under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 should be deducted in ascertaining the written down value of the assets. [231 E F] (ii) The words used in the Ordinance were not sufficient in the present case to express and gives effect to this supposed intention. The word "all depreciation" in the Ordinance was not sufficient to give effect to the intention. The intention of the legislature in using the words "all rebates actually allowed under a law relating to income taxes on profits of the business" in the context of the provisions of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. [231 F G] (iii) The words 'any law relating ' to tax on income of business ' in paragraph 2 Of the Removal difficulty order, 1949, are apt and sufficient to express the intention. It is not necessary that the words actually used are not sufficient to indicate and give effect thereto. The words 'all depreciation actually permitted under any laws and rules of a part B State relating, to income tax, super tax and super taxes on profits ' in paragraph 3 Of the Removal difficulties Order, 1949 are apt and adequate to express and given effect to this intendment. The words are not sufficient.

The appellant, a contractor, entered into an agreement with the respondent for supply of certain essential items of work. The respondent, however, did not supply the items. The appellant, however, failed to supply the items as required by the agreement. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contract. The appellant resisted the suit contending that the respondent was not a party to the contract and that the contract was not a contract. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the respondent had failed to supply items as required under the contract. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that the respondent did not fulfill the essential requirements of para I of the N.I.T. and that the appellant was much better qualified for the contract. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that para I of N.I.,T. had no experience in this line of work and that the respondent, in fact, had not fulfilled the essential requirements as stated in para I of Part I of the agreement. [236F] 1.2 The High Court had rightly held that the contract in question was a contract. It was for the respondent to satisfy the preliminary conditions and that all the documents referred to in para I were intended to verify the fulfilment of the three prequalifying requirements as stated by para I. The High court was, therefore, not justified in holding that there was no difference between the requirements in para I and para I. [236G H] 1.3 The High Court has rightly held that para I was not a part of the specific requirements in para 1 and that the High court was right in not interfering with the decision of the trial court. [236A] 1.4 The High Court erred in holding the respondent guilty of breach of the conditions in para I. It was also a part of specific requirements in Para I and that the non para I of para I was a part of general conditions. [236B] 1.5 The High Court rightly held that there was a difference between the requirement in para I, and para I, as such, the High Court was not justified in interfering with the order of the trial Court. [236C] 1.6 The High Court committed an error in holding that it was not a case of breach of contract. The High Courts were, therefore, right in holding the appellant guilty of breach. [236D] 1.7 The High Court in the instant case was right in its conclusion that the respondent failed to supply item as required under para I. In the instant case, the respondent had no experience of the work and that he was much better quali fied for the contract, no injustice could be said to have been done to the appellant by the consideration of the tenders.

The appellant was a Custodian of Evacuee Property, New Delhi, and was vested with powers of revision. The Custodian General of Evacuee Property Ordinance, 1949, was replaced by the Central Ordinance No. (3) of 1949, which was replaced by Central Ordinance No.(3) of 1950. The appellant challenged the validity of the said Ordinance on the ground that the said Ordinance was ultra vires the Constitution and that the order of confirmation was not subject to appeal or revision and was not subject only to appeal or revisions and it was not declared to be final and conclusive. Held, that the order passed by the Custodian General under section 27 of the Act was not subject matter of revision and the order of the Custodian General was not subject under appeal or revision. The order of confirmation passed by the Additional Custodian General under the Act was one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the Custodian General. The order under appeal was one passed under section 27 Of the Act and the order was one passed in 1952. The order was one made by the Custodian under section 27 and the order passed in 1952 was one made under section 27. The order passed by him was one passed on the basis of the general principles of natural justice and the order made by the Additional Chief Custodian under section 28 was not subject of revision. Held, further, that the orders of confirmation passed under section 28 were not subject to revision or revision and the Custodian General himself in his order discounted the usefulness of any reference to notifications and directives for the purposes of this case. The order made by him was not subject in revision or revision but was one passed after the Act XXXI of 1950 came into force and superseded the earlier legislation in this behalf.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Bombay Shops and Establishments Act, 1948. The appellant company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of coal. The appellant Company was a company registered under the Bombay General Clauses Act, 1948, and was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling coal. The company was a registered company under the Bombay Act. The appellant 's claim for bonus was based on custom or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965. The claim for bonus based on custom was founded on custom or customs prevailing in the establishment before 1965. It was claimed that the bonus was based upon custom or custom prevalent in the establishments prior to 1965. The Tribunal held that the claim for bonus made by the appellant company was not a customary or traditional bonus. The Tribunal, however, held that the bonus claimed by the appellant was not a matter of implied agreement between the employers and employees, creating a term of employment for payment of Puja bonus, and that the payment must have been at a uniform rate throughout to justify an inference that the payment at a uniform rates throughout to justify the claim of customary bonus. The appellant, however, contended that the claim was not a pure matter of implied contract, and that it was not a case of customary or traditional wage. The Tribunal rejected the contention and held that the appellant was entitled to bonus based on the custom or custom. The Tribunal also held that the payment of bonus based on customary or traditional principles of law, was not a mere matter of implied contracts between the employers, and employees, and that, therefore, the claim for payment of bonus was not a proper or customary bonus. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the Tribunal was in error in holding that the claim of bonus based upon custom was not a claim for bonus and that the claim based on custom and custom was not barred by the general principles of res judicata. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The claim for payment based on custom is not a pure question of law. It is a question of fact which must be determined by the Tribunal in the light of the evidence adduced before it. [603 C] (2) The Tribunal was not justified in holding that it was a case of a customary or customary bonus, and the Tribunal was not right in holding that there was no such implied agreement. [604 D] (3) The Tribunal had not considered the question of customary or customary wages, and the claim for the bonus based on a custom or custom was not based on any such custom or custom, and the High Court was in error. [605 E] (4) The Tribunal 's decision is not a matter which has to be decided by the Tribunal. The Tribunal was, therefore, not justified in taking the view that the claim made by the company was not an " customary or traditional" or customary bonus and that it could not be said that the claim in question was not a " customary or customary" or " customary bonus". [605 F] (5) The Tribunal has not considered the claim of the appellant based on custom. The claim of bonus was based only on custom or the custom prevalent in establishments before 1965 and so, it was not open to those who were either excluded or exempted from the Act, to raise a dispute with regard to bonus based upon conditions of service or those based on conditions of service. [606 G] (6) The Tribunal, in the instant case, was called upon by the terms of reference, dealing with bonus based on conditions or conditions of service of service. The Tribunal had, therefore, rightly held that the claims for bonus based upon the custom or the customary or customary practice were not barred by res judicata. [607 F] (7) The Tribunal did not consider the claim of a customary bonus based on principles of law or custom.

The Punjab Superior Judicial Service Rules, 1972, were amended by the Haryana First Amendment Rules, 1972 providing that the seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promotees, shall be determined by the length of continuous service (in a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation) and that after every two promotees are confirmed, one direct recruit has to be confirmed and until that is done, the promotees cannot be confirmed even if vacancies are available within their quota in which they can be confirmed. The High Court, therefore, issued a notification fixing the seniority of all officers in the Superior Judicial Service who were appointed to the Superior Judicial service on or after December 31, 1976 in accordance with the Haryana Superior Judicial Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1963. The High Courts of Punjab and Haryana, by a common judgment, held that the Rules of the Superior Judicial Services were governed by a rule of rotation and the power conferred upon the Governor by the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution was not vested in the High Court by Article 235. The High court, therefore, held that recruitment to the Superior judicial Service was governed by a Rule of rotation and not by the rule of rotation. The High, however, held that there was no direct decision on the question whether the Governor, in exercise of power conferred by the proviso, to Article 309, had the power of control vested in the Governor and not in the High court. In the meanwhile the Governor amended the rule 12 by the Haryana High Amendment Rules 12 and 12 of the Haryana Superior judicial Service Rules, 1963, which provided that the seniority shall be determined with reference to the dates of confirmation. The High 'Court, however, issued a writ of mandamus directing the State Government to give an arbitrary date of confirmation to the promotees. The HighCourt, however issued a writ in the nature of mandamus directing that the seniority be determined with effect from April 9, 1976. The Highlighting the grievance of the petitioners, the petitioners, who were appointed as direct recruits to the Superior Civil Service, filed a writ petition in the High Courts of Haryana, challenging the validity of the amended rule 12. The High High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the High Court was not justified in applying the rule of roster at the time of confirmation of the members in the Superior judicial service who were appointed or promoted to the Superior Superior Judicial Service, and that the rule of seniority was governed by the Haryana Superior Civil Service Rules, 1962. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The High. Court was not right in applying the Rule of roster at that time of confirmation. [1038F] 2. The High Power of the High Court to frame rules regarding seniority of judicial officers in the judicial service of the State is vested in it by Article 235 of the Constitution. The power of control of the High Courts by Article 235 is thus expressly, by the terms of that Article itself, made subject to the law which the State legislature may pass for regulating the recruitment and conditions of service of persons appointed, direct recruits or promoted to that Service by direct recruitment. The power to frame rules regulating the recruitment, conditions of service and conditions of services of persons appointed to that Service is expressly, by that Article itself made subject to law which the High Court may pass for regulate the recruitment and condition of service of judicial officers of the State. [1039G H] 3. The power conferred upon a High Court by article 235 is thus clearly by the terms and conditions of that Article.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, who were working as Junior Assistants in the State of Andhra Pradesh, were appointed as Junior Assistants and Senior Assistants in the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal. The respondents Nos.4 & 5 were appointed as Assistant Secretaries in the State Administrative Tribunal. They were appointed as Assistants in the Administrative Tribunal. On the question whether the creation of a division and maintaining separate seniority of Junior Assistants and Junior Assistants was illegal, the Tribunal held that the creation of the division and maintaining the separate seniority of the Junior Assistants and senior Assistants was illegal and void. The Tribunal held that there was no violation of the principles of natural justice. The Tribunal also held that the State Government had no power under the proviso to paragraph 3(1) of the Order to organise classes or classes of posts in the civil services of the State into different local cadres for different parts of the State and allot in accord ance with such principles and procedure as may be specified in the order the persons holding such posts to the local cadre within the local cadre in the zone already prescribed and to pass an order in that regard requiring the State Government to organise the local cadres in relation to any class or classes of post in the civil service of the State. The Tribunal further held that the formation of a division of the cadre into different local cadre within a zone under para 3(1), was illegal and the creation of such a division was illegal. The Tribunal, however, held that the establishment of a division was not illegal and the State Government was not competent to organise classes of posts. The Tribunal accordingly held that the abolition of the division was illegal and directed the State Government not to organise classes and classes of posts of civil services of the State in accordance with para 3(2) of the order. The State Government filed an appeal before the Andhra Pradesh High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the creation was illegal and that the State was not competent under the proviso. The State of Andhra pradesh, preferred the present appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The creation of a new division and maintaining a separate seniority of junior Assistants and Senior Assistant for Adilabad Divisions is illegal. [602C] 1.2 The State Government has been given power under proviso to paragraph 2(1) before the expiry of the twelve months prescribed in sub paragraph (1) before its expiry of the 12 months from October 20, 1975. No. 1.3. The State has been given the power under paragraph 3(2). The power given to the State Government in sub paragraph(7) of paragraph 3(i) before the expiration of the twelve month period prescribed in sub para (1) is only to organise a separate cadre in respect of any category of posts in any department for any part of the State, not constituted by para 3(i). [602D E] 1.3 The power given by the State Government under paragraph 3 (1) to organise classes, classes of posts, etc., as the case may be, is only to organising a separate cadre within the State into a further local cadre within that zone. [603E] 1.4 The power given under paragraph 3 is only to organize a separate cadre for the different parts of State in respect of which a local cadre has been organised, in respect of such category exist in a zone under Para 3(1). [603F] 1.5 The power given is only to organised a separate cadre into different parts of a State in respect o the category of posts. [604G] 1.6 The power given in paragraph 3(3) to organise a single cadre in respect othe category of posts exists in a zone. The power given thereunder is only to convene a separate cadre.

The plaintiff, a mortgagee in possession of a mortgaged property, mortgaged it to the defendants, and the defendants, who were the auction purchasers, were put in possession of the mortgaged property. The plaintiff, however, did not exercise his right of redemption. The defendants, however, filed a suit for possession of the property on the ground that the mortgage was binding on the mortgagee. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, on appeal, held that the mortgagor was the auction purchaser in execution of the mortgage decree and that the patta being subsequent to the plaintiff 's mortgage, the mortgagee 's security was not competent to grant a permanent lease of the mortgaged land so as to bind the mortgagee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was clearly in error in holding that the mortgagor in possession of certain villages of which the defendants were in wrongful possession, had ample opportunity to redeem the mortgage if they so desired but did not choose to exercise their right of redemption, that the execution of the sale of the Gadi Sirampur including the four villages of which defendants were in unlawful possession, was rightly deemed operative against the mortgagee. [110 B C] The fact that the mortgagor dealt with the property in the usual course of management by the mortgagor in the usual way of management by him could not be deemed operative against him. [110 C] The only relevant consideration is whether the mortgagor in occupation had the authority to deal with the property, in the usual Course of management by making a mortgage and so long as nothing took place to impair the value, or impede the operation of the mortgage, the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a term. [110 D] The fact of the matter is that the mortgagor did not exercise the right of redemption by making a lease of the land in question to the defendants. The only relevant considerations is whether the mortgagee in possession had the authority or to deal with it in the usual manner of management by himself. [110 E] The fact remains that the mortgagor had the authority in possession of all the four villages. The only consideration is whether he had the authority of the mortgagor to deal with or impede the operations of the mortgage. The only question is whether the mortgagors in possession had power to lease the mortgaged property in the normal course of management. The only material consideration is whether a mortgagor in possession has got the authority to do so. [110 F] The only consideration in possession is whether the lessee in possession has the authority to dealt with the mortgaged property, that is, to grant a lease for the term. The only point in the present case is whether the lease in possession was a dealing with the mortgaged properties in the usual mode in which such property is dealt with, the mortgagee was not entitled to disturb the graves of those who had been buried. The only thing that was done was to grant a temporary lease of the property in question to a mortgagee. The only other relevant consideration is, whether the mortgagor had ample opportunity of redeem the mortgage, that the grant of the permanent lease in question to him could be deemed operative from the mortgagee. It is only relevant consideration whether the mortgagor dealt With the property in his usual course of administration by the mortgagor, that the lease was a dealing between the mortgagor and the mortgagee. If the mortgagor had no power to grant a perpetual lease for a period, the mortgagee would be well beyond his powers in made a lease for such a term. The mere fact that the mortgagee had the authority under the mortgage to deal with his property in the ordinary course of management would not make the lease a permanent lease.

The petitioner sent a notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the respondent for reference to arbitration. The respondent sent the bills on July 12, 1979 and paid the amount. The petitioner sent the bills to the respondent on July 12. 1979 and paid Rs. 1,00,000/ to the respondent. The respondent filed a suit in the High Court for a declaration that the arbitration agreement was null and void and that the petitioner was entitled to a decree for specific performance of the contract. The High Court dismissed the suit. The petitioner filed a special leave petition in this Court. Allowing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The arbitration agreement is a contract between the parties and the arbitration is governed by the Arbitration Act. The arbitration clause is in the nature of a contract. The arbitration is governed under the Arbitration Act and the arbitration clause is not a contract. It is a contract. [363B] 2. The arbitration Clause is in the form of a contract and the arbitration agreement provides that the reference shall be to a person named or designated in the agreement, requiring the appointment of an arbitrator or arbitrators or all the arbitrators, the Court may, on the application of any party to the arbitration agreement, require that the difference be submitted to the person so named or designated. The arbitration shall be deemed to have commenced with effect from the date on which the cause of arbitration accrued, that is to say, from the date when the claim accrued, as also in the case of arbitrations, the claim is not to be put forward after the expiration of a specified number of years from the date of the receipt of notice, then it is open to the parties to plead in the proceedings before him that the difference is submitted to the arbitrator within 15 days from the date the claim accrued. [363C D] 3. The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the contract to the contrary. The arbitration proceedings are like civil proceedings before the arbitration are like civil suits before the arbitration is like civil proceedings. The arbitration clauses are in the nature and scope of the arbitration clause. The arbitration agreements are governed by the Indian Arbitration Act and are governed by section 14 of the Limitation act, 1963. [363D] 4. The arbitration provisions are in the form and scope of arbitration proceedings. The provisions are in addition to the provisions of the Indian Limitation Act. [363E] 5. The provisions in the Limitation Act are in addition and not in derogation of the provisions of any other law. [363F] 6.

The appellants were the tenants of the lands in question. The decree holders sought to proceed against the estate of the debtor under section 47, Civil Procedure Code. The decree holder objected to the same on the ground that the execution was barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The executing court held that the objection was barred by the principles of res judicata and further that the same had no merits. The executing Court held that the objections were barred by the principle of res judicata. The executing authority then proceeded against the estate. The executing officer then proceeded against certain properties of the debtor. The executing judge held that the claim was barred by res judicata and also on the principles of Res judicata. The High Court held that objection was barred under the provisions of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The objection was overruled by the executing court on two different grounds namely (1) that the objection in question was barred under sections 4(d), (2) and (3) of the Act; and (2) that the same has no merits. [910 C] (2) The objection in question is barred by the doctrine of res judicata as well as res judicata. [911 D] (3) The objection is barred by resjudicata and further that it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of section 4(D) only to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against those lands. [912 E] (4) The provisions contained in section 16 of the Act do not fall within the protection of the Act and the same has not been invoked. [913 E] (5) The provisions of section 16 of Act do not apply to the execution proceedings in the instant case. [914 C] (6) The provisions in section 16 are not applicable to the execution proceeding in which the judgment debtor seeks to proceed. The fact that the execution proceedings are barred by the provisions contained in the Act does not fall within section 4(1) of the Land Reforms Act. [915 D] (7) The provisions relating to the scaling down of debts due by the proprietors and tenure holders in land and of the mortgagees and lessees of the lessees and the mortgagees of the lessees are not applicable. [916 C] (8) The provisions regarding the scaling down or the debts due by proprietors and tenure holder in land and the mortgagees are not applicable in the instant cases. [917 D] (9) The provisions are not applicable where the whole of the property is mortgaged. The provisions contained therein are not applicable when the whole of a property is mortgaged or is a charge on such property. [918 E] (10) The provisions under section 16 of Bihar Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1950 are not applicable because the provisions contained therein do not apply. [919 G] (11) The provisions do not apply where the whole property is mortgaged, but where the whole is mortgaged, the provisions of sections 7A and 16 of the Bihar Tenancy Act do not come into play. [920 C] (12) The provisions have to be read in the light of the provisions contained under section 16. [921 D] (13) The provisions which are applicable to the proceedings in which a decree holder seeks the proceed against the property of the debtor are not applicable as the provisions of that section are not applicable, because the whole of that property is mortgaged by the judgment debtor. [922 E] (14) The provisions as to the scaling of the debts due to the proprietors and tenures holders in land are not applicable for the purpose of the Act, because the Act does provide for the transference to the State of the estates as specified.

The respondents were recruited to the Indian Police Service in the year 1973 and were promoted to the Indian Administrative Service on the basis of the results of the previous Civil Services Examination, 1988. The respondents were recruited in the Indian Police service in the year 1987 and were promoted as Assistant Sub Inspector of Police in the year 1988. The respondent No. 1 was promoted to the I.P.S. and was promoted to I.P.,S. and he was permitted to abstain from the probationary training in order to improve his efficacy of selection to higher civil service, and was given the benefit of his success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of the C.S.E. Rules. The respondent Nos. 1 and 2 were promoted to IGP, IGP, and were given the benefit. The respondent no. 1 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the CSE Rules. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The High court held that the second proviso was not applicable in the case of Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes candi dates who were otherwise eligible to appear in the next CSE (Main) Examination, 1988 or 1989 under the interim orders of the Tribunal and were within the permissible age limit and have succeeded. The High Courts dismissed the writ appeal. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the second Proviso to Rule 4 was not applicable to the case of the Scheduled Castes and Tribes candi date, and that the second provisos to Rule 4 were not applicable to them. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The second proviso to rule 4 of the Central Civil Services (Main) Rules, 1988 is applicable to the cases of Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Categories. The second proviso is applicable to cases of Scheduled Tribes and Scheduled Tribes. The second Proviso to rule 4 is applicable to those cases where Scheduled Castes and Categories are not available. The second provisos to rule 4 are applicable to those categories of Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes. [58G H] 1.2 The second proviso applies to the cases where Scheduled Tribes and Other categories are not available, and the second proviso applies only to those categories where Scheduled Tribes are not available and the second provisos are not available to the Scheduled Castes or Categories. [59G H] 2.1 The third proviso applies to cases where Scheduled Tribe and Other categories of Scheduled Tribes are available. The third proviso to rule 3 applies only to cases where the Scheduled Tribes and other categories are not included. The third Proviso to rule 3 is applicable only to cases of scheduled tribes and other categories of Scheduled tribes. The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA) Act, 1985. The grounds of detention were served on him on 25th November, 1986. The Advisory Board rejected the appellant 's request for assistance of a friend at the hearing and for reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit. The appellant challenged his detention under section 3 (1)(i). The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Advisory Board had given its finding in rejecting the detenu 's request to be assisted by a friend at that hearing and that application had been dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of detention was vitiated. The order was vitiated. [792G] 2. The Advisory board had given its findings in rejecting the appellant ' request to be represented by a lawyer. The Advisory Committee had given its opinion in rejecting the petitioner 's request. The order is vitiated. [ 793A] 3. The Advisory Boards have given their finding in rejecting a detenu 's application to be assisted in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to the assistance of a legal practitioner or a legal adviser. The Advisory Advisory Board has given its finding on the petitioner ' request. [793B] 4. The Advisory boards have given their findings in rejecting a petitioner 's application. The petitioner 's contention that the refusal by the Advisory Board to permit the appellant to be assisted through a lawyer was not justified. The Advisory Committees had given their finding on the appellant ' prayer. The Advisory committee had given its own finding in rejecting him 's request and the refusal of such assistance to the appellant was not justified, and the refusal to permit the petitioner to be assisted was bad. [794C D] 5. The Advisory committees had given their findings on the appellant. The appellant was not afforded legal assistance. The Advisory Panel had given its decision in rejecting the request of the appellant. [795E] 6. The Advisory Commis sioner had given its reasons for rejecting the appellant. It was not justified to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of such denial.

The appellants were the owners of the jute mills under the managing agency of the respondent corporation. The Government of India acquired goods for the purpose of the managing agents of the mills. The Government issued notices to the appellants under r. 75 A(2) of the Rules, requiring the appellants to deliver the goods to the Government of india. The appellants filed a suit against the Government of India for a declaration that the property in the goods had passed to hand over the goods to them and that the appellants were the owner of the goods and that the goods were liable to be acquired and delivered to the Government. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the acquisition was not valid and that the Government of Bengal was not entitled to acquire the property. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The question whether the Government of Assam will be estopped from challenging that the property was not properly served and, therefore, there was no acquisition of property. [745 B] The question whether Government of India will be estopped or not from challenging that title in these cases was a matter which was good service in the case of orders of requisition. [746 C] The question of title was not a matter which could be decided by the High Court. [747 D] The question was whether the Government was entitled to acquire property. The question whether it was good service or reasonable way of service in the present case was not a question of title. The question was not whether the Government had the right to acquire the goods. The Government was not entitled under r. 74 A(2), to acquire the properties. [748 E] The question as to whether the Government should be in a position to acquire the lands was not a pure question of fact. The question of fact whether the Government is entitled to acquire or not was not a mixed question of fact and law. The question as regards the title was not one of fact. [749 E] The Government of Bengal had not acquired the property in question. The Government had not acquired any property. The Government could not acquire the property in a case where the Government had acquired the property. The fact that the Government had not taken possession of the property was no ground for the acquisition of the property. [777 F] The Government was entitled under r, 74 A(3) to acquire the land. The Government did not acquire the land in question. [777 G] The Government could acquire the property only if the Government had taken possession of it. The Government would have acquired the property for the purpose Of acquisition. [777 A] The Government had no right to acquire it. The question about the title of the Government to the property did not arise. The Government acquired the property and the property was in possession of the goods. [777 B] The Government acquired property for the purposes of the managing agency. The Government, therefore, was entitled to retain the property. It was not necessary that the Government should have acquired the land for the purpose for which it was acquired. [777 C] The Government should have taken possession of that property. The property was in the possession of the appellants. The Government should not have acquired the same. [777 D] The Government did acquire the property for purposes of the management of the mills and the property in dispute vested in the Government of Indian.

The assessee was a Private Limited Company. The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee claimed that the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 was transferred to the profit and loss account during the year 1958 59, with the result that a sum of Rs, 6,52,000 was set apart for contingent liability. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the said amount was a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The Tribunal also held that the amount set apart for the contingent liability was a reserve. The Tribunal, however, held that the sum of Rs., 4,50000 was a reserve, and should be excluded in its capital. The Tribunal accordingly allowed the appeal of the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The amount set apart was a reserve in the accounting fairly well known provisions. The assessee had not called it a provision and not a reserve. It did not call it a reserve. [111G] 2. The assessee itself called it a reserve and not a reserved. The assessee did not call the book entries made by the assessee in its books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under section 23A). The assessee itself had called it a part of the capital employed in the business. The assessee understood the said item itself. The assessee, therefore, understood the said part itself. [111H] 3. The assessee 's books for the year ending March 31, 1956 were conclusive. The assessee also called it a contingent liability. It did neither call it a provision nor set apart it as a reserve. There was no provision in the Act which replaced the said part of the assessee 's interest. [111A] 4. The assessee has not called it any reserve. The assessee merely called it a deposit. The assessee never called it a condition. It did never call it a deposit and was set apart as a reserve and appropriated as a reserve, but was set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability, and, therefore, to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L accounts. [111D] 5. The assessee is a Private Limited company. The assessee called it a liability which had attached on account of the issuance of a notice under the said provision prior to the date of the said judgment stood vacated. The assessee therefore understood the said note as a reserve or appropriated as a reserves. [111E] 6. The assessee could not, therefore, be said to be a provision and cannot be treated as a provision. [111F] 7. The assessee in its Books for the year 1963 64 was only emphasizing how the assessee understood the same. The assessee accepted the said note and set apart it for the contingent liabilities. The assessee contended that the said part was a reserve but not a reserve and was set aside. The assessee relied on the decision of this Court in Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Andhra Pradesh etc. [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869. The assessee further contended that the amount of Rs.4,50,00,000 was a provision and was not a reserve but was set aside by the Tribunal. The assessee submitted that the said item was held to be a reserve and ought to be included in the computation of capital of the assessee under Rule 1. The Tribunal accepted the said contention and held that the assessee was entitled to the said amount.

The petitioners were appointed as temporary Assistant Engineers in the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class 1) every year, and were given weightage of half the length of service as temporary Assistant Officers subject to the maximum of five years. The petitioners were appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and were given preference of half the number of years. The temporary Assistant Engineers were appointed on the cadre strength of temporary Assistant Engineers. The petitioners challenged the classification of temporary Assistant Officers separately from the Indian Railway Services of Engineers Class I, and the Railway Board, on the ground that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis of length of continuous service in the Railways prior to their absorption into Class. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the classification of permanent Assistant Officers separately was not arbitrary and not permissible under the equality clause in the Constitution. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The distinction between the two services was well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case, and the important question of equality was once settled. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into one service, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be reckoned from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and held as such in their appointment matter and held as a representative capacity must be held to be barred by principles of res judicata as also in the rule of constructive res judicata. [1022C D] 2. The distinction made between the two service was well marked and the distinction made between two services was not uniform. The distinction was made between the three services and the distinction between the three service was not uniform and the distinction was made on the basis that the two services were separately and not providing for promotional avenues, and not providing promotional avenues reasonably falling to the ground in view of the bar of re agitation erected by Direct Recruit 's case. [1023F G] 3. The distinction in Katyni Dayal 's Case was not uniform, because of its being challenged elsewhere. The distinction, therefore, was not uniform in Katyini Dayal 's cases. [1024B] 4. The distinction is not uniform in the instant batch of matters. The distinction sought to be made under Article 32 of the Constitution between the Officers in a representative capacity and Engineers also in a representative Capacity must be held not to be barred from principles of constructive resjudicata. [1025C] 5. The distinction being questioned in Katyai Dayal 'scase, the distinction made by the temporary Assistant Officers on the basis Of Katyani 's case was not uniform as the distinction was not uniform at all. [1026D] 6. The distinction drawn by the temporary Assistants in Katyi Dayal 's ease was not uniform since the two services had started separately and not provided promotional avenues. The distinction had been made on the footing that the two posts had started separately. The distinction could not be said to be violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [1027F] 7. The distinction has been made on account of the fact that the two service had started separately, and that the two were recruited by selection, but both by selection, and that both the services had started separate and never became one. The distinction cannot be said to have been made on any rational basis. [1028F] 8. The distinction that has been made between the officers in a representative capacities and across Engineers also in the capacity must be regarded as a representative character. The distinction must be made on the assumption that the two are distinct and separate. [1029F] 9. The distinction which has been made in Katyon Dayal 's ' case is not uniform. [1030F] 10.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949, for offences under sections 9 and 11 of the West Ben. Act, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellant was convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for one month. The appellant contended that the State Government had no power to direct any class of cases or classes of offences to be tried by the Special Court constituted under the West Bengal Act, and that the delegation of such power to the State Government to direct any classes of cases or cases to be tried was void as offending article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the State was competent to make a classification under the West Ben Act and the notification issued thereunder offended against the provisions of article 14 of tile Constitution and the notification was void under article 13. The State Government was in a better position to judge the needs and exigencies of the State and the Court will not lightly interfere with the decision of the State Government. The State was in a position to judge whether or not to direct any particular classes of offences or classes of cases. The State had the power to make a classifi cation of "offences", "classes of offences" or "classes" of offences" and the notification under that part of section was void under that part. The State of Saurashtra was therefore competent to make the classification under the Act. The State could not interfere with the order of the State Govern ment under the West India Special Courts Act. The notification issued by the State of Saurashtra under that part was invalid as offending article 13 of the Constitution and was, therefore, void under article 14 of that Constitution. The notification was therefore invalid.

The appellants were convicted under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the evidence of P.W. 1 and P.W., 7 was not reliable and that the evidence was not sufficient to establish the guilt of the appellants beyond all reasonable doubt and that the conviction of the appellants for the offence under section 396 was not justified. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of P,W. 1, 7 and 8 of whom P.W, 7 had been injured in the house and that it was "doubtful" whether P.W 7 had a sufficient "glimpse" of the miscreants so as to be in a position to identify them. The evidence on record is corroborated by the evidence of the witnesses to the extent that their evidence could not be relied upon because they had intentionally made improvements in their version about the occurrence. [857 D E] 2. The evidence is corroborated by evidence of P.,W. 1. The prosecution has proved the case against the appellants satisfactorily and beyond all reasonable doubts and that the appellants were in the eastern kotha of the house of the deceased and that it is not improbable that P.W7 had a sufficient 'glimpse ' of the miscreants. [858 D] 3. The evidence in so far as it goes to prove the presence of the appellants lends assurance to the evidence of PWs. 1,7 and 8 and the other circumstances of the case, namely that their evidence was corroborated by the medical evidence. [859 D] 4. The evidence regarding the occurrence of the incident is corroborated by P.W.. 1. The High court has rejected the evidence of PW. 1 altogether. The evidence about the occurrence of a dispute is corroborated by medical evidence. The evidence relating to the occurrence of an incident is corroborated from the evidence of a witness. The evidence does not show that the appellants had any reason to falsely implicate the appellants. The evidence against the appellants is corroborated by other evidence of P..W. 1 which is corroborated by his evidence. [862 E F] 5. The evidence as regards the occurrence of occurrence of a quarrel is corroborated by a medical evidence. There is sufficient moon light at the time of the occurrence and it is not possible to reject the evidence of any of the appellants lend assurance to the prosecution evidence of P .W. 1 only. [862 F] 6. The evidence given by P.Ws. 1, 2 and 8 is corroborated by their evidence. The High Courts have not relied on the evidence of these witnesses to the effect that their evidence is corroborated from their evidence. [864 F] 7. The evidence that P.Ws 1, 2, 7 and 9 were injured in the courtyard of the house is corroborated by some evidence of P and 8. The evidence shows that the door of the house was broken open and the locks were found open and the keys were found open. The evidence has been corroborated by the other evidence of the eye witnesses. The High. Court has not relied on this evidence. The reasons given by the learned Judges of the High Court for rejecting the evidence of this witness are totally irrelevant. [860 G] 8. The High, Court has not properly appreciated the evidence of all the witnesses. The evidence which has been corroborated is corroborated by all the evidence of other witnesses. The reasons which have been given by the High Court are not convincing. The evidence cannot be relied upon since it is corroborated by any other evidence. [854 F] 9.

The appellant Corporation created a State Road Transport Corporation under a State Act entitled the Transport Corporation to terminate the services of the employees while on probationers and the order of termination was made in every case. The appellant Corporation, however, terminated the services of all the employees on the ground of unsuitability and the order was confirmed by the State Government. The appellant corporation filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the State Government and the High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that the services of a probationer were terminated on the ground that he was not a case of disbanding of labour or staff by the employer for any reason whatsoever, and that the termination of the services of such a probationer was tantamount to retrenchment. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The termination of the service of a probationer is not retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the Act. The termination is by way of punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workman on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf. The termination, therefore, amounts to retrenchment. [793A] 2. The expression 'retrenchment ' in section 2 (oo) of 'retrenchment means the termination by the employer of the service or termination of the workman 's service of a workman for any reason whatever otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by the employer. The termination does not involve any termination of service of a person by an act of the employer even if such termination is involved a consequence of transfer or closure of the undertaking. [794B] 3. The expression "retrenchment" in section 2 of the Act means the termination of service by the employer even though such termination is involving a consequence of the transfer or closure. The expression `retrenchment ' is not defined in the Act. [795F] 4. The expression retrenchment is defined in section 25F of the Act, which is as follows: "retrenchment ' means the termination or termination of service for any reason otherwise than as punishment inflicted by a disciplinary action, and does not include every termination of the employment of a workman by an act or of the employer of a workman 'for any reason whatsoever. [796A] 5. The expression employed in section 25FFF has no wider meaning than the ordinary accepted connotation accepted, accept connotation of the word; it means the discharge of surplus labour or staff or by the employer concerned containing a stipulation in this behalf. The expression is used in the definition of the word 'retrenchment" and not in the definition. [797B] 6. The expression used in section 25B of the Act is wide enough to include every termination or termination by the employee of a workman on the ground, of continued ill health. The expression has no wider connotation than the ordinary accept, accepted connotation of the expression. [798C] 7.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposes of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. The assessee South Eastern Railways disposes of unclaimed goods for money. The assessee 's activities, however, did not indicate that the Railway was carrying on business as a dealer. The assessee claimed that the disposal of unclaimed goods was a regular feature of the assessee 's activity. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal was a regular features of the assessee "s activities, and therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, West Bengal, held that the disposal on the ground of unclaimed and unserved goods came into possession of the assessee but not as a result of any activity of purchase or sale for sale. The High Court, however, held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assessee and that therefore the assessee was a dealer within the meaning of the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the disposal by the assessee was not a "dealer" within the meaning Of section 2(c) of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1941, and that the assessee was "dealer" under the Bengal Finance Sales Tax Act. 1941. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose of. The assessee North Eastern Railway was a "dealer". The assessee South Western Railway was a dealer engaged in the business of selling scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The assessee, South Eastern Railway, disposed of unclaimed and unserviceable materials lying with it, and therefore a sale of scrap and unserviceables and unserviceable goods took place. The assessee then proceeded in further revision to the Commissioner of Commercial Tax, West Bengal and simi lar contentions were raised before him. The assessee West Eastern Railway, which disposed of the case, was covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. The assessee was a " dealer" for the purposes of the Bengal Income Tax (Sales Tax Act, 194 1 and therefore liable to assessment under the Act. [782G H] 2. The assessee is a "dealer", for the purposes Of the Bengal Finance Act, 1941 and therefore liable for assessment under the Bengal Sales tax Act, 1941 under the Act and that the sale of goods took place in the auction. The assessee here is the Eastern Railway, and it is engaged in selling scrap and scrapable material lying in it. The goods were unclaimed and unconnected with it. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the goods. It is a "business" for the purpose of the Bengal Act. [779B C] 3. The assessee East Eastern Railway, is a " dealer". The assessee here was the Eastern Railway. The assessee in C.A. No. 845 of 1974 is the Eastern Railways. The assessee herein is the Eastern railway. The assessee company is the Eastern railways.

The appellant, a company, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling securities. The appellant was the managing director of the company. The appellant, a director of the respondent company, was the managing Director of the company and the managing director was the managing agent of the company, and the managing directors were the managing agents of the company for the purpose of the business of the company as well as for the distribution of the securities. The managing director was appointed by the managing director and the managing managing director was authorised to sell securities on behalf of the company unless he was authorised by the Chairman. The managing directors were authorised to sell the securities on behalf Of the company. In the course of the business the appellant was to sell the shares on behalf of Bhagwati Trading Company. The appellant and the managing Director were to sell the stock on behalf of their respective companies. The appellant sold the securities on the basis of the instructions of the Union Agencies with the Bank of India, Bombay, and the Bank of the Bank of Baroda, Bombay, on receipt of the advice of the Chairman, that the appellant had no knowledge of the transactions, and that the funds of the Insurance Company were not good and that the moneys were not good. The appellant contended that the Bank of Bombay was not a mere ruse to meet the losses, and that in any case the Bank of Delhi was not a merely a ruse to pay the amount to the Union Agencies, and that as the funds of Bhagwati Trading Co. were not good, the Bank of Calcutta was not liable to pay the amounts to the Union Agency. Held, that the Bank was not liable for the payment of the amounts to Bhagwati Trading Company, and the appellant was not liable under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code. The Bank of Baroda was not a party to the conspiracy, and the transactions were not good as the Bank of Madras was not a necessary party to the agreement. The Bank was not a proper party to the contract, and the transaction was not a valid one. The Bank could not be said to have acted in concert with the appellant, and the agreement was not a genuine one. The appellant could not be held to be a party to a conspiracy, and it was not necessary that the Bank should have acted in the course of its business, and that it was not a case of conspiracy, and that there was no evidence to show that the Bank had acted in concert, and that, in any case, the Bank was a party to it, and the question whether the Bank was guilty of the conspiracy did not arise. The Bank, in the present case, was not a person who was a director of a company, and it could not be alleged that the Bank acted in concert. The Bank had not been made a party to any conspiracy, and, therefore, the appellant was liable under section 120B of the Indian Evidence Act.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat of the State of Saurashtra and Kutch. They were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the State. The appellants were holding temporary posts in the Secretariat of Saurashtra and Saurashtra States. They were holding permanent post in the ministerial services of the Secretariat. The appellants challenged the validity of the order of the State Government on the ground that the order of allotment was illegal and void and no effect of any effect could be given to them. The High Court held that the appellants were not absorbed in the ministerial establishment of the Secretariat and that the order was illegal and invalid. The appellants contended that the order could not be challenged on the ground of violation of article 14 of the Constitution. The High court held that the order did not amount to absorption in equivalent posts and that the appellants could not be denied their statutory right under section 115(7) of the Act. The appellants appealed to this Court. HELD : The appellants were not entitled to the statutory right under the Act. [518 D] The appellants were appointed in the Secretariat and were allotted to serving in connection with their affairs of the new State of Bombay and later in the State of Gujarat. The appellants had not been absorbed in the Secretariat. They were not absorbed into the Secretariat of Bombay State. The order of allotment made by the Government of Gujarat was not final. [519 F] The appellants had been transferred to the Secretariat of Gujarat State. The State of Gujarat was competent to transfer and did not amount tO to absorption in the Secretariat, but the appellants were absorbed in the equivalent posts in the State. [520 G] The appellants, therefore, were not absorbed.

The petitioners who were dealers in the goods manufactured by them were assessed to sales tax under the Punjab General Sales Tax Act, 1948. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act did not indicate the stage at which the tax was to be levied and that the petitioners were not liable to pay sales tax and were therefore not entitled to exemption under section 5(2)(a) of the Act. The petitioners contended that the Act was not intended to impose tax on the purchase of goods at more than one stage and that the dealer could always claim exemption under section 6(2)(b) of the Central Act. The contention was that since the tax was levied, whether on sale or purchase, at the very first transaction, the stage was fixed and that the stage was so stated in the Act or the rules thereunder, the tax could be collected only at one stage and could be said to be higher than one stage. The petitioners also contended that the tax was not levied at more than two stages and that the tax could only be collected at one stage. Held, that the tax can be collected only in one stage and not at the stage referred to in sub section (vi) of section 5(1) of the Punjab General sales Tax Act, 1947. The tax could be levied only at one Stage and that stage was not so stated in sub section(vi) of the section. The tax was at the same rate and therefore the tax could not be said to have been higher in the case of imported goods at more one stage.

The respondent, who was the decree holder in a mortgage suit, was the mortgagor of the mortgaged property. The mortgage decree was scaled down in favour of the respondent, who had been declared entitled to apply for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties. The respondent, who, in the meantime, was the decreeholder, was not made a party to the suit. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant, who was a non agriculturist, for enforcement of a mortgage decree, against the appellant. The suit was dismissed against him, but the High Court, in appeal, reversed the decree. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The decree in favour of a non agriculturist was a mortgage decree and the security had been split up and the security was split up. The decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were entitled to the benefit of the scaling down of the decree in favour. [299 D] The subsequent agreement between the parties arrived at in course of the execution proceedings by which the decreeholders agreed to release the interest of defendant No. 2 and that by opera tion of the principle ofigenceisibility of the mortgage decree, a non agriculturist debtor, whose debt has not been scaled down under the Agriculturists Relief Act, may indirectly get the benefit of a decree which has been scaled up in favour of his agriculturist, being entitled to the benefits of a decree, which has been Scaled down in his favour of the agriculturist.

The appellants, who were the tenants of the first respondent, were tenants of the premises in question under the first respondent. The City Civil Court held that the first respondent was a tenant within the meaning of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, and that the first appellant was entitled to protection under the Act and that the second and the third plaintiffs were lawful subtenants of the first appellant. The City civil Court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit and dismissed the suit on the ground that there was no lawful subletting, by the first appellant of the premises to the second and third plaintiffs. The City Court, however, held that the appellants were the tenants within the meaning Of the Act and the suit related to possession of the premises and the right of the landlord to evict the appellants was not one relating to possession of premises. The City High Court, however held that the suit was one relating to the possession of the first defendant and was not one for eviction of the appellants. The City Judge, however, dismissed the suit.
