The High Court, on appeal, held that it was a tenant of the first plaintiff and was entitled to possession, use and occupation of the premises as subtenants thereof. The City judge, however, found that the first plaintiff was not a tenant within section 28 of the Act and dismissed the appeal. The High court, however, reversed the decision of the City Civil Court and held that the plaintiffs were the tenants in the first appellant 's suit. The City City Civil Court, however dismissed the suit holding that the first defendant was a tenant in the premises in dispute and that the appellants had been lawfully sublet to the second respondent. The High, however, allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The City Civil court had jurisdiction to try the suit. It was not one of the classes of cases in which a question of title arose out of the Act or any of its provisions. The City C.P.C. could not be determined by the City Civil court. The City of Bombay, the City Civil Courts, therefore, had jurisdiction to deal with such a suit. [374 D] (ii) The City civil court could not be said to have been lawfully sublet by the first respondent to the second defendant. The City court was not a court within the meaning ofs.28 of the Act. [374 E] (iii) The City C., Bombay, the city Civil Court, was not a Court within the meaningof the Act. The City District Civil Court could not be held to be a court within its jurisdiction. [374 F] (iv) The City City civil Court could not, therefore, be said to be a Court within its jurisdiction, and the jurisdiction to try such a suit was exclusively vested in the courts specified in section 28 and no other. [374 G] (v) The City District civil Court could be said to act within the jurisdiction of the City civil Court. The City, Civil Court could be held to have jurisdiction to try a suit relating to possession. [374 C] (vi) The City of Madras, the City civil court, was not one dealing with the question of title to the premises.

The appellant was a private company incorporated under the name of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd., hereafter called the Company. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba executed a registered deed of partnership with the appellant Govind. The appellant was appointed as the managing director of the Company by the will of Dadoba. The appellant 's appointment was to take over the business. On July 8, 1955, the appellant was appointed a director of the company by the will. The appellant made an application to the Company for appointment of the appellant as the managing Director of the Company. The Company rejected the appellant 's application. The appellant then filed a suit for a declaration that the appointment of the respondent was void under the section. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the appointment was void under section 312 of the new Act and that the appointment by the appellant was void under that section. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the proviso to section 86B of the old Act did not apply to the case. The proviso to section 2(1) of the new act did not apply in the present case. The appellant had no right to continue the business of the company. The proviso did not apply. The appellant could not claim to have a say in the appointment of his successor by a director. The proviso was not applicable to the case because the appellant had no power to appoint his successor. The proviso could not be applied to the case as the appellant had not exercised his option to continue the company.

The respondent landlord let out a shop to the appellant firm under clause 13(3)(iv) and (vii) of the Central Provinces and Berar Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The appellant filed an eviction petition against the respondent landlord on the ground that the respondent sublet the said shop let out to the said M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart without joining any of the partners of the said firm as respondents or serving them as partners and serving them as respondents or serve them as partners or serving them or serving them. The Trial Court held that the appellant had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet a shop to M/s Adeshwar Glass Palace without joining any firm of the partners. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal. The High Court, however, held that the respondent landlord had unlawfully and with the consent of M/sAdeshwar Glass Mart was liable to be evicted for subletting under the provision of Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease & Rent Control)Act, 1960. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondent was not entitled to the protection of Section 10 (2)(ii) (a) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the appellants had sublet the shop to M. The partnership firm was carried on business in the said premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business even for sometime during which the appellant firm had ceased not carry on the said business even for any time during which M/s adeshwar Glass Mart were carrying on business at the said premises. [420B] 1.2 The High Court had rightly held that the appellants were sub tenants. The appellants firm was carrying on business in those premises even for anytime during which they firm had ceased. The High court was in error.

The Andhra Pradesh Urban agglomeration (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, was enacted to provide for the imposition of ceiling on land situate within the urban agglomerations. Section 2(n)(A)(ii) of the Act defines "family unit" as meaning "a unit of land equal to one standard holding". Section 2(p)(A)(i) defines "family" as meaning a unit of land held by a person in excess of the ceiling area. Section 2 (p)(A) defines "land held by a member of a family unit" as including land held by any person in excess. Section 2 provides for the ceiling area of a family. Section 2 defines "family". Section 2 (n)(A) provides that "family unit of a family" means a unit of family unit. Section 2 lays down the ceiling area for the purpose of determining the ceiling area and lays down the procedure for determining the ceiling. Section 2 deals with the ceiling area, and lays down that the ceiling area shall be deemed to be an urban agglomeration. Section 2, which is a charging section, lays down the method of determining the extent of land held and the ceiling area to be taken into account for the purpose. Section 2 is a charging Section and lays down a procedure for determining ceiling area. The Andhra Pradesh Act, 1950, was enacted with a view to provide for imposition of ceiling of land situate within such area. Section 3(f) provides that the ceiling areas shall be deemed as urban agglomeration and the Andhra Pradesh Act shall not apply to land situate within any urban agglomeration. Section 2 empowers the State Government to make rules for the purpose and the manner in which the ceiling area is to be determined. Section 3 provides for the procedure for determination of ceiling area. Sub section (2) of section 3 provides that the State Government may, by notification, make rules for determining the extent to which the ceiling areas are to be taken. Section 4 provides for the determination of the ceiling areas. Section 5 provides for the fixation of ceiling areas. Sub section(2) provides that in the case of every individual who is not a member of the family unit, and in the caseof any other person shall be an extent of land equal and in the cases of any other person, shall be an area of land equal. Sub section provides that in case of any other individual who is a member of an family unit, the ceiling area would be liable to be determined as on 1st January 1975 under the Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling and Regulation) Act, 1976. The Andhra State Legislature, therefore, ceased to have competence to provide for levy of ceiling on lands situate within the Urban agglomeration.

The respondent workmen, who were directed to be taken back in employment, were put on notice of the Company that they were near Burnpur and might have joined the Company without any condition. The Company, however, refused to give the permission to the workmen to resume work without any condition and the workmen were not given any opportunity to meet the charges. The Company filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Calcutta challenging the validity of the order of termination of the services of the workmen. The High Court held that the workmen were near Burnapur and might have been joined the Company by the workmen without any condition, and that the workmen had failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence, and that they were not entitled to be taken in employment without any condition; and that the Company was not justified in refusing to give the workmen the permission to resume work. The Company appealed to this Court. Held, that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to interfere with the order of the Company, unless it found that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. The Industrial Tribunal was not justified on the footing that the workmen themselves tried to coerce the Company by 'slow down tactics ' and strike indulged in prejudicial activities to the Company and that the Industrial Tribu nal had no jurisdiction in interfering with the order. The Industrial Tribu ly had no jurisdiction under article 226 to interfere with an order of termination. The Industrial Court was not justified to interfere with a finding of fact. The Industrial Adjudicator had no jurisdiction. The Industrial Appellate Tribunal was not correct in interfering with a finding that the workmen did not attend the Company for a long time. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, was a special Act and the Industrial Tribunal was competent to interfere with it. The Industrial Tribunals were not justified in interfering with an order passed by the Industrial Tribunal. The Industrial Commis sioner had no jurisdiction, and the Industrial Tribun ly had jurisdiction to interfere.

The appellant University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Urea Kant Act, 1974, invited applications for appointment of Dr. Urea Kant as Professor in Botsany. The appellant University of Rajasthan invited applications for filling the post of professor in Bot any. Dr. Ura Kant who was already selected and kept in the reserve list was appointed as Professor in the department of Botany and his name was recommended in the reserve List. The Selection Commis sioner, after considering the objections, recommended the reserve list of the appellant. The appellant, however, did not join the post. The Selection Board constituted under section 6 of the Act, 1974 put a restriction that no teacher in any university in Rajasthan shall be appointed except on the recommenda tions of the Selection Committee constituted for the selection of teacher or officers for which the selection committee was constituted. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order by a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve list would be valid upto six months from the date of approval of the Syndicate as per the resolution of the Syndicate dated 10th July, 1978 and sub section (4) of Section 6 provides for the procedure of selection committee and sub section(4) of section 6 provides for selection of candidate for the post. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The selection committee constituted for the selections of a teacher or officers of an officer in the University, a Committee would be constituted for the selec tion of a teacher in the University. The selection committee, which is constituted for the Selection Committee, which is formed for the selection, is therefore, adjudged by the Selection Committee which is constituted. [419C D] 1.2 The selection committee shall prepare a list of candidates selected by it in order of merit and shall further prepare a reserve list in the same order and to the extent of 50% of the vacancies for the post in the post of teachers or officers for whom the selection committee is constituted. The selection Committee shall prepare a reserve List in the same manner as the reserve list. [420D] 1.3 The selection committee formed for the selections made by it in the last decade from the reserve list is also adjudged by the selection committee which is constituted, for the selection. The selection is therefore, declared by the Selection Commisioner, and the selection of the appellant, Dr. Ure Kant is also adjudged. [421G H] 1.4 The selection committee in its resolution dated 10th August, 1978 and the sub section (3) of Section 5 and the reserve list prepared by the duly constituted Selection Committee constituted in the present case was constituted for the selecting of a teacher. The selection of the appel lant was therefore, not valid for one year. [422D] 1.(a) The selection committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a person selected by the selection Committee has joined that post then selection made by the Committee which is formed, for selection of a teacher, or officers forwhich the selection committee had joined that post, then selection made, by the Committee constituted, for selection, which is constitute for selection of teacher in the university. [423E] 1.(b) The selection of a candidate for the concerned post of teacher or officer for which the Selection Committee was constituted, is therefore not valid for the reason that the selection committee constituted was not constituted for the concerned posts of teacher or Officer for which the select Committee was constituted. [406C] 1.(c) The selection Committee constituted for selection of teachers or officer for whom the Selection Committee had been constituted, is not a function of the Selection Com missioner.

The appellants were owners of certain lands in the development plan originally published on January 9, 1964. The appellants challenged the validity of the development plan on the ground that the land was earmarked for recreation centre and green belt by the first respondent in the development Plan finally adopted by the local authority. The appellants contended that the development plan was prepared in contravention of section 9 of the Act and that the local authority was obliged to make a declaration of its intention to prepare a development plan. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The development plan was submitted by the local authorities before the finalisation of the development plans. The draft of a section of the development Plan was prepared and published in the prescribed manner. The preparation of the development scheme was, therefore, nothing but a mere preparation of the final development plan. [284 B] (ii) The preparation of a development plan was an act of the local authority which could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. The preparation and final development plan was nothing which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local authorities. The preparation or final development plan could not be given without doing any violation to the development plan. It was not something which was left lo the pleasure or the discretion of the Local authority. [284 C] (iii) The preparation or the final development of a section could not be delegated to the local authority without doing any breach to the development scheme. The preparation, final development plan and the final development plans were nothing which was right to the pleasure of the local author ity. [284 D] (iv) The preparation and the final Development plan was a matter which was left for the pleasure or pleasure of the Local Authority. The preparation was nothing which could be delegated to local authority. [285 E] (v) The preparation was a matter of policy and the rules framed thereunder were binding on the local authority and the local authority had to guide itself. [284 G] (vi) The preparation, the final development scheme was prepared and the final plan was prepared. The draft was prepared and circulated in the prescribed form. The draft had to guide themselves. The preparation had to guide the local authority concerned. [284 A] (vii) The preparation for the development plan had to guide it. The preparation for a development plan had been made in the prescribed forms. The draft prepared was circulated in the manner prescribed by the rules. The preparation could not be said to be a mere preparation. The preparation did not amount to a preparation. The draft could not be sent to the local authori ty. The preparation would be a mere paper. The preparation may be a mere printing paper. The draft may be a paper. The printing paper may be a printing paper. It may be a printed paper. The printed paper may be printed in the form of a paper. It is not a paper. [284 E] (viii) The preparation may not be a paper but a paper. There is no question of printing. The preparation is a paper. A printing paper may not be printed in a paper. But it may be printed on a paper. In the present case, the preparation was made in the form prescribed by the Rules. The preparation in question was a paper. Therefore, the preparation could not have been made in a paper but it was a paper which was not printed in the manner required by the Rules and the rules. [284 F G] (ix) The preparation could be made only after the development plan came into force. The preparation must be made in the manner specified in the rules. If the provisions of the Act are borne in mind and the rules made thereunder comply with, as appears to have been done in these cases, there was little or no scope for the local authority acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the Act. [284 H] (x) The preparation in the development plans was made in accordance with the rules framed under section 13.

The appellants, who were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat, challenged the validity of the award of the International Tribunal, which held that the dispute was to be decided by arbitration, and that the award was binding on the parties. The appellants contended that the award of a foreign tribunal was binding on them and that the claim made by the claimants was not barred by article 19(1)(d) of the Constitution. The Tribunal accepted the claim and held that the area was in different state at different seasons in the year, for part of the year, and that there was no clear evidence of demarcation of a boundary acceptable to the parties now or in the past, and that no constitutional amendment was necessary. The Tribunal also accepted the claim. The High Court, however, held that the award did not amount to a binding award and that the appellants were entitled to the benefit of article 19(2) of the constitution. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Award did not amount either to a binding or a binding award, and that it was not a binding award. HELD: (i) The award did not purport to, nor did it operate as giving rise to an obligation to cede Indian territory and the rule laid down by this Court applies if no constitutional amendment is required the power of the Executive wing of the Government and no constitutional amendment could be exercised to correct boundaries now that they have been settled, and that in the present case the award did no more than define on the surface of the earth boundary which had at all material times remained indefinite, because of the nature of the terrain, the shifting nature of the border of what was called Rann. [289 F G] (ii) The award does not purport to give rise to an obligations to cedes any part of the territory which formed part of the State of Kutch before 1948, or was in de facto occupation and in respect of which sovereign authority was exercised by the British authorities governing Sind since 1843 over the Rann of Kutch. [289 A] (iii) The award is not a binding Award. The award does no more than defines on the surface the earth boundary as it was a part of India and has always been so from the establishment of the State. The award did no less than define on a surface of the soil boundary which has at all material time remained indefinite, since of the nature, the terrain of the border between Sind and the Rann. The award merely does not purport tain that the border of the border was now part of the territories which formed part the State of Saurashtra. [289 C D] (iv) The award was not binding on the claimants. The award was binding only on the State of Bombay and the Kutch State authorities. The award, therefore, did not amount only to a binding Award but also to a binding agreement between the parties. [289 D] (v) The award, though binding, did not purport tO make any provision for the acquisition of the territory of India.

The mortgagor, a proprietor of a five annas share in Mauza Bansjora, Simitanr, and certain interest in Mauza Banshora, Simitr, died in 1942 leaving behind his widow, his widow and two sons, the widow and two daughters, the widow of the mortgagor. The mortgagor, in execution of a money decree obtained against the mortgagor, his right, title and interest in Mauza Chunjora,imunder, Simitar and Bahaldih, was sold on January 16, 1937, and after th sale was confirmed, possession of Mauza Bansjorora, Simbatr, Simitor and Bahaldahih, was taken by the auction purchaser on April 7, 1937, by the auction purchasers who purchased the mortgagor 's rights in Mauza Banskora, Simritr, Simitan and Bahaldhih, and the mortgagee, in execution thereof, obtained possession of Mauza Chunjorora. The mortgagor 's right, title, interest and interest in the mortgaged properties was transferred to the Court auction purchaser who purchased the mortgaged property on January 16 , 1937, and the sale was confirmed. The mortgagor filed a suit on July 12, 1946, for a decree for enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of the mortgaged properties. The trial Judge rejected the defence raised by the contesting defendants and held that the suit in respect of the first mortgage was within limitation because the mortgage was partly simple and partly usufructuary and partly usufructuary. The High Court, however, held that the claim was within limitation. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was right in holding that the claim to enforce the mortgage was within time. The plaintiff 's suit to enforce the mortgages was within limitation since the mortgage was not redeemed within the period of limitation. The plaintiff was not entitled to the costs in respect of that mortgage. [100 C] (ii) The High court was right in not holding that the suit was barred by limitation because the mortgagee had lost his interest in Mauzas Bansjora and Simitar. The plaintiff could not rely upon part payment in respect of his mortgage dated August 27, 1922, as evidenced by the endorsement on the first mortgage deed, the mortgagee must be deemed to be in possession till the mortgagor 'S interest in the mortgage property was transferred, part payment will not extend the period of time for the suit. [100 D] (iii) The High Courts were right in holding, that the claim for the first mortgage in respect of a mortgage dated August 28, 1922, was barred by the law of limitation because the mortgagor had lost his right in Mauzis Bansjora. [100 E] (iv) The High, Court was right, in holding that there was no bar to the period of Limitation for the suit, because the mortgage money was not redeemed by the mortgagor within the period prescribed by article 120 of the Limitation Act. [100 F] (v) The High was right in dismissing the suit. The plaintiff had not relied upon any other part payment in the mortgage deed dated August 27 , 1922, as a evidenced by the endorsements on the first mortgages dated August 27.

The appellants, who were in supervisory grades, were charged at the rate of Rs. 2 per month for the transport of employees from Chinchvad to TELCO factory at Pimpri and back. The appellants contended that the tax was realised by the appellants only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in the supervisory grades. The High Court dismissed the appeals. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the tax could be levied only if the passengers were carried by a stage carriage. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word 'public service vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules. The word "public service vehicle" has not been used either by the legislature or by the rules. The word `public service vehicle " has not been mentioned either by the Legislature or by the Act nor by the Rules, but that does not create any difficulty, because having regard to the Preamble of the Act it is not disputed that the transport provided to the employees of the company was a public service vehicle. [362B C] 2. The word public service vehicle ' in the definition of `public service vehicles ' has not defined either by Act or by Rules. The words `public service ' have not been defined by the Act and by the Rules but have been defined in section 2(7) of the Act. [362C D] 3. The word used in the definition is "public service vehicles" and not "public service". The word `private service vehicle ' is defined in section 3(7) to mean a motor vehicle carrying or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver, which carries passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers, either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. The word, `public service motor vehicle ' has been defined in the Act to mean a public service vehicles. The word is defined in the definition to mean a vehicle carrying or designed to carry more passengers than six persons. The word has been defined by section 2(8) to mean any motor vehicle carrying more than six passengers. The word was defined in section 4(7) as meaning a motor vehicle which is of the nature of a public service Vehicle. The word vehicle ' has also been defined in Section 2(7). The word `Public service vehicle ' means a motor vehicle carried or adapted to carrying more than 6 persons excluding the drivers, which carry passengers for hire, reward or reward at different fares paid by the owner of a stage carriage, and includes such a carriage or other omnibus when used as a contract carriage within the meaning of the . [362E F] 4. The word vehicles ' has been used in the Act and the transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the aforesaid definition. [362F] 5. The word motor vehicle ' is not defined either in the Act or in the Rules but it does not create difficulty, because, having regard to its Preamble of the act, it cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of reasoning or Place of reasoning or from imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company.

The appellants, who were the residents of the village of the village, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court of Madhya Pradesh for a writ of mandamus directing the licensing authority to grant a "no objection certificate" to the appellants. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the detailed provisions for the grant of a "no objections certificate" were invalid as the District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there was a mosque, and a mosque, but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema having been re opened in the locality there was no need for a cinema house with a permanent cinema. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The detailed provisions for grant of a 'no objection certificate ' are invalid. The District Magistrate was, therefore, not justified in granting the same. [797G] 2. The District Magistrates were, therefore, justified in refusing the grant of no objection certificate. [798A] 3. The District magistrate was not justified in refusing to grant a 'no objections certificate '. [799B] 4. The District Collector was not justified to refuse a 'no Objection certificate '. The appellants being not entitled to challenge the grant of the 'no objection ' certificate, the order granting no objection certificate was violative of the principles of natural justice. [796C] 5. The High Courts were, therefore. justified in refusing a 'noobjection certificate '. There is, however, nothing in the Act or the rules which requires the licensing authority not to invite objections before grant of a quasi permanent cinema licence. [795D] 6. The appellants not being entitled to challenge a grant of a cinema licence on the same grounds which he took against the "no objection" certificate, when there was no statutory obligation on the licensing authority refusing to grant the "no objections" certificate, the appeal was decided at their back and thus the decision was rendered in violation of the principles Of natural justice. The High court was, therefore. in error in granting the writ of mandamus.

The appellant, a lessee of a mining lease, granted to the respondent, a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekan Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk, and claimed specific performance of the contract. The respondent contended that the contract was concluded on September 2, 1957 and that the appellant was at liberty to revoke the offer. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the respondent was at liberty, to revoke the contract and to remove the iron ore. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 was not an acceptance of the offer. It was not intended to be an acceptance. It was intended to be a acceptance. It is not usual to accept a business offer by a plaint. The plaint in the instant case was not an offer of the respondent 's offer. The respondent had made an offer to assign a mining lease. The offer was communicated to the appellant before November 6, 1957. The respondent, therefore, could not get a possessory right before execution of a conveyance of the mining lease. [584 D E] (ii) The plaint was not an accepted offer. The communication of an acceptance was not an agreement of acceptance. The respondent was at the liberty to revoke it. The correspondence between the parties showed that the appellant had agreed to assign the mining lease to the respondent. The correspondence showed that the respondent had agreed to transfer the mining lease, and that the respondent did not accept the offer. [584 E] (iii) The respondent had not agreed to purchase the mining lease and gave it the right to remove the goods. The correspondence did not indicate that the respondent 'fews had agreed to the transfer of the mining leases. The correspondence indicated that the respondent agreed to assign a lease to the appellant. The correspondence also showed that the offer was not made or communicated to the respondent before November 6. 1957. [584 A B] (iv) The correspondence showed the acceptance of the respondent. There was no concluded contract. The correspondence was not an oral agreement. The correspondence, however, showed that the acceptance was communicated to him before November 6 and that the acceptance of an application for the assignment of the mining Lease could not be lawfully made without the sanction of the State Government. [584 B] (v) The correspondence did indicate that the acceptance had been communicated to the parties. The correspondence clearly showed that the communication of the acceptance was not necessary. The correspondence had not indicated that the acceptance letter was communicated to all the parties. [584 C] (vi) The correspondence indicated the acceptance of a tender. The correspondence further showed that the letter of acceptance was not a formal acceptance. The correspondence could not be said to be an oral agreement, because the correspondence showed that it was an acceptance of an offer. [585 D] (vii) The correspondence was an acceptance and not an acceptance. The letter of acceptance did not indicate the acceptance of any offer. The correspondence made by the appellant did not indicate any acceptance of the application for the transfer of mining lease. There was, therefore, no concluded contract between the parties. There was nothing to show that the communication was made or communicated.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3 of the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937 for having committed an offence punishable under section 7 of the Act. The prosecution case was that the appellants were carrying on the business of manufacturing sugar and were selling sugarcane. The appellants were prosecuted for having committed the offence under section 7 read with section 7 of that Act. The trial court acquitted the appellants but convicted them under section 7 and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court, however, acquitted them. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The Bihar Sugar Factories (Control) Order, 1955, was enacted by Parliament in exercise of the concurrent power of legislation under Entry 33 of List III of the Constitution which empowers the Parliament to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of essential commodities and trade therein. The regulation of the price at which sugarcane may be bought or sold, and in addition to the Sugar Control Order, 1955 in the manner it did, it was well within the competence of Parliament to enact the Act and hence the power conferred on the Government ,under section 3 of that Act was well within its competence of Parliament. [616 D E] (ii) The power conferred on Parliament under section 3 is a legislative power in respect of the production, supply, distribution and distribution of foodstuffs. The power to regulate the movement of sugarcane is expressly dealt with by the Bihar Sugar Factory Control Act, 1950. The power conferred by the Act and the power conferred by it on the Government are well within the legislative competence of the State. [617 E] (iii) The power to legislate in regard to sugarcane is expressly conferred on the State Government under section 3. The power of the State Government to legislate in relation to the control of sugarcane is specifically dealt with by Bihar Sugar Factories Act, 1937. The power is expressly conferred by the Bihar Act and the State Government is also within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, the same being a part of agriculture. [618 E] (iv) The power of legislation in respect of sugarcane is clearly covered by Entry 33 of the List III of Seventh Schedule of the Constitution. [619 G] (v) The power under section 3 to legislate in the matter of sugarcane is not a legislative power but a legislative power. The power under the Act is a legislative function and the power is conferred on the Central Government under section 4 of the Act and not by the State Government. [620 C] (vi) The power given to the Central Government to make a law relating to the control and distribution of sugarcane is a legislative one and is not a judicial power. The Central Government is also a creature of the statute. The power given by the Central Government is a legislative and executive power. The State Government is a creature of statute and the power of legislation is not a part of the legislative power.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation and that the Government of Karnataka was committed 948 to a policy of rapid industrialisation. The Government of Karnataka, however, issued another order which recited that the incentives would be given to new industries requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or promise as it had sought to do by the order dated 12th January, 1977. The Government, however, did not grant the concession. The appellants filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the concessions granted under the said order dated 30th June, 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government of Mysore that the concessions given by the earlier order dated 30 th June, 1969 had been being misused and unduly advantage was being given to the new industries requiring investments of considerable funds. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The doctrine of Prom Estoppel is not applicable in this case because the benefit given to new industrial units by way of refunds was by way of refund of sales tax paid to the new industrial units requiring investment of some funds and the government was not entitled tO go back or promised that promise as it has sought to do so by the order. [950G] 2. The doctrine is not applicable to the present case. The benefit of the concessions given to new units by the earlier orders dated 30th September, 1969 was being misused and unreasonably advantage was being granted to the new units by way Of refunds. [951A] 3. The doctrine must be regarded as good law in view of the recent decision of this Court in State of Bihar and Anr. vs Usha Martin Industries Ltd., [1987] 65 STC 430, wherein this Court held that doctrine of Prom estoppel could not be regarded as a good law in the present cases because it was held that the doctrine was not applicable to cases where the source of power under which it was issued was not stated in an order but could be found on the examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. [952B] 4. The doctrine has to be construed in the light of the decision of this court in State of Kerala and Anr. etc. vs UshaMartin Industries Ltd. [1987]65 STC 430. [954C] 5. The doctrine cannot be said to be a good law for the reason that it is not a rule of law that a person who has been granted a right to get refund of sales Tax paid by him should be granted a refund. [955D] 6.

The appellants were charged with the offences under Sections 147, 148, 323, 379 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. and Section 302 read with 149 I. P.C. The Trial Court acquitted A 1 and A 2, but convicted them under Sections 148 and 302 readwith 149 I.PC. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants under Sections 148, 302 and 302 read and Section 34 I.P.,C. and acquitted them. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court fell into error in confirming the conviction and the sentence of the accused under Sections 148 & 302 read with section 34 I. P.,C. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The non applicability of Section 149 IP.C., is, therefore, no bar in convicting the appellants under Section 7 of the I.P,C. [813C] 2. The non application of Section 149, I.P C. is, therefore no bar in conviction of the appellants Under Section 302 read and section 34 I P.C., for having committed offences. [814D] 3. The non operation of Section 149 is, therefore. no bar in convicted the appellants under section 302 read with s 34 I.PC., for having caused the instantaneous death. [815E] 4. The non compliance of Section 149 of I.P.; is, therefore not bar in convicting them under Section 302 read. [816E] 5. The nonapplicability of Section 149 to the appellants under the said sections is, therefore; no bar in convict the appellants under sections 148 and 302 I.P;C. [916F] 6. The non invocation of Section 149 does not bar the conviction of the accused appellants under Section 302 I. P,C. for having committed the offences. [917F] 7. The non availability of Section 149 in convicting the accused under Section 302, read with Section 34 I P,C., is therefore no bar. [918F] 8. The non com mission of offences is, therefore a bar in convicting under Section 302 and Section 34, I. P.;C. [ 918F] 9. The non provisions of Section 149 are, therefore, not bar in conviction under Section 302.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax on the total income of the assessee. The assessee claimed that the transfer was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of the liability of the assessee to tax on capital gains on the basis of the transfer exceeded the full value of the consideration declared by the assessee. In the assessment proceedings the Income tax officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500/ as the consideration for the transfer and it was enough to attract the applicability of sub section (2) of section 52. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax Officer. The assessee filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that the High Court was in error in holding that the transfer of the capital asset was not a condition precedent to attract the application of sub section(2) of Section 52. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that there was no question of the assessee having received more than what was declared by him. [603G] 2. The High court was in error of holding that the assessee had actually received more than the full value declared by him and the assessee had not actually received more or less than 15% of the value so declared. [604B] 3. The High Courts were in error in not holding that the fair market value of the capital assets transferred by the assessee as on the date of the transfer exceeds the full value. [605C] 4. The High. Court was in wrong in holding that sub section (1) of section 53 of the Act was not applicable. [606D] 5. The High, Court was in the error in holding, that the fair value of the transfer was not the condition precedent to the applicability of the sub section (3) of section52. [607D] 6. The High ' Court was in a wrong position in holding that section 52(2) was not applicable to the facts of the present case. [608D] 7.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, and was convicted by the Sessions Judge. The High Court acquitted him but convicted him under section 7 (i) of that Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the evidence of the Food Inspector was more probable because it was more probable that there was talk about the purpose for which the. Til seeds were sold to the Food Inspector. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The evidence of the prosecution witnesses was more probable. The evidence of P.W. 2 was more probable and was rightly rejected by the High Court. [330 B] (2) The evidence was more probable, for reasons already given by this Court. The evidence was not reliable. The evidence could not be implicitly relied upon in this case. The evidence had been corroborated by the evidence of P, P.W., 2. The Food Inspector who said that Tambe was not present at the time when the seeds were sold by the appellant to the Food inspector. The evidence showed that Tambe had been sold for pooja. The evidence did not show that Tambe sold was not present when the seeds had been sold to the appellant. The evidence, therefore, could not be relied upon in the absence of any other evidence to corroborate the food Inspector. [330 C D] (3) The evidence showed the presence of Tambe at the time of the occurrence. The evidence also showed that the appellant had a grain shop. The evidence further showed that the name of Tambe was also not mentioned in the cash memo. The evidence clearly showed that Tamwas sold for pooj. The appellant had a shop. The Food inspector who said that the black Tils were sold to him for pooja and not for pooja, was not examined. The evidence shows that Tambe 's testimony tends to demolish more than corroborate to corroborate the version of the Food inspector that Tambe used as food. The evidence does not show that the appellant was guilty of adulteration of food. The appellant was not prosecuted on the ground that he sold it in an adulterated condition. The evidence on the other hand showed that the Food Inspector had clearly told the Food Inspector that the blackTils were sold for poos. The Food Inspectors had clearly told him that they were not meant for human consumption. The Food Controller, after examining the whole evidence, concluded that the version of P. W. 2 was not more probable.

The plaintiff, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh, was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th of January, 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August, 1966. The plaintiff 's suit was one to obtain a declaration that the order of dismissal was bad and he continued to be in service. The plaintiff filed an appeal to a Divisional Commissioner and the Divisional Commissioner dismissed the appeal. The plaintiff preferred an appeal before the Divisional Commissioner. The Divisional Commissioner dismissed his appeal on 31st March, 1966. On appeal, the Divisional Commissioner allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. The plaintiff then preferred an appeal against the dismissal of the plaintiff 's appeal. The Divisional Commis sioner dismissed the appeal on 31.8.1966. The plaintiff moved an appeal to this Court. The plaintiff contended that the order merged in the order of the lower authority in the order passed in appeal therefrom and in the final order of dismissal, the appeal was dismissed. The plaintiff also contended that the appellate order of dismissal merged in the final orders of dismissal passed in appeal from service and that appeal had been dismissed on 31.3.1966. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of merger applicable to decrees of courts would not apply to departmental tribunals, and if the High Court has no jurisdiction to issue a writ to the appellate authority it cannot issue a writ of certiorari to the appellate authori ties. [48G H] 2. The principle that the principle of merger applies to decrees of Courts would not apply in every case only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of action shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on the expiry of six months from the date of preferring of the appeal or making of the representation, the right to sue and representation provided by Law is disposed of. [49A] 3. The principle is that the original order merged in an appellate order of the State Government and it is the appellate decision which is the operative order and if the State Government has no jurisdiction, the appeal or the representation provided by the law is disposed off. [49B] 4. The principle applies to decrees passed in a civil suit under the Code of Civil Procedure by the Court of first instance and the appellate decision of the State Govern ment is not regular courts. [49C] 5. The principle has been applied to decrees passed by the State Government, and it is not open to attack under article 226 of the Constitution. [49D] 6. The principle in the instant case is not applicable to the proceedings under Article 226 of the Consti tution. [49E] 7. The principle applied to decrees of the courts of law would not be available to the appellant. [49F] 8. The principle would apply to decrees passed before the State Government. The Civil Court 's jurisdiction has been taken away by the Act and, therefore, the High Court was right in its view that the suit was within time.

The appellant, who was the decree holder of a decree for a sum of Rs. 1,000/ was the decreeholder of a decree. The appellant applied for leave to appeal to the Privy Council under article 133(1) of the Constitution. The application was dismissed by the Privy Council. The appellant then applied for leave under article 133 (1) of The Constitution to appeal to this Court. Held, that the word "decision" in article 133(i) should mean the whole of the appellate decree and not the portion of the decree. The word "decision " in article 133 (i) should not mean the whole. The word 'decision" in the context of the word "judgment" in article 134(i) must mean the whole and not the decision of the appellate court. The word `decision ' in article 133 of the Constitution means the whole of a judgment or a decree. It is not a part of the decision or the grounds given for it but the decision of that court. The words "decision" are not to be construed in a narrow sense and they are not to have a narrow meaning. The word is not to be interpreted in a narrow or pedantic sense but in a narrow and pedantic sense. The word must be construed in the sense in which it is used in the statute. The word has to be construed according to its ordinary meaning. The words of the statute must be construed according, to their ordinary meaning. In the present case the appellate court made a variation in the decision of a trial court and not by reference to the whole of it. The High Court was right in holding that the word 'decision ' in the context in which it was used in the Act was a part of a decree and that the variation was made in favour of the intending appellant and not against him. The appellant was entitled to go to the Privy council and the High Court was in error in holding that if the appellate decree makes any variation in the judgment of the trial court it is not a decree of affirmance.

The High Court had exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, to entertain a revision petition filed under section 115, Code of Civil procedure, against the revisional orders of the District Court under section 115. The High Court had no jurisdiction under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act, to entertain revision petitions filed under section 25. The High Courts had exclusive jurisdiction to exercise revisional powers under section 115 and the District Court had exclusive power under section 115 to the District Court in other cases. The High court had exclusive jurisdiction in respect of cases arising out of original suits of the value of Rs. 20,000 and above. The High Curt had exclusive jurisdiction over the case. The High, however, held that the revisional jurisdiction under section 100, Code of Criminal Procedure, was not maintainable. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had jurisdiction under section 114, Code of civil Procedure, to entertain the revision petitions under section 115 in respect of an order of the District Judge under section 25 of the Provincial Small Cause Court Act disposing of a revision petition on and after that date, irrespective of the valuation of the suit out of which the case arose, the case would be amenable to the revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under section 25; and that the High Courts had jurisdiction under Section 115, Code, of Civil Procedure. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The High. Court is not vested with revisional jurisdiction under Section 25, Provincial Civil Procedure Code. [975F] 2. The High ' Court is not invested with revisional jurisdiction in respect to any case decided by a District Court under Section 115. [976F] 3. The High courts have jurisdiction under section 24, Code of C.P.C. to entertain a petition under section 115 for consideration as a petition under Article 227 of the Constitution. [977F] 4. The High High Court is not within its revisional jurisdiction under the revisional jurisdiction conferred on the High Court. [978F] 5.

The respondents, who were owners of certain lands, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Rajasthan, challenging the validity of the notification issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of the Act for the Urban Improvement Trust, Jaipur, and the High Court quashed the notification issued under section 52 (1) of Act. The Division Bench of the High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the acquisition of the land under section 52 was not for a public purpose, namely, for the implementation of a development scheme at public expense, viz. the Civil Lines Extension Scheme, the Civil Lines Scheme, the City Improvement Trust, Jodhpur, and the notified land vested in the State Government free from all encumbrances. The High Court also quashed the notification dated February 8, 1984 issued by the Government under section 53(1) and the order of the Special Officer, Town Planning Department, Jaipur under section 52 of the Act. The State Government issued the impugned notification dated February 9, 1984 under section 52, which was published in the Official Gazette on February 8,1984. The respondents challenged the validity of this notification by filing a writ petition before the High Court. The High court dismissed the writ application holding that the notification issued on February 8. 1984 under section 53 (1) was not for public purpose, as the acquisition of land under section 51(1) was for a public purposes, namely, the implementation of the development scheme at the public expense viz. the civil Lines Scheme, and the notification issued thereunder. The High Courts also quashed the notifications issued by the Central Government under section 51 (1) and directed the appellants to pay the compensation to the respondents. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High courts have rightly held that the acquisition was for a purpose wholly or partly in part and that the notification under section 52 had been issued by the appropriate authority. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of a land under section 53 of the Act arose within the State of Rajasthan i.e. within the territorial jurisdiction of the Rajasthan High Court at Jaipur Bench. [605G H] 2. The High 'Court at Jaipur Bench was not justified in quashing the notification issued in the year 1984 under section 51 of the Act and the notification under Section 52(1). [605H] 3.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the appellant from the premises in suit. The appellant contended that the building in question was constructed by a co operative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the new Rent Act had no application to the building in suit and the appellant cannot get any protection of the new Rent Acts. The Additional District Judge held that the building was constructed by the co operative society, and the landlord was in possession of it from the Society and, therefore the new Rent Ordinance had no application. The High Court, however, accepted the finding of the Additional District Judge that the building would be deemed to have been completed on the date of assessment of house tax and water tax held that the appellant would be entitled to the benefit of s.39 of the new Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that the building had become ten years old on the date the assessment of house taxes and water tax was held to be completed on 1st October, 1971, the date of the assessment of the house tax and the water tax held by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was in error in holding that the building will be deemed to be completed only on the date on which the first assessment was made. [337B] 2. The High Courts were in error in not holding that the appellant was entitled to the benefits of s.40 of the new rent Act. [338C] 3. The High. Court was in error. The appellant would be entitle to the benefit under s.39. [339D] 4. The appellant was entitled for the benefit of section 39 of the newRent Act. [340D] 5. The appellant is entitled to the protection of the old Rent Act. [341E] 6. The appellant cannot get the benefit of the new Amending Act.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of a building contractors. The respondents entered into three contract for the construction and construction of a buildings contractor. The respondents were the contractors for the construction. The respondents filed a suit for the enforcement of the contract. The respondents contended that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of the bills, and that the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not be brought within item 12 of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant date, and it was therefore void. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the agreement for reference to arbitration was not one of the contracts, and that it was not one which was not a contract relating to the execution of works, and that therefore it fell within item 12. The High court held that the award passed in proceedings founded thereon was a nullity and that the award was a nullity. Held, that the award which was sent by the arbitrator to the Superintending Engineer whose decision was to be final, and that as the agreement was one relating to the arbitration, it was not a valid reference to arbitration. The award was not one in which case the arbitrator did not prepare the award in triplicate, and that under section 35 of the Stamp Act there could be validation only of the original, when it was unstamped or insufficiently stamped, that the original was not a copy of the award. The award in proceedings founded on it was a nullity, and the question whether the award was sent by a person who was authorised to do so by the Governor, and in consequence there was a valid reference, was not one regarding execution of the contract, and that, therefore, it fell within the item 12.

The appellant, a retired Executive Engineer in Public Works Department, was working as Executive Engineer in the Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. He was working as a Executive Engineer in PWD in the State. He was charged with criminal misconduct under Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, 1934. He was convicted and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and in default to undergo rigorous rigorous imprisonment for one year. The High Court quashed the First Information Report and convicted him under Rule 2(2) of the Punjab civil Service Rules, and sentenced him to undergo rigorous Imprisonment for two years. The State appealed to this Court. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The third proviso to clause (b) of Rule 2.1 of the Punjab Criminal Service Rules, which is in the nature of a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the Rule has been framed. The embargo on prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of a period of four years from the date of cause of action or event mentioned therein is not to be interpreted as laying down an absolute or general embargo on prosecution. [920D] 1.2 The embargo on the prosecution of a Government servant on the expiration of a periodof four years from his date of cause or event mentioned in the Rule is not to place an embargo on prosecution on the expiry or of four years of the cause of action. [921D] 1.(a) The third proviso is in the very nature of a statutory provision and in case the conditions stated therein are satisfied, the benefit of a government employee on the expiry thereof cannot be extended to a government servant. [922D] 1(b) The third Proviso to clause (a) of Rule 3.2 is in the character of a beneficient legislation and in the case of doubt had to be interpreted In the light of the scope of the power to frame a rule under Article 309 and the purpose of Rule 2, there is no doubt with regard to the interpretation of the said rule. [923F] 1(c) The third provisos to clause (c) of Rule 1.2 are in the nature and of a beneficative legislation and in cases of doubt has been framed for a different purpose namely to provide an exception to the power of the government in the matter of withholding or withdrawing or withdrawing or withholding or withdrawing pension of a retired government servant contained in clause (b). [924D] 1 (d) The third sub clause (b), of Rule 2 is in the manner of a beneficential legislation and in a case of doubt having to be interpreted, in favour of a person for whose benefits the Rule has already been framed. [924E] 2(e) The third and the purpose for which the Rule has come to be framed is not to placed an embargo on the institution of judicial proceedings as against a person referred to therein for prosecution in respect of a cause of action which arose or an event which took more than four years prior to the institution of the departmental proceedings.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 ordinary share of Rs. 7,000 preference shares of Rs. 10,000 preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to a fixed dividend of 71 per cent on the face value of the shares, with no right in the balance of the profits. The respondent company was registered as a public company under the Companies Act 1913. The authorised capital was 7,500 ordinary shares and 8,000 ordinary shareholders. The authorised share capital of the respondent company was 7.000 ordinary shares. The authorised shares of Rs, 10,000 were not held by the public. The respondent was a public limited Company. The authorised shareholders of the respondent Company were not shareholders of the public. In the assessment year 1949 51 the Income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 23 A of the Indian Income tax Act for any of the three years and on that footing answered the question in the negative. The High Court held that the provisions of section 23 A were correctly applied for the three relevant years. The High court held that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23A was in reality a clause which defines what a company in which the public are substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such companies, if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company is held by the parent company or by the nominees thereof. The High. Court further held that the explanation to sub section(1) of that section applied only to the company which was a public company in which it was substantially interested and not to a subsidiary Company of such companies. The High, Court, on a reference, held that the respondent company had no jurisdiction under section 23A to pass the orders under section 23. The High 'Court held that the proviso to sub section 1(1) applied only to a company in whose shares the public were substantially interested and that the company was not a public company within the meaning of section 23(A) of the Indian Incometax Act. The High ,Court held that section 23 A was correctly applied for three relevant years and that the Explanation was not applicable to the company in which its public were substantially affected. The HighCourt held that in the present case the Explanation to section 23 A applied only to companies in which the Public were substantially interested, and that the proviso was not applicable. The High Courts, however, held that in determining whether the provisions of the section were correctly applied, the test laid down by the High Court was whether the provisions were correctly applied. Held, that the Explanation applied only to private companies which were substantially interested. The Explanation applied only in respect of companies which were not substantially interested. It was not necessary that the company should be a public company. The Explanation was not applied to private companies. The Explanation did not apply to private companies in which they were substantially interested; it was not necessary to apply the Explanation to private companies, because the Explanation applied to private Companies. The Explanation merely applied to private company which was substantially interested. In the present case, the Explanation applied not only to private company but also to private companies also. The Explanation applies only to private Companies which were substantially owned by the public and not by the nominees of the company. The proviso applied only to those companies which were owned by the company.

The first appellant, who was the agent of the first appellant, was authorised to take delivery of the bales on behalf of the first respondent. The first appellant sent them to Dharsi Moolji on behalf of another quota holder Beharilal Bajirathi. The first respondent sent them to the first appellant on 17th February, 1947, but the goods were not physically delivered to the first respondent on 21st February, 1947. The first information report was lodged on the same day. The first informant sent a letter to the first Appellant on 21st March, 1947, stating that he had been authorised to take possession of the bales and that the goods had passed, and that he had received payment in advance from the first appellant for the goods, and that the balance amount was to be paid by the first appellant to the first informant on 21st April, 1947. On the same day, the first appellant sent a letter, to the first information appellant, stating that the bales were delivered to the second appellant on 21st May, 1947, and that they were in the physical possession of the first Appellant at all material times and were not physically delivery to the quota holder or his agent. The first Appellant sent a letter on 21st June, 1947, to the second Appellant, stating that his firm had received payment for the goods and that the first appellant had delivered them to the second respondent on 21th June, 1947. In the meantime, the first Appellant sent the goods to Dharsi on behalf of himself and his agent. On the next day, the second appellant sent them on 21st July, 1947, saying that he had delivered them on 21th July, 1947. Thereafter, the first information report, on the same date, was lodged by the first Appellant. The first Information Report was lodged on 21st August, 1947, after the goods had been delivered to the appellant. The first and second appellant, who were the agents of the second appellant, sent them toDharsi on behalf, and sent them to their godown. The first first appellant sent the goods on 21st September, 1947, for delivery to Dharsi. The first, appellant, however, sent them on 22nd September, 1947 to Dharsi, and sent the goods back to Dharsi and the goods were delivered to Dharsi in the godown. The second appellant, however sent them to his godown on 22nd October, 1947, on the ground that the bales remained in the physical custody of the first, appellant at all material time and were not actually delivered to the quota holders or his agent and as Dwarkadas Khetan was not the agent of Dharsi, the statement was inaccurate and misleading. The first. appellant, however. sent them to Amsi on behalf Of another quota holder.

The respondent was a public servant. He was prosecuted under section 5(1)(d) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, for having committed the offence of criminal misconduct in the discharge of his duty. The respondent was convicted by the trial court and sentenced to imprisonment for one year. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that the High Court was in error in holding that the respondent was a "public servant" within the meaning of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code, keeping in view the nature and the nature of the duties which he was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of any public duty. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that there was no abuse of position as a public servant although the abuse of position was of a nature which could well be regarded as public servant. [723 B] (2) The use of the word "obtains" in clause (d) of the Eighth clause of the Eighth Clause is not decisive. The use of words "obtains", "obtains". "obtains "obtains," and "obtains the words "obtain" in clause(d) of that clause. [724 C] (3) The use "obtains ' in the discharge or his duty" is clearly implied. The use is not decisive of the question whether the abuse of the position would be the necessary ingredient of the offence. [725 D] (4) The use is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. The abuse of the status would be the essential ingredient of the charge. [726 E] (5) The abuse of position would be a necessary ingredient of offence under section 5 (1) (d) and the abuse being either by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as a Public servant. [771 B] (6) The use in the instant case was not of a public servant but was merely a abuse of position. The abuse being either in the discharge, or by other means of the nature mentioned in Narayanan Nambiar ' Nambiar ' Nambiar" was clearly implied. [727 C] (7) The use was not of any public character. The use was of a very wide nature and the use of the words "public servant " in the discharge and his duty" in clause 2 of the Eighth paragraph was not decisive of its nature. [728 D] (7)(a) The use by the respondent was of a wide nature and was not of the essence or essential ingredient of an offence under section 161 of the Indian penal Code. [729 C] (b) The use being either by the corrupt or illegal or by other mode of the nature described in Narayanan Nambiar, it was clearly implied that the abuse of a position as apublic servant was of the essence of the offence under section5 (1) of the Corruption Act because the liability of a public officer had been made absolute and it was not necessary that the remuneration by any of the methods mentioned in Narayanan Nair Nambiar ' Nambiar should be paid by the Government as a public officer. [730 D E] (c) The use made by the respondent in the instant cases was not of public character. [731 D] (d) The use for the purpose of the opening part of section 5 (2) (d), was not of an essential ingredient of that offence. [772 D] (e) The use, however, was not of such a nature as to make it punishable under section 161. [732 E] (f) The use did not amount to abuse of position which was consistent with the provisions of the sub s.5 (1)(d).

The petitioners, who were working as casual labourers in the Construction Department of the Signal Unit in the Signal unit in the Signals Department of the Construction Department, filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the validity of the Railway Board 's orders on January 1, 1984, and January 1,1984, on the ground that the same were discriminatory and that the petitioners were entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the Railway Board. The petitioners contended that the Railway Board had no power to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and that the Railway Administration had no power under the Railway Board to treat them as temporary servants and that the said retiral benefits were not available to them at par with the maintenance workers and should be treated as temporary servants. The petitioners also contended that the Railways had no power in the matter of granting temporary status to the petitioners and that the same was discriminatory and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The petitioners further contended that the petitioners had been discriminated against by the Railway Administration and that the impugned orders were violative of Articles 16 and 16 of Constitution. The respondents contended that the writ petitions were not maintainable as the petitioners had not been given the same pay as was admissible to temporary railway servants after attaining temporary status. The petitioners, therefore, contended that the impugned order was violative of Articles 19 and 16 of constitution. The petitioners have also contended that since the petitioners were project employees and do not belong to the open line, their case should be considered as temporary servants, and that the respondents should be directed to treat the Petitioners at par with permanent employees and that the pensionary benefits are not admissible to either category of employees. The respondents have also contended in their counter affidavit that the petitioners are project employees and doing not belong to any open line. The petitioners had also contended that as per the existing rules, temporary status will be first given in the cadre of Khallasi and then promotion to skilled category after conducting the trade test is admissible. The petitioners alleged that the Railway administration had no power, under the Railway Boards ' Manual, to treat the employees at par with temporary railway servants and that they are entitled to all the privileges as applicable to open line. Allowing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The petitioners are project workers and do not belongs to the open Line. The petitioners are Project employees and do Not belong to the Open Line. The Railway Administration is anxious to take appropriate steps to remove the difficulties faced by the casual labour but there is hardly slackness in enforcing them. [144C D] 1.2 The Administration is anxious and to take appropriate action to remove the difficulty faced by the Casual labour but there are hardly slackerness in enforcing the petitioners. [144E] 1.3 The Administration is conscious to take appropriate measures to remove the problems faced by the causal labour but there was slackness of enforcing them.

The Forward Markets Commission was constituted under the Forward Markets Commission Act, 1956, which was to be deemed to be a proper authority for the purposes of the Act. The Forward Markets Commission, in exercise of the powers conferred by section 12 of the Act, framed a bye law, called the Forward Markets Act, 1956. The said bye law was amended by the Forward Markets (Amendment) Act, 1956 and the powers of the Central Government under section 12 of that Act were vested in the Commission. The Forward Market Commission was constituted by the Forward Market Commission. The said Act was amended by Act No. 11 of 1956, which came into force on January 21, 1956. By section 12(1) of the Act the Central Government was empowered to make bye laws with retrospective effect. The said power was vested in the Central Government by section 12(2) of the Forward Markets Regulation Act, 1956 (Act No. 11 Of 1956). The said bye laws were made by the Central Government in exercise of its powers under section 12(3) of the said Act. The said rules were made by a notification dated January 24, 1956, issued by the Central Board of Agricultural and Rural Development, Government of India, under section 12 (1) of that Act. The appellant, a member of the Forward Market Committee, was appointed by the Central Govt. under section 12A of the Forward Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1957, to function as the Forward Markets Committee. The said Committee was to consist of the Forward Marketing Commission and the members of the Forward Committee. The Forward Marketing Commission was to consist Of the Forward Markets Commissioner and the members to be nominated by the Central Govern ment. The said Commission was to be a body corporate having perpetual succession and a common seal with power to acquire, hold and dispose of property, both movable and immovable, and to enter into contracts for the sale and purchase of any property, both moveable and immovable, in the State of Bombay. The Forward Contracts (Regulations) Act, 1951, was passed by the Forward Contracts Act, 1956 which was to come into force on the 1st day of April, 1956. Section 12(1), of the Forward Contract (Regulation) Ordinance, 1956, provided that the Forward Markets Commis sioner shall be the principal executive and executive of the Forward Co operative Societies and shall be responsible for the proper management and administration of the Forward contracts. The Forward Co operative Society was to consist in the Forward Markets Co operative Societies. The Forward Contract (Regulations) Ordinance, 1957, was passed in exercise of that power. The Forward Service Commission was to function as a Forward Markets Commission. The Commission was to exercise the powers conferred on it under the Act, and the Forward Markets Regulations were to be framed by the Central Gov ernment. The Commission, however, was to function under the Act as the Forward Market Commis sions. The Commission had to function as an advisory body and the Commission was to act as the delegate of the Commission. It was, however, not competent to make a bye law under section 12. The Commission could not, having regard to the terms of the statute under which it was created, be a proper recipient of the power conferred on it by or under the Act. It was not competent to frame bye law under the Act to make a Bye law with retrospective effect and, therefore, the new bye law made on January 21. 1956, in so far as it purports to operate retrospectively, was invalid. The Commission therefore, could not, in the exercise of its power under section 12, be said to have made a bye law with retrospective operation. The Commission did not, therefore, have the power to make a rule under section 12 and the Association under section 12 was not competent.

The assessee, a shareholder of a company, was a shareholder of the Ukhara Estate. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts distributed to him as dividend, the assessee was not taxable as dividend, but only a part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire amount for each year was income in the hands of the assessee, but only part of it was being dividend, and the remaining amounts were not taxable as dividends, and the balance amount was not taxable, since they were declared out of capital gains of the company which comprised salami or premia received by it as consideration for grant of long term leases after the 31st March, 1948, was not in the hands ofthe assessee, but merely a part of the same being dividend, in the hands Of the assessee, and taxable as dividend.
