The Appellate Tribunal held that the whole amount for each of these three years was income in its hands, but only of the part of it, being dividend, outside the meaning of the section 2(4A) of that Act, and that the distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to salami received by it was not taxable. The High Court, however, held that the distribution of dividend out of capital gain was taxable as dividend and the remaining amount was not liable to tax under section 12 of the Indian income tax Act, 1961. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The distribution of dividend by the assessee to the shareholders of the company was taxable as income of the assessee from other sources. The distribution to the shareholders was taxable as dividends within the meaning Of section 2(5A) of Income tax Act. [33E F] (2) The distribution to a shareholder of an assessee is of a capital nature and interest which forms part of the fixed assets of a company is of a Capital nature. The distribution of the capital gains, to the shareholders, out of those capital gains, is of a revenue nature. [33F] (3) The distribution is taxable as dividend under section 12. [33G] (4) The distribution in the hands is taxable as dividends. The distribution is not capital gain, but interest which is statutorily payable on compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land for public purposes. [33H] (5) The distribution was taxable as the income of the company from other sources, and the distribution to a company out of those profits was taxable as a dividend within the meaning ofs. 2(6 A) of the Act. [34F] (6) The distribution must be deemed to be exempt from liability to tax under s.12 of the Act, and the provisions of section 12 of that Act are not applicable to the distribution of the dividend. [33D] (7) The distribution made by the assessee was taxable as "other sources" under section 12, and the amount attributable thereto was not capital gain. [33A] (8) The distribution by the assessee of capital gains was taxable as capital gains. [33C] (9) The distribution, in the present case, was of a capital character and interest which formed part of the assets of the fixed asset which forms part the fixed assets. [33B] (10) The distribution did not amount to capital gains, but only capital gains. The distribution was not capital gains, and the assessee was entitled to the distribution. [33 F] (11) The distribution could not be regarded as capital gains, because the distribution was not of capital gains. It was not a capital asset.

The respondent was prosecuted for offences under the Kerala Forest Act, 1963, alleging that Sandalwood oil was not a forest produce within the meaning of section 2(f) (i) of the Act. The trial court acquitted the respondent. The High Court, however, held that Sandal wood oil was not 'wood oil ' as defined under section 2(g) (i), (f) of the Kerala Forest (Amendment) Act, 1972. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Sandal Wood Oil is not a forest product within the meaning Of section 2(e) (i). Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'forest produce ' in the definition of forest produce ' in section 2(k) of the Forest Act, 1968, is a wider meaning than the word 'forest '. The word wood oil is not static and ideas of concepts and concepts as they are bound to do in any country like ours with the establishment of a democratic structure based on agalitarian values, the meaning and content of the word wood oil ' in section2(f) of that Act. [164B C] 2. The word "forest produce" in the definition is not static or ideas of concepts or concepts and as they are governed by the definition of 'forest produce'. The word ' forest produce ' is not static nor ideas of concepts, but as understood in commercial parlance. The word forest produce ' has to be construed in the sense in which it is being understood in commercial sense in which its meaning is being understood. [164F] 3. The word Forest produce ' in its definition of forest produces is not static but ideas of concepts. The word `forest produce ' is a generic term which is commonly used in commercial parlance in commercial parlance and in commercial parlance, it cannot be restricted in such a manner so as to defeat the principle object and purpose of the Act.[164F] 4. The word timber oil is a forest produce which includes wood oil. The word, wood oil is a natural produce of the forest directly derived as an exudation from living trees in the forest belonging to the family of the Dipterocarpucoae trees while wood oil is an essential oil. The dictionary meaning of the word ' forest produces ' is to say, the 'enumerated items in Clauses 1 and 11. 'wood oil is a bye product from sandalwood (including wood oil). The word ' wood oil ' is a natural product from sandalwood. The word is to be construed as a dictionary meaning in which it was being understood in the sense which it is used and the purpose of the statute. [164G H] 5. The word trees is a natural commodity from sandalwood (excluding wood oil). It must be construed in its technical sense but in an exhaustive manner it cannot be limited in such a way so as to frustrate the principle and object of the Act, when there is nothing in the context or the subject matter to the subject matter of the Act to defeat the principles and object of that Act.[164G H; 164A] 6. The word saw oil is a 'forest produce which includes timber oil. The expression is not static, but in an inclusive definition has to be interpreted in its technical meaning. The word must be construed as meaning in its technical and being part of an inclusive definition. [164D] 7. The wordwood oil is not a wood oil as defined under Section 2(f)(i) of that act. The word earth oil is a mineral oil which is being used in commercial sense.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The High Court acquitted the appellant on the ground that there was no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment of acquittal. The appellant contended that there was nothing compelling reasons for the reversal of the acquittal and that there was sufficient evidence against him to warrant a conviction and that there were no compelling reasons justifying interference with the judgment of the High Court. Held, that the High Court was in error in accepting the testimony of the doctor P. W. W. 4 who was present on the spot by using the statement of the deceased alleged to have been made in the circumstances of this case. The High court was in error on its findings in accepting the evidence of the doctor and that the evidence of P. W., P. W, was not in accord with the opinion expressed in books on Medical Jurisprudence by authors like Modi and Lyon. The High Courts were, therefore, in error in holding that the evidence in the present case was sufficient to sustain a conviction. The High, Court was in a position to record a finding that the evidence was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt of the accused could properly be drawn. The High. Court was in the error in accepting a dying declaration of the deceased. The High ' Court was in fact in error in rejecting the testimony of these two eye witnesses in support of the dying declarations. The High , Court was in wrong in accepting the statement of a man who was present at the spot by use of the statement of another man who was not present on the scene.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In the course of its business, it had two factories, at Jamshedpur and the factory at Jamshedpur, and had two factories at Jamshedpur. The appellant company was a whole time establishment. The workmen of the appellant company were employed in the factory at the Jamshedpur, and the factory was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. The appellant Company was an allIndia complex having its own establishment at Jamshedpur. In the year 1964, the appellant company was incorporated in Bihar and the factory of the appellant was situated at Jamshedpur. On the basis of the agreement between the management and the workmen, the appellant Company was constituted under the Bihar Factories and Establishments Act, 1947. The appellant 's workmen represented by the Indian Oxygen Workers ' Union, were also paid wages at double the ordinary rate of wages as provided in the Bihar Shops & Establishments Act, 1948. The appellant, a company, was incorporated in the Bihar and Orissa Shops and Establishments (Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1961. The appellant was a company incorporated in Bihar. The appellant filed a petition under section 10(2) of the , for a reference under section 10 of the , alleging that the dispute between the management of the appellant ' company and its workmen represented by its employees represented by the Indco Labour Union was a dispute between the appellant and the workmen represented by their workmen represented by Indco Labour Unions. The Tribunal held that the dispute raised by the union was in respect of the employees of the appellant Company and that the dispute was between the management, of the appellant and its workmen, and that the Tribunal 's award was not justified. The appellant appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the Tribunal was justified in refusing to grant special leave to the appellant company to grant special Leave to the appellant. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the dispute referred to the Tribunal was only those set out in the said agreement and the said statement, any award made by the Tribunal in respect of those disputes must necessarily be confined to the disputes referred to it, the parties who had agreed to refer those disputes for adjudication. HELD: The Tribunal was justified. The Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant company 's employees to grant special special leave to it. [507 D] The Tribunal was right in refusing to give special leave to appeal. [508 E] The Tribunal 's conclusion, therefore, that the union 's union was duly amended on January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was only those sets out in the agreement and the same statement and the said Statement, any award was made by the tribunal in respect of workmen of the company 's factory at Jamshedpur and not the workmen of its other establishments, was clearly without jurisdiction. [509 F] The Tribunal, on the aforesaid considerations, was not justified, in obliging it to grant special permission to attend the meetings of the executive committee of the union, and that it had amended its constitution on January 6. 1963 and that the said statement was not binding on the appellant company. [510 F] The appellant company, a whole time employee, was not entitled to special leave under section 10. [511 F] The fact that the dispute regarding the employees of a company was referred to the tribunal by the appellant company, was not disputed by the appellant. The Tribunal, therefore, was not right in refusing the special leave to this appellant.

The assessee was a partnership firm carrying on business in timber at Abdullapur in the name of M/s Hakam Malani Tani Mal. The firm was dissolved on March 31, 1939, and the business of the firm was taken over by the assessee. The firm, in the assessment proceedings for 1943 44, was dissolved on April 1, 1939, after April 1, 1942, and the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer held that the firm was not carrying on business at the commencement of the Indian Incometax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939, and that firm alone was entitled to the benefit provided in section 25(3) or 25(4). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the assessee was not carrying out business at the end of the period between the end of March 31, 1944, and the first succession which took place on April 1. 1939, and, therefore, the firm alone was liable to be assessed to tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1918. The Appellate Tribunal, however, took the view that the assessee had been carrying on business immediately after the dissolution of the firm, and that the firm alone had become separate from the 1st of April, 1939, before the Income tax (Amendment) 7 of 1939. The High Court, however, disagreed with the view taken by the Tribunal and held that the business of Messrs. Hakam Mal Tani Mal was liable to tax under section 25 (4) of that Act. The High court, however, agreed with the view of the Tribunal and the High Court that the assessee could not be said to have been carrying on the business at the date of dissolution of the partnership firm. The High, however, found favour with the Tribunal and in the view of that Court, the assessee was at the commencement, of the Indian income tax (Amendment). The High Court agreed with the Tribunal that the assessee 's firm was not carried on the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution of that firm in March 1943, and that it succeeded to the business on April 1 , 1939, after the dissolution. The High. Court, however held that the partnership firm was not entitled to relief, under section 25 of the Indian Act, 1922, and that, in the absence of other evidence, it could not be held that the income, profits and gains of the previous year shall be deemed to have been the previous year for which the Indian Incometax Act, 1918, was brought into force. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The assessee was carrying on business as timber at the commencement Of the Indian Income taxes (Amendment) Ordinance 7 of 1939 and the business at Abdullpur was settled on March 31 , 1939, and thereafter the business of M/S. HakamMalani TaniMal was settled on April 1 . 1939, and there was no other evidence in that behalf. [601 B C] (ii) The assessee, was constituted to carry on the timber at the time when the Indian Income Act, 1918 was brought into being. The assessee was constituted to carrying on the timber in timber which was carried on by the undivided family of Hakam Mal Malani T. Malani Mal. T. Malni Malani Malani Malini Malani Malni Malini Malini Malni Malni Mali Malini Mali Malni Malnani Malini T.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the , for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimoga. The appellant produced the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit. The appellant filed a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the order of the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the order of stay. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the issue of the permit was made beyond the prescribed period of limitation under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963, and rule 151 of the old Rules was replaced by rule 119 of Mysore Motor Vehicles rules, 1945 (old Rules) and rule 151 was in force and rule 151 had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The appeal must be dismissed. The appeals before the State Transport Tribunal and further in second appeal by the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal are, therefore, not competent under section 64 of the Act. [190B] The appeals before this Court are, therefore not competent under rule 120 of the Mysore 1939 Motor Vehicles Rules. [190C] The appeals to the Mysore Revenue Tribunal are, however, not competent. [190D] The appeals were, therefore, competent under section 65 of the Act and both the Tribunals had no jurisdiction. [190E] The appeals of the appellant were, therefore not incompetent under section 64.

The appellant was a sitting member of Parliament. He was alleged to have been assaulted by the workers of the Republican Party. The appellant alleged that at the meeting which was held at Hapur on February 7, 1967, the appellant and his supporters entered the office of the Republica Party. The respondent was alleged to be a member of Parliament and the appellant was alleged to belong to a particular caste and sects. The appellant denied the opportunity of meeting. The respondent denied the allegation of the appellant that the meeting was held at the Town Hall Maidan. The appellant 's case was that the meeting of the Republic of the Party was held at night and the appellant and the supporters of respondent Prakash Vir Shastri were alleged to have chased the constituency. The appellant contended that the meeting could not be held at Hapur and the supporters were not mentioned at all either in the Vir Arjun published on February 8, 1967 or in the Hindustan dated 7 February, 1967. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The evidence of the appellant was not sufficient to establish that respondent Prakash Vir Gandhi committed any corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of the appellant. The evidence of P.W. 18 was not sufficient. The evidence was not sufficient for the appellant to prove that respondent Vir Shastri committed any corrupt practices in relation to personal character and Conduct of the appellant and that the appellant was guilty of corrupt practice. [895 C D] (2) The evidence was sufficient to prove that the respondent Vir Shastri and his election agent committed any corrupt Practice in relation to his personal character and the conduct of the respondent. The evidence showed that the meeting at Hapur was held at Meerut on February 7. 1967 and there was no complaint by the appellant to the Election Commissioner. The evidence did not mention the name of the appellant as having been assaulted or chased or chased or assaulted or chased. The evidence clearly showed that the appellant had been assaulted or assaulted or attempted to be assaulted or chased by the respondent. [896 D E] (3) The evidence showed the presence of the appellant at the Town hall Maidan, Hapur on February 8. 1967. The evidence further showed that the respondent was a member of the Parliament and the supporters at the Town Centre were alleged to be assaulted by the appellant with the consent of the respondent Prakash Vir. The evidence shows that the appellant and respondent Vir Shastri were the supporters of the respondent and the supporters. The evidence also showed that the supporters of Prakash Vir Shastri and the supporters had been assaulted by them. The evidence, therefore, showed that the attack on the office of Prakash Vir Gandhi was unacceptable.

The respondent, a Hindu Undivided Family, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for delivery of possession of the property purchased by him. The application was dismissed by the District Judge, Jaipur City, Jaipur, holding that in view of the provision of Explanation I to section 47 of the Code, the application for delivery of the possession of the mortgaged property purchased by the respondent was maintainable and not barred by limitation. The respondent filed an application for setting aside the sale on the ground that in view thereof, the application of the decree holder auction purchaser for delivery of posses sion of the property sold was maintainable and non est. The District Judge, however, dismissed the application holding that in the view of the provisions of Explanation I, the application was within the period of limitation as prescribed by Article 136 of the . The respondent filed a revision petition before the High Court which dismissed the same holding that the application for settingaside the sale was within the time of limitation as provided by Article 136. The respondent then filed a writ petition before the Division Bench which allowed the same holding, that the application was beyond the period of 12 years as prescribed by the Article 136 of th e Limitation Act. The Division Bench also took a similar view that after the amendment of section 47 of CPC by Section 20 of the Code the application for set aside the sale was made within one year of the dismissal of the application for the setting aside the auction sale. The Division bench also took a view that after amendment of section47 of the Code by Section 20, the application could be filed only after the decree was put into execution within the period prescribed by Article 137 of the . In the circumstances, the Division Bench held that Article 134 will apply to an application under order XXI Rule 95, and not Article 134 of the would apply. The Division Court also took a contrary view that after insertion of Explanation II to Section 47 of the CPC, an application for set ous tion of possession could also be made within a period of 12 year from the date of the dismissal. The Division Judge took a similar views that after the insertion of Explanation I in the Code of civil Procedure, an application under Rule 95 of Order XXI of the Code will be governed by Article 136 and not Article 136 of t he would apply. In the circumstances the Division Bench took a similar opinion that after the Amendment of Section 47 of CPC, an applica tion for setting aside sale can also be made in a period of twelve years from the date on which the decree has been passed, as provided in clause (a) of Explanation II of Section 47, an application filed for setting aside a sale can also also be made after the decree is put into execution. The Division Co operative Court, however, took a similar decision that after the addition of Explanation II, all questions relating to delivery of possession can also be raised on other grounds as mentioned in the said Rules. The Division Commis sion of City, Jaipur City was confirmed by the Single Judge of the High Court. The Division of the High Commis sions of City, Bangalore, in the Letters Patent Appeal, took a contrary stand. The Division Benches took a similar stand and held that the application of Explanation II was within the limitation as prescribed under Article 136 of The would apply. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The application for setting off the sale was filed within one year from the dismissal of application for setting it aside the sale by the judgment debtor for setting aside an ex parte decree. The Division Benami decree holder had filed the application for restoration of possession of property sold in execution of a decree. The application had been made within one month of the dismissal and the application for condonation of delay was also within the period. [367B C] 2. The application filed for restoration of the possession was within the prescribed period as prescribed by article 136 of the Limitation Act. [367D] 3.

The appellant, a candidate for election to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from the Mattancherry Constituency No. P 14, was declared elected. The appellant challenged the election of the first respondent on the ground that the said poster was published in the presence of the workers of the first appellant and that the said wall poster was pasted on a wall at the instance and with the consent of the appellant 's election agent. The High Court held that the said posters were published in the manner alleged by the appellant and that it was not defamatory or that it was intended to create an impression and did create an impression that the incident had taken place a previous day but it was an admitted fact that the said display was meant to create an assurance and did create impression that the occurrence had taken place. The High court also held that the publication was intended to creating an impression and that it did create an assurance. The High Cou rt held that the appellant was guilty of the corrupt practice within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The publication by a candidate or his agent or by any other person with the consent or knowledge of a candidate or of his election agent or by some other person with his consent of a candidate, being a statement reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus of that candidate 's election. [701C D] 2. The publication was intended merely to create an apprehension and did create a impression that the event of murders had taken place, a previous day prior to the election. The appellant 's cross examination of this witness was also not only his own testimony but also his own testimony as well as on the testimony of his witnesses. [702C D] 3. The appellant was not guilty of the charge of the corrupt practices within the meaning Of Section 123(5) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. [703E] 4. The appellant had not been able to establish that he had taken the photographs in question on the said days. He had also in his examination in chief stated that he had not seen the wall poster together with exhibit P 1. He had not seen it on the said day prior to election. He had only stated that he was going to examine only in connection with the pasting of the poster on the said one wall. He had seen the actual pasting. He had, therefore, seen the actual present pasting. [704C D] 5.

The respondent No. 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for the construction of a five star hotel. The Municipal Corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan. The Municipal Commissioner rejected the plan. The respondent No. 2, however, rejected the plan holding that it was intended to earmark a certain land under reference. The Municipal Council rejected the plan and the High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Municipal Corporation that the proposed revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was not justified in merely relying upon a proposal for revision of the draft plan or that such a revision was under contemplation. The High court was not justified merely relying upon the proposal for revision. The High Courts were, therefore, not justified in rejecting the plan on that ground. [924B] 2. The High. Court was not right in holding that the proposed revised plan was no longer tenable. The High, however, was justified in rejecting a plan on the ground that there was a proposal for the revision of a draft revised development plan. [925C] 3. The High ' Court was not correct in merely relying on a proposal for a revision of the revised development plan, and the High court rejected the plan submitted by the respondent No. 4. [926D] 4. The High was not justified. The High Curt was not justified on the ground of the rejection of the plan on account of the clear provisions of sections 46 and 31(6) of the Act and having regard to the position that the draft revised development plans had since been published and the plan submitted to the Municipal Commissioner was not justified, merely relying upon an approved plan submitted by respondent No. 3, the High Court was justified in holding that in granting the exemption, the Municipal Corporation had not considered the plan submitted and the plan approved by the respondent no. 2.

The appellants, who were the employees of the two concerns, were dismissed from service by the Industrial Court. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Industrial Court had framed an issue whether the employers had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing a lock out and had thus committed unfair labour practice. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Industrial Court was not justified in rejecting the complaints filed by the appellants. The Industrial Courts have not gone into the question whether the employer had imposed a lockout or has closed down the industrial undertaking. The Industrial court has to determine whether the employer has imposed a lock out or has closed the industrial undertaking and whether the closure was a bonafide one or was a device to determine whether it was a device or was a pretence to determine the intention and bonafides of the employer at the time when it resorts to lock out. [67F G] 2. The Industrial Tribunal has not decided to close down the industrial establishment. The Industrial Disputes Act, 1974 is an unfair labour practices. The Industrial courts have not gone through the evidence produced before it and have come to the conclusion that the closure was not a bonafide one. The Industrial Tribunals have not gone in the matter from this angle. The Industrial tribunals have not gone to the correct approach. The Industrial disputes Act, 1974 has to be construed in the light of the principles of natural justice. [67G H] 3. The Industrial Appellate Tribunal has not gone into this question. The Industrial Adjudicator has not gone to correct the approach of the Industrial Court before rejecting the complaints. The Industrial Tribu nal has not gone in this case. The Industrial Commis sion has not gone beyond the scope of the Industrial Disputes Act. [67H] 4. The Industrial adjudicator has not considered the question whether a closure was a bona fide one or was an unfair labour Practice. The IndustrialTribunal has not gone through that aspect. The Industrial Corpo rationality has to be determined with accuracy whether the closure is a bonafide one and not a pretence to decide the services of workmen or whether it is bonafide and for reasons beyond the control of the employer. [67A B] 5. The Industrial Dismis sion is an unfair Labour practice. The Industrial Con sion has to be fair and just. The Industrial adjudication has to be done in accordance with the principles of justice. The Industrial (Tribunal) has to be slow and judicious in interfering with the order of the employer in the matter of termination of the services of the employees. [67B] 6. The Industrial Labour Court has not gone wrong in interfering with an order of the management in the matter.

The assessee company was a dealer in shares, securities and properties. The objects set out in the memorandum of association and the previous assertion made by the assessee company that it was a dealer and not an investor, were the properties of the assessee company, could not be taxed as business profits. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee company was not a dealer in securities and properties and dismissed the appeals. The High Court, on a reference, held that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities, securities and immovable properties of the company could be taxed as profits. The assessee company then applied to the Appellate Tribunal under section 66(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 for a reference of the questions of law for the opinion of the High Court. The Tribunal held that in the case of the assessee, the assessee company could be treated as a dealer in investments and properties and that the profits or losses arising from sale of shares and securities and immovable property of the assessee Company could be taxed under section 66 (1) of that Act. The High court, however, held that in view of the objects contained in the memorandum, the assessee was a dealer. The High, Court, however, allowed the appeal on the last occasion and set aside the judgment of the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question as to what are the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor is a mixed question of fact and law. The question as framed at present is a mixed questions of fact and fact. The final conclusion of the Tribunal can, therefore, be challenged on the ground that the relevant legal principles have been mis applied by the Tribunal in reaching its decision on the point; and such a challenge is open under section 66 of the Act to the High Court and the Appellate Tribunal should be asked to make a fresh statement of the case. [527 C D] (2) The question whether the profits and loss arising from the transfer of shares, shares, securities or immovable properties of a company can be taxed as income profits depends on the facts and circumstances of each case. The question whether profits and losses arise from the sale or securities and immovable assets of the assessee is a mixed issue of fact and it is a mixed mixed question of law and fact. [528 D E] (3) The question of law involved in this case was not a pure question of fact but was a mixed question Of fact and law and it was a mixed mixed questions of law and law. [529 E] (4) The question involved in this appeal was not a mixed question and it was not a question of pure fact but was mixed question of facts and law. It was a mixed issue and it was, therefore, necessary in the interest of justice that the questions should be modified as suggested by the assessee in its petition under section 66. [530 F G] (5) The question was not a purely question of fact.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as Munsif in 1935. He was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was promoted to that office. The appellant was promoted to his office on June 19. 1950, and was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. The appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the grounds, inter alia, that the order of the Government of Madras, after October 1, 1953, was without jurisdiction, and that the proceedings of the High Court were without jurisdiction, that the proceedings were without jurisdiction and that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution, and that, therefore, the proceedings of that Court were without authority, and that as the authority which appointed him was the Governor of the Province, it was only that authority which appointed the appellant, that the High Court could not quash the order of his suspension, and that in any case, the proceedings were not without jurisdiction, but were, therefore, illegal. Held, that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under article 311 of The Constitution. The order of suspension was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government, and that it was not one of dismissal or removal from service within article 311 of Constitution. The Government was bound to hold a fresh enquiry and decide the matter finally, that the findings given by the High Court on January 28,1954, were without jurisdiction. The order passed by the High court on January 28 was merely one, and the order of dismissal was merely one. The order was merely one and the order was one of dismissal and the order passed by it was only one. The Government could not, therefore, interfere with the order of transfer. The order made by the High, Court on January 27, 1954, was merely one in contravention of the provisions of article 311 Of the Constitution. The High Court was, therefore, right in holding that the order made by it was not an order of dismissal or discharge within article 311 Of Constitution. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled under article 311 Of The Constitution to have his case referred to and determined by the Tribunal in accordance with Rule 4 (1) (a) of the Madras Civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules, 1948, which was the rule in force when the enquiry against the appellant was started, and that he had a right to have his say referred to and decided the matter finally.

The assessee, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company, a private limited company, was assessed to income tax under section 23(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, on the basis that the assessee had not died. The assessee claimed that the income received by him before his death was assessable to income tax in the hands of his legal representative when the order of the Income tax Officer pursuant to which the income was to be deemed to be distributed became effective after the death of the shareholder, and may be enforced against him or his legal representative in the manner and to the extent the statute permits. The Income tax Officer, however, rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the assessee was not liable to be taxed in the hands Of the legal representative of the deceased person in the hands. The Appellate Tribunal, however, allowed the appeal. The High Court, on a reference, held that section 24B did not authorise the levy of tax on receipts by the legal representative when he was the legal representative, when the order was made, became effective after his death, and that received by his legal representatives after the death was made after the death. The High court, however, dismissed the reference. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The expression "assessee" in section 24B of the Indian income tax Act, 1961, means a person by whom income tax is payable. The legal personality of a deceased person is to be regarded as extended to the end of the year in which such notional income must be deemed to have been received by the legal representatives of the deceased. [597 G] (ii) The legal personality is to be treated as extended to a person by fiction to have been receiving income of the legal representative. The Legislature has not made any provision generally for assessment of income receivable by the legal heirs of a deceased. The Legislature had not made any provisions generally for assessment. But if the Legislature has failed to set up the procedure to assess such income, the Courts cannot supply it. [597 A B] (iii) The expression 'assessee ' in section 24 B of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 means a person who dies, his legal representative, and not a person by whose estate income tax is due. The Legislature having not made any such provision generally for the assessment of income received by a legal representative of a deceased, has no power to tax the income. [597 C] (iv) The expression `assessee ' in the section means a person whose income tax is paid by him under the Act. The Legislature, having made provision generally for income tax, has to charge income tax on such receipts. The Legislature cannot supply it, and the Legislature has not provided that the income which may be deemed by fiction to be received by a Legal representative of the estate of a deceased cannot be deemed to he taxed in the eyes of the heirs and legal representatives who cannot be deemed as assessees for the purpose of assessment in regard to those years. [597 D] (v) The expression, 'assessee ' has been used in section 24A of the Indian Act, 1922. The Legislature did not provide that the income should be deemed to, have been received in the hands or by the legal Representatives of the deceased, and that the Legislature had not provided that income which may he deemed to have received by the deceased, had been received by such legal representative. [597 E] (vi) The expression has been used to indicate that the income must be regarded as received by the assessee or his legal representatives before the end of that year. The Legislature was not competent to make any provision for assessment of the income received or of the loss sustained by the legal or representative of the assessee. [597 F] (vii) The expression is used in section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Income Tax (Amendment) Act 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, with effect from May 1, 1952.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Baster. He was a Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution. The appellant was the Ruler of the said villages. The Ruler of the appellant was the Maharaja of Baster and was a Ruler. The appellant claimed that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owners of the villages mentioned in Schedules A, B and B of the petition under articles 227 and 227 of The Constitution. The High Court held that the appellant was still a Ruler and was entitled to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such villages. The appellant contended that the provisions of the Act did not apply to a Ruler or to the private property of a Ruler which was not assessed to land revenue. Held, that the appellant had no right to recover rent and revenue from persons held land in such village. The appellant had no such right to recover or revenue from the persons holding land. The appellant could not be regarded as a Ruler of an Indian State. The appellant 's rights under article 363(22) of the Constitution were not affected by the provisions of article 363(2) of the constitution. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled to recover or be revenue from personsholding land in such cases. The appellant must be regarded as an ex Ruler and as he was also a maufidar, he was a maufiidar. The appellant did not claim any right to recover any rent or revenue or from persons holding lands in such villages, nor was he entitled to recover any revenue or revenue from such persons holding land, in such villages in such villages; nor was he a mauiidar entitled to recover such rent or revenue. The appellant cannot be regarded as the Ruler of an 'Maufidar ' within the meaning of article 366(22) Of the Constitution.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uauri) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. The respondent was transferred to Pauri. The respondent challenged the order of his transfer before the Central Administrative Tribunal, Guwahati. The Tribunal quashed the order of transfer on the ground that the guidelines contained in the administrative instructions/guidelines contained in the Administrative instructions/guides contained in the instructions issued by the Government on the subject. The Tribunal also quashed the order on the ground of mala fides on the part of the respondent. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Tribunal. The High Court quashed the order. The respondent contended that the guidelines issued by the Central Government are not an unfettered one but are circumscribed by various circulars/guideline contained in the executive instructions/guices contained in the guidelines issued in the administrative instruction/guide guidelines contained in administrative instructions/Guidelines contained therein. The respondent also contended that the order of her transfer was vitiated by mala fides on her part and that the Tribunal had exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order of transfers. The Tribunal held that the respondent was liable to transfer anywhere in India. The Tribunal further held that the guidelines were applicable to the case of the respondent and that the respondent had no locus standi to challenge the order of transferring. The Tribunal, however, quashed the order and directed the respondent to continue at Shillong. The Tribunal directed the respondent not to continue at the same place. The respondent preferred an appeal before the Central Adminis tional Tribunal. The Tribunal dismissed the appeal. The respondent then filed a writ appeal before the High Court. The High court quashed the order holding that the guidelines are applicable to the cases of the respondent, and that the order passed by the Tribunal is not an arbitrary one. The High Commis sion of the High Court quashed that order of the Tribu nal. The High Cou rt held that the Tribunal exceeded its jurisdiction and acted in violation of the statutory provisions. The High Courts also held that the order was vitiated by malafides and was therefore aware of the norms and constraints of the writ jurisdiction.) The High Court also held that if the respondent was not in a position to make any representation with respect to his transfer, the administrative needs and the claim of other employees should not be interfered with. The High Cour t held that the transfer was vitiated mala fide on the part o f the respondent. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of the High Cour sary Authority is not an Appellate Authority sitting in judgment over the orders of transfer. The Tribunal is not a Court or Tribunal merely where it is passed malafide or is made in violation of any statutory provisions, the Court or the Tribunal can quash the order of transferred. [475B] 2. The order passed by a Tribunal is akin to the jurisdiction of the High Courts under Article 226 of the Constitution of India in service matters. The Administrative Tribunal is not the Appellate Authority sitting over the orders passed by the subordinate authority. The Tribunal cannot interfere with it. The Tribunal has also exceeded its jurisdiction. The Tribunal does not even support the respondent 's contentions instead of supporting them. The High chal ly has exceeded its jurisdiction, and the Tribunal has exceeded its jurisdication in interfering with it. [476C D] 3. The Tribunal exceeded its juris dication in interfering in the order of t he transfer. The Administrative Tribu ny is not an appellate Authority sitting in appeal over the order of a subordinate authority. [477D] 4. The Tribunal had exceeded the jurisdiction in interfering in an order of transfer. [478E] 5. The Tribunal was not an Appellate authority sitting in judgmentover the orders of the subordinate authority (competent authority). The Tribunal has exceeded the jurisdiction.

The appellants were tried for the murder of Jawahar. The prosecution case was that the appellants were tried under Sections 147 and 148 I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder. The prosecution alleged that the appellants had assaulted the deceased with aruval (bill hook) and a stick (spear stick) and that the deceased had inflicted multiple injuries on the person of the deceased. The Trial Court acquitted the appellants. The High Court affirmed the acquittal of A1 to A3. The appellants contended before this Court that the participation of the appellants in the occurrence was proved beyond doubt. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325, I.P.,C. and not convict under Section 325,I.P. C. [312B] 2. The intention was to cause death, but the offence committed was of grievous hurt and not merely causing simple and simple injuries to the deceased. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all the accused had caused simple and simple hurt to him. Even accordingto Jawahar 's evidence the appellants could have intended to cause the death of Jawahar. Even according the deceased had caused simple injuries to him. The appellants were convicted under Section 304 Part I, I. P.C. and instead of under Section 325 read with Section 34, I.PC. [313C D] 3. The appellants are entitled to the benefit of Section 325 I.P,C. and the sentence of imprisonment already undergone by them is set aside.

The appellant Bank was constituted a special Indian law by the Indian Legislature. The Banking Companies Act, 1949, was enacted to protect the British economic interests and though such a law could justifiably be enacted under the General Clauses Act, 1897, the Banking Companies Act was a special law enacted by the Indian Parliament. The Banking companies Act, 1949 was enacted to provide for the establishment of a special law for the regulation of banking and other matters connected therewith. The Banking Company Act, 1949 came into force on the date of the enactment of the Banking Companies (Amendment) Act, 1949. Section 4(e) of the Act provides that the Banking Companies Acts shall apply to a corporation formed by or under a special law made by the Parliament. Section 4 (e) of that Act provides that a corporation formed or constituted by or under the law itself shall be deemed to be a special law in force in India. Section 4 of the Act empowers the Central Government to make rules for the regulation and management of banking and the other matters connected with banking. Section 4 provides that the Central Government may make rules for regulating the regulation and the management of banking. Section 5 provides that the rules made under the Act shall be published in the Official Gazette. Section 6 provides that the General Clauses (Amendment) Rules, 1949 shall apply to the Banking Companies as they apply to a Corporation formed by orunder the law itself. Section 7 provides that the provisions of the Act shall apply to every Corporation formed by a third party in pursuance of the Banking companies Act. Section 4 lays down that the General clauses (Amendment) shall apply to any Corporation formed by the law itself in pursuance of an Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom and shall apply to such Corporation. Section 7 lays down that every Corporation formed or constituted under the law shall be deemed always to have been a corporation formed and administered by the Central Government. Section 8 provides that the Corporation shall be deemed, for the purposes of this Act, to be a Corporation formed and administered under the law made by Parliament. Section 9 provides that the general law shall be in force in the United Kingdom. Section 9(1) provides that the Act shall not apply to a banking company formed by or Under the law itself, and the Banking Companies shall be deemed not to have been incorporated in the Act. Section 9 (2) provides that a Corporation formed or administered by the law shall continue to be a corporation formed under the law and shall be deemed never to have been formed by or on behalf of the Central Government and shall continue to function under the law. Section 9 lays down that a corporation shall be deemed for the purposes Of this Act to be a company formed by the Central Govern ment. Section 9 is in the nature of a special provision enacted by the Parliament and not by the law. The Banking company Act, 1949 is a special law passed by the Parliament, and not by a special law. The banking Companies Act, therefore, is a special Act enacted by the British Parliament. [968D E] Krishna Murthy vs Krishna Murthy, ; , referred to.

The petitioners who were manufacturers of sugar in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, challenged the validity of the impugned notification on the ground that the impugned notification was violative of the fundamental rights of the petitioners guaranteed under article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. Held, that the impugned Act was not violative of the rights guaranteed under article 14 of the Constitution and the impugned notification must be struck down as invalid. The impugned notification was not violative Of the fundamental rights guaranteed under articles 19(1) (g) and (h) of the constitution. The impugned Act was therefore invalid. The petitioners were not entitled to any relief under article 32 of the Constitution on the ground of discrimination. The impugned order was therefore invalid and the petitioners were not justified in contending that the impugned order was invalid. The State of Uttar Pradesh vs M/s. M. P. Sugar Mills Ltd., ; , followed. The impugned Notification was therefore invalid as it contravened article 19(2) (g). The impugned notification did not authorise the Central Government to fix the price at a loss, (ii) it fixes the price arbitrarily, and (iii) there was discrimination in effect, because the impugned notification merely fixes the price at the ex factory level. The impugned notifications were therefore invalid. Held, further, that the object of the Act was to secure equitable distribution of the commodity to the consumer at a loss. The impugned act was therefore invalid, and the impugned Act could not be said to have been proved to be beyond the ambit of authority conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of the Act and the Order did not authorise it to fix the prices at a loss; but it did not follow from this object that the price fixed by the Government by the impugned notification could in no circumstances be said to be proved to be below the cost of production. The impugned Government was therefore not justified in holding that the impugned Government was not justified in fixing the price at an arbitrary and unreasonable price.

The appellant company was a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, and was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling of pharmaceutical products. The company was incorporated under the Companies Act, 1956, and the appellant company was incorporated in the Indian Companies. The company had its registered office at Calcutta. The appellant company was carrying on the business of manufacture and sale of pharmaceutical products and was carrying on its business in Calcutta. The company, however, did not carry on its business at Calcutta. It was alleged that the company had been carrying on its manufacturing business in Calcutta and that the company was not in a position to carry on its manufacturing activities in Calcutta. It also alleged that the appellant company had been doing business in Calcutta, and that the business of the company was being carried on in Calcutta. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the working class cost of living index was not a relevant factor for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class of living cost of living Index. The Tribunal was right, in holding that there was a substantial change in working class cost and the corresponding entries in regard to the working class manials and the corresponding entry in regard to working class menials and corresponding entries in respect of the working class men and the corresponding corresponding entries in the Monthly Digest, West Bengal, for ascertaining the working class costs of living index, and complained that similar entries for all the relevant years had not been produced. The Tribunal rightly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal. The Tribunal wrongly relied upon Exhibit 4, corrected on its basis of information given by it. The Tribunal, in fact, relied upon Exhibit 5, corrected on that basis of information furnished by the State Government. The Tribunal also relied upon Exhibit 6, corrected on a different angle, and held that the working classes of living index were not relevant for all the years. The Tribunal relied upon Exhibit 7, corrected on an erroneous basis of the report of the State Statistical Commis sioner. The Tribunal held that the work of living index in the year 1951 was a substantial increase in the working classes and the corresponding Entries in regard to their working class men were not produced. The appellant Company was not prepared to produce the said report. The Tribunal further held that the report of a State Statistical Bureau was not a conclusive evidence of the working classes in the year 1957, and that it was not a case of substantial change in its working class cost. The Tribunal accordingly held that the award dated June 21, 1951, was not terminated under section 19(6) of the Act and therefore the present reference was bad in law and without jurisdiction. The appellant, however, contended that the award was binding between the parties and therefore the reference was bad. Held, further, that the award of the Tribunal was binding between them and the parties and the reference was not bad in law. The Tribunal had rightly relied upon the report of an expert body and the report of such expert body was not a piece of evidence. The Tribunal erred in relying upon the report. The report of the expert body was a piece of document and the Tribunal was justified in relying upon it. The report was not a mere piece of evidence and the Tribunal had rightly held that the Tribunal had wrongly relied upon the same. The Tribunal has rightly relied upon it.

The appellant, a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva Mutt, was the Matadhipati of Sri Gavi Mutt, which was a religious institution, dedicated to the promotion and promotion of its endowments. The appellant, who was the Matada Mutt, was appointed as the Executive Officer of the said Mutt. The appellant challenged the validity of the scheme on the ground that the scheme was not consistent with the relevant provisions of the earlier Act and that the scheme had been framed under the relevant provisions Of the earlier Act. Held, that the scheme framed under the earlier Act was consistent with the appropriate provisions of the latter Act and was not warranted by the provisions of the later Act. The scheme was framed under the provisions of earlier Act and was valid when it was framed. The scheme had not been completely reconstituted and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. The scheme could not be deemed to be settled or modified under the earlier scheme. The scheme, therefore, was not valid when it came into force. The scheme framed under section 63 of the earlier Acts was not valid. The scheme did not contravene the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution. The scheme which was framed under section 62 of the earlier act was not valid until 1952. The scheme in question was framed under a different Act and the Executive officer was appointed as a Executive Officer of that Mutt. The scheme having been framed under section 61 of the earlier acts, the appellant was not entitled to seek the protection of article 19(1)(f) and the High Court was right in holding that the scheme did not violate the fundamental rights under article 19(f) and that the appellant was entitled to seek protection of article 31(1)(g) of the Constitution.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in a school in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. He joined his school with repeated spells of 89 days and 89 days. He joined service with repeated spells. He joined school with repeated spell of 89 days. The appellant continued to serve the school with repeated periods of 89 days, and 89 days, but later on his appointment was made available, and the appellant continued to work with repeated spells, and the managing committee of the school was appointed on July 12. 1982. The appellant was appointed on ad hoc basis on July 12 1982. He continued to serve in the school with successive spells of 89 day appointments, and the school was also functioning with the approval of the authorities of the school. The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution of India before the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Teacher with effect from July 12,1982. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High court erred in denying the benefit of the Validation Act to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue replaced until a candidate from the select list. The High Courts erred in denying him the benefit of Validation Act to his initial appointment in a school with effect from 7.12.1982. [901C] 2. The High 'Court read into the Act what was of the view that the appellant was still continuing to serve the School under the orders of the managing committee. The High Curt erred in denying to the benefit of validation Act to the petitioner on the ground of discrimination. [902D] 3. The High. Court erred in denying benefit of validation of the Validation act on the ground, that his initial appointments for 89 days were conditioned by the condition that he would continued to replace by a candidate from select list. [903E] 4.

The respondent was a Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti. He was elected to the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, and the ground that he was disqualified from being a candidate was based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samiti and Zila Parishads and Non official Members (Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965. The respondent was elected to a Panchayat Samiti and the ground was that he was not disqualified from being an office of Chairman of a Zila Parishad. The respondent challenged the election of the appellant on the ground that the appellant was disqualified from contesting the election on the ground of his having been disqualified from being chosen as a member of a Panchayat Samitis and the ground of disqualification was based on the Rules 3 to7 of the Punjab Panchayats Samitis and Zila Parishad Rules, 1965, and that the appellant had failed to establish that the allowances paid under rules 3 to 7 were in addition to the payment of the consolidated monthly allowance. The High Court held that the allowances were paid under rules 8 to 7 of Rules 3 to 8 of the Rules, and that, therefore, the appellant was not entitled to mileage allowance under r. 3 to 7. The appellant contended that the allowance paid under r. 7 was in addition to payment of the daily allowance under rs. 3 to 8 and that the respondent was disqualified from appearing in the election. The High court held that the allowance was not payable to the Chairman of a panchayat Samiti and that the order of the State Government was correct in arriving at the conclusion that the allowances granted under r. 8 to 7 were not in addition to or in addition to any allowance to which he might have been entitled in order to compensate him for expenses incurred in connection with the discharge of his official duties. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was perfectly correct in arriving on the conclusion that allowances paid under r 3 to 7 was in lieu of the travelling allowance and daily allowance under rr. 3 to7 were in addition only to the payment to the Chairman and the Chairman. [401 C] (ii) The payment of travelling allowance and Daily allowance under r 3 was in addition onlyto the payment of daily allowance under rule 3 to 7 and not in addition thereto. [402 D] (iii) The payment was clearly meant only to cover additional expenditure and out of pocket expenses of the Chairman and, while no evidence has been advanced to show that out of the amount received as daily allowance the Chairman will in fact invariably make a saying, it cannot be held that this payment would result in gain so as to make the office of profit. [403 E] (iv) The payment to the appellant was in addition not to the payment at a higher rate to the Chairman. The payment was in addition, to the payment made to the Chairman, and, consequently, it must be held that the Chairman must be making gain out of the payment to him of daily allowance. [404 F] (v) The payment made to a Chairman for travelling allowance and monthly allowance under r, 3 to 7 is in addition to a payment of the monthly consolidated allowance under r., 3 to 7, and not in the addition to the amount of expenditure which he would have to incur for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties.[403 G] (vi) The payment is clearly meant only for the payment of monthly consolidated allowance and out of the pocket expenses of Chairman and, therefore, it must also be held that it must be made an office of profit, and, therefore. it must be assumed that this payment was really meant only to covering additional expenditure and Out of the pocket expense of Chairman and the chairman, while no proof has been advanced that out of this amount, the Chairman will normally make a saying it cannot be said that this payment will result in gain, so as to render an office of profits.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop in the premises in question. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction against the appellant on the ground of subse quently occupying the premises. The appellant contended that the tin shed marked by letters ABHG had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents and that the tin sheds marked by letters CDGH had been constructed in the form of kitchen and bathroom. The trial Court held that the partition wall did not constitute material alteration, and that the appellant had failed to prove that the tin roof and the partition wall were permanent in nature. The first appellate court held that the roof and the roof were permanent and that the roof was not affected at all by the disputed tin shed. The High Court, however, held that the appellant subse quent had been constructed on the open land adjacent to the accommoda tion. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High Court was in error in interfering with the findings of fact recorded by the first appellate court. The High court in second appeal interfered with the findings recorded by the First Appellate Court on the question whether tin shed and the partition wail was permanent in nature, and they could be removed without causing any damage to the accommodation. The High Courts in second appeal did not interfere with the findings. The High Cou rt was in error of interfering with the finding of fact recorded. [771A] The High Court in second appeal had found that the roof, the partition wall and the roof formed a material alteration in the accommodation. One portion of the tin shed was already in existence on the open space adjacent to the accommodation, and it was enclosed by Bamboo structure, and it formed a material alterations in the accommodation, it took care to use the word materially altered the same were temporary and they could not be removed without causes damage to the premises.

The respondent company filed a suit against the appellant for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent firm on 22 4 1975. The appellant filed a suit for setting aside the ex parte decree on 22 4 1974. The trial court decreed the suit on 29 7 1975. The respondent firm filed an appeal before the Second Additional District Judge, Indore. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the exparte decree on 22 5 1975. The High court set aside the judgment of the Trial Court and upheld the passing of the ex parte order. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The words "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. The meaning of clause (b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in order 5 which is meant for issue of service and summons on natural persons. The meaning has got to been understood in the context of the provisions in Order 5 which is intended for issue of a service and summons upon natural persons. [1032E F] 2. The meaning given to clause (b), has got to he understood in the light of the provisions contained in Order 5. [1033E F] 3. The meaning and scope of clause (a), has got a to be understood as the meaning of clause(b) of Order 29 of the Code. The meaning is that the words "Principal officer" in clause(a) of Order 5 would include managing agent and it can. under this rule be on a juridical person. [1034F] 4. The meaning to clause (a of Order 29 is that the word "Principal Officer", in clause (b). has got to mean any person who is entitled to be served on behalf of the company in accordance with sub clause (a). [1034G] 5. The meaning assigned to clause (c) has got a meaning which is meant to be understood by the word as to what is meant by service of summons on the company in the sense as to what was meant by service. [1035E] 6. The meaning which is given to clause(b), has to be understood according to the provisions of Order 5. The word "Principal officer", in clause(b)(i) has got the meaning of the word "principal officer" in the first part of clause (c). [1035F] 7. The meaning attributed to the word " Principal Officer" in the second part of clause(c) has to be interpreted in the background and context of the provision in Order 5, which is meant of service of summons upon natural person. [1134G] 8. The meaning ascribed to the word 'Principal Officer ' in clause (c), has got the same meaning as in the first paragraph of Order 29. [1036F] 9. The meaning attached to the word `Principal Officer ' is to be understood to mean the principal officer of the corporation. [1037F] 10. The meaning, which is given in the first para of Order 29, is to be interpreted by the word 'principal officer ' in the first portion of clause (d) of Order 6. The word 'principal ' in clause(c), has to mean the Principal Officer of the corporation, or the principal officer, of the corporation or the principal Officer of the Corporation, or the Principal Officer. [1038F] 1035A] 11.

The respondents were tried under section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for the offences under sections 145 and 145 of the Indian Penal Code for having committed breach of the peace. The Magistrate passed the final order on 17th July, 1978 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. The Magistrate, after a full enquiry as provided by section 145, passed the final orders on 17th August, 1978 declaring him to be in actual possession of the lands in dispute. On the basis of a police report, the Magistrate passed the order on 17.7.1978 declaring the appellant as in possession of land in dispute, and the final order was confirmed by the Magistrate. The High Court, however, allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the final order of the Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of peace existed at the time the order was passed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The finding of the Magistrate in the final order in favour of the appellant is implicit in the final orders passed by the Magistrate so it was not necessary for the Magistrate to repeat what he had said in the preliminary order in the final and final order. Once a preliminary order drawn up by the Magistrate sets out the reasons for holding that a breach of the law exists, it is not necessary that at the time of passing the final order the apprehension of breach of peace should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence to show that the dispute has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section (5) of section 145. [94A B] 1.2 The High Court in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction would not go into the sufficiency or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the Magistrate is based. But once a preliminary order is drawn up by a Magistrate, the High Court in revision cannot go into the question of sufficiency or otherwise the materials on record as to whether a breach of peace exists or is not sufficient to vitiate the order passed by the magistrate so it was necessary for the magistrate to repeat what the Magistrate had said in his final order. [94C D] 1.3 The High Court was in error in holding that a finding of existence of breach of the Act existed at the stage when a final order was drawn up by an Magistrate so it could be said that no dispute existed as contemplated under section 145. The High court in the exercise Of its revisional jurisdiction could not go into this question of sufficiency of material which has satisfied the Magistrate so as to attract the extraordinary jurisdiction of the High Court under section 482 of Cr. It is, therefore, manifest that a finding about the existence of a dispute likely to cause a breach of law exists even in the final or final order.

The appellant, a resident of Madras, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1941 42, 1942 43 and 1943 44. The appellant contended that the profits had accrued to it both in British India and in the legal sense and that liability to tax had arisen. Held, that the question whether the profits had been accrued to it, was a mixed question of fact and mixed question of law and fact. The finding of the Tribunal on the facts found was not liable to be set aside on the ground that there was no evidence in support of it or that on the evidence it was perverse. The finding on the question whether it was a mixed fact or mixed question of facts was a question of law. The finding was not a pure question of fact. The question whether the income had accrued to the appellant or not was a mixed one of pure fact or mixed questions of law and facts. The finding must be based on the evidence and the inference drawn from the facts found must be based upon the evidence and not on the ground of mixed law or mixed question. The finding is a pure question Of law and fact and must be based merely on the assumption that the finding of the tribunal on the facts was perverse. In the present case, the finding of fact must be based not only on the ground but on the ground as it was not supported by any evidence or that it was perverse and was not based on any evidence or was perverse. Held, further, that the finding on the facts could not be said to be perverse. The question of law which could be reviewed by the court was a mixed point of law and law and it was not open to attack on any of the grounds on which such a finding could be challenged in a reference under section 66(1). The finding of fact was a pure question and mixed question Of law. The question was one of pure law and mixed question and mixed questions of fact and law. The decision of the Tribunal was a pure finding of fact and was not open for challenge to any of the contentions on which such finding could be assailed in a reference. The decision in Com Missione vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co. (1) was not open.
