The Appellate Tribunal held that the commission paid to Shri Vaish was not really paid wholly for the purpose of carrying on business and that the commission was paid to Shri J.P. Vaish. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax, however, held that the amount of Rs. 77,733 paid to the general Manager was not really a receipt laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose for the business of the assessee and was wrongly disallowed by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The High Court, however, took the view that the post was of General Manager and not of the Director and that the Commission paid to Shri O Vaish was in no way related to the proprietors of the firm and the commission paid was not really earned wholly or exclusively in the purpose of the business of assessee. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The High Court was wrong in holding that the post is of General Manager. The High court was wrong in accepting the view of the Income Tax Officer that the rate of commission paid to him was reasonable and the allowance was therefore restricted to half of the amount claimed by the assessee. [733 D] (ii) The principle of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure was wholly and exclusively laid out for the purpose or exclusively for carrying on business has to be decided on the facts and in the light of the circumstances established by the assessee and not on the basis of any other evidence. [734 E] (iii) The principle is not applicable to the present case. The principle of industrial expediency is not applicable in the present case because the assessee was not a trader or it was not laid out wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business. The principle is applicable to the case. [735 E] (iv) The principle applies to the present cases. The principle applies only to cases where the assessee is a firm or a firm. The principle has no application to the present facts of the case. The assessee was not carrying on business. The assessee had not been carrying on business in the manner contemplated by the Act. The assessee, therefore, was not entitled to the benefit of the principle of industrial necessity. [736 F] (v) The principle has not been applied to the present appeal. The principle applied to the instant case is that the assessee was entitled to the deduction of the amount paid to Shri U Vaish. The High, Court, however held that the rate was reasonable and was not justified.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company (Private) Limited, since October, 1943, when the appellant filed his application for separate representation, the Secretary of the Union, who was the Secretary of that Union, made an award in terms of the petition of compromise. The appellant filed his objection to the award on March 13, 1957, and the Secretary of a Union, who made the award, was not a party to the proceedings. The appellant contended that the Tribunal committed a serious error in rejecting his application to be represented by a person of his own choice instead of Fateh Singh, the Secretary, the Union, and that he did not want his case to be represented through a person of the Union. Held, that the Tribunal was in error in refusing the appellant 's prayer for a writ. The Tribunal committed a grave error in rejecting the appellant ' s application for a writ, and the Tribunal committed an error in refusing to record the compromise in so far as it related to the appellant 'S case and to give its award without reference to the settlement and on proper adjudication of the matter. The Tribunal was in fact a party to a dispute between an individual workman and an employer, and the appellant was not independently of the Union which had espoused his cause. The Tribunal had committed a serious mistake in rejecting the application for a Writ. The Tribunal, therefore, committed a serious illegality in refusing the appellants ' prayer for a Writ, and the High Court was in error. The appeal must be allowed. The appeal should be allowed.

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the respondents on the allegation that the surviving appellants constituted a joint Hindu family and the surviving plaintiffs could continue the appeal in view of the provisions of O.XXII, r. 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court set aside the decree and dismissed the suit. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the appeal must be dismissed. The provisions of 0. XLI, r. 3 of the Code were not intended to apply to an appeal which was not a competent appeal against a party under the Code or under the Letters Patent of the High Court. The provisions Of 0. XLI r. 4 were not intended by the Legislature to apply to the proceedings when an appeal is filed and empowers one of the plaintiffs or defendants to file an appeal against the entire decree in pursuance of the provisions Of 0, XLI, r., 4 when the decree proceeds on a common ground to all the plaintiffs or the defendants, if all the plaintiffs were negligent in taking steps for substitution, the Court was not to exercise its discretion in favour of such a party. The provisions were intended to apply only to appeals which were not a competent one against a party. It was not possible for the appellants to continue as tenants of one of the landlords and not as a tenant of one of them when all the appellants had a joint right to eject him or to have him as their tenant. The provisions could not have been intended to apply in an appeal which had not been a competent appeal.

The respondents were the employees of the Assam State Electricity Board. They were dismissed from service by the Assam State Government. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of dismissal. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The High court held that the order of the Governor was not justified because the Governor had to arrive at the subjective satisfaction that in the interest of the security of the State it was not expedient to give the government servant an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The High, however, held that the Governor had no power to dismiss or remove a person from service. The High ' Court held that the Government had to arrive to the subjective satisfaction on the basis of the evidence adduced during the course of the inquiry and that the Governor was satisfied that in the interests of the security, it was not necessary to give the Government servant an opportunity to show cause against the proposed action proposed to he taken in regard thereto. The High. Court, however, dismissed the writ application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Governor 's satisfaction under the unamended clause (2) of article 311 was not necessary because the Governor was also satisfied that in his interest it was not reasonably practicable to give the said person an opportunity of show cause against his action proposed to been taken in regard thereof. HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the Governor did not have the power to dismiss the respondent. [487 B] The Governor was also of the opinion that in the public interest it was necessary to give an opportunity of being heard to the respondent. The satisfaction under the amended clause (2), therefore, that the Governor should arrive at the satisfaction that in public interest it is not expedient to issue an opportunity of hearing to the respondent was not necessary. [487 C] The Governor 's opinion was that in the circumstances of the case the Governor was of the opinion, that in the larger interest of the public it was not desirable to give the respondent an opportunity of making his representation against the action of the proposed action. The Governor 'has to be given an opportunity of explaining the reasons for the proposed action to be taken. The Governor is further satisfied under sub clause (c) of the proviso to clause (2). [487 E] The Governor is also satisfied that the Government servant, and under the proviso, the Governor 'has been satisfied that in public interests it was not practicable to give an ' opportunity of showingcause against the action to be proposed to be initiated in regard to the action proposed proposed to be adopted in regard to them. [487 E F] The Governor has to arrive at his satisfaction that in order to be able to give an adequate opportunity of showing causes against the action sought to be taken, the Governor has to give the concerned Government servant an adequate opportunity to show that he is satisfied that in order that he is likely to be dismissed or removed or reduced in rank he has been given a reasonable opportunity of showing that he is not reasonably practicable. [487 F G] The Governor must also satisfy himself that in the course of his inquiry, the Government servant is satisfied that the circumstances of his case justify the action proposed. [487 A] The Governor, therefore, has to satisfy himself that the circumstances are such as to justify the action to take in regard to a Government servant.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. The petitioner company was assessed to sales tax in accordance with the provisions of the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, and the impugned notification was issued on March 31, 1956, and the petitioner company was registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1956. The State of Uttar Pradesh imposed a tax on the sale proceeds of jute goods. The petitioner company filed an application under article 226 in the High Court of Allahabad calling in question the validity of the impugned notification and the impugned order was passed on March 31. 1956, and in consequence the impugned notification dated March 31,1956, was issued. The High Court held that there was no power in the State to issue the impugned notification under section 3 A on March 31 1956, and that the impugned notification must be held to be within the saving of the Validation Act. The petitioner contended that the impugned Act was ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54, and that in consequence the said notification was not saved by the new Act. Held, that the Validation Act was intra vires the powers conferred on the State Legislature under entry 54 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution and any other provisions of the Constitution bearing on the question as to when such a tax could be imposed, and in the exercise of that power, it must be held that the validation Act was intravires. The impugned notification was not ultra vires the power of the legislature to enact a law with retrospective operation. The impugned Act was intra vocabulary and intra vires the power conferred on the Government under entry 54. The impugned order was therefore ultra vires the provisions of entry 54, because the impugned notification did not affect the competence of the legislature. The impugned Notification was therefore ultravires.

The assessee, a limited company dealing in land, was assessed to income tax. The Income tax Officer treated the sum of Rs.7,37,190 payable to the assessee as compensation payable in terms of the award dated July 29, 1956 of the Arbitrator and a sum of Rs,7,37190 payable to him in terms of his award dated July 30, 1956. The assessee claimed that the amount of compensation received by him related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assessee, that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquired land which was his stock in trade, and was therefore, a capital receipt of a revenue nature liable to tax. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the claim and held that the compensation was received by the assesee, and that the compensation paid by the assessee was not a receipt of a capital nature. The High Court, however, rejected the first contention and held that in the circumstances of the case, the Revenue could claim that the sum of compensation received was not a receipts of a revenue character. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the amount received by the Revenue related to the purchase of land which is the stock intrade of the assessee and was, thus, a trading receipts of the business, and was a trading receipt, and that, therefore, the receipt of a compensation could be said to have accrued to the assessee on the date when possession of the land was taken by the Government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court is right in the view taken by it and, therefore, it is right in holding that the mere claim by the assessee after taking possession of the property at a particular rate or for a certain sum is admitted and the only quantification of the amount payable is left to be determined in accordance with settled principles. [439C] 2. The High Courts are right in the conclusion that the mere claims by the assessee before the Collector could be said not to have accrued or deemed to accrue, whether in fact paid or not, whether in reality or not, were not payable. [440D] 3. The High, Court is right in its view that the mere claiming by the assessee without furnishing a security bond for refunding the amount in question cannot be said to be a receipt of revenue nature liable for tax. [441E] 4. The High. Court is right, in the view of the High Court, in Harish Chandra Raj Singh vs The Deputy Land Acquisition Officer & Anr., [1962] 1 SCR 676 that the amount which had already been assessed to tax in respect of the additional amount of compensation claimed by the assessee could not be said to amount payable to the assesee merely quantifying the amount to be received, and cases where the right to receive payment is admitted and is in dispute and it is not a question of merely quantifying an amount to be paid, and cases, where the right is in dispute, and it is the question of merely identifying the amount payable, and cases when the right to receiving payment is admitted, and the only conclusion is left to the be determined in accord or settled principles.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground of bona fide requirement of the respondent landlord. The appellants filed a compromise petition in the Trial Court which passed a decree for eviction and other reliefs in January, 1968 in accordance with the terms of the compromise. The compromise was accepted and the suit was decreed. The appellants then filed a suit in the Trial court for a decree for possession in respect of the suit premises and other reliefs. The Trial Court decreed the suit. The appellants ' appeal to the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the compromise was legal and was in accordance with law and was not binding on the parties. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The compromise decree was clearly valid and executable. The compromise decree clearly was legal and is within the purview of the plaint. The protection of a tenant based upon public policy, is inherent in the language of Order 23, Rule 3 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise. the Court shall pass a decree on the basis of the compromise." [881 B] In the instant case, the compromise decree was duly valid and executable and the suit had been decreed in accordance with Order 23, rule 3. The appellants got about three years ' time to vacate the shop in dispute from the date of the compromise decree, they were ill advised to fight the litigation and further cause delay in vacating the shop. The appellants had got about three year ' time to file a suit for possession in accordance with their conditions of compromise. The suit was decreed in accordance therewith. The appellants, therefore, filed a suit against the respondents for a decree of eviction and other relief in January, 1969. The suit having been decreed, the appellants filed a petition in the High Court for a decree in terms of the decree. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellants appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ Held: (1) The compromise decree in terms was clearly valid. The compromise in terms of paragraph 1 of the compromise petition was binding on the appellants. The compromise had to be read in the light of the pleadings of the parties and in the light thereof it was held that the compromise decree in the instant case was legal and valid. [882 B] (2) The compromise in the instant appeal was binding on all the parties. The compromise could not be treated as a decree in accordance with section 12(1) (f) of the Act. The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly agrees to suffer a decree for ejectment because the landlord, in the circumstances is entitled to have such a decree under the law. [883 C D] (3) The compromise must disclose either on its own or in the context of other materials, in the case, that the agreement is lawful, as in any other suit so in an eviction suit so in the circumstances of a particular case, to be in violation of a particular Rent Restriction or Control Act, the Court would refuse to record the compromise as it will not be a lawful agreement. [886 D] (4) The compromise is binding on all parties. The Court can pass a decree in the absence of any other material in the case. The Court may pass a decree for the eviction of the tenant in accordance with Section 12(1)(f) of Act. [887 E] (5) The compromise should indicate either on the face or in any of the statutory grounds mentioned in Section 12(i) of the . [887 F] (6) The compromise cannot be treated as an agreement between the parties. [890 C] (7) The compromise does not create any interest in the property. The compromise is not a lawful agreement between the landlord and the tenant.

The assessee, a company, was carrying on the business of manufacturing and selling cotton yarn. In the assessment year in question, the assessee claimed that the loss on the ground that it related to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency of the company was a capital loss. The Income tax Officer, however, rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the loss was a capital gain and incurred by the company in earlier years and that the loss in the value of the shares of the company in Elphinstone Mills Ltd. was due to the loss of Rs. 12,00,000/ on account of depreciation in the value. The Appellate Tribunal, however, allowed the assessee 's appeal. The High Court, however, reversed the order of the Income tax Officer and held that in view of the capital loss of Rs, 12,00/ on account thereof, the loss on account of the depreciation in the price of the shares held by the company was not reasonable. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The assessee had suffered a capital loss of about Rs. 12 lakhs in the year in question. The company did not declare any dividend for the year in dispute. The company had suffered a loss of Rs 12 lakhs in view of depreciation in its value of the share of the company. The company, therefore, hardly any doubt that the assessee had suffered loss of Rs 10 lakhs in the earlier years and to the smallness of profits made. [864C D] (2) The assessee was a company carrying on the trade of manufacturing and sale of cotton yarn. The company was not a mere shareholder of the company and the dividend was not a capital loss but a capital loss, because the company had suffered loss in the earlier year. The company could not be said to have suffered a capital gain. [865D] (3) The company did neither declare any dividend nor a larger dividend than declared by the company. It was not open for the Income tax officer to constitute himself as a super Director. The company having failed to declare any dividend, it was not open to the Income tax. [866E F] (4) The High Court was right in holding that in view Of the said loss, any reasonable body of Directors of a company would have done just what the Directors of a Company would have done. The form of the word used in the section is to prevent evasion of tax. The form must be worked from the standpoint of the tax collector but from that of a businessman. [868F] (5) The word 'having regard only to losses previously incurred by the Company ' would be unreasonable within the meaning of section 23A of the Act. The form is to prevent the evasion of tax, the provision must be worked out from the stand point of the tax Collector but from thatof a businessman. The form cannot be worked from a standpoint of tax collector but the form of the words used in the Section is to prevent avoidance of tax. [876E F; 87A] (6) The word "having regard only" in the section means that the company has suffered a capital losses. The form has to be worked out by taking into account the losses incurred by the assessee and the smallness or the smallness thereof. [874C] (7) The word used in section 23A is to prevent evaded tax. The word 'has to be understood in the context of the section. The form may be used in the context in which the word 'has been used. The form in which the words 'have been used is to indicate the intention of the legislature. The form used in the provision must, therefore, be understood in its context. [875D E] (8) The word has to be understood as used in the Act.

The respondent, a displaced person, filed a suit against the appellant, for a declaration that the order of the Civil Judge, Aligarh, was illegal and void. The Civil Judge, on an objection, held that the Civil Judge was not justified under section 15 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1947, and dismissed the suit. The High Court, on appeal, held that an appeal lay under section 39 of the Act, and that the Civil Court was not justified in modifying the award. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The effect of section 37 of the Act is to apply sections 15 and 39 of the U P. Consolidation of Holding Act, 1947. The effect of sections 46 and 47 of the Act was that the decision of the arbitrator under sub section (4) shall be final. [651 C] (ii) The effect is that the decision under sub section(4) shall not be final. The effect is to apply section 39 of that Act to arbitrations under section 12(4) of the Act. [652 D] (iii) The effect, of section 37 is that the Civil judge, who shall refer it to the arbitrator, shall refer it, to the arbitrator. The effect, therefore, is that the civil judge, who will refer it to him, is final. [663 E] (iv) The effect that section 37 of Act applies to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holdings is that the proceedings under the Act shall be final and the decision of an arbitrator under sub s.(4) shall, be final. In the present case, the Civil Judge had no jurisdiction to modify the award made by the Civil Judge. [664 C] (v) The effect was that the Civil court was not justified to modify the order of a Civil Judge modifying the award made in favour of the appellant. [661 D] (vi) The effect would be that the Civil Courts would be competent to modify the awards made by the civil judge.

The respondent Corporation passed a resolution, for the first time, making 75 per cent of the posts of superintending Engineers available to the executive Engineers holding degrees and 25 per cent to the Executive Engineers who were diploma holders. The resolution was also not a regulation made under the said section 64 of the Maharashtra Industrial Development Act, 1961. The Corporation passed a Resolution, for the second time, making 76 per cent of posts of superintend Engineers available to executive Engineers holding degree and 25 percent to the Executive Engineer who were diploma holder and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. The resolution also provided that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to the cadre of Executive Engineers. The resolution further provided that graduates would be eligible for promotion to the post of superintending Engineer, since they belong to the same cadre of Executive Engineer. The resolution provided that graduates should be eligible for the promotion to the said post on the basis of educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the cadres of Executive Engineers and did the same work. The resolution, however, did not provide for any such classification. The resolution of the Corporation was challenged by the petitioner by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the resolution of the corporation was not a regulation framed under section 64 of Maharashtra Industrial Development Corporation Act, 1961, and that the classification was discriminatory in nature and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification made on the basis o f educational qualification which is not permissible in law though the creation of selection grade in the same category on the basis thereof on the basis Of educational qualification which was not permissible in Law though the creation or selection grade in that behalf on the same basis of their qualification which is neither the basis of their qualifications nor the basis of the educational qualification which the is not permissible, in law, though the creation and selection grade in such behalf on the basis other than that in the case before the classification was already made, taking into consideration the nature of work, the requisite qualification for the work and the necessity for making such a classification, should be upheld. [75F G] 1.2 The Court has clearly held that the classification made on a basis of educational qualifications which is not permitted in law though, the creation of the selection grade in a similar category on the ground of educational qualification which are not permissible in fact merely of their qualification, which is not available in law, although the creation of such selection grade in similar category on that basis of educational Qualification which is not impermissible in law, even though the creation is not permissible.

The petitioner, a retired Judge of the Supreme Court, was appointed as a Judge of the High Court of Orissa. He was appointed as the Chief Justice of India. He was promoted as the Chief Judge of the Orissa High Court. He was confirmed in the post of Chief Justice of the High Courts. He was later promoted as the Judge of the Kerala High Court. The petitioner was appointed as Chief Justice of Orissa High Court on the recommendation of the Chief Justice. He was transferred to the High Court. On the question whether the Chief Justice was competent to transfer him to the High Courts, the Court, HELD: 1. The Chief Justice of a High Court is not a constitutional functionary having a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Government. He is not a Judge of a High court. He is a Judge of High Court. [460C D] 2. The Chief justice of India is the best judge of the situation and there is an element of immediacy in the matter of appointment to the Supreme Court and the High Courts of the High courts. [460E] 3. The Chief Judge of India is not a Constitutional functionary having a consultationative role and power of appointment reside solely and exclusively with the Central Government . [460F] 4. The ChiefJustice of India is a constitutional functionary who has a consultative function and the power to appointment resides solely with the Central Govern ment. He is an independent constitutional functionary having an independent role and the powers of appointment resides exclusively and exclusively in that Central Government. [460G] 5. The Chief Justices of the High Cou rt are merely constitutional functionaries having a consultatiative role and, therefore, the Chief Justice is not a member of the Commission. [460F G] 6. The Chief Judges of the High court and other Judges of the Supreme court are merely constitutional functionary having constitutional functionaries having an consultative role, the power of appointments resides solely and primarily in the Central Governmen t. [460H] 7. The Chief CJI of India is an independent Constitutional functionary having an consultatiative function and is merely a constitutional functionary. He is the sole constitutional functionary having the constitutional functionaries having the constitutional authority and the power and appointment resides solely in the Central Govt. . [460G H] 8. The Chief CJ of India is also a constitutional functionary exercising a consultative power and the power is merely constitutional functionary. The Chief Chief Justice of an Indian High Court and other Judges are merely constitutional authorities having a consultat ion and the power cannot be equated with the power of the appointment of the Chief Justices of India. [460A B] 9. The ChiefCJ of India is, therefore, not a constitutional authority having a consulta tion and the power vested in him is merely constitutional functionaries. [460B] 10. The Chief Law Minister of the State of Orissa is an independent statutory functionary having a constitutional role and the authority of appointment resides primarily and exclusively in a Central Government. The Chief Minister of the state of Orissa is not a statutory functionary having an constitutional role and is merely an administrative functionary having a legal role. [460D] 11. The Chief Secretary of the State is not a legal functionary having a role and the duty of appointment resides mainly and exclusively in an executive capacity. [460 F] 12. The Chief Ministers of the State are not a constitutional functionaries having any constitutional role and they are merely executive functions. The Chief Secretaries of the State cannot be equated to the Chief Minister of a State.

The respondent C.A. No. 3071 of 1988 was appointed as Enquiry Officer under the Chief Executive Officer 's Order dated January 9, 1979, authorising him to appoint Enquiry Officers and Appellate Authorities under the provisions of Chapter 19 of the Bi parettlement Settlement dated 19th October, 1966, authorising him, to appoint Enquiry Officer and Appellate Authorities. The respondent C. A. No. 3081 of 1988 filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of punishment and directing that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the impugned order got merged in the appellate order, the initial defect, if any, stood removed, was repelled by the learned Judge on the ground that 'as the original order was without jurisdiction or competence, there was nothing for the Appellate Authority to confirm. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in quashing the impugned order of punishment. [199C] 1.2 The High Court had rightly held that the impugned order was bad in law. [199D] 1.3 The High Court has rightly held that since the original order stood removed, the initial defects, if any , stood removed, stood removed. [199F] 1.4 The High Court ought to have remitted the matter to the competent Disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry Officer. [199G] 1.5 The High Court should have remitted the mater to the competent disciplinary Authority to take fresh decision based upon the report of Enquiry Officer. No useful purpose can be served by adopting the procedure suggested by Shri Shetye. [199E] 1.6 The High Court, therefore, was right in quash the impugned order. [199H] 1.7 The High Court rightly held that in Pulin 's case the initial defect was removed, if any. The High court was right in holding that the impugned punishment was bad in fact. [199A] 1.8 The High Court erred in directing payment of all consequential benefits to which the respondent would be entitled on superannuation. [199B] 1.9 The High Court is right in quashing that order of punishment but because the technical plea of incompetence or lack of jurisdiction of Shri Shetyke could be saved because both sides to the proceedings had not raised any objection to the continuance of the enquiry by the said Enquiry Officer and therefore the High Court ought not to have permitted the respondent to question the competence or jurisdiction of ShriShetye.

The appellant, a Zonal Development Plan, was sanctioned by the Corporation under section 336 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, for the development of a building. The appellant, who was the owner of the property, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Commissioner refusing sanction. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the order of sanction was legal and was justified by the provisions of cl. (a) of sub section (2) of section 336 of Delhi Municipal Corporation, 1957, and that the proposed user mentioned by them in the plan was not in contravention of the Master Plan. HELD: (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the proposed building or the use of the site for the building, by the respondents, would contravene the provisions of sub section 2 of section 14 of the Development Act. [167 D] (ii) The High court was in error. The High court had rightly held that the proposed use mentioned by the appellant in the Master Plan was not in accordance with the Master Plan and, therefore, the order of rejection passed by the Commissioner was legal and justified. [167 E] (iii) The High Courts were in error in not accepting the contention of the appellant that there was no violation either of the Master plan or any provisions of the Development Rules or any other law. [167 G] (iv) The High courts were in error. [167 A] (v) The High. Court was in wrong in holding that there was violation of section 14. [167 B] (vi) The High, Court was in the error in holding, that the proposed construction was not in conformity with the Master plan. [167 C] (vii) The High was in error because the plan was prepared for the area, before it came into operation, and if that was so, there was no contravention of either the Master Plan or any provisions thereof. [167 F] (viii) The High ' Court was in a wrong position in holding that cl. (b) of sub s. (2) was not applicable.

The appellant no. 2 was a member and the appellant was the Secretary, and the appeal of the appellant No, 1 was dismissed. The appellant 's appeal to the High Court was dismissed. Held, that the appeal must be dismissed. The appeal must be allowed. The appellant was the Minister, and the respondent No. 1 had the requisite amount with him and the offence under section 161 would not have been committed. The appellant had no connection with the commission of the offence of bribery or illegal gratification by the appellant No., 1. The appellant, No. 1, was the Secretary and the appellant, No, 2, was the Minister for the judiciary. There was no evidence to show that the appellant No 1 had brought these moneys from his home these moneys were proved to have been provided by the police authorities and given to Nagindas when the raid was organised and were the instruments of the offence. The evidence given by the appellant no, 1, in regard to the statement made by the appellant, was not sufficient to establish the falsity of the allegation made by the prosecution. The evidence of the two witnesses, Nagindas and Pannalal on the one hand and the police witnesses as well as Shanti Lal Ahuja, the Additional District Magistrate, and come to the conclusion in regard to his guilt of the appellant no., 1.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable. He was convicted and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months each. The respondent was served with a show cause notice before the impugned order was passed. The respondent filed a second appeal before the Additional District Judge, who heard the appeal. The Additional District Judge dismissed the respondent 's appeal. The respondent preferred a second appeal to the High Court which was dismissed. The High Court dismissed the second appeal. The High court, however, dismissed the second appel lant 's appeal against the judgment of the Additional District judge. The respondent appealed to this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit for finding out whether the suit was barred by limitation and whether the order of dismissal was illegal on the ground of arbitrariness and there fore, the bar of limitation would not apply. [824F] 2. The High Cou rt should have examined plaint for finding Out the cause of the action for the respondent. The High Cour t should have examined this plaint for finding off the cause of actions for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. [825F] 3. The High tiffs order of dismissal had been passed by an authority not compe tent in this case. The High Commis sion in the judgment of this Court after a very brief discus sion in favour of the respondent had been accepted by the first appellate court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the plaintiff in certain conditions, and the direction about the payment of the salary and other emoluments. [826F] 4.

The appellant was a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. The Income tax officer held that the transactions involved merely transfer of delivery notes and not actual delivery of the goods to the transferee, that transaction was speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on Explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the transaction involved merely transfer delivery notes and did not actual delivery. The Tribunal held that the sales in question were speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 4 of the Act. The High Court held that the sale in question was speculative transactions within section 24(I) of the Act and that the losses suffered by the assessee in these transactions could not be set off against the profits made by the assessee 's non speculative transactions within that meaning of explanation 1 to section 24. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The explanation to section 24 of the Act is qualified by the first proviso which permits the set off of a loss in speculative transactions so as to put them in a special category for income tax purposes. The object of the explanation is not to invalidate the transaction which are not completed by actual delivery of goods to the purchaser. The object is not to vitiate the transaction which is otherwise speculative in nature may yet be speculative in nature. [184G] (2) The explanation is qualified by Explanation 2 to Section 24(1). The object of Explanation 2 is not to affect any transaction of sale which is otherwise illegal. The object was not to invalidate a transaction of sale where the speculative transactions are of such a nature as to constitute a business, the business shall be deemed to be distinct and separate from any other business. The object could not be defeated by mere sale of the commodity or the scrips. [184A B] (3) The explanation does not make any difference in the nature of the transaction which was not completed by the actual delivery of a commodity or the shares. The explanation does no more than make the transaction a speculative transaction. The object does not make the transaction of sale a speculative transaction which could be allowed to be set off only against a profit in a transaction of the same nature. [185D E] (4) The explanation has to be read in the light of the circumstances of each case. The object and purpose of the explanation are not to invalidate any transaction of sales which is otherwise commercial in nature. The object or purpose of the Explanation is not to render any transaction of the kind referred to in the explanation a speculative transaction of sale. [185F G] (5) The explanation cannot be read in isolation. The object sought to be achieved by the explanation is to make the transaction more workable. The explanation is not intended to invalidate the transactions which are not complete by actual delivery. [185G] (6) The explanation must be read in conjunction with the explanation. The object must be gathered from the circumstances of the case. The explanation must not be read in a narrow or pedantic sense. The object should be to avoid a conflict between the main provision and the explanation.

The appellant was a double member constituency. He was declared elected to the Legislative Assembly. The appellant challenged the election of the respondent on the ground that the respondent had failed to comply with the provisions of section 33(1) of the Act. The Election Tribunal held that the respondent was guilty of corrupt practice under section 123(2) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The appellant contended that the respondent could not be declared elected because he had failed to do so. The Tribunal held that section 33(2) was mandatory and enjoined the Returning Officer to refuse any nomination when there had been "subscribe" in its ordinary sense and its ordinary meaning was to "sign" in the special way prescribed by the Act but in the ordinary way the word "subscribe " was used in the sense of making a signature and the word " Subscribe" in the general sense. The High Court held that the Returning Officer had failed to refuse any nominations when there had not been " subscribed " because of some slip on his part and it could be proved that he was satisfied at the proper time, the matter might be different because the element of his satisfaction at the proper place was of the substance, which is of the substance. Held, that the word "Subscribe" in section 33(i) of the was not used in the same sense in the Act but it was also clear that the word 'subscribe ' in its ordinary meaning and its ordinary sense was to be used in the ordinary sense and it was not necessary that the word should be used in its ordinary and ordinary sense. The word "subscribers" in its normal sense means "subscribe". The word " Subscribers" is not defined but it is equally clear when the Act is read as a whole along with the form in the second schedule, that "subscribe", can only be used in, the sense of giving assent to, or attest to, or writing to, or signing, or to attest, or to sign, or to do, writing, or to execute, or to give assent to, and to, or to, sign, or do, writing or to sign. The word 'subscribers ' in its normal meaning and its normal meaning is to "sign". The word ' Subscribe" is not used in its normal and ordinary sense but it is also clear when the statute is read as "subscribe"; and the word ' Subscribers ' is not defined.

The appellants, who were working as workmen of the Company, were dismissed by the Company on September 7, 1972, on the ground that they had abandoned the service of the Company. The Company sent separate communications to the appellants and others informing them that since they had abandoned service of the company, they were not interested to continue in service of the appellants. The Company, however, sent separate communications, to the appellants, asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972, failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the Company from the rolls of the company. The appellants, however, filed complaints before the Labour Court, Bombay, alleging that the Company had abandoned the services of the Company and had completely abandoned the Company 's service. The Labour Court, on the basis of the evidence adduced before it, held that the action of the Company in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls was illegal and arbitrary and that the appellants had abandoned the Company. On appeal, the Industrial Tribunal held that the appellants were not interested in the service of a Company and had not abandoned the Company, and that the action was mala fide, and that they had not abandoned their service of the appellant. The Tribunal, however, held that in the circumstances of the case it could not be said that the appellants abandoned the service and had not voluntarily abandoned the service. The appellants appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the Company ' had voluntarily abandoned the services and had not even abandoned the service, and that it had lost its right to continue in the Company ' service. The High court, however, dismissed the appeals. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the action on the part of the Company was mala fide and that the acts of the Company amounted to a change in the conditions of service of the workmen during the admitted pendency of the industrial dispute before the Labour court which affected them and could not be countenanced. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned action on the basis that the Company was voluntarily abandoned the Service of the appellants in the aforesaid circumstances, the impugned action on its part amounted to a changing in the condition of service of its workmen during the disputed pendency of the dispute before the labour court which adversely affected them and was not merely temporary and could not by any stretch of imagination be construed as voluntarily abandonment by them of the Company ' 's service, was purely temporary and could by no stretch of imagination, be construed as abandonment by them. [619B C] 2. The impugned actions on the part Of the Company clearly amounted to a transfer of service of a workman during the disputed period. The impugned acts of the appellants were wholly illegal and arbitrary. [620D] 3. The impugned act on the part, of the Company clearly amounts to a change of the conditions of the service of its employees during the disputed service. [621D] 4.

The appellant was the trustees of a public trust. The trustees executed a mortgage deed in favour of the appellant. The appellant was the trustee of a public Trust. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under the mortgage. The trustees failed to pay the instalments. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under the decree. The trial court held that the sale was not prohibited by section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950. The trial Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the amount due. The High Court set aside the decree and remanded the case to the District Court for decision on all the points correctly arising out of the matter. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The expression 'sale ' in section 36(a) includes a sale of the property of a public trusts in execution of a decree. The High court was not bound to follow that precedent. [462 B] (2) The High Court was not bound by the precedent of the Full Bench of the Gujarat High Court. The Full Bench of that High Court was in error in holding that the decision of the Full Court of the Gujarat high Court was binding upon the appellant. [462 C] (3) The High court had no power to set aside the sale held in execution of the decree. [462 D] (4) The High Courts were not bound to consider the question whether a judgment delivered by a Full Bench of a Division Bench of the High Court after due consideration of the points before it was liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that Court on the round of some alleged irregularity in the constitution of the Full Benches. [462 E] (5) The High, Court was not right in holding that a judgment delivered in execution of such a decree was not binding on the appellant. It was not necessary for the High Court to consider the questions of law arising before it. [462 G] (6) The High was not right. The High Courts had no power under section 36 of Bombay Public Trusts act, 1950 to set aside a sale held in the execution of a money decree. [461 A] (7) The High 'Court was not bound under section 36 to set aside an auction held in execution. The High ' Court was not entitled under section 36. [462 A] (8) The High. Court was not justified in setting aside the sale in execution of an execution decree.

The respondent was a clerk in the Post and Telegraph Department. He joined the Post and telegraph Department as a clerk on June 4, 1935. He was promoted as a clerk in June, 1935. The respondent was promoted as an officer on June 4. 1935. He joined service in June, 1934. He was given three months ' notice or pay in lieu of such notice. He was retired on June 4 and was given three month ' notice or salary in lieu of the notice. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of retirement. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The respondent filed a special leave petition in this Court. The question for consideration was whether Rule 2(2) of Pension Rules could only be made to retire a Government servant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and February 8, 1956 lay down that the retirement under Rule 2(1) of Pension Rule should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. The memorandum has not been issued under Article 309 of the Constitution. The memorandum is in the nature of executive instructions issued in the name of President of India as required under Article 77(1) and (k) of the Constitution of India. [799G H] 2. The memorandum was in the nature and nature of executive instruction issued in the names of President of Indian. The memorandum had not been issued in the form of executive instructions but was in the manner of executive instructions. The memorandum does not have any parity with Rule 2(3) of Pension rules. [798A] 3. The memorandum in the name is in the manner prescribed under Article 77 of the Constitution and as such cannot be statutory. [797B] 4. The memorandum issued under Article 162 of the Constitution is in the form in the nature, of executive instructions and is not statutory. The memorandum cannot be said to be statutory. The Memorandum is in the character of executive instructions as required under article 77(1). [799C] 5.

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable accounting period was 1st April, 1941 to 29th September, 1941. The chargeable account ing period was 1 st April, 1941to 29th September 1941. The assessee was an registered firm carrying on the business of manufacture of katecu. The assessee claimed that the deficiency of profits during the chargeable accounting period ending 31st March, 1941 to 31st March 1943 should be allowed a set off in computing the excess profits for the chargeable accounting periods ending 31st December, 1940 to 31st December 1942. The assessee contended that the deficiency in profits pertaining to the chargeable accountingperiod ending 31st January, 1941 to 30th September, 1942 should be allowed set off in computation the excess profits during the accounting period ending March 31, 1941 to March, 1941 and that the deficiency should be set off in calculating the excess profits. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, held that the deficiency was attributable to the manufacturing activity alone and there could be no deficiency of profits. The High Court, however, allowed the assessee 's appeal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the deficiency could not be said to have suffered any deficiency during the chargeable chargeable accounting period commencing 31st March 1944 and ending 31st May, 1941, and that the standard profits as provided in the Act became the deficiency of the said two chargeable accounting periods. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the deficiency attributable to the manufacture of kathaechu was part of its business within the meaning of the third proviso to section 5 of the Act. [601C] 2. The High Courts were right in holding, that the deficiency did not fall within the mischief of the third Proviso to section 5. [602D] 3. The High. Court was right in not accepting the opinion of the Tribunal that the deficiency had been attributable to the production of katcechu. [603E] 4. The High, Court was right, in holding, in the circumstances, that the profits of a part of the business, the manufacturing activity, between 28th OCtober, 1940 to 29th November, 1941 could be attributed to the manufacturing activities alone and there were no sales, therefore, no part of the profits realised upon the sales effected during the chargeable period ending 31 st March, 1941. [604B] 5. The High ' Court was right. In the instant case, the question was whether the assessee could be said to be liable to income tax. The High tions of the High Court were right. [605C] 6.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for the posts of Civil Engineering and Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University and the Kerala Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). The applications were rejected by the Public Service Commission. The appellants filed a Writ Petition in the High Court challenging the selection of the appellants and the method of selection. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petitions. The appellants contended that the KPSC had advised candidates according to the separate list prepared by the Public service Commission and there after in an interview held by it. The appellants also contended that the Public Service commission had advised candidates belonging to the same category and that the Public Services Commission had advised candidates for the same post. The High court dismissed the Writ Petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the Kerala Public Service commission was directed to prepare separate lists and publish separate rank lists after the written test and the interview held by the KP SC was not directed to prepare a common list. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The Kerala Public Service Commissions were directed to prepare two separate rank lists, one for Civil Engineering and the other for Mechanical Engineering graduates. The KPSC prepared the two rank lists for Civil Engineering (Civil) and Mechanical Engineering (Civil). The KP SC prepared the two ranks list for Engineering (Civil), and Mechanical Engineering graduates on the basis of examination already conducted. The K.P.SC prepared the second rank list for Engineering and Mechanical engineering. The K PSC prepared the separate rank lists for Engineering ( Civil) and Mechanical engineering graduates on the foundation of examination already held. The KSC prepared the three rank lists for the Mechanical Engineering and Mechanical Engineers. The KMPSC prepared the four rank lists for Mechanical Engineering and the Mechanical Engineering graduates and the rank list for Mechanical Engineering. The KMSC prepared the combined rank list for the Mechanical engineering graduates. The appellants, who had qualified in Mechanical Engineering and had qualified in Civil Engineering, had also been appointed. The KKPSC had also prepared the two separate rank list for Civil Engineering graduates. It was contended that there were directions to the KPCSC to prepare separate list. The KpSC had also stated in its counter affidavit that there were instructions to the K.PSC to prepare two different rank lists for civil Engineering and Mechanical graduates. The Kerala State Public Service Commission was directed to prepared separate lists for Civil engineering graduates and the other. The KCSC prepared the common list for Civil engineering graduate and the Mechanical engineering graduate on the basis thereof. The K KPSC also prepared the separate list for Civil Engg. graduates on the ground that the K.K.PSC had recommended candidates according to separate list for civil engineering graduates. It is also stated that the KKP SC prepared two separate rank Lists for Civil Engineering, Mechanical Engineering and Electrical Engineering. The Kerala Government or the KP.SC accepted the directions given by the High Court.

The plaintiff respondent No. 1, a partnership firm, was a proprietary business belonging to Abdul Samad, father of the plaintiff and defendant Nos. 1 and 2. The plaintiff, who was a partner of a partnership firm and was a proprietary concern, was assessed to income tax under section 7(iv)(f) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The plaintiff filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and valuing at Rs.50 for profit to the share of the plaintiff arising out of the business. The plaintiff 's case was that the plaintiff had laid claim to a sum of Rs.1,26,796.72 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income tax department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint. The plaintiff alleged that he was a partner in a partnership firm. The plaintiff also alleged that he had taken part charge of the business and excluded the plaintiff from the business. He also alleged that the plaintiff was a partner and was not entitled to any relief. The trial court dismissed the suit. The plaintiff preferred an appeal before the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the plaintiff has not laid claim to the sum of Rs,1,26796.73 as his share. The plaintiff has filed a suit in the High Court for dissolution of the partnership and valuations at Rs.150.50 for the profit for the year 1979 79. The plaintiff contended that the valuation given by the plaintiff as grossly undervalued and arbitrary was arbitrary and unreasonable. The High Courts in the country have consistently confirmed this right of the plaintiff. The plaintiff was not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. The plaintiff had not established any decision to the contrary. The High court, however, rejected the valuation put by the plaintiff on the plaint. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the plaintiff that the valuation put in by the plaintiff was arbitrary and irrational and that the court had no jurisdiction to examine the matter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The plaintiff cannot arbitrarily and deliberately under the value of the relief claimed in the suit. It is true that in a suit for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choosing an unreasonable and unfair figure for that purposes. [501C D] 2. The suit is governed for the purpose of court fees by section 7(v)(f) and the plaintiff has the absolute right to put on the plaint any value he wishes to place any valuation whatever on such relief and where the plaintiff manifestly and deliberately under valuation put a tentative value upon the suit. [502C D] 3. The plaintiff is not entitled to ask for any valuation on the plaint, but he has not discovered any decision to contrary. The plaintiff can give an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the suit. If the court comes to the conclusion that the tentative valuation of the suit would be beyond its pecuniary jurisdiction, it shall pass an appropriate order under Order VII of the Code of Civil Procedure. [503D E] 4. The plaintiff could not have valued the suit at the rate of Rs.150 per share. The valuation put by him was arbitrary and unacceptable. The plaintiff did not choose an unreasonable or arbitrary figure for the purpose. The valuation was put by the defendant before the court. The plaintiff failed to establish any decision to that effect. [504B C] 5. The plaintiff in the instant case has not established any such decision to the detriment of the plaintiff or he has not established that the valuation was arbitrary or unreasonable. The plaintiff having failed to establish that the valuation of the plaintiff was unreasonable and arbitrary, the court may reject such valuation.

The respondents in these two appeals are manufacturers of various industries. They were registered as dealers in the State of Madhya Pradesh. They were granted exemption from payment of tax under the Madhya Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1958. The respondents in these appeals were registered as dealer in the State. They were also registered as dealers of the other two units. The respondents were registered as manufacturers of various other industries. The State Government issued a notification dated 1st April, 1981 exempting the class of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule to the notification from payment of sales tax under the said Act for the period specified in column(2) of the said Schedule. The respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the said notification. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the State that the exemption granted by the 1981 notification was in the nature of an alterna tive to the notification excluding "traditional industries" from the notification. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The exemption granted by 1981 notification is in the nature and nature of an alteration to the notification. The exemption is only in the nature or of an alteration in the notification excluding 'traditional industries ' from the notification and not on the basis of any further requirements not so set out in the notification. [601C] 2. The exemption under the 1981 notification is not available to traditional industries. The exemption cannot be given to a notification rescinding an exemption granted earlier. The exemption can be given only prospectively. The exemption has to be prospective only prospectively. [602D] 3. The exemption in question is only in respect of the industries mentioned by it. The exemption was not available to such traditional industries. [603E] 4. The exemption could be given only to those industries listed in rule 14. The exemption would be available to traditional units only if they are eligible for the concession of deferment of tax. [604B] 5. The exemption should be given to traditional industries only if they have set up the new entrepreneur al Units. [605C] 6. The exemption may be granted only prospectively. But the exemption is not available in respect of industries mentioned by the notification. It is clear from the language of the notification that traditional industries are excluded. The exemption does not carry the State 's case that the industries run by them are "traditional Industries" from the exemption. [606D] 7. The exemption, therefore, cannot be given retrospective effect to. [607E] 8. The exemption will be available to new industrial units who opt for the alternative concession of deferment. [608D] 9. The exemption shall be available to the new industrial units which opt for the concession. [609E] 10. The exemption so granted by the notification is not applicable to traditional industries because of the condition that the new industrial unit who opt for alternative concession of deferring the payment of tax shall be entitled to the exemption on the terms and conditions set out in rule 14 particularly when rule 14 specifically provides that the certificate shall be issued to the new unit who opt to avail the alternative concession. [709E] 11. The exemption of the old industrial units who opted for the alternative concessions of deferment of payment of tax is only in nature of an altered tive to that provision for exemption and the former is not available. [610E] 12. The exemption to be granted under the 1981 Notification is not available for traditional industries. It is not necessary for the State to specifically provide that they will not be available to those industries specified in rule 14 especially when rule 14 is clear that while a notification under it can be prospective or retrospective only prospective operation can be given to such units.

The Delhi Judicial Service Rules, 1973 were framed under the Delhi Judicial Service (Recruitment) Rules, 1973. Rule 16(1) provided that temporary posts shall be filled in, in consultation with the High Court, from amongst the members of the Delhi Judicial service who were appointed in a substantive capacity to a temporary capacity. Rule 16 (2) provided that the first vacancy shall be filled by a direct recruit, the first vacancy by promotion, and the promotees who were appointed on the basis of selection from amongst the member of the Delhi judicial Service who were appointed substantively in substantive vacancies, could be made within the framework of the Rules and had to be made, if at all, from amongst members of the Haryana Judicial Service who were recruited in consultation with High Court. Rule 16 provided that temporary vacancies shall be filled, in consultation, with the High Courts from amongst the persons of the Delhi and the promotees appointed under Rule 16. Rule 16 was amended by the Delhi Judicial Services (Recruitment) (Amendment) Rules, 1976. Rule 16 of the said Rules provided that temporary appointments shall be made by the Administrator on the recommendation of the High Court. The appellants who were appointed as Additional District & Sessions Judges in the Delhi Judicial services were appointed to temporary posts of Additional District & Session Judges in the Service under Rule 16(2) of the Rules. The appellants were appointed to the temporary posts of District & Sessions Judge in the Delhi Higher Judicial Service. The appellants challenged the validity of the said Rule on the ground that the said Rule was violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed. The appellants contended that the Rules were violative of Articles 16 and 16 of Constitution. The appellants also contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the Rules of 1973 were violative of Article 16 of the constitution. The High court dismissed the writ petitions. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Rules are violative of Articles 15 and 16 of constitution and that the appellants were not entitled to any relief. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Rules of 1973 are violative of Article 14 of the Constitution and are not violative of Articles 19 and 16 of Part III of the Constitution of India. [419C] 2. The Rules are violative Of Articles 14 and 19 of the Constitution as they are not violative either of Articles 14 or 16 of the Consti tution of India. The Rules do not violate Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution inasmuch as they are made in consultation with a High Court. [420D] 3. The Rules have been framed under the Act and the Rules are made in exercise of the powers conferred by the Act. The Rules cannot be said to violate Articles 14 or 19 of the constitution and the Rules do not contravene Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution.[421E F] 4. The Rules were framed under Rule 16 of Delhi Judicial Service as required under Rule 16 (1) and if such posts have been filled in consultation with, the High Court from amongst the Members of Delhi Judicial Services, the seniority must be governed by the rules of continuous officiation in the cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a member of the Haryana judicial Service is appointed in a temporary capacity to a substantive capacity. [422C D] 5.

The Income tax Officer assessed the appellant as "the income of the family of Parshad". The Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of the Income tax Officer and directed that the income in the three assessment years be assessed in the hands of the family. The Appellate Assistant commissioner set aside the assessment order of the income in respect of the income of the appellant. The Tribunal held that the income belonged to the family of the appellant and the income from the business was liable to be brought to tax on that footing. The Tribunal also held that the business was carried on by an association of persons and the income was liable to tax on the income of a family. The Tribunal, however, set aside the orders of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and directed that he may be personally assessed by the Income tax officer in respect of income. The Tribunal further held that the Income tax Act was not barred by the law of limitation. The High Court, however, held that the assessee was not a stranger to the assessment proceedings and the Appellate Assistant commissioner had no jurisdiction to direct the Income tax authorities to amend the assessment proceedings. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that the Income Tax Officer was not competent to make the direction in the case of Ambala Flour Mills. HELD: (i) The Income tax Officer was competent to set aside the direction of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal was competent to make that direction. The power of the Appellate Tribunal was not and could not be referred to the High Court. [882 C] (ii) The Income Tax Officer had no jurisdiction under section 33A of the Income Tax Act to make the impugned direction. The Income tax officer was competent to give directions with regard to the assessment of the income. The Income Tax officer was competent not to make the order of assessment by the Income Tax officer. The Incometax Officer was competent not only to make the assessment but also to make the necessary order. The Income taxes Officer was competent under section 33B of the Act to make an assessment on any partner of the firm or association of persons. [883 D E] (iii) The Incometax officer was competent under the Act to set aside an order of assessment made by the Incometax Officer. The Appellate Asstt. commissioner was competent to remand the case to the Income tax Authorities for making the impugned direction by which they sought tomodify the order of Income tax Officer. The Income 'tax Officer was not entitled to make the said direction. [884 E] (iv) The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner was competent to modify the order of income tax Officer. But on the question referred to the Tribunal, no inquiry into the power of the Incometax officer to make the original direction was competent.

The appellant, who was the plaintiff, filed a suit for partition of his share in the suit properties. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court held that the proper court fee paid by the appellant in respect of his claim for partition was not a proper court fee and that the proper Court fee paid was to be paid on the memorandum of appeal. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the High Court was in error in directing the appellant to pay court fees on the memorandum. The appellant was entitled to amend his plaint and set out the amount specifically mentioned in the plaint as the value of the appellant 's claim for partition. The proper court fee payable in respect of the value of his relief of partition was not only the value given by the appellant but also on the memorandum and the plaint. The proper Court fee was to be determined under section 7(iv)(b) of the Act and it was not open to him to make any jurisdictional valuation. The proper courts fee was to have been paid on the plaint and on the memorandum, appeal on the memorandum was to be valued for the purposes of court fees and the valuation was to be taken to be the value even for the purposes Of court fees. The proper Courts fee was to the value of Rs. 15,00,000 as the value for the purposes. of court fees. It was not open for the appellant to claim the value of a relief claimed for the purposes for the purposes ofs.7(iv)(c) of the Madras High Court Fees and Court Fees Act, 1959, for the purpose of court fees, and it was open to him under section 7 (iv)(b), to amend his valuation for the purposes mentioned therein. The proper forum was to be fixed by the court in computing the court fees payable in respect Of the value of relief claimed for partition.

The appellant, a Municipal Committee, was constituted under the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957, to provide for the safety of the refuge areas in the ratio of one sq. metre per person. The appellant, a statutory body, was also a statutory body. The appellant was also a Municipal Committee. The Municipal Committee, in its meeting held on 18.2.1989, decided to accept the appellant 's objections to the plans and to accept them. The appellant 's grievance was that the plans were not in conformity with the Bye law and the Chief Fire Officer, who was not competent to accept them, was not permitted to do so. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the decision of the NDMC on the ground that the plans provided for adequate fire safety measures, and that the construction of the buildings was not a "external wall" for purposes of the Bye law. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the NDMC did not raise, at the appropriate stage, any specific objections to the plan on the ground of its sanction, did not raise at the appropriate time any specific objections regarding the plans on the ground, that they were not in compliance with Bye law 16.4.8.1, and that, therefore, the clearance given to the plan by the Chief Fire officer was implicit in the clearance given by the Chief fire Officer. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The construction of the building was not a 'external wall ' for purposes of bye law 16.1.8. The construction of such pedestrian walk way was not an "external walls" for purposes. The construction work according to bye law 16, was an "ex internal wall" for the purposes of the said bye law. [604B C] 1.2 The construction of a building is not a "External wall" within the meaning of bye law 17.1. The construction is not a 'External wall ' within the meaning Of bye law 17, but a 'ex internal wall ' for the purposes. [605C] 1.3 The construction of buildings is not a part of the "external structure" for purposes, of the Bye laws 16.4, the zonal development requirements in this behalf and the difficulties and probity in this behalf, and the difficulties inherent in the insistence upon construction of such AUGrian walk way. [606D] 1.4 The construction of building is not an "External structure" within the ambit of bye law. The construction would be at the risk of the respondents 1 and 2 to the effect that whenever the policy to implement the Zonal Developmental requirements in this regard is considered to provide for safety in a better measure than those envisaged by the Bye laws. [607D] 1(a) The construction of an outer wall is not an 'external structure ' within the ambit Of bye law 16 of the NDMC. [608C] 1(b) The construction is an integral part of the Bye Law 17.1, the zonal developmental requirements in this respect are not inflexible and that in appropriate cases, where the plans and incorporate fire safety measures are considered to provide adequate fire safety in accordance with its bye laws or in a better manner.

The appellant, a joint family business, was still a joint family and that he had a right to ask for accounts of that business subsequent to March 31, 1946, that accounts of the motor business should be taken up to March 31 , 1946, and that the compromise accounts of the Motor business should be kept up to March 30, 1946, and the date of the final decree for payment of the amount found to be due would be the date on which a final decree for the payment of the said amount would be made. The appellant, who was the owner of the motor shop, filed a suit for partition and possession of the shop on the ground that the compromise was made after due deliberation, that accounts should be taken into account for the subsequent years. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that the suit was barred by res judicata and by order II, rule 2, of the Code of Civil Procedure. The appellant appealed to this Court. Held, that the cause of action in the two suits being the same, the suit was not barred by resjudicata or by order II. Rule 2(3) of the Code Of Civil Procedure, 1908, which provides that where the parties omitted to provide in the compromise accounts that account of the motor businesses should be taken down to March 31 1946, only implicitly relinquished their claim to the account for the later years, the date of final decree would be the end of the previous suit. The cause of action for the subsequent period was the desire and intention of the parties, but the parties did not care to ask that accounts of those businesses should be keptup to March 31. 1946, only impliedly relinquished their claims to the account up to March 3, 1946, only explicitly implicitly relinquished his claim to the accounts for the subsequent periods. The cause for action in the first suit was the desire of the plaintiff to separate the accounts of the business after the 31st March, 1946, even implicitly relinquished the claim to theaccount for the subsequent year. The cause was different from the cause of actions in the first. suit. The suit was barred under Order II, rule 1, of the Civil Procedure Code. The cause in the first case was the desire, and intention of parties, but not the intention of the plaintiff, and the consent decree was passed by the Court, and the plaintiff was bound by the terms of the compromise and the consent decrees for accounts of those business after the 1st April, 1946, merely implicitly relinquished her claim to the Account for the subsequent two years. The cause, of action in both the suits being the one, the suit being the same and distinct and separate, and not separate and distinct, and that, the suit be barred under Order I, rule 2(3), of the Code.

The appellant was employed as a servant in the Salt Works. He was prosecuted under section 92 of the Indian Factories Act, 1948, for the contravention of the provisions of the Act. The trial court acquitted him but the High Court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The appellant was employed in the Salt works and the salt works were carried on in the appellant 's Salt Works. The appellant was not a factory. The salt works were not in the open air and not in the premises. The appellant 's salt works were in the premises of the Salt Works and were not in a building. The appellant had been rightly convicted of the offence of an offence under section 92. [659 B] The appellant ' was employed in a Salt Works and was not in the same position as that of a factory. [660 C] The appellant was rightly convicted of an offence of manufacturing process.
