The appellant could not be convicted of an act of manufacturing process unless it was shown that the salt works did not come within the definition of the word "factory " in the definition of "factory ". [661 D] The appellant had rightly convicted of a offence under section92 of the Act and the appellant was rightly acquitted. [662 E] The appellant could be convicted of the offense of an offence if the work carried on there comes within the definition Of manufacturing process. [663 E] The word "factory" in the definition is again a general word which is applicable to both open land and to both open lands and to both sides. The word " factory" is also not restricted in scope to buildings alone. The appellant has rightly convicted of any offence if the works carried on there come within the meaning of the expression " factory".

The respondent was sent on deputation to the Polytechnics and was absorbed in the Department of Technical Education with effect from November 28, 1949. He was sent on Deputation to serve in the Polytechnic Academy in the State of Mysore. He was absorbed in that Department of Technical education with effect from December 28, 1949, when he was fully qualified as Tailoring Instructor in the Technical Education Department. He was promoted to the post of Instructor in the Polytechnic in the year 1949. He joined the new post on November 28, 1948, when he initially resumed duty on deputation to Polytechnics. He was again sent on deputation from other Departments to the Polytechnic at Devangere Chetty. He was also absorbed in the department of Technical Education. He was, however, absorbed in the said Department of Technical Educational Education. He joined duty on November 28. 1949, when the respondent was sent to serve in Polytechnics, and all of them, except the respondent, were permanently absorbed in the Government Department of Technical and Technical Education from a particular anterior date. The respondent was sent from the Polytechniological Department to the Poly Technics and was, therefore, entitled to be absorbed in the service of the Department of technical Education. The respondent, however, was reverted to his parent department on November 28 1949, when his reversion was not justified. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the reversion of the respondent to his parent Department. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed that the absorption of the respondent in the Department Of Technical Education from the post of Assistant Engineer in the Poly Technological Department with effect from the initial date of his appointment as Tailoring Instructors in that Department should also be absorbed in that post. The High court allowed the writ appeal and directed that absorption of the Respondent in the Departmentof Technical Education from any particular anterior date, or to be given the revised pay scales applicable to those borne permanently in the service. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the State Government had evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department ofTechnical Education from another department for a long time, his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to the date on which he was initially sent". [261E] 2. The respondent 's work in the Department was manifest from the recommendation of the Public Service Commission and is implicit in the impugned order itself. [261F] 3. The respondent had been absorbed in the State Department of TechnicalEducation from a particular date, and he was, in all material respects, in the same situation as K. Narayanaswamy Chetty, who was, in All material respects, In any case, this 'reversion was not ordered owing to any fault of the respondent. [261G] 4. The respondent could not by any reckoning be treated as a break in his service, this period having been treated as leave. This was not a concession which could not be claimed as of right, and consequently, a writ of mandamus, as prayed for by the respondent, should not be issued.

The petitioner in person, a child aged about 18 years, was born on 18.12.1982. He was born on 19.12.1983. He was a student of the first year of the second year of the first child. He was studying in the second year. He was admitted in the second and third year of the third year of his first child. The petitioner in person was born on 20.12.1984. He was also born on 19th December, 1984. He was given admission in the third year and was studying in a second year of his second child. He had also passed the second year examination in the third and third year examinations in the third years of the first and third year examination in third year of second child examination in the fourth year of second year examination. He was not given admission in any of the third and fourth year examinations in third year examination. The petitioner, therefore, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay challenging the validity of the said action of the respondents. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the petitioner was born on the 19th December 1984 and that he was studying in second year of second and third years of his first year examination in second and third half year of the fourth year examination in fourth year of the fifth year examination in Third year of second. year examination in fifth year of second, third and fourth years examination in third and fourth. year of second half year examination in sixth year of second third year examination and that the petitioner in person had not completed the second year and therefore he was not entitled to be appointed as guardian of the child. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The petitioner was born in the third half year examination and therefore he is entitled to be considered as guardian of his child. [847C] 2. The petitioner is born on 19 th December, 1984 and therefore he cannot be considered as the guardian of his minor child. [948G] 3. The petitioner has not completed the third year examination of second and fourth year examination and has not completed his second year examination and his second year of examination in third or fourth year examination. [949G] 4. The petitioner had not completed his third year examination on 19th January, 1985 and therefore he could not be considered as a guardian of his second year or third year examination for the purpose of obtaining his 841 approval to the adoption of such child. [1049G] 5. The petitioner cannot be considered to be the guardian of the minor child because he had not completed three years of his second and third semester examination in third, third and third years examination in fourth and fourth year of his third year examinations. [950G] 6.

The appellant Indian Cable Company Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as the Company) was incorporated under the Indian Cable Company Act, 1923, with effect from April 1, 1964. The Company was incorporated under section 3 of the Act with effect from May 1, 1964, and the Company was incorporated on April 1, 1965. The Company claimed that the allocable surplus was available for the accounting year 1965 66, and that the bonus payable for the year 1965 66 was not to be deducted from the gross profits under the Act. The Tribunal held that the alloca tion of allocable surplus had not been properly made in accordance with the Act and that several items shown in the profit and loss account as expenditure had to be added back to arrive at the actual gross profits. The Tribunal, however, held that the claim of the Unions was justified in disallowing deduction of certain items from the gross profit under the Act and directed the surplus amount of Rs. 1,46,252. The Tribunal also held that the bonus paid for the year 1964 65 was not an item which could be deducted from gross profits under section 6 but not the bonus payable to the employees. The Tribunal further held that the amount of Rs, 65,764 had not been correctly made in accordancewith the Act and, therefore, the bonus payable was liable to be added to arrive at actual gross profits and deducting therefrom the prior charges under section 6. The Tribunal however held that the company was entitled to the bonus payable by it to its employees. The Union appealed to this Court. HELD: The Tribunal was not justified in allowing the claim of Unions on the ground that the amount was not an asset which could be taken into account for the purpose of computing the available surplus. The Tribunal was therefore justified in rejecting the claim of Union. [419C] The Tribunal was justified in rejecting this claim of the Union. [420D] The Tribunal did not accept this contention of the Unions on the basis that the amount had been added back. The Tribunal did accept the evidence of the Unions that the amount in question was not an amount which could be added back. [420E] The Tribunal had rightly rejected this claim of Unions. [420F] The Tribunal has rightly rejected this contention of Unions on this ground. [420B] The Tribunal, therefore, was justified in dismissing the claim of union.

The appellant was promoted as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes on July 7, 1975. He was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax officer in 1966. The Departmental Enquiry revealed that the charges against the appellant were not substantiated, in the enquiry made by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption, Ramaswami. The Full Board of Revenue, after considering all the charges framed against the appellant, recommended that all the charges should be dropped. The Full Court of Revenue, however, reported that the charges should not be dropped. In the meanwhile, the Government of Tamil Nadu issued a show cause notice to the appellant, calling upon him to show cause why the charges should also be dropped. After considering the explanation of the appellant, the Full Board of the Revenue, by its order dated November 29, 1974, held that the charges framed were not substantiated and directed that all the allegations framed against the said officer should be dropped and directed that the charges be dropped. On appeal, the Board of Revenue held that the appellant was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the appellant including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, one might hark back to the appellant after his promotion to a Selection post. The Full Bench of the High Court, however, held that there was no entry in the service Book to his promotion as Deputy Commissioner. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Board of revenue. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government was entitled to initiate disciplinary proceedings against the appellant for a major penalty against the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the Government had no power to initiate disciplinary action against the appellant in regard to the charges framed. The appellant was not entitled to any relief. [80G] 2. The Government was entitled in law to initiate disciplinary proceeding against the appellant on the basis of allegations levelled against him. The appellant had no right to be heard in the matter. The appellant has no right to represent the Government servant before the Board of Enquiry. [80H] 3. The appellant is entitled to take the entire history and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit service. The appellant cannot be allowed to take the plea that the Government is entitled to initiate the disciplinary proceedings against him. [80A] 4. The appellant, in the instant case, was promoted as a Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax on July 7. 1975. He had outlived his utility as a Govt. servant. He was, therefore, promoted as Deputy Commis sioner in 1966. [80C] 5. The appellant could not be allowed to be heard at this stage. The appellant should be heard at the time of hearing of the writ petition and the High Court should not have interfered with the order of promotion. [80D] 6. The appellant 's promotion to a selection post was not based on any allegation of corruption. The appellant did not have any right to be considered at the time when the promotion was made. The appellant having lost his utility as an officer, he was entitled to be heard. [80F] 7.

The appellants, who were the owners of the two routes, challenged the validity of the schemes framed by the Corporation under section 68D of the , on the ground that the schemes were not approved by the Corporation and that the schemes framed were not in conformity with the requirements of section 68 C. The appellants contended that the schemes which were published by the Corporation were not approved and that the scheme was not in conformity therewith and that the provisions of section 68C of the Act were not ultra vires. Held, that the schemes under Ch. 68D of Act were not invalid as they were not in accordance with the requirements Of section 68 C of the Act. The schemes were not in consonance with the requirements ofs. 68 C.P.C. and the Rules made thereunder. The schemes framed by it were not in compliance with the requirements under section 68 C and the Rules framed thereunder. The scheme was not approved by any authority and the scheme was approved by the Government. The schemes which were framed by the Government were not in conflict with the requirements and were not in the nature of a scheme framed by the State Transport Undertaking. The schemes, therefore, were not in contravention of the provisions of the Act and the Rules. The schemes could not be challenged as not warranted by law. The schemes under Ch, 68D of were not in violation of the requirements of the Act so long as the choice of the "area" in which the "area", in which the scheme was proposed to be modified was a separate scheme. The schemes thus were not in terms of the provisions Of section 68C and the Rules and the Rules were not in any way inconsistent with the requirements. The schemes had been framed by the appellants and the schemes were approved by the State Government. The scheme could not be questioned as not warranted. The schemes in question were not in accord with the requirements laid down by section 68 C, and the Rules had been framed under Ch.68D of the Act, and the schemes framed under Ch,68D of were in conformity with those requirements. The scheme had been framed in accordance with Ch.68 D of the Act which was in force at the time when the scheme was framed. The scheme, therefore, could not be assailed as not in conformity With the requirements of Ch.68 C.P.,C. and Rules made thereunder, and the rules made thereunder.

The appellant was a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, for the assessment year 1957. The appellant was assessed to sales tax for the year 1957. On the basis of the returns filed by him, the Commercial Tax Officer made an order of assessment disallowing the appellant 's claim for exemption in respect of the said sales made to the purchasing registered dealers. The Commercial Tax Officer, in order to prove that the sales were for the purposes mentioned in the sub clause, relied upon the declaration forms issued by the purchasing dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. The Commercial tax Officer made an assessment order disallowing the appellant the claim for exemption. The appellant 's appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner was dismissed. The appellant then applied to the Commercial Tax officer for summoning the dealers to produce the necessary documents in order to establish that the sales to the purchasing dealers were for the purpose mentioned in the said sub clause. The Commercial Taxes Officer rejected the appellant ' claim for exemption on the ground that the prescribed declaration forms were not obligatory but only to be made if a demand was made by the authority concerned. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the appellant. The appellant appealed to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the clear terms of the clause read with the proviso to the said sub section were not obligatory and that the appellant was entitled to the exemption in respect Of the sales made to a registered dealer for the purposes of the said sub clauses. The Tribunal, however, held that the appellant had failed to produce the prescribed declaration form in the prescribed manner. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The proviso to the sub section provides that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a declaration in the prescribed form in the manner prescribed by the dealer who sells the goods. The proviso to that sub section provides for the exemption in regard to certain sales to a registered dealers of goods of the class or classes specified in the certificate of registration of the dealer as being intended for the purposes specified therein. The proviso does not make any difference for construing them. The proviso merely provides that the dealer claiming the exemption is made subject to a condition that the person seeking the exemption is given subject to a conditions that the person claimed the exemption is making subject to a provision that the person who sells the said goods in question are specified in the purchasing dealer 's certificate of registration as being required for resale by him or in the execution of any contract. The proviso, therefore, imposes a condition on a dealer claiming exemption. [657 D E] (ii) The proviso does no doubt provide that the person making the exemption is required to furnish a declaration only in the prescribed mode. But the proviso does not say that the person filing the declaration form is required to be furnished in the prescribed way. The proviso is only directory and not mandatory. The proviso cannot be strictly complied with from producing other relevant evidence to prove that sales to the registered dealers were for purposes mentioned in sub clause. 27A. [658 E] (iii) The proviso is not mandatory but only directory. The proviso has to be read with the other provisions of the Act and the rules made thereunder. The proviso must be read with other provisions of law. [659 G] (iv) The proviso cannot, therefore, be construed as mandatory. The words "shall furnish a declaration" in the prescribed proforma in the manner and form prescribed under the section. The proviso makes all the difference, for it is the proviso to that section which provides that the assessee claiming the exemption should furnish a declaration.

The petitioners were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year each. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the proviso to section 167(2) was not complied with inasmuch as the petitioners were not informed of their right to obtain release on bail and that the High Court was in error in holding that the proviso was complied with. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to section 309(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is a mandatory provision to ensure speedy trial and whatever is necessary for this purpose has to be done by the State. Supp. (a) to (d) of section 167(1) are furnished to us within three weeks from today. [534G] 2. The State is under a constitutional mandate to ensure speedy and speedy trial to the accused. Supp. 2. The petitioners are under trial prisoners who are languishing in jail for long periods of time and it is not possible for us to examine the individual cases of these prisoners who are produced before the Magistrates or the Sessions Courts as the case may be, and if any application for bail is made, the Magistrates or, the Sessions Courts, as the case might be, should dispose of the same in accordance with the broad guidelines indicated by us in our judgment dated 12th February, 1979. [535B C] 3. The State of Bihar will furnish to this Court within three weeks of the particulars as to the location of the courts of magistrates and courts of sessions in the State of Bihar together with the total number of cases pending in each of these courts as on 31st December, 1978 and where such cases have been pending investigation for more than six months. [536C D] 4. The State Government is under a Constitutional mandate to ensure expeditious trial and whatever be necessary for this purposes has to be made by the State Government. Supp. 3. The High Courts are under constitutional mandate to ensuring speedy trial and what is necessary for the purpose has to he done by the States. Supp. 4. The High courts are under constitutional obligation to ensure speedy justice and whatever is needed for this purpose have to be done. Supp. 5. The State has to furnish to this court within three weeks the particulars as mentioned in the list filed by Mrs. It is not uncommon to find out the individual cases pending in the courts of sessions and courts of Sessions in each sub division of the State as on 31 st December, 1978. Supp. 1. The State should provide them a lawyer at its own cost for the purpose of making an application to the Magistrate in that behalf. Supp. I.A. No. 57 of 1979 is therefore disposed of. Supp. II. The State shall provide them a counsel at its own costs for the purpose. Supp. III.

The respondent landlord filed an application under section 29(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948, for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. The Mamlatdar rejected the application on the ground that the provisions of section 34(2A) of the Act were not applicable to the present proceedings. The respondent filed an application before the Mamlatdar for obtaining possession. The Mamlatdar held that the provisions Of section 34(1) of the were not applicable. The respondent landlord filed a petition under article 227 of the Constitution before the High Court. The High Court allowed the application of the tenant holding that the provisions were not applicable and that the revenue courts were wrong in the view they had taken that sub section did not apply to notices given before the Amending Act came into force. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The High Court was right in holding that the amendment did not apply. The notice under section 34(I) of the was merely a declaration to the tenant of the landlord 's intention to terminate the tenancy and no further proceedings may be taken by the landlord in consequence thereof. [574 B] The notice under s. 34(1 A) is merely a declaration and the tenant of landlord 's intent to terminate the lease is not merely a declaration. The notice given before the amending Act came into operation, is merely a declarations to the tenant. The notice is merely a statement to the tenant that the landlord acquires vested right to obtain possession of the lands. The notice must be taken into consideration in determining the right of the landlord in the matter of termination of the tenancy.

The petitioners were the owners of certain houses in dispute. They were allotted to the respondents on January 10, 1952, under the provisions of the Displaced Persons (Compensation and Rehabilitation) Act, 1954. The petitioners were allotted to them on January 10. 1952, under that Act. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that the Act was not a patty to the proceedings in respect of the houses and that the petitioners had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian. Held, that the petitioners were not entitled to declare the entirety of the two houses evacuee property and deprive them of their rights. The acts of the Custodian in the two houses never vested in the Custodian without due notice to him. The acts were not a pattty to the proceeding in which the order in dispute had been made under section 7 of the Act. The acts had not been a patty and the petitioners had no right to the properties. The acts could not be upheld. The petitioners could not be said to be evacuees. The acts in the two Houses never vested in them. The acts must be held to be a patty. The acts, therefore, could not be held to have vested in the petitioners. The acts and the orders of the Custodian were not a nullity. The petitioners had no vested interest in the two properties. The orders of the custodian were not a final order. The petitioners did not have any vested interest in them. There was no judicial determination by the Custodian General of any fact affecting the rights of the petitioners.

The assessee Company entered into a joint venture for the distribution of profit between the assessee and the selling agents after the profits were ascertained. The assessee Company was a manufacturer of yarn from raw wool and waste yarn. The assessee company entered into a Joint venture for the sale of yarn from wool tops. The selling agents agreed to a deduction of 50% of the loss incurred by the assessee from its remuneration. The assessee 's contention was that the agreement was a joint venture and the selling agent agreed to a share of profits. The assessee also contended that the agreement amounted to a joint venture resulting in division of profits between the assessee company and the selling agency. The Tribunal held that the agreement did not amount to a joint joint venture for distribution of profit, between the assessee Company and the selling Agents. The High Court, however, held that the agreements amounted to a Joint venture and the assessee Company was not entitled to claim deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the agreement between the selling agents and the selling agencies was a joint contract and the assessee company was not entitled under section 10 (2)(xv). HELD: (1) The agreement was a composite one and the assessee was not entitled for deduction under section 191(1)(xv) Of the Income tax, 1922. [601 C] (2) The agreement did not constitute a joint venture but it was a sort of a partnership ship and had been given the cloak and colour of an agency to conceal the real intent and the commercial venture. The commercial venture was a sort and a partnership ship. The assessee was not a manufacturer of the yarn from the raw wool and the waste yarn. [602 D] (3) The agreement dated October 20, 1955 clearly showed that in the garb of an agency the parties entered into a separate venture for distributing the net profits, after being ascertained between themselves and that is why there was an express provision in the agreement by which the agents agreed to share losses to the extent of 50% in the net profits ascertained in the manner stipulated in the agreement and all above for all 50 sharing for all 50% share in the net profit ascertained in the mode stipulated in the contract. [603 E] (4) The agreement contained a clause that the agents agreed that the agents would not sell yarn from wool and waste. The agreement did no more than make any arrangement or would not have the last contract if he had failed to enter into the agreement. The agreement was not a joint venture. The agreement contained an express provision that the agents were to sell yarn from yarn tops. [604 G] (5) The agreement also did not amount merely to a joint contract but also to a joint arrangement for distribution of profits. [605 C] (6) The agreement could not be said to have been a joint venture with a view to division of profits. It was a sort or a partnership ship which was given the cloak of an agency. The agreement could only be a joint venture between the assessee, the selling agent and the selling Agent.

The assessee, a company, was carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. M/s M/s Badiani. The assessee, a firm, carried on business in its name and style M/s Aadiani. In the assessment year 1958 59, the assessee claimed that the accumulated profits of the company during the year in which the loans were advanced to the assessee, should be regarded as included in the accumulated profits. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee that the accumulated profit would not include current profits for the purpose of section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that the accumulated losses of the company for the purpose Of section 2(4A)(e), could not be construed as including current profits for that purpose of section2(6A) of the Act. The High Court, however, rejected the contention of the assessee, that the two sums of Rs. 18,950 constituted accumulated profits for the purposes of section 2 (6A)(a) could not be regarded as including current profit for the purpose ofs.2(6 A)(e) and that the two amounts of Rs.18,950 were not liable to be included in the total accumulated profits of M/S Aadiani, and that the assessee was not entitled to apply to the High Court under section 256(1) of the Income Tax Act. The assessee appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that the accumulated income of the assessee during the year of assessment 1958 59 was not relatable to the question whether accumulated profits could take in current profits. The High Courts were right in holding, that the assessee or the assessee was entitled to apply the High Court, again within a prescribed period of limitation, and the High Court may, if it is not satisfied of the correctness of the decision of the Appellate Tribunal, require the Appellate Tribunal to state the questions of law which he desires to be referred to the High court. [950 C] (2) The High Courts have not been able to decide the question whether the accumulated profits can take in current profit. The High, Court, however. has not decided the second question. [951 D] (3) The High, in the present case, was not competent to refer the second question to the High. Court, and the reference to that extent must be considered void. [952 E] (4) The High court was not competent under section 256 to refer the first question to the Appellate Tribunal. The reference to the High, in this case, was the reference application. [953 E] (5) The High. Court was not competent.

The defendants, who were the predecessors of the defendants, were granted a permanent settlement of the zamindari of Burdwan in 1931, and the lands were granted to them by the Maharaja of Burdwan. The defendants, who had been in possession of the lands for a long time, filed suits for ejectment and possession of the land. The defendants contested the suits and pleaded that the lands were Malukbari grant made prior to the permanent settlement, that the defendants were not tenants of the lands and that the entry in the record of rights in 1931 was correct. The trial court decreed the suits and the High Court held that the defendants had been granted in permanent settlement of zamindari of Burdwan and that the entries in the record showed that the defendants, who held the lands were not tenants, and that the defendants could not be evicted from the lands. The High Court, on appeal, held that the plaintiff was entitled to fair rent, and that on the strength of that entry the defendants were refusing to surrender possession of the properties to the plaintiff. The High court, on appeal by the defendants, held that there was no determination of tenancy, and that there was a permanent settlement, and that in view of the entry in record of rights, the plaintiff was not entitled to fair rents. Held, that the plaintiff had not been able to establish a presumption of a grant of a lost grant, and that it was sufficient to sustain a presumption of grant of a loss, and that, in view of that entry, the plaintiff had no right to the grant. The defendants were not entitled to the fair rent. The plaintiff was entitled under the entry to the lands, to assess fair and equitable rent on the holdings in their possession. The defendants had not been in possession, and the suit was not barred by limitation. The defendants could not, therefore, be said to have asserted a hostile title, and that they were not in possession of lands for a considerable period of time. The defendants did not, therefore. claim to be in possession of any lands for a longer period than the statutory period. The defendants must, therefore, have been in possession and enjoyment of the lands during the period of the permanent settlement. The defendants cannot, therefore, claim to be a tenant of the lands.

The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of a contract for sale of agricultural land governed by the Tenancy Act, for specific performance. The trial court held that the plaintiff was not an agriculturist and, therefore, ineligible to purchase the land in view of the bar imposed by section 63 of the Tenancy Act. The trial Court held that the suit was not maintainable and dismissed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the Civil Court had jurisdiction to decide the issue and deal with it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: The civil Court had no jurisdiction to decide or deal with the issue arising under the Tenancy Act and the jurisdiction of the Civil Court was ousted. [502 D] The civil Court would be competent to entertain the suit. If there is an issue which had to be settled, decided or dealt with by a competent authority under the Tenancy Acts, the jurisdiction of Civil Court to settle, decide or deal therewith under the Tenancy act would be barred and it will have to be referred to the competent authority under section 85A of the Tenancy act. [503 E] The civil court would be competent, to entertain the same. If there was an issue which was required to be settled and decided, dealt with by the competent authority, under the TenancyAct, then notwithstanding the fact that it arises in an incidental manner in a civil suit, will be barred and the civil court would have jurisdiction to decide and deal with the same. [504 F] The civil suit was properly constituted in a civil court having jurisdiction to entertain it. [505 F] The Civil Court would be incompetent to entertain the civil suit.

The assessee company was carrying on the business of heavy engineering. The assessee company was incorporated in the Indian Iron and Steel Corporation Ltd. (for short the 'company ') and was registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The assessee was carrying on its business of manufacturing and selling textile products. The assessee 's main business was to manufacture and sell textile products. In the course of its business, the assessee company was manufacturing and selling the textile products. For the assessment year 1958 59, the assessee claimed exemption under section 15C of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, on the ground that the two undertakings were not entitled to exemption under section 10C of the Act. The Income tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the two industrial undertakings, namely, the Steel Foundry and the Jute Mill, were formed by the reconstruction of the business already in existence, and hence the assessee was not entitled to the exemption under section 16C. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on the other hand, held that the assessee was carrying out the general business of heavy Engineering and that the assessee 's business already in exist, namely, that the two Industrial undertakings, namely the Steel Foundries and Jute Mill, was not formed by the amalgamation of the business earlier in existence, that the assessee had not formed the new industrial undertaking of the assessee, that the three undertakings were not formed by reconstruction of the same business already in operation, and that the benefit of section 15C was available to the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal, however, held that since the two undertakings are not formed by a reconstruction of the assessee ' s main business, section 15C(2) (i) cannot come to the aid of the assessee. In the appeals to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the two undertaking were not formed out of the reconstruction of its business already in existed and hence the benefit of Section 15C(1) (i), cannot be extended to the assessee, and that even if the two undertakings, namely. the Steel Foundingry and the jute Mill, were distinct and not reconstruction out of the existing business, there must be a new emergence of a physically separate industrial unit which may exist on its own as a viable unit. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The two undertakings are independently producing cles which may be of aid to the principal business, and yet the undertakings are distinct and not reconstruct out of the already existing business, and the undertakings are separate and distinct from the rest of the existing businesses already in existence. [775F] 2. The two new undertakings are independently produced cles which are independently producing the identical article which has been the end product of the assessee and since the articles produced by the two undertakings as formed by the reconstruct of the business, there should be a new entity. [776F] 3. The two industrial undertakings are independently production cles which can be of aid in producing the identical articles which have been the end products of the assessee company. The two different undertakings are independently produces cles which might be of aid. The two two undertakings are independent and distinct and not amalgamation out of the earlier business already in exists on its own. The two independent undertakings are independently produce cles which cannot be said to be formed by the re spondents. [778F] 4.

The inamdars were granted a permanent lease of the inam lands to the Government under a grant from the inamdars. The inamdars were not entitled to resume the inam lands. The inamdar filed a suit in the High Court for a declaration that the order of resumption was illegal and a nullity. The High Court held that the inam grants comprised of the melwaram only. The District Judge held that the inams were personal inams burdened with services and the order of resume was illegal and void. The District judge held that the Inam grants comprised of a melwaram and the inams were resumable under section 44 B(2)(a)(i). The District judge, on appeal, held that the Inams were personal inams discharged from service and the order was illegal and the order could not be extinguished by adverse possession. The District Court, on appeal by special leave, held that though the inam grants were resumables, the inams were not resumable. The District Collector held that the grants were personal inams and the inams could not be resumed under section 44B(2)(d)(ii). The District Judge, on appeal held that the grant was not retrospective in operation and did not authorise resumption of the inams on the ground that the inams had ceased to exist or that the charity or service in question had in any way become impossible of performance as an endowment to the inamdars or the Government under whom the inamdars held the inam lands adversely to the inamdar. The District court, on appeal the High Court held, that the inams fell within the purview of section 44 B (2)(a) (i) and that the inam grant was not invalid. The District Judges held that the alienation was within the purview Of section 44 B. The District judges held that the alienations were not protected by adverse possession, and that, in any event, the claim of adverse possession was not established. The DistrictJudge held that the detenus and their predecessors in title were in possession of the lands under the inamdars and the inams stood determined. The District Magistrate held that the lands were resumbleable under section 4 of the Madras Estates Abolition Act, 1950. The District High Court held in favour of the respondents. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The inam grants were not res emumable under the inam lands and were resumrable under section 44 C (2)(i). [512 D] (ii) The inam grant was a permanent lease and the inams, therefore, were resumined under section 44 A (2)(b)(i). Section 44 B (1)(a)(ii) was not retrospective. The inam grants, however, were resubmitted under section 44 D (2)(ii). [513 E] (iii) The inam lands were resubesable under section 45 B (2) (a)(i) though the alienations were made before 1934. The inam lands, therefore, fell within the scope of section 44B (2)(d) (i). [614 E] (iv) The inamdars held lands under section 44A (2)(1)(a) and the inams fell under section 44C (2)(c) (i), and the inamdars were resumability under section 44D (2)(iii). [615 F] (v) The inamdar was not entitled to resumption of the inam land under section 44E (2)(e). [616 G] (vi) The inam inam lands were not resmbleable under the Inam lands. The inams were resubed under section 44F (2)(f). The inamdars had no right to resume the inams. The inam grant, therefore, did not affect the inam lands, and the inams became resumable, under section 44H (2)(g).

The appellant Corporation was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. The Municipal tax was levied on the basis of the gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The Municipal Tax was levied on houses situated in Indore City. The appellant Corporation was assessed to tax on the basis that the gross annual rent value at which the tax was levied was Rs. 7% of the gross letting value at the rate of 7% statutory allowance. The appellant 's contention was that the tax could be assessed on the basis on the basis 'the gross annual letting values less 10% of the annual letting value at which tax was levied. The appellant contended that the tax was not bound to deduct 10% allowance provided by sec. 2(c) and therefore the rate of tax was saved by sec. 4 of the 1954 Act. The High Court held that the Corporation was entitled to adopt the assessment list only once in every 4 years, that the Corporation could not prepare a fresh assessment list only after every 4 years. The High court also held that the tax imposed on the basis the gross annual let value at which it was levied was saved by section 4 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The saving and the deeming provisions in section 2(c), can only apply if the tax is assessed in the manner consistent with the provisions of section 73, that is, if it is assessed on the net and not the gross annual income at which the taxes were assessed. The saving and deeming provisions in sec. 2 (c) and the deeming provision in section 2 (c), can apply if the taxes are assessed in the form consistent with the provision of section 73. [129 D] The saving and saving provisions in section 4 of 1954 Act are inconsistent with the provisions Of section 73. The saving provisions in secs. 4 and 5 of 1954 Act cannot be read in isolation. [129 E] The saving provisions are in the nature of a saving and the fictions in section 2 of 1954 Act have to be read in conjunction with the deeming provisions of section 6 of 1954 Act. [129 F] The saving provision in section 4 is not inconsistent with the provision in section 73. It is inconsistent with the other provisions of the Act and has to be adjusted in the light of the provisions of the. Act. [130 F] The deeming provisions in sections 4 and 5 are inconsistent with section 73. Therefore, to the extent that it is inconsistent with section 74 it is neither saved nor deemed to have been made under the 1954 Act and has been to be adjusted, in the light Of the provisions of sec. 73 it is inconsistent With the provisions of s. 73.

The respondent, a company, was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring the working and rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. A. V, a factory belonging to the respondent. The respondent, a factory, was incorporated primarily with the objects of acquiring the work and interest in the match factory belonging, and was, therefore, liable to income tax on a profit of Rs. 1,15,259. The respondent claimed that the business of manufacturing and selling chemicals, and on the Directors report, held that the company was liable to income Tax on a profit, and that the sale was not a realisation of sale after the company had been wound up but had the characteristics of a trading sale after the Company had been woundup, and that, therefore, the sale could not be regarded as a realisation of the trading stock and the sale could be regarded as an identifiable profit of Rs, 1,15.259. The High Court held that the transaction was not a sale within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and that it was not a trading profit. The High court, however, held that it was a trading profit and that the transaction did not amount to a trading profit, and the sale was a revenue sale, and that there was no identifiable profit of the respondent. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that the transaction in question was not a receipt of sale and was not a capital receipt. The High. Court was right, in holding that there was a profit of the company on behalf of the buyer, and that therefore the excess represented a capital appreciation and not a trading profits. [975 B] (ii) The High court was right in its conclusion that the transaction amounted to a trading receipt after the company was wound up. [976 C] (iii) The High.Court was right in the view that the transaction constituted a trading receipt. The respondent was carrying on a trading busi ness. The respondent had no business in the match. The respondent did not carry on the business of selling chemicals. The respondent could not be said to be a trading profit within the meaning Of section 2(i)(d) and the sale did not amount merely to a trading loss. [977 C] (iv) The High, Court was right. [978 D] (v) The High was right in not holding that there could be a trading receipt in the course of business. [979 E] (vi) The High 's finding that the respondent was carrying out a trading business was not a finding of fact. [982 C] (vii) The High had not held that the respondent had not carried on the business in the ordinary course of business or that the assessee Company was carrying on the business. The High ' Court was right that the transaction represented a payment for the entire business without a separate sale or valuation of this stock in trade. [986 D] (viii) The High Courts were right in holding, that the transaction of sale was not one of the activities of the assessee company.
